relationships.description: Connects CPU Profiling & Flame Graphs to jvm internals and garbage collection in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Sampling CPU profilers capture call stacks at fixed intervals (e.g., 99 Hz) with <1% overhead, and Flame Graphs aggregate those stacks into proportional width rectangles so hot code paths jump out immediately.

spark.summary: Sampling CPU profilers capture call stacks at fixed intervals (e.g., 99 Hz) with <1% overhead, and Flame Graphs aggregate those stacks into proportional width rectangles so hot code paths jump out immediately.
spark.keyTakeaway: Flame Graphs measure inclusive time on the horizontal axis—not chronological time—so wide plateaus reveal where your CPU actually spends cycles, even when scattered across thousands of calls.

concept.whyItMatters: Instrumenting every function entry/exit distorts timings by 10x–100x (the observer effect) and misses kernel/libc time. Statistical sampling profilers like Linux `perf`, `async-profiler` (JVM), `pprof` (Go), and `py-spy` (Python) inspect instruction pointers at 99–999 Hz with <2% overhead in production. Visualizing millions of raw stack traces as a Flame Graph turns unreadable megabytes of text into an instant structural map of CPU bottlenecks, lock contention, and unexpected allocations.
whenToUse: Diagnosing high CPU utilization, tail-latency spikes (p99), or throughput plateaus in production services with <2% overhead.
Comparing before/after performance of a refactor using Differential Flame Graphs (red = regression, blue = speedup).
Uncovering hidden runtime tax such as JVM safepoint bias, Go GC mark/sweep overhead, JSON serialization, or kernel syscall time.
whenNotToUse: Debugging threads blocked on network I/O, disk reads, or mutexes—on-CPU sampling ignores sleeping threads; use off-CPU profiling (`offcputime` eBPF) or distributed tracing instead.
Measuring single-digit nanosecond microbenchmarks where sampling period (1–10 ms) is 1,000,000x coarser than the function; use hardware PMU counters (`perf stat`) or `criterion`/`JMH`.
Tracing rare, single-request logic bugs that occur once in a million requests; statistical sampling will likely miss the event.
keyPoints: Sampling at a prime-adjacent frequency like 99 Hz or 997 Hz prevents lockstep aliasing with periodic 10 ms or 100 Hz application timers.
The X-axis of a Flame Graph is sorted alphabetically by frame name (not chronological time); the width of each box represents the percentage of total samples containing that frame.
The Y-axis represents call-stack depth (bottom = root/entry point, top = leaf function currently executing on CPU); wide flat tops ('plateaus') indicate self-time hotspots.
Missing frame pointers (`-fomit-frame-pointer` in C/C++/Rust) break fast kernel stack unwinding unless DWARF unwinding (`--call-graph dwarf`, slow) or ORC/SFrame tables are used.

Safepoint bias in traditional JVM profilers skews samples to GC safepoints; tools like `async-profiler` use `AsyncGetCallTrace` + `perf_events` to capture true async stacks across native and Java frames.

examples.title: Eliminating 38% CPU Waste in a Go gRPC Gateway
examples.scenario: A Go API gateway hit 85% CPU at 12k RPS. Running `go tool pprof -http=:8080 http://pod:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30` generated a Flame Graph.
examples.outcome: A wide 38%-width plateau appeared under `regexp.Compile` inside a per-request routing middleware; hoisting regex compilation to `init()` dropped CPU usage from 85% to 51% and cut p99 latency by 42 ms.

examples.title: Catching Kernel `futex` & TLS Overhead via `perf` + `async-profiler`
examples.scenario: A Java microservice showed low `jstack` activity despite 100% CPU saturation on 16-vCPU containers.
examples.outcome: `async-profiler -e cpu -d 30 -f flame.html <pid>` revealed 44% of samples inside `libcrypto` / `G1ParScanThreadState` and kernel `sys_futex`, pinpointing unpooled TLS handshakes and oversized allocation rates.

tradeOffs.pro: Higher frequencies (999 Hz) capture short-lived bursts and reduce variance in shorter 10-second profiles.
tradeOffs.con: Increases interrupt/unwinding overhead, ring-buffer drops, and profile file size on high-core-count machines.

tradeOffs.factor: Frame Pointer (`fp`) vs. DWARF Stack Unwinding
tradeOffs.pro: Frame-pointer unwinding (`-fno-omit-frame-pointer`) walks stacks in ~100 ns inside the kernel with tiny ring-buffer records.
tradeOffs.con: DWARF unwinding (`perf record --call-graph dwarf`) copies 8 KB of raw stack per sample, causing 5%–15% overhead and disk I/O spikes, though it works on stripped binaries.

tradeOffs.pro: On-CPU sampling has near-zero overhead because it only fires when a core is actively executing instructions.
tradeOffs.con: Completely blind to lock contention, `epoll_wait`, and disk stalls; off-CPU eBPF tracing instruments every context switch, which adds overhead under high scheduler churn.

failureModes.name: Broken Stacks (`[unknown]` Frames)
failureModes.description: Compiled binaries built with `-fomit-frame-pointer` or stripped JIT symbols produce single-frame towers labeled `[unknown]`.
failureModes.mitigation: Compile production C/C++/Rust services with `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` (now default in Fedora/Ubuntu and <1% cost on x86_64), keep debuginfo packages, and generate `/tmp/perf-<pid>.map` for JIT runtimes.

failureModes.name: Lockstep Sampling Aliasing
failureModes.description: Sampling at exactly 100 Hz (10 ms) synchronizes with a 10 ms ticker or cron loop, causing that task to appear as 0% or 100% of CPU.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use non-divisor frequencies such as 99 Hz, 499 Hz, or 997 Hz.

failureModes.name: JVM Safepoint Bias
failureModes.description: Profilers relying on JVMTI `GetAllStackTraces` only sample threads when they reach a JVM safepoint, blaming allocation-heavy or loop-exit lines instead of tight compute loops.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `async-profiler` or JFR with `AsyncGetCallTrace` + Linux `perf_events` rather than safepoint-based samplers.

failureModes.name: Misreading X-Axis as Wall-Clock Time
failureModes.description: Engineers assume left-to-right frames executed sequentially in time and chase narrow transient spikes.
failureModes.mitigation: Read bottom-to-top for call hierarchy and look strictly for wide horizontal plateaus (high self-time) or wide subtrees (high inclusive time).

commonMistakes: Profiling an idle or under-loaded staging instance where 90% of samples sit in `idle` or `epoll_wait`, hiding real lock and cache bottlenecks.
Forgetting that Flame Graphs normalize to 100% of *captured samples*, not 100% of machine capacity—a 50% bar at 5% total CPU is only 2.5% of a core.
Leaving `perf.data` un-collapsed on production hosts until it fills `/tmp` (999 Hz DWARF can write >50 MB/s).
Looking only at self-time (`top` view) and missing a death-by-a-thousand-cuts caller allocating objects across 20 tiny helper functions.
Comparing two Flame Graphs visually by eye instead of generating a Differential Flame Graph (`difffolded.pl`).

sections.content:
## The idea

CPU profiling answers one question: *which code paths are consuming CPU cycles?* Instrumenting every function call adds prohibitive overhead and skews short functions. Instead, modern profilers use **statistical sampling**: a kernel hardware timer or PMU (Performance Monitoring Unit) interrupts each CPU core at a fixed rate (e.g., 99 times per second), records the currently executing instruction pointer and its call stack, and resumes execution.

Raw stack samples are noisy—thousands of identical stacks repeated in arbitrary order. Brendan Gregg's **Flame Graph** solves this by folding identical call stacks together, summing their sample counts, sorting sibling frames alphabetically on the X-axis, and plotting stack depth on the Y-axis. The width of any rectangle is directly proportional to the fraction of CPU time spent in that function and its descendants.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose we profile a Rust/C++ service on Linux with `perf` for 30 seconds at 99 Hz:

1. **Capture**: `perf record -F 99 -a -g --call-graph fp -- sleep 30`
   - `-F 99` avoids 100 Hz timer aliasing.
   - `-g --call-graph fp` walks the `RBP` frame-pointer chain in kernel space (or use `dwarf` if frame pointers are omitted).
2. **Collapse**: `perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded`
   - Converts raw addresses + symbols into single-line semicolon-delimited stacks with counts, e.g.:
     `main;handle_req;parse_json;serde_json::from_slice 1420`
     `main;handle_req;verify_sig;ed25519_verify 890`
3. **Render**: `flamegraph.pl out.folded > cpu.svg`
   - Total samples = 2,310. `main` and `handle_req` span 100% width at the bottom.
   - `parse_json` spans 61.5% (1420/2310) on the left; `verify_sig` spans 38.5% on the right.
   - At the top of `parse_json`, `serde_json::from_slice` forms a flat plateau—confirming JSON parsing is the primary self-time hotspot.

sections.content:
## Reading & interpreting flame graphs

When reading a Flame Graph, ignore colors (in standard Flame Graphs, warm colors are randomized for contrast; only in **Differential** or **eBPF/JIT** graphs do colors encode kernel vs. user space or regression vs. speedup).

Look for two shapes:
- **Wide plateaus (flat tops)**: Functions at the top of a wide stack with nothing above them. These are **self-time** hotspots—tight loops, hashing, compression, or serialization.
- **Wide towers with many thin spires**: A parent function is wide, but its children split into many narrow calls. This indicates high **inclusive time** caused by calling a helper too often (e.g., logging, locking, or small allocations inside a loop).

Always check the **bottom-most kernel frames** if system CPU (`%sys`) is high: frames like `entry_SYSCALL_64 -> sys_futex` or `tcp_sendmsg` indicate lock contention or unbuffered small writes.

## Profiler matrix by runtime

| Runtime / Language | Recommended Tool | Unwind Mechanism | Typical Overhead | Key Gotcha |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **C / C++ / Rust** | Linux `perf` / `cargo-flamegraph` | Frame Pointer or DWARF | <1% (FP), 5%+ (DWARF) | Needs `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` & debug symbols |
| **Go** | `runtime/pprof` (`go tool pprof`) | Go runtime stack walker | <1% (100 Hz default) | Excludes Cgo/kernel frames unless using `perf`/eBPF |
| **JVM (Java/Kotlin)** | `async-profiler` / JFR | `AsyncGetCallTrace` + `perf` | 1%–2% | Avoid `jstack`/JVMTI samplers due to safepoint bias |
| **Python** | `py-spy` / `austin` | External `process_vm_readv` | <1% | Must correlate C-extension frames (`--native`) |
| **Node.js / V8** | `perf` + `--perf-basic-prof` / `0x` | FP + V8 JIT map | 1%–3% | JIT recompilation shifts addresses without map files |

## Failure modes

1. **Container permission denial**: Docker/Kubernetes drops `CAP_PERFMON` and `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` by default, blocking `perf_event_open()` unless configured via `seccomp` or privileged sidecars.
2. **Inlined functions hiding bottlenecks**: Aggressive `-O3` inlining collapses hot helpers into their callers; enable DWARF inline info (`-g`) so the symbolizer can reconstruct virtual inline frames.
3. **Missing JIT symbol maps**: Profiling JVM or V8 without `--perf-basic-prof` or `async-profiler` leaves 80% of the Flame Graph as hexadecimal addresses.
4. **Ignoring off-CPU latency**: A service with 10% CPU and 500 ms p99 latency is waiting on I/O, DNS, or mutexes—an on-CPU Flame Graph will only show the 10% active work and mislead the investigation.

## Continuous production profiling

Ad-hoc profiling fails when incidents are transient. Continuous profilers (Parca, Pyroscope, Google Cloud Profiler, Datadog Continuous Profiler) run eBPF or runtime profilers as a DaemonSet across every node at ~19–99 Hz, uploading collapsed profiles every 10–60 seconds.

This enables **Differential Flame Graphs** between canary and baseline deployments (e.g., `v2.4.1` vs `v2.4.0`): frames that grew wider turn red and frames that shrank turn blue, catching 5% CPU regressions before full rollout.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Build native binaries with `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` and split debug symbols (`-g`).
- [ ] Sample at a non-divisor frequency (99 Hz or 997 Hz) under realistic load.
- [ ] Verify `perf_event_paranoid <= 1` or grant `CAP_PERFMON` in container specs for eBPF/perf.
- [ ] Check `%usr` vs `%sys` before profiling; include kernel frames if `%sys` exceeds 15%.
- [ ] Use Differential Flame Graphs to validate optimizations rather than eyeballing widths.
- [ ] Switch to off-CPU (`offcputime`) or mutex contention profiling whenever CPU is low but tail latency is high.

interviewProblems.title: CPU Profiling & Flame Graphs
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on CPU Profiling & Flame Graphs. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Sampling CPU profilers capture call stacks at fixed intervals (e.g., 99 Hz) with <1% overhead, and Flame Graphs aggregate those stacks into proportional width rectangles so hot code paths jump out immediately.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Symbolizer & Folder applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Flame Graph (SVG/HTML).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Flame Graph (SVG/HTML) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Compile production C/C++/Rust services with `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` (now default in Fedora/Ubuntu and <1% cost on x86_64), keep debuginfo packages, and generate `/tmp/perf-<pid>.map` for JIT runtimes.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Flame Graphs measure inclusive time on the horizontal axis—not chronological time—so wide plateaus reveal where your CPU actually spends cycles, even when scattered across thousands of calls.
Avoid trap: Profiling an idle or under-loaded staging instance where 90% of samples sit in `idle` or `epoll_wait`, hiding real lock and cache bottlenecks.
Avoid trap: Forgetting that Flame Graphs normalize to 100% of *captured samples*, not 100% of machine capacity—a 50% bar at 5% total CPU is only 2.5% of a core.
When to reach for it: Diagnosing high CPU utilization, tail-latency spikes (p99), or throughput plateaus in production services with <2% overhead.
When to reach for it: Comparing before/after performance of a refactor using Differential Flame Graphs (red = regression, blue = speedup).

putItTogether.title: Putting Cpu Profiling Flamegraphs Together
putItTogether.summary: Flame Graphs measure inclusive time on the horizontal axis—not chronological time—so wide plateaus reveal where your CPU actually spends cycles, even when scattered across thousands of calls.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Cpu Profiling Flamegraphs before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: A wide 38%-width plateau appeared under `regexp.Compile` inside a per-request routing middleware; hoisting regex compilation to `init()` dropped CPU usage from 85% to 51% and cut p99 latency by 42 ms.

concepts.name: CQRS & Event Sourcing

relationships.description: Events connect write side to read projections.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

concepts.tagline: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.

spark.summary: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use CQRS without Event Sourcing whenever read and write shapes diverge; adopt Event Sourcing only when an immutable audit log, temporal replay, or multi-projection architecture justifies handling eventual consistency and schema evolution.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional CRUD architectures force a single normalized schema to serve both transactional invariant checks and complex denormalized UI/reporting queries, creating lock contention and N+1 join bottlenecks. Combining CQRS with Event Sourcing—used in financial ledgers (TigerBeetle, Stripe-style double-entry), collaborative editors, and high-throughput order books—gives you append-only write throughput, deterministic state replay for debugging/auditing, and independently scalable read models (PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, Redis).
whenToUse: Financial ledgers, healthcare records, or compliance-heavy domains requiring a cryptographically or structurally immutable audit trail of every state change.
Systems with extreme read/write asymmetry (e.g., 100:1 reads to writes) where read queries need specialized denormalized views in Elasticsearch or Redis.
Domains needing time-travel queries, retroactive bug-fix replays, or spawning new downstream analytics projections from historical events.
whenNotToUse: Standard CRUD domains (user profiles, CMS, simple inventory) where overwriting the current row in PostgreSQL is simpler and faster.
Flows requiring immediate strong read-your-own-writes consistency across complex cross-aggregate views without extra client versioning.
Small teams lacking operational maturity for idempotent consumers, event schema upcasting, and projection lag monitoring.
keyPoints: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) and Event Sourcing are orthogonal: you can run CQRS over a plain relational DB, and you can use Event Sourcing with synchronous projections.

On the write side, an Aggregate reconstructs its state by replaying its event stream (up to a snapshot), validates the Command's invariants, and appends new Events using optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`).
Read models (Projections) asynchronously tail the event store (via EventStoreDB subscriptions, Kafka, or Postgres CDC/Outbox) and update denormalized tables idempotently.
Snapshotting every N events (e.g., every 100–500 events) bounds aggregate hydration latency so long-lived streams do not degrade write p99.
Because events are immutable facts, schema changes cannot mutate old records; consumers use **upcasters** (versioned event transformers) or weak-schema deserializers.

examples.title: Double-Entry Payment Ledger with EventStoreDB & Projections
examples.scenario: A fintech settlement service processes 8,000 transfers/sec while compliance and merchant dashboards query 90-day balance summaries.
examples.outcome: Commands append `FundsReserved`, `TransferSettled`, and `FeeAssessed` events to an append-only stream with `expectedVersion` checks, while asynchronous workers project into PostgreSQL read tables and ClickHouse analytics without locking the write path.

examples.title: E-Commerce Order Fulfillment with Outbox + Elasticsearch
examples.scenario: Customer support needs instant full-text search across 50M orders by SKU, shipping status, and customer email, which caused heavy `LIKE` queries on the primary OLTP database.
examples.outcome: Separating the write model (PostgreSQL + Transactional Outbox) from an Elasticsearch read projection cut OLTP CPU by 62% and reduced search p95 from 1.4 s to 28 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Decoupled async projections let write and read databases scale and fail independently.
tradeOffs.con: Introduces replication lag (typically 10–200 ms), meaning a user who submits a command may refresh and see stale data unless the UI tracks a `streamVersion` watermark.

tradeOffs.pro: Every historical state and the business reason ('why' it changed) is preserved forever for replay and debugging.
tradeOffs.con: Ad-hoc queries against raw event streams are painful; every new query shape requires writing and backfilling a dedicated projection.

tradeOffs.pro: Adding a new read-model column only requires replaying events into a new projection table.
tradeOffs.con: Renaming or splitting an existing event type requires maintaining backward-compatible upcasters for the lifetime of the store.

failureModes.name: Projection Lag & Stale Read-Your-Writes
failureModes.description: A burst of 50,000 events backs up the projection consumer, causing users to see outdated balances or missing orders right after a `200 OK` command.
failureModes.mitigation: Return the committed `streamPosition` in the command response and have read queries wait (briefly) or fall back to reading the aggregate until the projection reaches that checkpoint.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Split-Brain
failureModes.description: Writing an event to PostgreSQL and publishing to Kafka in two separate calls fails midway, leaving the read model permanently out of sync.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a dedicated Event Store (EventStoreDB) as the single source of truth, or use the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC.

failureModes.name: Non-Idempotent Projection Handlers
failureModes.description: At-least-once delivery replays an `OrderPaid` event after a worker crash, double-incrementing a merchant's total revenue counter.
failureModes.mitigation: Store the last processed `(streamId, eventNumber)` or `eventId` in the same transaction as the read-model update and skip duplicates.

failureModes.name: GDPR / Right-to-Erasure Conflict
failureModes.description: PII stored inside immutable events violates legal deletion requests.
failureModes.mitigation: Use **crypto-shredding**: encrypt PII fields with a per-user key stored in a mutable KMS/vault, and delete the key upon erasure request.

commonMistakes: Applying Event Sourcing across an entire monolith instead of isolating it to core subdomains that genuinely need auditability or temporal replay.
Designing 'CRUD events' (`UserUpdated`) instead of domain-meaningful events (`SubscriptionUpgraded`, `ShippingAddressCorrected`), losing business intent.
Calling external HTTP APIs or generating non-deterministic `time.Now()`/`uuid.New()` inside projection replay handlers.
Allowing aggregates to grow unboundedly across millions of events without snapshots or stream archiving (e.g., monthly account closing events).
Blocking synchronous HTTP responses while waiting for 5 downstream projections to finish updating.

sections.content:
## The idea

**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits an application's data model into two distinct paths: a **Command** side that validates business rules and mutates state, and a **Query** side that reads pre-shaped, denormalized views.

**Event Sourcing** changes *how* the Command side persists state. Instead of executing `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 150 WHERE id = 42`, it appends an immutable domain event (`MoneyDeposited{amount: 50}`) to an append-only log. Current state is simply the left-fold (`reduce`) of all events in that stream. When paired together, the write model focuses purely on invariant enforcement and optimistic concurrency, while asynchronous projectors continuously fold the event log into optimized read databases.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `WithdrawFunds(accountId='acc-9', amount=40)` command:

1. **Hydrate**: The command handler loads `snapshot@v100 (balance=120)` plus events `v101..v103` (`-10`, `+20`, `-30`), folding them to `currentBalance = 100`, `version = 103`.
2. **Validate**: Since `100 >= 40`, the aggregate emits `[FundsWithdrawn{amount: 40, txId: 'tx-77'}]`. (No DB mutation happens inside the domain object.)
3. **Atomic Append**: The repository appends the event to stream `acc-9` with `expectedVersion = 103`. If another concurrent request already wrote `v104`, the store rejects with `WrongExpectedVersion` (HTTP 409).
4. **Project**: The `AccountSummaryProjector` tails the global event log (`$all`), sees `v104`, verifies `last_checkpoint < global_pos` inside a PostgreSQL transaction, executes `UPDATE account_views SET balance = balance - 40, last_pos = ...`, and commits.

edges.title: Aggregate hydration
edges.description: Reads latest snapshot and subsequent events to reconstruct current in-memory state.

edges.label: 2. Append(expectedVersion)
edges.title: Atomic event commit
edges.description: Appends new domain events if stream version matches; rejects concurrent conflicts.

edges.label: 3. Stream / CDC
edges.title: Ordered log delivery
edges.description: Pushes committed events in global commit order via subscription or outbox CDC.

edges.label: 4. Idempotent upsert
edges.title: Update read view + checkpoint
edges.description: Applies projection logic and records global offset in the same transaction.

edges.label: 5. Query / UI read
edges.title: Fast zero-join reads
edges.description: Clients query pre-computed read tables without touching the write-side event log.

data.caption: CQRS + Event Sourcing decouples transactional appends from asynchronous, idempotent read-model projections.

sections.content:
## Consistency, versioning & snapshots

Event-sourced systems trade immediate global consistency for **stream-level linearizability** plus **eventual read consistency**.
- **Write-side concurrency**: Optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`) guarantees no two commands overwrite each other on the same aggregate. Cross-aggregate invariants (e.g., transferring funds between two accounts) are coordinated via Sagas/Process Managers rather than distributed 2PC.
- **Read-your-own-writes**: Commands return `ETag: "v104"` or `X-Min-Position: 98412`. The query API polls or waits briefly for the projection checkpoint `>= 98412` before serving the requesting client.
- **Snapshotting**: A separate background worker periodically serializes aggregate state at `v500`, `v1000`, etc., keeping write-side hydration bounded to O(100) events.

## Architecture pattern comparison

| Pattern | Write Storage | Read Storage | Consistency | Audit Trail | Operational Complexity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Standard CRUD** | Normalized OLTP | Same OLTP | Strong (ACID) | Manual audit table | Low |
| **CQRS + State DB** | Normalized OLTP | Replica / Elastic via CDC | Eventual reads | Optional | Medium |
| **CQRS + Event Sourcing** | Append-only Event Log | Multiple Projections | Stream-strong, read-eventual | Native & immutable | High (upcasting, replay) |

## Failure modes

1. **Poison-pill event**: A malformed or un-upcasted event crashes the projector in an infinite retry loop, stalling all downstream read updates. *Fix*: Dead-letter queue (DLQ) per stream or alertable circuit breaker after N retries.
2. **Blue/green projection rebuilds**: Rebuilding a 500M-event projection in-place breaks live reads. *Fix*: Write to a versioned table (`orders_v2`), catch up to live tail, then atomically swap the DB view/alias.
3. **Eventual consistency surprises**: Automated tests or UIs immediately `GET` after `POST` and see 404. *Fix*: Propagate causal position tokens or return the updated state summary in the command response.
4. **Side effects during replay**: Sending emails or charging cards inside a projection handler re-executes during a historical rebuild. *Fix*: Isolate external side effects to a live-only Process Manager that checks `isLiveMode` or deduplicates via idempotency keys.

## Schema evolution & GDPR

Because historical events are immutable facts, you never run `UPDATE events SET payload = ...`. Instead:
- **Additive changes**: Add optional fields with defaults.
- **Breaking changes**: Introduce `OrderPlacedV2` and register an **Upcaster** (`V1 -> V2`) in the deserialization pipeline before events reach aggregates or projections.
- **GDPR Erasure**: Store PII (name, email, SSN) encrypted with a per-subject AES-256 key (`user_key_42`) held in a separate mutable key store. Deleting `user_key_42` renders all historical PII fields cryptographically unreadable without breaking event-stream hashes or structural replay.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Confirm Event Sourcing is restricted to bounded contexts that require auditability, replay, or temporal queries.
- [ ] Enforce optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`) on every event append.
- [ ] Guarantee atomic write + publish via an Event Store or Transactional Outbox + CDC (never dual-write).
- [ ] Make every projection handler idempotent using `(streamId, eventNumber)` or global log position checkpoints.
- [ ] Implement crypto-shredding for any PII stored inside immutable event payloads.
- [ ] Test full projection rebuilds from event 0 into a shadow table before going to production.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Cqrs And Event Sourcing

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Async Projector applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Denormalized Read Model.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Denormalized Read Model experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Return the committed `streamPosition` in the command response and have read queries wait (briefly) or fall back to reading the aggregate until the projection reaches that checkpoint.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use CQRS without Event Sourcing whenever read and write shapes diverge; adopt Event Sourcing only when an immutable audit log, temporal replay, or multi-projection architecture justifies handling eventual consistency and schema evolution.
Avoid trap: Applying Event Sourcing across an entire monolith instead of isolating it to core subdomains that genuinely need auditability or temporal replay.
Avoid trap: Designing 'CRUD events' (`UserUpdated`) instead of domain-meaningful events (`SubscriptionUpgraded`, `ShippingAddressCorrected`), losing business intent.
When to reach for it: Financial ledgers, healthcare records, or compliance-heavy domains requiring a cryptographically or structurally immutable audit trail of every state change.
When to reach for it: Systems with extreme read/write asymmetry (e.g., 100:1 reads to writes) where read queries need specialized denormalized views in Elasticsearch or Redis.

concepts.name: CRDTs & Conflict-Free Replicated Data

relationships.description: Connects CRDTs & Conflict-Free Replicated Data to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are replicated data structures whose concurrent updates commute or form a mathematical join-semilattice, guaranteeing every replica converges to the exact same state without coordination or consensus.

spark.summary: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are replicated data structures whose concurrent updates commute or form a mathematical join-semilattice, guaranteeing every replica converges to the exact same state without coordination or consensus.
spark.keyTakeaway: CRDTs eliminate consensus round-trips for local-first apps and geo-distributed active-active stores by trading coordination latency for metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, or per-element IDs).

concept.whyItMatters: Consensus protocols like Raft and Paxos require a quorum round-trip (50–150 ms across WANs) and stall during network partitions. Real-time collaborative editors (Figma, Notion/Linear-style local-first apps, Yjs, Automerge) and active-active distributed databases (Riak, Redis Enterprise Active-Active, Cassandra counters) need sub-millisecond local writes even offline. CRDTs mathematically guarantee **Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC)**: any two replicas that have received the same set of updates—in any order, with any duplicates—hold identical state.
whenToUse: Local-first collaborative applications (rich-text editors, whiteboards, offline-capable mobile apps) where edits must apply locally at 0 ms and merge cleanly upon reconnection.
Multi-region active-active databases tracking distributed counters, feature flags, shopping carts, or user presence sets without cross-region locks.
Edge/IoT telemetry aggregation where intermittent nodes push deltas over unreliable networks.
whenNotToUse: Strict global invariants such as preventing negative bank balances, enforcing unique usernames, or inventory reservation under scarcity (requires consensus or single-leader serialization).
Large binary blobs or relational joins that cannot be decomposed into monotonic state transitions.
Memory-constrained systems with high churn of deleted items where tombstone metadata cannot be garbage-collected.
keyPoints: State-based CRDTs (**CvRDTs**) ship full or delta state (`delta-CRDTs`) and merge via a **join-semilattice** operator `⊔` that is associative, commutative, and idempotent (ACID-free convergence).
Operation-based CRDTs (**CmRDTs**) ship small operations, requiring reliable causal broadcast (exactly-once or idempotent causal delivery) and commutative concurrent operations.

Core primitives include **G-Counter** (per-replica monotonic map), **PN-Counter** (two G-Counters for inc/dec), **LWW-Register** (timestamp + replicaId tie-breaker), and **OR-Set** (Observed-Remove Set using unique add-tags).
Sequence CRDTs (**RGA**, **YATA/Yjs**, **Fugue**) assign unique fractional/tree-ordered IDs to characters so concurrent insertions at the same cursor never interleave or corrupt text.
CRDTs guarantee *convergence*, not human *intention*—e.g., LWW-Register silently drops one concurrent write, and concurrent add+remove in an OR-Set resolves to add-wins or remove-wins by design.

examples.title: Real-Time Collaborative Rich Text via Yjs (YATA CRDT)
examples.scenario: 50 concurrent editors type, format, and paste offline/online in a shared browser document over WebSockets and WebRTC.
examples.outcome: Yjs encodes each character insertion with a `(clientId, clock)` ID and left/right origin pointers, merging 10,000+ out-of-order updates in <5 ms in-browser with zero central lock server.

examples.title: Active-Active Global Shopping Cart in Redis Enterprise
examples.scenario: Users in Mumbai and Frankfurt modify the same shopping cart across two active-active regional clusters during a transatlantic link flap.
examples.outcome: Using an Observed-Remove Set (OR-Set) CRDT with vector clocks, concurrent `add(SKU-A)` and `remove(SKU-B)` operations merge deterministically across regions once the link heals, avoiding lost cart items.

tradeOffs.pro: CvRDTs tolerate dropped, duplicated, and reordered messages over plain gossip/HTTP because `merge()` is idempotent and commutative.
tradeOffs.con: Shipping full state scales poorly with object size; delta-CRDTs mitigate this by shipping only recent state diffs.

tradeOffs.pro: Keeping tombstones (deleted item IDs) prevents 'zombie resurrection' when stale replicas sync late.
tradeOffs.con: Tombstones accumulate indefinitely in high-churn sets/documents unless compacted via causal stability barriers or epoch GC.

tradeOffs.pro: 100% write availability under network partitions (AP in CAP/PACELC) with 0 ms local write latency.
tradeOffs.con: Cannot enforce global uniqueness or non-negative bounds (e.g., `stock >= 0`) without adding a coordination layer.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Corrupting LWW-Registers
failureModes.description: An LWW-Register using raw wall-clock `Date.now()` allows a replica with a 5-minute fast NTP clock to silently overwrite all newer edits from other nodes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) combining physical time with a monotonic logical counter and `replicaId` tie-breaker.

failureModes.name: Tombstone Bloat & OOM
failureModes.description: A collaborative document or OR-Set with millions of add/delete cycles grows 10x larger than its visible data because deleted elements remain as tombstones.
failureModes.mitigation: Run distributed garbage collection once all known replicas acknowledge a causal version vector, or compact via periodic epoch snapshots.

failureModes.name: Zombie Item Resurrection
failureModes.description: Pruning tombstones aggressively before an offline mobile client reconnects causes that client's stale state to re-introduce deleted items.
failureModes.mitigation: Never drop tombstones below the minimum causal frontier of active replicas, or force stale offline clients (>30 days) to re-bootstrap from a fresh snapshot.

failureModes.name: Replica ID Collisions
failureModes.description: Two browser tabs or cloned VMs share the same `replicaId` in a G-Counter or OR-Set, causing updates to overwrite each other and break convergence.
failureModes.mitigation: Generate a cryptographically random 64-bit/128-bit `clientId` per session/instance rather than reusing user IDs or hostnames.

commonMistakes: Using CRDTs to enforce invariants like 'only 1 seat left' or 'account balance cannot go below 0'—CRDTs cannot reject concurrent valid local writes.
Implementing a naive G-Counter keyed by `userId` instead of `replicaId`, which breaks when a user opens two tabs.
Assuming LWW-Register preserves all data—it explicitly discards losing concurrent writes.
Sending full CvRDT states on every keystroke instead of batching delta-CRDTs.
Forgetting to persist the local causal clock/vector alongside the CRDT state across restarts.

sections.content:
## The idea

Traditional replication relies on consensus (Raft/Paxos) to agree on a single global total order of writes. **CRDTs** invert the problem: instead of agreeing on *when* operations happened, design the data structure so that *order does not matter*.

Formally, a state-based CRDT (CvRDT) forms a **bounded join-semilattice** `(S, ⊔)`. Every local mutation moves the state monotonically upward in the partial order, and merging two replicas computes their least upper bound `A ⊔ B`. Because `⊔` is **associative** `(A ⊔ B) ⊔ C = A ⊔ (B ⊔ C)`, **commutative** `A ⊔ B = B ⊔ A`, and **idempotent** `A ⊔ A = A`, replicas can gossip updates over lossy, out-of-order networks and still converge identically.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an **Observed-Remove Set (OR-Set)** with add-wins semantics across two disconnected replicas `R1` and `R2`:

1. **Initial state**: Both hold `{('milk', tag_1)}`. `R1` and `R2` go offline.
2. **`R1` removes `'milk'`**: `R1` moves `tag_1` into its `tombstones` set -> visible set is `{}`.
3. **`R2` concurrently removes and re-adds `'milk'`**: `R2` tombstones `tag_1` and generates a fresh unique tag `tag_2` -> visible set is `{('milk', tag_2)}`.
4. **Merge (`R1 ⊔ R2`)**:
   - `adds = {('milk', tag_1), ('milk', tag_2)}`
   - `tombstones = {tag_1}`
   - Visible elements = `adds \ tombstones` = `{('milk', tag_2)}`.

Unlike a naive set where `remove('milk')` would wipe out `R2`'s concurrent re-add, tagging each addition with a unique `(replicaId, seq)` ensures a remove only cancels the specific additions it *observed*.

edges.description: Replica A applies mutation locally in 0 ms and queues a compact delta or tagged op.

edges.label: 3. Deliver in any order

data.caption: Strong Eventual Consistency: concurrent updates travel asynchronously and converge deterministically via the join operator.

sections.content:
## State-based vs. operation-based vs. delta

- **CvRDT (State-based)**: Replicas exchange full states and call `merge()`. Dead simple transport (works over plain HTTP polling or UDP gossip), but bandwidth is O(state size).
- **CmRDT (Op-based)**: Replicas broadcast tiny operations (e.g., `insert(pos, 'a')`). Low bandwidth, but requires **reliable causal broadcast** (no dropped or out-of-order ops).
- **Delta-state CRDTs (δ-CRDT)**: The modern sweet spot used in Riak, Yjs, and Automerge. Each mutation produces a small delta `δ` that is itself a valid CvRDT fragment. Replicas ship deltas and merge them idempotently, combining small payloads with loss-tolerant transport.

## Core CRDT catalog

| CRDT Type | Semantics | Metadata Overhead | Typical Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **G-Counter** | Increment-only counter | O(N replicas) integers | Distributed page views, rate counters |
| **PN-Counter** | Increment & decrement | 2 * O(N replicas) | Active user counts, inventory deltas |
| **LWW-Element-Set** | Add/remove via timestamps | O(items) + HLC timestamps | User profiles, config flags |
| **OR-Set** | Add-wins / remove-wins | O(adds) unique tags + tombstones | Shopping carts, collaborative tag lists |
| **YATA / RGA / Fugue** | Ordered text/list sequence | O(total chars incl. deleted) | Real-time collaborative text editors |

## Failure modes

1. **Wall-clock drift in LWW**: Relying on unsynchronized client clocks lets a skewed device win every conflict forever. *Fix*: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) bounded by server time.
2. **Unbounded tombstone growth**: High-churn documents accumulate megabytes of deleted character metadata. *Fix*: Run causal-barrier compaction when all peers acknowledge a version vector, or use run-length encoding (RLE) of contiguous IDs like Yjs/Automerge.
3. **Interleaving in naive sequence CRDTs**: Early sequence CRDTs (Logoot, LSEQ) could interleave two users' concurrently typed words (`hweolrldo`). *Fix*: Use modern non-interleaving algorithms like **Fugue** or **YATA**.
4. **Broken global invariants**: Two replicas concurrently decrementing a `PN-Counter` from 1 to -1 cannot be prevented locally. *Fix*: Use Escrow/Bounded-Counter patterns (pre-allocating per-replica quotas) or fall back to consensus for scarce resources.

## Compression & production libraries

Production CRDT engines avoid storing a JSON object per character:
- **Yjs**: Uses doubly-linked blocks (`Item` structs) with **ID run-length encoding**—typing `"hello"` creates 1 struct of length 5 instead of 5 structs, keeping memory ~1.5x raw text.
- **Automerge 2.0**: Stores columnar compressed change logs (inspired by Apache Arrow/Parquet) so a 100,000-edit document loads in ~10 ms and compresses 10x smaller than JSON.
- **Redis Enterprise CRDTs**: Implements native `G-Counter`, `PN-Counter`, `OR-Set`, and `LWW-Hash` inside C modules across active-active clusters.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify your domain does not require strict global invariants (e.g., uniqueness, non-negative stock).
- [ ] Assign a unique, persistent `replicaId` per client instance/tab—never reuse user IDs.
- [ ] Replace raw `Date.now()` with Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) for any LWW conflict resolution.
- [ ] Use delta-CRDTs with run-length-encoded IDs (e.g., Yjs or Automerge) for sequences and large maps.
- [ ] Define a tombstone compaction / snapshot strategy before high-churn workloads hit memory limits.
- [ ] Fuzz-test `merge(A, B)` for associativity, commutativity, and idempotency under random network reordering.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Crdt Replicated Data Types

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are replicated data structures whose concurrent updates commute or form a mathematical join-semilattice, guaranteeing every replica converges to the exact same state without coordination or consensus.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Gossip / Delta Channel applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Join-Semilattice Merge (⊔).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Join-Semilattice Merge (⊔) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) combining physical time with a monotonic logical counter and `replicaId` tie-breaker.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: CRDTs eliminate consensus round-trips for local-first apps and geo-distributed active-active stores by trading coordination latency for metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, or per-element IDs).
Avoid trap: Using CRDTs to enforce invariants like 'only 1 seat left' or 'account balance cannot go below 0'—CRDTs cannot reject concurrent valid local writes.
Avoid trap: Implementing a naive G-Counter keyed by `userId` instead of `replicaId`, which breaks when a user opens two tabs.
When to reach for it: Local-first collaborative applications (rich-text editors, whiteboards, offline-capable mobile apps) where edits must apply locally at 0 ms and merge cleanly upon reconnection.
When to reach for it: Multi-region active-active databases tracking distributed counters, feature flags, shopping carts, or user presence sets without cross-region locks.

concepts.name: CSRF Defense Patterns

relationships.description: Connects CSRF Defense Patterns to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.

spark.summary: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.
spark.keyTakeaway: Modern CSRF defense stacks three layers: `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookies, `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata validation, and unpredictable per-session Synchronizer Tokens for legacy or cross-site flows.

concept.whyItMatters:
Whenever authentication relies on ambient credentials—HTTP cookies, HTTP Basic Auth, or client TLS certificates—any malicious website can submit a hidden `
` or `` request that the browser happily signs with the victim's cookies. A single CSRF flaw can trigger unauthorized wire transfers, email/password resets, or OAuth account takeovers. Because browsers now ship `SameSite` defaults and `Sec-Fetch-Site` headers, understanding how modern browser defenses interact with legacy endpoints and CORS is critical for zero-gap web security.
whenToUse: All browser-facing web applications using session cookies (`Set-Cookie`) for authentication on state-changing (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) endpoints.
OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization flows, which must bind the authorization callback to the user's session via the `state` parameter (or PKCE) to prevent login CSRF.
Single-Page Applications (SPAs) and APIs that share a parent domain (`app.example.com` and `api.example.com`), where `SameSite` alone does *not* block sibling-subdomain attacks.
whenNotToUse: Pure machine-to-machine or mobile APIs that authenticate *strictly* via explicit `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` headers read from memory—browsers never auto-attach `Authorization` headers cross-site.
Idempotent, read-only `GET`/`HEAD` endpoints (provided they never mutate state—if a `GET` endpoint mutates state, fix the HTTP verb first).
keyPoints: `SameSite=Lax` (the modern browser default) withholds cookies on cross-site `POST` forms and `fetch()` calls, while still sending them on top-level `GET` navigations; `SameSite=Strict` withholds them even on inbound links.

Fetch Metadata headers (`Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin | same-site | cross-site | none`) are browser-enforced forbidden headers that cannot be spoofed by JavaScript, letting servers reject `cross-site` state changes in 5 lines of middleware.

The **Synchronizer Token Pattern** embeds a cryptographically random, per-session (or per-request) secret in forms or custom headers (`X-CSRF-Token`) and compares it using constant-time equality (`hmac.Equal` / `crypto.timingSafeEqual`).

The **Stateless Double-Submit Cookie** pattern must bind the token to the user's session using an HMAC (`HMAC(secret, sessionId + random)`) rather than a raw random cookie; otherwise, an attacker on a compromised subdomain can overwrite the cookie.

CORS preflights (`OPTIONS`) block custom headers and `application/json` cross-origin `fetch()` calls, **but** simple requests (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, `text/plain`) bypass CORS preflight completely.

examples.title: Bypassing Naive CORS via `text/plain` Simple Request
examples.scenario: An engineering team assumed `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` protected their `POST /api/transfer` endpoint, which parsed JSON bodies without checking `Content-Type`.
examples.outcome: An attacker's page sent `fetch('https://api.example.com/api/transfer', {method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: {'Content-Type': 'text/plain'}, body: '{"to":"attacker","amount":5000}'})`. Because `text/plain` skips CORS preflight, the browser sent the session cookie and executed the transfer—fixed by enforcing `Content-Type: application/json` + `Sec-Fetch-Site` + CSRF tokens.

examples.title: Subdomain Cookie Overwrite Defeated with Signed Double-Submit
examples.scenario: A marketing blog on `blog.example.com` had an XSS flaw, and the main app on `app.example.com` used an unsigned double-submit CSRF cookie.
examples.outcome: The attacker set a `Domain=.example.com` CSRF cookie from `blog.example.com` and submitted a forged form to `app.example.com`. Switching to an HMAC-signed token bound to the `HttpOnly` session ID closed the subdomain bypass.

tradeOffs.pro: `SameSite=Strict` blocks all cross-site cookie transmission, including top-level link clicks.
tradeOffs.con: Breaks inbound links from emails, Slack, or Google Search—users appear logged out when clicking a link into your app.

tradeOffs.factor: Stateful Synchronizer Token vs. Signed Double-Submit
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronizer tokens require zero extra cookies and are trivial to invalidate on logout.
tradeOffs.con: Requires server-side session state (Redis/DB), whereas HMAC-bound double-submit works in stateless JWT-in-cookie architectures.

tradeOffs.pro: `Sec-Fetch-Site` explicitly classifies `same-origin` vs `same-site` vs `cross-site` without brittle URL parsing.
tradeOffs.con: Very old browsers or corporate proxies may strip `Sec-Fetch-*` headers, so pair it with `Origin` or a Synchronizer Token fallback.

failureModes.name: Simple-Request CORS Bypass
failureModes.description: Relying solely on CORS `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` without rejecting `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, or `text/plain` lets HTML `<form>` and `fetch()` skip preflight.
failureModes.mitigation: Strictly validate `Content-Type: application/json` on JSON APIs AND enforce `Sec-Fetch-Site` or a CSRF token.

failureModes.name: SameSite Sibling-Subdomain Blind Spot
failureModes.description: `SameSite=Lax` treats `evil.example.com -> api.example.com` as `same-site` (same registrable eTLD+1), attaching cookies to cross-subdomain attacks.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `__Host-` cookie prefixes (`__Host-session=...; Secure; Path=/; HttpOnly`) and check `Sec-Fetch-Site == 'same-origin'` or `Origin` exact-match.

failureModes.name: Login CSRF & OAuth State Omission
failureModes.description: Skipping CSRF protection on `POST /login` or omitting `state` in OAuth callbacks lets an attacker log the victim into the attacker's account to harvest subsequent activity.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply CSRF tokens or `Sec-Fetch-Site` to login/logout endpoints and enforce cryptographically bound `state` + PKCE on OAuth.

failureModes.name: HTTP Method Override Abuse
failureModes.description: Frameworks supporting `_method=DELETE` query parameters or `X-HTTP-Method-Override` let a cross-site `GET` or `POST` form trigger `DELETE` handlers.
failureModes.mitigation: Disable method-override middleware or run CSRF validation before method rewriting.

commonMistakes: Mutating state on `GET` requests (e.g., `GET /logout` or `GET /unsubscribe?confirm=1`), which `SameSite=Lax` explicitly allows cross-site.
Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (or blindly echoing the request `Origin` header).
Using `==` string comparison instead of constant-time comparison (`timingSafeEqual`) when verifying CSRF tokens.
Exposing the CSRF token in URL query parameters, which leaks it via `Referer` headers and browser history.
Believing HTTPS/TLS alone prevents CSRF—an attacker's `https://evil.com` page can still submit HTTPS forms to `https://bank.com`.

sections.content:
## The idea

Web browsers automatically attach **ambient credentials** (cookies, HTTP Basic Auth) to every request targeting an origin—regardless of *which* page initiated the request. If `victim` is logged into `bank.com` and visits `evil.com`, a hidden `<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">` submitted by `evil.com` arrives at `bank.com` with `victim`'s valid session cookie.

**CSRF Defense** breaks this confused-deputy problem by requiring proof of **origin** or **intent** that a cross-site page cannot forge: either telling the browser not to send the cookie cross-site (`SameSite`), inspecting browser-enforced origin metadata (`Sec-Fetch-Site` / `Origin`), or requiring an unpredictable secret (`X-CSRF-Token`) that `evil.com` cannot read due to the Same-Origin Policy (SOP).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how a defense-in-depth `POST /api/v1/payout` request is evaluated:

1. **Browser Layer (`SameSite=Lax` + `__Host-` prefix)**:
   - Session cookie is set as `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=...; Secure; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax`.
   - If `evil.com` submits a cross-site `POST` form, the browser strips `__Host-sid` before the packet leaves the client.
2. **Edge/Middleware Layer (Fetch Metadata)**:
   - Server inspects `Sec-Fetch-Site`. If the header is `cross-site` (and the endpoint is not a public webhook/OAuth callback), the server immediately returns `403 Forbidden`.
3. **Application Layer (Synchronizer Token + Content-Type)**:
   - For `same-origin` or legacy clients lacking `Sec-Fetch-Site`, the SPA reads an HMAC-bound token and sends `X-CSRF-Token: <token>` with `Content-Type: application/json`.
   - Because `X-CSRF-Token` and `application/json` trigger a CORS preflight and `evil.com` cannot read the token across origins, the server verifies `timingSafeEqual(expected, actual)` and processes the payout.

sections.content:
## SameSite nuances & subdomain risks

A common misconception is that `SameSite=Lax` eliminates CSRF completely. Three edge cases remain:
1. **Same-Site != Same-Origin**: `SameSite` uses the *registrable domain* (eTLD+1). If `static.example.com` or `staging.example.com` is compromised, it is considered `same-site` to `app.example.com`, so `SameSite=Lax` and `SameSite=Strict` cookies **are sent**.
2. **Lax+POST 2-minute window**: Chromium historically allowed cookies on top-level `POST`s for 120 seconds after cookie creation if `SameSite` was omitted (default Lax). Explicitly setting `SameSite=Lax` removes this grace window.
3. **`GET` state mutations**: `SameSite=Lax` still sends cookies on top-level `GET` navigations (`<a href=...>` or `window.location=...`). Any state change on `GET` remains vulnerable.

## Defense mechanism comparison

| Defense Pattern | Server State | Protects Subdomain? | Legacy Browser Support | Key Caveat |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`SameSite=Lax` Cookie** | None | No (`eTLD+1` scope) | Modern browsers | Fails if `GET` mutates state or sibling subdomain is untrusted |
| **`Sec-Fetch-Site` Header** | None | Yes (`same-origin`) | Chrome 76+, FF 90+, Safari 16.4+ | Must check `Sec-Fetch-Mode` & fallback for older clients |
| **Synchronizer Token** | Session store | Yes | Universal | Requires server-side session lookup |
| **Signed Double-Submit** | None (HMAC key) | Yes (with `__Host-`) | Universal | Must bind token to session ID via HMAC |
| **`Bearer` Header (No Cookies)** | None | Yes | Universal | Vulnerable if XSS steals token from `localStorage` |

## Failure modes

1. **CORS misconfiguration with `credentials: true`**: Reflecting arbitrary `Origin` headers with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` lets an attacker read CSRF tokens from `GET /csrf-token` cross-origin, defeating Synchronizer Tokens.
2. **Unsigned Double-Submit Cookie**: Comparing `cookie.csrf == header.csrf` without HMAC binding allows a sibling-subdomain XSS or MITM on plain HTTP to plant a matching cookie.
3. **CSRF token leaked in `GET` URLs**: Passing `?csrf=...` leaks the token in server access logs, `Referer` headers to third-party images, and browser history.
4. **OAuth Login CSRF**: Omitting `state` on `/oauth/callback` lets an attacker force a victim's browser to link the attacker's OAuth identity to the victim's session.

## Framework & Go/Java implementation notes

- **Go 1.25+ `net/http.CrossOriginProtection`**: Implements Fetch Metadata (`Sec-Fetch-Site`) + `Origin` checks in standard library middleware with zero token state.
- **Spring Security (Java)**: Enables `CsrfFilter` by default using `XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler` (BREACH-mitigated masked Synchronizer Token) and `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` for SPAs.
- **BREACH mitigation**: When embedding a CSRF token inside compressed HTTPS HTML responses, mask the token with a per-response random one-time pad (`XOR`) so attackers cannot infer the secret via compression-ratio side channels.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Ensure `GET` and `HEAD` endpoints are strictly read-only and never mutate state.
- [ ] Set `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` (and `__Host-` prefix where possible) on all session cookies.
- [ ] Add Fetch Metadata middleware rejecting `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on state-changing routes.
- [ ] Enforce `Content-Type: application/json` on JSON APIs so simple `<form>` / `text/plain` requests fail fast.
- [ ] Use HMAC-bound Synchronizer or Double-Submit tokens verified with constant-time comparison.
- [ ] Validate `state` and PKCE on all OAuth/OIDC callbacks and protect `/login` against Login CSRF.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on CSRF Defense Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: CSRF Token & Content-Type applies the primary invariant and coordinates with State-Changing Handler.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, State-Changing Handler experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Strictly validate `Content-Type: application/json` on JSON APIs AND enforce `Sec-Fetch-Site` or a CSRF token.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Modern CSRF defense stacks three layers: `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookies, `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata validation, and unpredictable per-session Synchronizer Tokens for legacy or cross-site flows.
Avoid trap: Mutating state on `GET` requests (e.g., `GET /logout` or `GET /unsubscribe?confirm=1`), which `SameSite=Lax` explicitly allows cross-site.
Avoid trap: Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (or blindly echoing the request `Origin` header).
When to reach for it: All browser-facing web applications using session cookies (`Set-Cookie`) for authentication on state-changing (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) endpoints.
When to reach for it: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization flows, which must bind the authorization callback to the user's session via the `state` parameter (or PKCE) to prevent login CSRF.

putItTogether.title: Putting Csrf Defense Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Modern CSRF defense stacks three layers: `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookies, `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata validation, and unpredictable per-session Synchronizer Tokens for legacy or cross-site flows.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Csrf Defense Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: An attacker's page sent `fetch('https://api.example.com/api/transfer', {method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: {'Content-Type': 'text/plain'}, body: '{"to":"attacker","amount":5000}'})`. Because `text/plain` skips CORS preflight, the browser sent the session cookie and executed the transfer—fixed by enforcing `Content-Type: application/json` + `Sec-Fetch-Site` + CSRF tokens.

spark.keyTakeaway: Move analytical ownership from a central data engineering bottleneck to the domain teams that produce the operational data, enforced via automated platform contracts rather than manual gatekeeping.

concept.whyItMatters: Centralized data warehouses and lakes collapse under organizational scale: a single data engineering team cannot understand the semantics of 40+ upstream microservices, leading to brittle ETL pipelines, silent schema breakages, and 6-week backlogs for simple metric changes.
whenToUse: Organizations with 10+ autonomous product or domain teams shipping independent microservices and schemas.
When a central data team spends >60% of its sprint capacity fixing broken upstream ingestion rather than building analytics.
When multiple downstream consumers (ML, BI, finance) need guaranteed SLAs, lineage, and semantic stability from operational domains.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage startups or teams under ~30 engineers where a single dbt + Snowflake/BigQuery project is faster and cheaper to operate.
Organizations lacking a dedicated platform engineering team to build self-serve storage, catalog, and CI/CD templates.
Domains with zero analytical engineering maturity where teams cannot own schema contracts, backfills, or on-call alerts.
keyPoints: Domain-oriented ownership: the Checkout team owns both the operational Postgres/Kafka events and the analytical Checkout Orders data product.
Data as a product: every exposed dataset has an explicit owner, SLAs (freshness < 15 min, 99.9% completeness), discoverable metadata, and versioned schemas.
Self-serve data platform: platform engineers provide Terraform/Helm templates for Iceberg tables, Kafka topics, dbt runners, and DataHub registration so domains don't reinvent infra.
Federated computational governance: global rules (PII masking, retention TTLs, Avro/Protobuf compatibility) are enforced automatically in CI/CD and query engines, not by review boards.
Polyglot output ports: a single data product can expose both a streaming Kafka topic and a batch Apache Iceberg table backed by the same canonical schema.

examples.title: Fintech Payments Domain Productization
examples.scenario: A payments company had 18 microservices feeding a central Redshift cluster via brittle Airflow scrapers. Whenever the Ledger service renamed a column, downstream regulatory reporting broke for 3 days.
examples.outcome: The Ledger domain adopted Data Mesh using Protobuf contracts in Confluent Schema Registry, Debezium CDC to Iceberg, and automated Soda quality gates. Schema-breaking PRs are now blocked in CI, and regulatory report freshness improved from 24 hours to 12 minutes.

examples.title: E-Commerce Search & Recommendations Mesh
examples.scenario: Clickstream and Catalog teams maintained conflicting definitions of 'active_sku' across separate Spark jobs, causing 14% discrepancy in conversion attribution.
examples.outcome: Each domain published a canonical data product in Unity Catalog with semantic tags and OpenLineage tracking. A federated governance policy enforced standardized ISO-4217 currency and SKU IDs, eliminating reconciliation tickets.

tradeOffs.pro: Domain teams ship analytical updates at the same cadence as product features without waiting on a central queue.
tradeOffs.con: Multiple domains may duplicate common transformations (e.g., currency conversion or sessionization) unless shared platform libraries are curated.

tradeOffs.pro: Self-serve templates standardize encryption, lineage, and cost attribution across dozens of teams.
tradeOffs.con: Building the self-serve control plane (catalog, IAM automation, CI/CD checks) requires 6–12 months of upfront platform engineering effort.

tradeOffs.factor: Decentralized Storage vs. Cross-Domain Join Latency
tradeOffs.pro: Domains isolate compute budgets and avoid noisy-neighbor warehouse contention.
tradeOffs.con: Cross-domain joins via federated query engines (e.g., Trino) incur network shuffle overhead unless co-located on shared object storage.

failureModes.name: Siloed Data Swamps
failureModes.description: Domains dump raw operational tables into S3 without documentation, SLAs, or semantic modeling, recreating a fragmented data swamp.
failureModes.mitigation: Require every data product PR to pass automated catalog registration (DataHub/OpenMetadata), owner assignment, and schema contract validation before deployment.

failureModes.name: Platform-as-a-Bottleneck
failureModes.description: The central platform team builds bespoke pipelines for domains instead of self-serve abstractions, recreating the original central bottleneck.
failureModes.mitigation: Measure platform success by self-serve adoption time (e.g., < 30 minutes to scaffold a new Iceberg data product via CLI/Terraform).

failureModes.name: Cross-Domain Join Explosion
failureModes.description: Analytical queries join 8+ domain products across different regions or storage formats, causing OOM errors and 10x compute bills.
failureModes.mitigation: Standardize on open table formats (Apache Iceberg / Delta Lake) on a shared cloud object store and materialize high-fan-in consumer-aligned products.

failureModes.name: Unenforced Breaking Schema Changes
failureModes.description: A domain team alters column types or drops fields in production without versioning, breaking downstream ML feature pipelines.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE compatibility in Schema Registry and require major-versioned output ports (v1/v2) with 90-day deprecation windows.

commonMistakes: Treating Data Mesh as a pure technology migration (e.g., buying Snowflake or Trino) without changing team topologies and domain ownership.
Exposing internal operational database schemas directly as data products instead of modeling clean, consumer-facing analytical contracts.
Skipping the self-serve platform layer and expecting microservice engineers to hand-write Spark, Airflow, and IAM policies.
Creating a governance committee that manually reviews every dataset instead of encoding PII, retention, and naming rules as OPA/CI policy-as-code.
Allowing domain teams to define bespoke, incompatible identity keys (e.g., user_id vs. account_uuid) without a federated entity-resolution standard.

sections.content:
## The idea

Data Mesh applies Domain-Driven Design (DDD) and platform thinking to analytical data. Instead of extracting operational data into a centralized monolith owned by a separate data team, each business domain (e.g., Orders, Inventory, Billing) owns its analytical data end-to-end as a first-class product.

This model rests on four interdependent pillars:
1. **Domain Ownership**: Analytical pipelines live inside the domain's codebase and CI/CD lifecycle.
2. **Data as a Product**: Datasets are discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, self-describing, interoperable, and secure—backed by explicit SLOs.
3. **Self-Serve Data Platform**: A dedicated platform team abstracts away infrastructure complexity (compute, Iceberg tables, Kafka, IAM, lineage) behind declarative specs.
4. **Federated Computational Governance**: A council of domain leads and platform architects defines global interoperability and compliance rules that execute automatically in CI/CD and runtime engines.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an e-commerce **Checkout Domain** publishing a `checkout.orders.v2` data product:

1. **Contract Definition**: The Checkout team defines an Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) YAML specifying Avro/Protobuf schemas, `order_id` uniqueness, `< 10 min` freshness SLO, and `PII` tags on `customer_email`.
2. **CI/CD Policy Gate**: On pull request, an OPA (Open Policy Agent) check verifies that `customer_email` has a `sha256` masking policy attached and that the schema is backward-compatible with `v1`.
3. **Self-Serve Provisioning**: Merging the PR triggers Terraform modules that provision a Kafka topic, a Flink/Spark streaming job writing to an Apache Iceberg table in S3, and an IAM role scoped to the Checkout domain.
4. **Automated Registration & Consumption**: OpenLineage emits run metadata to DataHub. The Finance domain discovers `checkout.orders.v2` in the catalog, requests read access via automated RBAC approval, and queries it via Trino without ever filing a ticket with Checkout engineers.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Data product anatomy and output ports
sections.content:
## Data product anatomy and output ports

A production data product is an architectural quantum containing code, data, metadata, and infrastructure definitions:

- **Input Ports**: Consumed upstream events (Kafka/Debezium CDC), operational snapshots, or other domain data products.
- **Transformation Logic**: Versioned SQL (dbt), Spark, or Flink jobs that clean, deduplicate, and model entities into stable analytical schemas.
- **Output Ports**: Standardized, read-only interfaces—typically a **batch/analytical port** (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake table) and a **streaming port** (Avro/Protobuf Kafka topic). Both ports must reflect identical business semantics.
- **Control & Observability Port**: Exposes `/health` or OpenLineage/Prometheus metrics reporting row counts, freshness lag, and contract test pass rates.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Centralized vs. Data Fabric vs. Data Mesh
sections.content:
## Centralized vs. Data Fabric vs. Data Mesh

| Dimension | Centralized Warehouse / Lake | Data Fabric | Data Mesh |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ownership** | Central Data Engineering team | Central team + automated metadata layer | Domain product teams (source-aligned & consumer-aligned) |
| **Architecture** | Monolithic ETL/ELT into single store | AI-assisted integration & virtualization over silos | Distributed data products on shared self-serve platform |
| **Governance** | Manual tickets & central DBA approvals | Metadata-driven automated cataloging | Federated computational policies in CI/CD & runtime |
| **Scaling Bottleneck** | Central team backlog & domain context loss | Metadata inference accuracy on messy schemas | Platform maturity & domain engineering skill |
| **Best Fit** | < 100 engineers, unified BI | Legacy enterprises with immovable silos | 100+ engineers, high microservice autonomy |

## Failure modes

- **Distributed Monolith**: Domains couple directly to each other's internal staging tables instead of public output ports, causing cascading breakages.
- **Governance Theater**: Creating a 15-person Data Mesh steering committee that adds 2 weeks of manual review to every dataset, defeating domain velocity.
- **Unbounded Compute Sprawl**: Without per-domain FinOps tagging and query quotas on the self-serve platform, runaway Trino/Spark joins spike cloud bills.
- **Inconsistent Global Identifiers**: If Orders uses `cust_id` (int64) and Support uses `user_uuid` (UUIDv4) without a federated mapping product, cross-domain analytics becomes impossible.

## Federated computational governance in practice

Governance only scales when it is **computational** (automated) rather than manual:

1. **Policy-as-Code in CI**: Use Conftest/OPA to fail builds if a dataset lacks an `owner_slack_channel`, `retention_days`, or `pii_classification`.
2. **Fine-Grained Runtime Access**: Enforce row-level security (RLS) and dynamic column masking in Trino, Databricks Unity Catalog, or Snowflake based on IdP groups (Okta/Entra ID) rather than cloning tables for each consumer.
3. **Standardized Interoperability**: Mandate ISO timestamps (UTC), ISO-3166 country codes, and OpenLineage-compliant job metadata across all domains.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Identify 2–3 high-value pilot domains (e.g., Orders, Payments) with strong engineering maturity rather than boiling the ocean.
- [ ] Define a machine-readable Data Product Specification (ODCS YAML) covering schema, owner, SLOs, and PII tags.
- [ ] Build a self-serve Terraform/CLI template that provisions storage (Iceberg/Delta), compute, IAM, and catalog registration in < 30 minutes.
- [ ] Enforce backward schema compatibility (`BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE`) and PII policy checks in CI/CD.
- [ ] Instrument OpenLineage and freshness alerting so domain on-call rotations own data SLO breaches.

interviewProblems.title: Data Mesh Principles
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Data Mesh Principles. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Data Mesh decentralizes analytical data ownership to domain teams, treating datasets as versioned, SLA-backed data products built on a shared self-serve platform and governed by federated computational policies.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Governance Plane applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Consumer Domain.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Consumer Domain experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Require every data product PR to pass automated catalog registration (DataHub/OpenMetadata), owner assignment, and schema contract validation before deployment.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Move analytical ownership from a central data engineering bottleneck to the domain teams that produce the operational data, enforced via automated platform contracts rather than manual gatekeeping.
Avoid trap: Treating Data Mesh as a pure technology migration (e.g., buying Snowflake or Trino) without changing team topologies and domain ownership.
Avoid trap: Exposing internal operational database schemas directly as data products instead of modeling clean, consumer-facing analytical contracts.
When to reach for it: Organizations with 10+ autonomous product or domain teams shipping independent microservices and schemas.
When to reach for it: When a central data team spends >60% of its sprint capacity fixing broken upstream ingestion rather than building analytics.
