concepts.name: Data Quality Checks

relationships.description: Connects Data Quality Checks to data warehousing lakehouse in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Data quality checks validate schema, freshness, volume, distribution, and business invariants across ingestion and transformation stages so corrupted data is quarantined before reaching dashboards or ML models.

spark.summary: Data quality checks validate schema, freshness, volume, distribution, and business invariants across ingestion and transformation stages so corrupted data is quarantined before reaching dashboards or ML models.
spark.keyTakeaway: Shift data quality left into CI/CD and ingestion contracts, and pair deterministic rule assertions with statistical anomaly detection and circuit-breaker quarantining.

concept.whyItMatters: Silent data corruption—such as a timezone shift, nullified join key, or duplicate Kafka consumer offset—erodes executive trust, trains broken ML models, and triggers costly regulatory or billing errors long before an infrastructure alert fires.
whenToUse: At ingestion boundaries (Bronze/Raw) to enforce schemas, non-null primary keys, and freshness SLAs via data contracts.
Inside transformation pipelines (dbt, Spark) using Write-Audit-Publish (WAP) before promoting tables to production.
On critical downstream metrics and ML feature stores where silent distribution drift degrades model accuracy.
whenNotToUse: Running heavy full-table statistical profiling on every micro-batch (e.g., 10-second streaming windows) where it adds unacceptable latency.
Applying rigid static thresholds (e.g., row_count == 10000) to organically growing or seasonal traffic without dynamic bounds.
Duplicating identical checks across 5 pipeline stages without clear ownership or actionable alerting.
keyPoints: Five core dimensions: completeness (null rates), uniqueness (duplicate keys), validity (regex/enum/range), timeliness (freshness lag), and consistency (referential integrity).
Deterministic vs. probabilistic checks: use hard assertions (`amount >= 0`, `pk_unique`) for invariants and statistical checks (z-score, PSI, seasonal EWMA) for volume and distribution drift.
Write-Audit-Publish (WAP): stage new data in an isolated branch or snapshot (e.g., Iceberg branch / Nessie), run quality gates, and atomically fast-forward production only on pass.
Severity tiering: route blocking failures (`ERROR`) to quarantine/DLQ and halt promotion, while routing soft drift (`WARN`) to Slack/observability without breaking SLAs.
Contract-first enforcement: validate producer payloads at the Kafka Schema Registry or API gateway before malformed records enter the lakehouse.

examples.title: Write-Audit-Publish on Daily Billing Mart
examples.scenario: A SaaS billing pipeline occasionally ingested duplicate Stripe webhook events, inflating daily ARR reports by 8% until finance caught it manually at month-end.
examples.outcome: The team implemented WAP on Apache Iceberg using dbt tests (`unique` on `invoice_id`, `not_null`, and a custom SQL invariant checking `net_amount == gross - discount`). Failed runs stay on the staging branch and page on-call, reducing billing discrepancies to zero.

examples.title: ML Feature Drift Detection in Fraud Scoring
examples.scenario: An upstream mobile SDK update accidentally changed `device_os_version` from `17.2` to `iOS 17.2`, causing a fraud model's categorical encoder to default to `UNKNOWN` and spike false declines by 3.4%.
examples.outcome: Adding Soda Core distribution checks (categorical set membership + Population Stability Index > 0.2) caught the schema-valid semantic drift within 15 minutes of deployment.

tradeOffs.factor: Strict Circuit Breaking vs. Data Freshness
tradeOffs.pro: Halting publication on failed checks guarantees downstream consumers never see corrupted numbers.
tradeOffs.con: False-positive alerts or minor non-critical column nulls can freeze entire executive dashboards during peak hours.

tradeOffs.factor: Full-Table Scans vs. Incremental Partition Checks
tradeOffs.pro: Full-table checks catch cross-partition duplicates and global referential integrity violations.
tradeOffs.con: Scanning multi-terabyte Iceberg/BigQuery tables on every run explodes compute costs; partition-scoped checks are 10–100x cheaper.

tradeOffs.factor: Static Rules vs. ML Anomaly Detection
tradeOffs.pro: Static rules (`price > 0`) are deterministic, explainable, and have zero false positives.
tradeOffs.con: Static rules miss subtle volume drops (e.g., 40% drop in EU traffic) that adaptive time-series baselines detect automatically.

failureModes.name: Alert Fatigue from Noisy Thresholds
failureModes.description: Teams configure dozens of uncalibrated `WARN` checks on volatile columns, causing engineers to mute the Slack channel and miss real outages.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict severity tiers: only page on Tier-1 contract invariants; calibrate statistical bounds using 28-day seasonal baselines.

failureModes.name: Check-After-Publish Race Condition
failureModes.description: Quality tests run asynchronously after the production table is overwritten, meaning BI tools and ML jobs already consumed bad data.
failureModes.mitigation: Adopt the Write-Audit-Publish (WAP) pattern using Iceberg/Delta branching or blue-green table swaps.

failureModes.name: Quarantine Black Hole
failureModes.description: Invalid records are routed to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) or quarantine table that nobody monitors or replays, causing silent data loss.
failureModes.mitigation: Track DLQ volume as an SLI with an alert when > 0.1% of records are quarantined, and automate replay scripts after schema fixes.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Scan Cost Explosion
failureModes.description: Unpartitioned `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` or regex checks run hourly across 5 years of history, spiking Snowflake/BigQuery spend.
failureModes.mitigation: Scope checks to the incremental partition (`WHERE event_date = CURRENT_DATE`) and use approximate sketches (HyperLogLog) for cardinality.

commonMistakes: Testing only for NULLs and data types while ignoring business invariants (e.g., `refund_amount <= order_total` or `ship_date >= order_date`).
Running data quality checks only in production instead of executing unit/contract tests in CI on synthetic or sampled staging data.
Treating row-count > 0 as sufficient validation, which misses silent 50% drops or duplicate-row inflation.
Writing custom one-off Python validation scripts per pipeline instead of declarative frameworks (dbt tests, Soda, Great Expectations, SQLMesh audits).
Failing to attach lineage and owner metadata to quality alerts, leaving responders guessing which upstream microservice broke.

sections.content:
## The idea

Data quality checks are automated assertions and statistical monitors placed at key boundaries of a data pipeline to verify that datasets are **fit for purpose** before consumers rely on them.

A mature quality architecture separates **structural/contract checks** (schema, types, non-null keys, enum values), **semantic/business invariants** (balance equations, state transitions, referential integrity), and **observability/drift checks** (freshness lag, volume anomalies, distribution shifts). Rather than fixing corrupted tables after dashboards break, modern pipelines combine **shift-left contracts** at ingestion with **Write-Audit-Publish (WAP)** gates during transformation.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an hourly **Clickstream & Revenue** pipeline loading events into an Apache Iceberg table:

1. **Ingestion Gate (Kafka + Schema Registry)**: Producers serialize events in Avro. Malformed payloads missing `event_id` or `timestamp_utc` are rejected at the producer or routed to `events.dlq`.
2. **Write Stage (Isolated Branch)**: Spark reads the hourly Kafka micro-batch and writes transformed records to an isolated Iceberg branch `audit_2026_11_12_10`—invisible to BI users querying `main`.
3. **Audit Stage (Soda / dbt / SQLMesh)**: Automated checks run on the branch:
   - `unique(event_id)` and `not_null(user_id, revenue_usd)`
   - `revenue_usd >= 0 AND revenue_usd < 100000`
   - `row_count` within 3 standard deviations of the same hour over the past 4 weeks.
4. **Publish or Quarantine**: If all `ERROR`-tier checks pass, Iceberg atomically fast-forwards `main` to the audited snapshot. If a check fails, `main` remains untouched, the bad batch stays in `audit_*` for inspection, and PagerDuty alerts the owning domain.

sections.content:
## Deterministic rules vs. statistical observability

Relying solely on one style leaves blind spots:

- **Deterministic Assertions**: Explicit SQL/Python rules (`not_null`, `accepted_values`, `relationships`, `expression_is_true`). Ideal for primary keys, currency codes, and accounting identities (`assets == liabilities + equity`). Zero ambiguity, fast to execute on incremental partitions.
- **Statistical Observability**: Automated profiling of metadata and distributions over time—freshness (time since last commit), volume (row count z-score / Prophet seasonality), and distribution drift (KL-divergence, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, PSI). Essential for catching upstream bugs that remain schema-valid (e.g., an ad campaign tracker dropping UTM parameters for Safari users).

## Comparison of data quality tooling

| Tool / Pattern | Execution Layer | Primary Strength | Best For | Key Limitation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **dbt / SQLMesh Audits** | Warehouse SQL (Snowflake, BigQuery, Trino) | Tightly coupled with SQL models & Git CI | Transformation-layer invariants & WAP | Limited statistical/ML drift detection |
| **Soda Core / SodaCL** | SQL & Spark DataFrames | Human-readable YAML checks & anomaly detection | Cross-team contracts & freshness SLAs | Advanced observability features require cloud tier |
| **Great Expectations** | Python / Spark / SQL | Rich library of 50+ built-in statistical expectations | Complex Python/Spark data engineering pipelines | Verbose configuration & higher boilerplate |
| **Schema Registry + DLQ** | Kafka / Pulsar / API Gateway | Prevents malformed records at the source | Real-time event streams & microservices | Validates single-record syntax, not cross-row aggregates |
| **Monte Carlo / Elementary** | Metadata & Query Logs | Zero-config freshness, volume & lineage alerts | Broad warehouse monitoring across 1,000+ tables | Can miss domain-specific business logic bugs |

## Failure modes

- **Silent Schema Evolution**: Adding a nullable column or changing an enum value upstream causes downstream `CASE WHEN` statements to fall into `ELSE NULL` without raising an error.
- **Late-Arriving Data False Positives**: Mobile clients offline for 48 hours flush batched events, triggering volume spike alerts or failing `event_timestamp >= partition_date` checks.
- **Quarantine Accumulation**: Routing bad rows to a DLQ without retention policies or replay automation turns the DLQ into an unmonitored graveyard of lost revenue events.
- **Test Suite Drift**: Engineers disable failing dbt tests (`severity: warn` or `# skip`) during an incident and never re-enable them.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Production patterns: quarantine, backfill, and SLIs
sections.content:
## Production patterns: quarantine, backfill, and SLIs

1. **Row-Level Quarantine vs. Batch Halt**: For non-critical dimensions (e.g., optional user survey fields), tag bad rows with `_dq_error_reason` and route them to a quarantine table while letting valid rows proceed. For financial ledgers, halt the entire batch.
2. **Partition-Scoped Incremental Audits**: Always filter checks by `_ingested_at >= window_start` or Iceberg snapshot diffs (`SELECT * FROM table.changes`) to keep audit latency under 30 seconds.
3. **Quality SLIs**: Track **Bad Record Rate** (`quarantined_rows / total_rows`), **Time-to-Detect (TTD)**, and **Freshness SLO Attainment** per data product.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce schema contracts (Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema) at ingestion boundaries with a monitored DLQ.
- [ ] Implement Write-Audit-Publish (WAP) on Tier-1 tables so unverified data is never visible on `main`.
- [ ] Cover all 5 dimensions: completeness, uniqueness, validity, freshness, and business invariants.
- [ ] Scope audit queries to incremental partitions or snapshot deltas to control warehouse compute costs.
- [ ] Separate `ERROR` (blocking/paging) from `WARN` (observability/Slack) to eliminate alert fatigue.

interviewProblems.title: Data Quality Checks
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Data Quality Checks. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Data quality checks validate schema, freshness, volume, distribution, and business invariants across ingestion and transformation stages so corrupted data is quarantined before reaching dashboards or ML models.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Quality Engine applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Production Table.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Production Table experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce strict severity tiers: only page on Tier-1 contract invariants; calibrate statistical bounds using 28-day seasonal baselines.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Shift data quality left into CI/CD and ingestion contracts, and pair deterministic rule assertions with statistical anomaly detection and circuit-breaker quarantining.
Avoid trap: Testing only for NULLs and data types while ignoring business invariants (e.g., `refund_amount <= order_total` or `ship_date >= order_date`).
Avoid trap: Running data quality checks only in production instead of executing unit/contract tests in CI on synthetic or sampled staging data.
When to reach for it: At ingestion boundaries (Bronze/Raw) to enforce schemas, non-null primary keys, and freshness SLAs via data contracts.
When to reach for it: Inside transformation pipelines (dbt, Spark) using Write-Audit-Publish (WAP) before promoting tables to production.

putItTogether.title: Putting Data Quality Checks Together
putItTogether.summary: Shift data quality left into CI/CD and ingestion contracts, and pair deterministic rule assertions with statistical anomaly detection and circuit-breaker quarantining.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Data Quality Checks before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The team implemented WAP on Apache Iceberg using dbt tests (`unique` on `invoice_id`, `not_null`, and a custom SQL invariant checking `net_amount == gross - discount`). Failed runs stay on the staging branch and page on-call, reducing billing discrepancies to zero.

concepts.tagline: A Data Lakehouse unifies the low-cost, open-format object storage of a Data Lake with the ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and fast SQL performance of a Data Warehouse—typically organized via Medallion (Bronze, Silver, Gold) layers.

spark.summary: A Data Lakehouse unifies the low-cost, open-format object storage of a Data Lake with the ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and fast SQL performance of a Data Warehouse—typically organized via Medallion (Bronze, Silver, Gold) layers.
spark.keyTakeaway: Store data once in open table formats (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) on cloud object storage, using Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers to progressively refine raw events into governed, query-ready business tables.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional two-tier architectures force teams to pay twice: raw files sit in an ungoverned S3 Data Lake for ML, while curated subsets are copied into an expensive proprietary Data Warehouse for BI—creating data silos, sync lag, and vendor lock-in.
whenToUse: Organizations running both BI SQL analytics and Python/Spark ML workloads over the same multi-terabyte datasets.
When avoiding proprietary storage lock-in (e.g., querying the same S3 data from Snowflake, Trino, Spark, and DuckDB) is a priority.
When teams need ACID mutations (GDPR deletes, CDC upserts, time travel) on cheap object storage.
whenNotToUse: Small datasets (< 1 TB) with purely SQL/BI needs where a managed serverless warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, DuckDB) requires zero compaction or file-management overhead.
Sub-10ms point-lookup OLTP workloads, which belong in PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, or Redis—not a lakehouse.
Real-time operational alerting requiring < 100ms end-to-end latency, better served by ClickHouse, Apache Pinot, or Flink.
keyPoints: Open table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi) add a metadata transaction log (manifests/JSON commits) on top of Parquet files in S3/GCS/ADLS.
ACID & Time Travel: optimistic concurrency control enables atomic writes, snapshot isolation for readers, and instant rollbacks (`AS OF VERSION` / `TIMESTAMP`).
Medallion Architecture: Bronze (raw, append-only history), Silver (cleansed, deduplicated, conformed entities), Gold (aggregated, business-level star schemas & feature tables).
Compute-storage separation: stateless engines (Trino, Spark, Snowflake, DuckDB) scale independently while reading shared Parquet files via catalog APIs (Iceberg REST, Unity Catalog).
File maintenance is mandatory: background compaction (`OPTIMIZE`), Z-ordering/clustering, and snapshot expiration (`VACUUM`) prevent the small-files problem.

examples.title: Media Streaming Platform Lakehouse Migration
examples.scenario: A video platform stored 400 TB of clickstream logs in S3 Parquet and copied 60 TB into Redshift nightly. Nightly `COPY` jobs took 4.5 hours, and GDPR deletion requests required rewriting entire monthly partitions.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Apache Iceberg on S3 with Spark + Trino eliminated the Redshift copy step, cut storage + compute costs by 42%, and enabled row-level GDPR deletes via Iceberg Merge-on-Read.

examples.title: Logistics Medallion Pipeline for Fleet Telemetry
examples.scenario: IoT GPS pings arrived out-of-order from 80,000 trucks, causing duplicate trip calculations in downstream BI reports.
examples.outcome: The team built a Medallion pipeline on Delta Lake: Bronze ingested raw JSON from Kafka; Silver deduplicated by `(truck_id, event_ts)` via `MERGE INTO`; Gold materialized hourly route-efficiency aggregates for ops dashboards.

tradeOffs.factor: Open Lakehouse vs. Proprietary Cloud Warehouse
tradeOffs.pro: Zero storage lock-in, multi-engine interoperability (Spark, Trino, DuckDB), and 5–10x cheaper raw storage ($23/TB/mo on S3).
tradeOffs.con: Requires managing table maintenance (compaction, vacuuming, manifest rewriting) unless using a managed catalog service.

tradeOffs.pro: CoW delivers fastest read performance because no delete files need to be merged at query time.
tradeOffs.con: CoW rewrites entire 256 MB Parquet files for a single-row update; MoR speeds up CDC writes at the cost of slightly slower reads until compaction.

tradeOffs.pro: Materializing Bronze, Silver, and Gold creates clear replayability, auditability, and decoupled SLAs.
tradeOffs.con: Materializing every intermediate hop triples storage writes and adds end-to-end latency if Silver is needlessly duplicated.

failureModes.name: The Small-Files Problem
failureModes.description: Streaming jobs commit thousands of 50 KB Parquet files per hour, causing query planners to spend minutes listing metadata and exhausting memory.
failureModes.mitigation: Schedule asynchronous bin-packing compaction (`rewrite_data_files`) to target 128–512 MB Parquet files and buffer streaming writes into 1–5 minute micro-batches.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Snapshot & Orphan File Bloat
failureModes.description: Frequent streaming commits accumulate tens of thousands of historical snapshots and unreferenced Parquet files, inflating S3 bills and planning time.
failureModes.mitigation: Run automated snapshot expiration (e.g., retain 7 days) and orphan-file cleanup (`VACUUM`) while preserving tagged compliance snapshots.

failureModes.name: Medallion Layer Leakage
failureModes.description: BI dashboards query Bronze raw JSON directly or Silver tables contain unmodeled business-specific KPIs, breaking clean separation of concerns.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict BI tool service accounts to Gold schemas via catalog RBAC, and enforce Silver-to-Gold modeling in dbt/SQLMesh.

failureModes.name: Concurrent Write Contention
failureModes.description: Multiple Spark jobs or compaction workers update the same partition simultaneously, triggering optimistic concurrency `CommitFailedException` loops.
failureModes.mitigation: Partition writes cleanly by ingestion date/region, use isolated Iceberg branches for backfills, and schedule compaction off-peak or with lock-free MoR.

commonMistakes: Treating Bronze, Silver, and Gold as rigid physical folders that must always be 3 separate materialized tables even when a simple view suffices.
Partitioning tables on high-cardinality columns (e.g., `user_id` or `timestamp_ms`), creating millions of tiny partitions and killing query pruning.
Ignoring Parquet row-group sorting (Z-ordering / Hilbert curves) on high-selectivity filter columns like `tenant_id` or `order_id`.
Running `VACUUM` with a 0-hour retention window while long-running queries are still reading older snapshots, causing `FileNotFoundException`.
Leaving raw PII unencrypted or unmasked in Bronze without strict IAM isolation, turning Bronze into a compliance liability.

sections.content:
## The idea

Data platforms evolved across three generations: **Data Warehouses** (schema-on-write, fast SQL, expensive proprietary storage), **Data Lakes** (schema-on-read, cheap object storage, no ACID transactions or schema enforcement—often degrading into data swamps), and **Data Lakehouses**.

A Lakehouse places an **open transactional metadata layer** (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, or Apache Hudi) directly over immutable Parquet/ORC files in cloud object storage. This gives object storage full ACID transactions, snapshot isolation, schema evolution, and partition pruning without copying data into a proprietary warehouse. To keep transformations maintainable, Lakehouses commonly structure data through the **Medallion Architecture** (Bronze -> Silver -> Gold).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a single **Order Event** through a Medallion Lakehouse:

1. **Bronze (Raw Ingestion)**: Debezium streams Postgres `orders` CDC events into Kafka, and Flink appends them as-is into `bronze.orders_raw` (Iceberg) with `_ingested_at` and `_source_offset` metadata. Zero transformations—if a downstream bug is discovered 6 months later, Silver can be replayed from Bronze.
2. **Silver (Conformed & Deduplicated)**: An hourly dbt/Spark job reads incremental Bronze snapshots, deduplicates by `order_id` keeping the latest `op_ts`, casts currencies to `DECIMAL(18,2)`, masks `customer_email`, and `MERGE`s into `silver.orders`.
3. **Gold (Business Aggregates)**: A downstream model joins `silver.orders` with `silver.customers` and `silver.fx_rates` to materialize `gold.daily_revenue_by_region`—a Z-ordered, BI-optimized table powering Looker/Tableau and ML churn features.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / How open table formats achieve ACID on object storage
sections.content:
## How open table formats achieve ACID on object storage

Object stores (S3, GCS) only support immutable object writes, not in-place file updates. Open table formats solve this via **snapshot-based metadata trees**:

- **Apache Iceberg**: Maintains a `metadata.json` pointer (swapped atomically via catalog CAS) -> `manifest list` (per-snapshot partition bounds) -> `manifest files` (per-file min/max column stats) -> `Parquet data files`. Readers prune 99% of files using manifest stats without calling `S3 ListObjects`.
- **Delta Lake**: Uses an ordered `_delta_log/*.json` transaction log plus periodic Parquet checkpoints. Writers use conditional `PutIfAbsent` (or a lock service) to claim the next sequential log version.
- **Hidden Partitioning (Iceberg)**: Decouples physical partitioning (`days(event_ts)`) from logical query filters (`WHERE event_ts >= '2026-11-01'`), preventing user errors that cause full-table scans.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake vs. Data Lakehouse
sections.content:
## Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake vs. Data Lakehouse

| Feature | Data Warehouse (e.g., Redshift, Snowflake) | Classic Data Lake (e.g., S3 + Hive Parquet) | Data Lakehouse (e.g., Iceberg / Delta + Trino / Spark) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Storage Format** | Proprietary internal columnar format | Open Parquet / ORC / JSON | Open Parquet + transactional metadata log |
| **ACID Transactions** | Full ACID | None (eventual consistency, partial writes) | Full ACID with snapshot isolation & time travel |
| **Schema Enforcement** | Strict schema-on-write | Loose schema-on-read (prone to swamp) | Configurable schema enforcement & safe evolution |
| **ML / Unstructured Support** | Limited (requires external export) | Native (Python, PyTorch, Spark) | Native + SQL BI on the exact same copy |
| **Storage Cost** | Higher (bundled or proprietary markup) | Raw cloud object storage (~$23/TB/mo) | Raw cloud object storage (~$23/TB/mo) |
| **Ops Overhead** | Low (fully managed vacuum/clustering) | High (Hive Metastore, manual partitions) | Medium (requires compaction & snapshot expiration) |

## Failure modes

- **Metadata Bottleneck**: Uncompacted Iceberg/Delta tables with 100,000+ small files cause coordinator OOMs during query planning.
- **Over-Partitioning**: Partitioning by `hour` + `country` + `device_type` creates sparse 200 KB files that destroy Parquet compression and I/O throughput.
- **Dangling Delete Files (MoR)**: Heavy CDC `MERGE` workloads using Merge-on-Read accumulate thousands of positional/equality delete files, degrading read latency by 10x until compacted.
- **Catalog Divergence**: Writing directly to S3 Parquet paths bypassing the Iceberg/Unity Catalog causes stale metadata and invisible rows.

## Maintenance and performance tuning

Keep a Lakehouse fast with four automated jobs:

1. **Bin-Packing Compaction**: Merge small files into 256–512 MB Parquet files every few hours for streaming tables.
2. **Data Clustering / Z-Ordering**: Sort rows inside Parquet files by common filter/join keys (`customer_id`, `tenant_id`) so min/max row-group statistics skip 95%+ of blocks.
3. **Snapshot Expiration & Vacuum**: Expire snapshots older than 7 days and delete orphan files > 24 hours old to cap S3 storage growth.
4. **Deletion Vectors / Puffin Stats**: Enable deletion vectors (Delta) or Puffin NDV sketches (Iceberg) to accelerate `MERGE` mutations and join reordering.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Standardize on an open table format (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) backed by a unified catalog (Iceberg REST, Unity Catalog, AWS Glue).
- [ ] Enforce strict separation: Bronze (raw, restricted PII), Silver (deduplicated, conformed), Gold (BI/ML-ready).
- [ ] Target 128–512 MB file sizes and coarse partitioning (e.g., `day` or `month`, never `user_id`).
- [ ] Automate background compaction, Z-ordering, and snapshot expiration jobs.
- [ ] Enable time-travel retention (e.g., 7 days) for instant rollback after bad pipeline deployments.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Store data once in open table formats (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) on cloud object storage, using Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers to progressively refine raw events into governed, query-ready business tables.
Avoid trap: Treating Bronze, Silver, and Gold as rigid physical folders that must always be 3 separate materialized tables even when a simple view suffices.
Avoid trap: Partitioning tables on high-cardinality columns (e.g., `user_id` or `timestamp_ms`), creating millions of tiny partitions and killing query pruning.
When to reach for it: Organizations running both BI SQL analytics and Python/Spark ML workloads over the same multi-terabyte datasets.
When to reach for it: When avoiding proprietary storage lock-in (e.g., querying the same S3 data from Snowflake, Trino, Spark, and DuckDB) is a priority.

concepts.tagline: B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.

spark.summary: B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.
spark.keyTakeaway: Choose B-Trees for read-heavy OLTP workloads needing predictable p99 read latency and in-place updates; choose LSM-Trees for write-heavy ingestion, time-series, and high-compression workloads.

concept.whyItMatters: Every database query and write path is governed by its storage engine's index structure: picking the wrong engine turns high-throughput writes into random-I/O stalls (B-Tree page splits) or turns point reads into multi-SSTable fan-out spikes (LSM read amplification).
whenToUse: Use B-Trees (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) for read-heavy OLTP workloads, frequent in-place updates, and strict p99 read latency guarantees.
Use LSM-Trees (RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Pebble) for write-intensive telemetry, event logging, and key-value stores where sequential append throughput dominates.
Use LSM-Trees when storage compression matters: immutable SSTables compress 2–4x better than fragmented B-Tree pages.
whenNotToUse: Avoid B-Trees on spinning HDDs or high-churn append streams where random 8–16 KB page writes saturate IOPS.
Avoid LSM-Trees for workloads dominated by uncached, random-key range scans across heavily updated keys without sufficient Bloom filter/block-cache RAM.
Avoid creating secondary indexes indiscriminately on write-heavy tables—every secondary index multiplies write amplification.
keyPoints: B-Tree structure: balanced tree of fixed-size pages (8 KB in Postgres, 16 KB in InnoDB) with high fan-out (typically 3–4 levels for 100M+ rows), yielding O(log N) reads.
LSM-Tree write path: writes append to an on-disk Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and insert into an in-memory MemTable (skiplist/red-black tree), flushing sequentially as immutable SSTables.
The RUM Conjecture: no index can simultaneously minimize Read, Update (Write), and Memory (Space) amplification—B-Trees optimize reads; LSM-Trees optimize writes and space.
Bloom filters & fence pointers: LSM-Trees use per-SSTable Bloom filters (~10 bits/key for 1% false-positive rate) to skip non-matching files on point lookups.
Compaction trade-off: Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS) minimizes write amplification for append-heavy loads, while Leveled Compaction (LCS) bounds space and read amplification.

examples.title: IoT Telemetry Ingestion on InnoDB vs. RocksDB
examples.scenario: A fleet platform ingested 120,000 sensor writes/sec into a MySQL InnoDB table indexed by random UUIDv4 primary keys. Buffer pool thrashing and random 16 KB page splits pinned NVMe IOPS at 100%.
examples.outcome: Moving raw telemetry to a RocksDB-backed store (LSM-Tree) turned random writes into sequential WAL + SSTable flushes, cutting write IOPS by 6x and disk footprint by 55% via Zstd SSTable compression.

examples.title: E-Commerce Order Lookup with Covering B-Tree Index
examples.scenario: A PostgreSQL `orders` table (400M rows) suffered 45 ms p99 latency on `WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` due to heap fetches.
examples.outcome: Creating a composite covering B-Tree index `(customer_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (status, total_cents)` enabled Index-Only Scans, dropping p99 latency from 45 ms to 1.8 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: B-Trees check a single root-to-leaf path (1 disk/cache lookup at the leaf), giving tight p99 read latency.
tradeOffs.con: LSM-Trees may probe the MemTable plus multiple SSTable levels on cache misses, though Bloom filters mitigate point-lookup overhead.

tradeOffs.pro: LSM-Trees batch writes sequentially and pack SSTables densely (~100% fill factor vs. ~67% average B-Tree page fill).
tradeOffs.con: LSM background compaction rewrites data multiple times (10–30x in Leveled Compaction) and can cause latency spikes if it saturates NVMe bandwidth.

tradeOffs.pro: B-Trees keep keys physically contiguous inside leaf pages, making `BETWEEN` range scans fast.
tradeOffs.con: LSM-Tree deletes write tombstone markers; heavy delete workloads without compaction force range scans to skip millions of tombstones.

failureModes.name: LSM Compaction Stalls (Write Stop)
failureModes.description: Sustained writes outpace background compaction, causing L0 SSTable count to hit `level0_stop_writes_trigger` and freezing client writes.
failureModes.mitigation: Monitor L0 file count and compaction pending bytes; allocate dedicated compaction threads, rate-limit bursts, or use NVMe SSDs with higher sustained write IOPS.

failureModes.name: B-Tree Random UUIDv4 Page Thrashing
failureModes.description: Inserting random UUIDv4 keys into a clustered B-Tree forces constant random leaf-page reads, page splits, and dirty-page eviction.
failureModes.mitigation: Use time-ordered identifiers (UUIDv7, ULID, or monotonic sequences) so inserts append to the rightmost leaf page.

failureModes.name: LSM Tombstone Accumulation
failureModes.description: Queue-like workloads that insert and delete keys rapidly leave millions of tombstones in L0–L2, slowing `SELECT` range scans from 2 ms to 2 seconds.
failureModes.mitigation: Avoid queue patterns in LSM stores, or enable `PeriodicCompaction` / TTL-aware compaction (e.g., Cassandra TWCS) to purge expired keys.

failureModes.name: B-Tree Index Bloat & Dead Tuples
failureModes.description: Heavy `UPDATE`/`DELETE` churn in MVCC B-Trees (like PostgreSQL) leaves dead index entries that bloat tree depth and cache usage.
failureModes.mitigation: Tune `autovacuum` aggressiveness and run `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` or `pg_repack` when index bloat exceeds 30%.

commonMistakes: Using random UUIDv4 as a clustered primary key in MySQL InnoDB, destroying buffer pool locality and causing 50% page fragmentation.
Assuming LSM-Trees have zero read penalty without sizing RAM for Bloom filters and the block cache.
Over-indexing OLTP tables with 8+ secondary indexes, multiplying write amplification on every `INSERT` or `UPDATE`.
Using a leading wildcard (`LIKE '%foo'`) or wrapping an indexed column in a function (`LOWER(email)`), bypassing the B-Tree entirely.
Neglecting `compaction_throughput` limits in RocksDB/Cassandra, allowing compaction to starve foreground query I/O.

sections.content:
## The idea

Storage engines balance three competing costs—**Read Amplification** (bytes read per query), **Write Amplification** (bytes written to disk per logical write), and **Space Amplification** (disk bytes stored per logical byte). Two dominant architectures resolve this trade-off differently:

- **B-Trees (Update-in-Place)**: Store sorted keys in fixed-size mutable pages (8–16 KB). Lookups traverse 3–4 levels from root to leaf in O(log N). Updates modify leaf pages in place (buffered in RAM and persisted via WAL), splitting pages when full.
- **LSM-Trees (Log-Structured Merge-Trees, Out-of-Place)**: Append all writes sequentially to an in-memory **MemTable** (backed by a WAL). When full, the MemTable flushes as an immutable, sorted **SSTable** on disk. Background compaction merges overlapping SSTables to reclaim space and bound read fan-out.

## Concrete walkthrough

Compare `PUT(k='user:42', v='active')` followed by `GET('user:42')` across both engines:

**B-Tree Path (PostgreSQL / InnoDB)**:
1. Write logs the change to the WAL, then locates leaf page #8812 via root -> internal -> leaf traversal (3 page lookups, usually cached in Buffer Pool).
2. Leaf page #8812 is dirtied in RAM; if full, it splits into two 50%-filled pages and updates the parent.
3. `GET('user:42')` traverses the exact same 3-level path to leaf #8812—1 leaf read, deterministic latency.

**LSM-Tree Path (RocksDB)**:
1. `PUT` appends to the sequential WAL and inserts into the active **MemTable** (~microseconds, zero random disk seeks).
2. Once the MemTable hits 64 MB, it freezes and flushes sequentially to **L0 SSTable**.
3. `GET('user:42')` checks the active MemTable, immutable MemTables, and then probes L0 SSTables (which may have overlapping key ranges) and L1..Ln SSTables. Per-file **Bloom filters** skip 99% of SSTables that don't contain `'user:42'`, reading only the matching block.

sections.content:
## Compaction strategies and Bloom filters

LSM-Tree performance hinges on two mechanisms:

- **Bloom Filters**: A compact bit array (~10 bits per key = ~1.2 MB per 1M keys) stored in each SSTable's metadata. Before reading a data block from disk, the engine hashes the key into the Bloom filter: a negative result guarantees the key is absent (zero disk I/O), while a positive result has a ~1% false-positive rate.
- **Leveled Compaction (LCS, e.g., RocksDB default)**: Each level `Li` is 10x larger than `Li-1` (L1 = 256 MB, L2 = 2.56 GB, etc.) with non-overlapping key ranges from L1 downward. Space amplification is low (~1.1x), and point reads check at most 1 file per level, at the cost of higher write amplification (~10–30x).
- **Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS, e.g., Cassandra default)**: Merges SSTables of similar size when `N` accumulate. Write amplification is low, but space amplification can temporarily reach 2x (requiring 50% free disk headroom).

## B-Tree vs. LSM-Tree comparison

| Metric / Characteristic | B-Tree (Postgres, InnoDB) | LSM-Tree (RocksDB, Cassandra) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Write Path** | Random in-place page updates + WAL | Sequential WAL + MemTable + sequential flush |
| **Write Amplification** | High on random keys (rewrites full 8–16 KB page for 100B row) | Tunable (low in STCS, moderate in LCS) |
| **Read Amplification** | Low & predictable (1 leaf lookup; O(log N)) | Higher on cache miss (MemTable + L0 + L1..Ln, mitigated by Bloom) |
| **Space Amplification** | ~1.3x–1.5x (internal fragmentation, ~67% page fill) | ~1.1x in LCS (~100% packed + Zstd/LZ4 block compression) |
| **Range Scans** | Fast (contiguous leaf pointers) | Slower (merge-iterator across levels + tombstone skipping) |
| **Concurrency Control** | Latch crabbing on tree pages | Lock-free/immutable SSTables; simple MemTable latches |

## Failure modes

- **LSM Write Stalls**: If L0 SSTables pile up faster than compaction can merge them into L1, RocksDB throttles or halts all writes to prevent read amplification from exploding.
- **B-Tree Page-Split Storms**: Bulk-loading out-of-order keys triggers cascading page splits, doubling WAL volume (full-page writes after checkpoints in Postgres) and saturating disk bandwidth.
- **Out-of-Memory Block Cache**: If Bloom filters and index blocks exceed RAM, every LSM `GET` requires extra disk seeks just to read the Bloom filter.
- **Tombstone Read Amplification**: In LSM-Trees, deleting 90% of a key range leaves tombstones that must be scanned until compacted into the bottommost level.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Modern optimizations: Bw-Trees, Prefix Bloom, and Tiered Storage
sections.content:
## Modern optimizations: Bw-Trees, Prefix Bloom, and Tiered Storage

- **Prefix Bloom Filters**: Store a Bloom filter on key prefixes (e.g., `tenant_id`) so short range scans (`WHERE tenant_id = 'acme' AND ts > ...`) can also skip irrelevant SSTables.
- **Composite & Covering Indexes (`INCLUDE`)**: In B-Trees, appending non-key payload columns to leaf pages (`CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (status)`) avoids random heap table lookups.
- **Time-Window Compaction (TWCS)**: Groups time-series SSTables into fixed time buckets (e.g., 1-day windows) and drops expired windows instantly without compaction overhead.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use time-ordered primary keys (UUIDv7, ULID, Snowflake IDs) on B-Tree tables to keep inserts sequential at the right edge.
- [ ] Keep B-Tree composite index columns ordered by equality predicates first, then range predicates (`(tenant_id, created_at)`).
- [ ] Size LSM-Tree RAM so 100% of Bloom filters and index blocks remain pinned in memory.
- [ ] Monitor `l0_num_files`, compaction pending bytes, and tombstone-to-live-row ratios on LSM engines.
- [ ] Leave at least 30–50% free disk headroom on LSM nodes for compaction temporary space.

interviewProblems.title: High-Throughput Financial Time-Series Ledger
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are building a crypto transaction ledger storing 2,000,000 write events per second while supporting point-in-time range queries for balance auditing. How do you design the storage engine indexing strategy?

dimensions.name: Storage Engine Selection
dimensions.description: Choosing LSM-Tree with SSTable compaction for write throughput.

dimensions.name: Bloom Filter Read Optimization
dimensions.description: Using Bloom Filters to prevent unnecessary SSTable disk reads.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Use an LSM-Tree storage engine (RocksDB/Cassandra) for sequential disk write ingestion. Pair each SSTable with an in-memory Bloom Filter to eliminate disk reads for non-existent keys during balance lookups.
commonPitfalls: Using a single B+ Tree PostgreSQL table which locks under 2M writes/sec.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: B-Trees organize sorted keys into fixed-size mutable pages optimized for fast, predictable point and range reads, whereas LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted runs to disk for high write throughput.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: B-Tree Buffer Pool applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Fixed 8-16KB Pages.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Fixed 8-16KB Pages experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Monitor L0 file count and compaction pending bytes; allocate dedicated compaction threads, rate-limit bursts, or use NVMe SSDs with higher sustained write IOPS.

concepts.tagline: Database isolation levels control what concurrent transaction anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew—are permitted in exchange for lower locking or coordination overhead.

spark.summary: Database isolation levels control what concurrent transaction anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew—are permitted in exchange for lower locking or coordination overhead.
spark.keyTakeaway: Read Committed does not prevent lost updates or read skew; Snapshot Isolation prevents read anomalies via MVCC but still allows write skew unless you use explicit `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or true Serializable isolation.

concept.whyItMatters: Most databases default to Read Committed (PostgreSQL, Oracle) or Repeatable Read (MySQL InnoDB), which silently permit race conditions like double-spending, inventory overselling, and broken invariants under concurrent requests—bugs that pass all single-threaded unit tests.
whenToUse: Use Read Committed for high-throughput, independent single-row writes and non-critical reads where slight point-in-time skew is acceptable.
Use Snapshot Isolation / Repeatable Read for consistent multi-table reporting, backups, and read-only analytics without blocking writers.
Use Serializable (SSI or 2PL) or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` when enforcing cross-row invariants (account balances, double-booking prevention, quota limits).
whenNotToUse: Blindly setting global `SERIALIZABLE` on high-contention OLTP workloads without retry logic, which causes high `40001` serialization-failure abort rates.
Using `READ UNCOMMITTED` for any financial, inventory, or user-facing state—dirty reads expose rolled-back data.
Relying on Repeatable Read alone (without row locks) for read-modify-write counters, which suffers from lost updates or write skew.
keyPoints: ANSI SQL anomalies: Dirty Reads (reading uncommitted writes), Non-Repeatable Reads (row changes between reads), and Phantom Reads (new rows match a `WHERE` predicate).

Beyond ANSI: Read Skew (seeing half of a transfer), Lost Updates (two concurrent `x = x + 1` reads), and Write Skew (two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint rows, breaking an invariant).
MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): readers read a consistent snapshot (`xmin/xmax` or HLC timestamp) without blocking writers, and writers don't block readers.
Snapshot Isolation vs. Serializable: Snapshot Isolation eliminates read skew and phantoms, but only Serializable (e.g., Postgres SSI or Spanner 2PL+TrueTime) prevents Write Skew.
Application retry loops are mandatory: optimistic/SSI engines abort conflicting transactions with SQLSTATE `40001` (`serialization_failure`), requiring idempotent client retries.

examples.title: On-Call Doctor Write Skew under Snapshot Isolation
examples.scenario: A hospital scheduling app required at least 1 doctor on call per shift. Under PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation), Alice and Bob both queried `SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE on_call = true` (saw `2`), and each updated their own row to `on_call = false`.
examples.outcome: Because they modified disjoint rows, Snapshot Isolation committed both—leaving 0 doctors on call. Switching the transaction to `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI) detected the rw-antidependency cycle and aborted Bob's commit with `40001`.

examples.title: Flash-Sale Inventory Lost Update under Read Committed
examples.scenario: Two checkout requests read `stock = 1` simultaneously under `READ COMMITTED`, computed `new_stock = 0` in application code, and ran `UPDATE inventory SET stock = 0 WHERE sku = 'X'`—overselling the last item.
examples.outcome: Replacing read-modify-write with an atomic `UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku = 'X' AND stock > 0 RETURNING stock` eliminated the race without escalating isolation.

tradeOffs.factor: Consistency Guarantees vs. Throughput / Abort Rate
tradeOffs.pro: Serializable isolation eliminates all concurrency anomalies, letting engineers reason about transactions as if they ran one-by-one.
tradeOffs.con: High-contention keys trigger frequent `40001` serialization aborts (under SSI) or lock waits (under 2PL), reducing effective throughput.

tradeOffs.pro: Pessimistic `SELECT FOR UPDATE` guarantees the winner finishes without wasted work when contention is high (> 10% conflict rate).
tradeOffs.con: Pessimistic locks hold resources across network round-trips and risk deadlocks; SSI excels when conflicts are rare.

tradeOffs.factor: MVCC Version Retention vs. Garbage Collection
tradeOffs.pro: Readers never block writers on long-running analytical queries.
tradeOffs.con: Long-running `REPEATABLE READ` transactions prevent `VACUUM` / undo-log purge, causing table bloat and OOM.

failureModes.name: Missing Retry Handler for SQLSTATE 40001
failureModes.description: Enabling `SERIALIZABLE` or `REPEATABLE READ` without exponential-backoff retries surfaces raw `could not serialize access` 500 errors to users.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap serializable transactions in an idempotent retry loop (3–5 attempts with jittered backoff) at the repository/DAO layer.

failureModes.name: Write Skew on Disjoint Rows
failureModes.description: Assuming `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation) prevents all race conditions leads to broken cross-row invariants (e.g., double-booking a meeting room).
failureModes.mitigation: Use `SERIALIZABLE` isolation, materialize a parent lock row (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on `rooms`), or use Postgres `EXCLUDE USING gist` constraints.

failureModes.name: Long-Lived Snapshot Bloat
failureModes.description: An idle-in-transaction `REPEATABLE READ` session stays open for 6 hours, blocking MVCC garbage collection across the entire database.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s'` and route long analytical exports to a read replica.

failureModes.name: Deadlock Cascades under 2PL
failureModes.description: Transactions acquire row locks in inconsistent order (`A -> B` and `B -> A`), stalling threads until the deadlock detector aborts one.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce a canonical lock acquisition order (e.g., sort `account_id` ascending before `SELECT FOR UPDATE`).

commonMistakes: Believing PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` allows phantom reads—in Postgres it implements Snapshot Isolation, which actually prevents phantoms, unlike the ANSI minimum.
Confusing MySQL InnoDB's `REPEATABLE READ` (which uses gap locks on `FOR UPDATE` to prevent phantoms, yet still permits write skew on plain `SELECT`s) with `SERIALIZABLE`.
Doing `SELECT balance` -> check in Java/Python -> `UPDATE balance` under `READ COMMITTED` instead of atomic SQL updates or `FOR UPDATE`.
Holding a database transaction open while making an external HTTP/Stripe API call, exhausting connection pools and holding row locks.
Testing concurrency bugs with sequential integration tests instead of parallel stress tests (e.g., Jepsen/Elle or concurrent goroutines).

sections.content:
## The idea

Database isolation (the **I** in ACID) defines how much concurrency side effects one transaction is allowed to observe from others. The 1992 ANSI SQL standard defined four levels—**Read Uncommitted**, **Read Committed**, **Repeatable Read**, and **Serializable**—based on three phenomena (Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, Phantom Read).

However, modern MVCC databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, CockroachDB) exposed critical gaps in the ANSI definitions: **Snapshot Isolation (SI)** prevents all three ANSI anomalies yet still suffers from **Write Skew** (where two concurrent transactions read an overlapping premise and write to disjoint rows, violating a global invariant). Achieving true **Serializability** requires either **Two-Phase Locking (2PL)** or **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **Write Skew** vs. **SSI Detection** on a `rooms(room_id, slot, booking_id)` constraint:

1. **Setup**: Room `101` at `10:00` has 0 bookings. Policy: at most 1 booking per `(room_id, slot)`.
2. **Snapshot Taken**: Tx1 and Tx2 both start under Snapshot Isolation at `T=100`.
3. **Concurrent Reads**: Tx1 queries `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings WHERE room_id=101 AND slot='10:00'` (sees `0`). Tx2 runs the same query (also sees `0`).
4. **Disjoint Writes**: Tx1 inserts `(id=501, room=101, slot='10:00')`. Tx2 inserts `(id=502, room=101, slot='10:00')`. Because `501 != 502`, there is no row-level write-write conflict.
5. **Outcome**:
   - Under **Snapshot Isolation (`REPEATABLE READ` in Postgres)**: Both commit -> **double-booked**!
   - Under **Serializable (`SERIALIZABLE` SSI)**: Postgres tracks `SIREAD` predicate locks on the index range `(101, '10:00')`, detects the dangerous `rw-antidependency` cycle (`Tx1 reads -> Tx2 writes` and `Tx2 reads -> Tx1 writes`), commits Tx1, and aborts Tx2 with `SQLSTATE 40001`.

sections.content:
## How databases implement isolation levels

Two engines claiming the same ANSI level can behave differently:

- **PostgreSQL**: Uses pure MVCC. `READ COMMITTED` takes a fresh snapshot per statement; `REPEATABLE READ` implements **Snapshot Isolation** (one snapshot per transaction, prevents phantoms, allows write skew); `SERIALIZABLE` adds **SSI** (`SIREAD` locks).
- **MySQL InnoDB**: Uses MVCC for plain `SELECT`s and **Next-Key Locks** (record + gap locks) for `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` / `UPDATE`. Plain `REPEATABLE READ` can still exhibit subtle write skew, whereas `SERIALIZABLE` converts every plain `SELECT` into `SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE` (2PL).
- **Distributed SQL (CockroachDB, Spanner)**: CockroachDB defaults directly to `SERIALIZABLE` using Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC), write intents, and timestamp-pushing; Spanner uses 2PL + TrueTime atomic clocks for External Consistency.

## Isolation levels vs. anomalies matrix

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Read Skew | Lost Update | Write Skew |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Read Uncommitted** | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| **Read Committed** (PG Default) | Prevented | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| **Repeatable Read** (InnoDB Default) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented (gap locks on writes) | Prevented | Possible (on plain read-then-write) | Possible |
| **Snapshot Isolation** (PG Repeatable Read) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented (First-Committer-Wins) | Possible |
| **Serializable** (PG SSI / CockroachDB) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

## Failure modes

- **Silent Read Skew in Billing**: Generating a multi-table invoice under `READ COMMITTED` reads `orders` before a concurrent `INSERT` commits and `order_items` after, producing mismatched totals.
- **False-Positive SSI Aborts**: Because `SIREAD` locks operate at page or index-granularity under memory pressure, unrelated transactions on the same index page can trigger unnecessary `40001` aborts.
- **Gap-Lock Deadlocks in MySQL**: Concurrent `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` under InnoDB `REPEATABLE READ` acquires overlapping gap locks, causing frequent deadlock rollbacks (`Error 1213`).
- **Transaction Wraparound / Undo Bloat**: Long-running `REPEATABLE READ` transactions pin old MVCC tuple versions, degrading sequential scan performance.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Choosing the right tool for the invariant
sections.content:
## Choosing the right tool for the invariant

You don't always need global `SERIALIZABLE` isolation to enforce correctness:

1. **Atomic Single-Statement Updates**: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 50` is safe even under `READ COMMITTED`.
2. **Database Constraints**: `UNIQUE` indexes and PostgreSQL `EXCLUDE USING gist` (e.g., non-overlapping booking ranges) enforce invariants at the engine level without application retry loops.
3. **Pessimistic Row/Parent Locking**: Lock a single parent entity (`SELECT * FROM rooms WHERE id = 101 FOR UPDATE`) to serialize concurrent child inserts.
4. **SSI (`SERIALIZABLE`) + Retries**: Best for complex multi-table invariants where locks would be too coarse or deadlock-prone.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Never perform `SELECT` -> compute in app -> `UPDATE` under `READ COMMITTED`; use atomic SQL expressions or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
- [ ] Verify your specific engine's guarantees (e.g., Postgres `REPEATABLE READ` = Snapshot Isolation; CockroachDB = `SERIALIZABLE` by default).
- [ ] Implement an idempotent retry wrapper for `SQLSTATE 40001` (serialization failure) and `40P01` (deadlock).
- [ ] Keep transactions short: never hold a DB transaction open across external HTTP/RPC calls.
- [ ] Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` to protect MVCC garbage collection from abandoned snapshots.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Database isolation levels control what concurrent transaction anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew—are permitted in exchange for lower locking or coordination overhead.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: MVCC Snapshot Engine applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SSI Conflict Detector.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SSI Conflict Detector experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Wrap serializable transactions in an idempotent retry loop (3–5 attempts with jittered backoff) at the repository/DAO layer.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Read Committed does not prevent lost updates or read skew; Snapshot Isolation prevents read anomalies via MVCC but still allows write skew unless you use explicit `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or true Serializable isolation.
Avoid trap: Believing PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` allows phantom reads—in Postgres it implements Snapshot Isolation, which actually prevents phantoms, unlike the ANSI minimum.
Avoid trap: Confusing MySQL InnoDB's `REPEATABLE READ` (which uses gap locks on `FOR UPDATE` to prevent phantoms, yet still permits write skew on plain `SELECT`s) with `SERIALIZABLE`.
When to reach for it: Use Read Committed for high-throughput, independent single-row writes and non-critical reads where slight point-in-time skew is acceptable.
When to reach for it: Use Snapshot Isolation / Repeatable Read for consistent multi-table reporting, backups, and read-only analytics without blocking writers.

concepts.tagline: Horizontally partitioning a dataset across independent database nodes by a shard key—using either contiguous key ranges or consistent hashing—to scale write throughput and storage beyond a single primary's CPU, IOPS, and memory ceiling.

spark.summary: Horizontally partitioning a dataset across independent database nodes by a shard key—using either contiguous key ranges or consistent hashing—to scale write throughput and storage beyond a single primary's CPU, IOPS, and memory ceiling.
spark.keyTakeaway: Range partitioning preserves ordered range scans at the cost of hot-spot risk on monotonic keys; hash partitioning spreads writes evenly at the cost of scatter-gather range queries.

concept.whyItMatters: Vertical scaling hits physical and economic walls around 64–128 vCPUs and NVMe IOPS saturation, while single-primary replication only scales reads, not writes. When a PostgreSQL primary crosses ~15,000–25,000 write TPS or its B-tree indexes exceed RAM, vacuum lag, WAL replication delay, and lock contention degrade p99 latency across every tenant. Sharding splits the write path and working set across autonomous primaries so each node holds a bounded slice of data and indexes.
whenToUse: Write throughput or index working-set size exceeds what the largest single-node primary can sustain without p99 latency spikes or vacuum/compaction stalls.
Data exhibits a natural isolation boundary—such as tenant_id, account_id, or region—so 95%+ of queries can route to a single shard.
Regulatory data residency (e.g., GDPR EU vs. US data) requires physically pinning subsets of rows to geographically separate storage clusters.
whenNotToUse: Read traffic is the sole bottleneck and read replicas, connection pooling (PgBouncer), or Redis caching can absorb the load without splitting the write primary.
Core business workflows rely heavily on multi-row ACID joins, foreign-key constraints, or global secondary index aggregations across arbitrary entities.
Dataset size is under ~2–5 TB and write QPS fits comfortably on a single modern primary, where sharding adds operational complexity without measurable gain.
keyPoints: Range partitioning (used by CockroachDB, TiKV, and HBase) maps contiguous key intervals like [A–F] or [2026-01–2026-03] to shards, enabling fast ordered scans (`WHERE created_at BETWEEN ...`) via a metadata routing table.

Hash partitioning (used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, and Vitess `xxhash`) applies a deterministic hash to the shard key and maps to virtual buckets, eliminating monotonic write hotspots at the expense of scatter-gather range queries.
Choosing the shard key is practically irreversible without a dual-write backfill; a poor key causes either cross-shard fan-out on every read or severe skew where one shard handles 80% of traffic.
Vitess and Citus separate logical shards (keyspace IDs / 1,024–4,096 virtual buckets) from physical database hosts so resharding moves small chunks incrementally rather than rehashing all rows.
Cross-shard transactions require two-phase commit (2PC) or asynchronous Sagas with an outbox table, trading single-node sub-millisecond commits for 2–4x network round-trips or eventual consistency.

examples.title: Multi-tenant SaaS ledger in Vitess on MySQL
examples.scenario: A B2B billing platform reaches 4 TB in a single MySQL 8.0 primary, with `invoices` and `ledger_entries` suffering 400ms p99 write stalls during end-of-month batch runs.
examples.outcome: The team deploys Vitess with `tenant_id` as the primary Vindex (`xxhash` across 64 logical shards on 8 physical MySQL primaries). Single-tenant queries hit one shard in 2ms, while Vitess VReplication resharded hot enterprise tenants onto dedicated shards with <2s cutover downtime.

examples.title: Time-series IoT telemetry with range-split CockroachDB
examples.scenario: An industrial sensor platform ingests 120,000 events/sec keyed by `(device_id, timestamp_utc)`. Pure timestamp range partitioning would hammer the newest range on a single Raft leader.
examples.outcome: Keying ranges by `(device_id, timestamp_utc)` distributes writes across all 24 nodes while keeping each device's time-series contiguous on disk, cutting 7-day range scan latency from 850ms to 35ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Range partitioning executes ordered scans (`BETWEEN`, `ORDER BY`, prefix lookups) on 1–2 shards without scatter-gather.
tradeOffs.con: Monotonic keys (auto-increment IDs, `now()`) concentrate 100% of inserts onto the tail shard unless prefixed with a high-cardinality tenant or hash byte.

tradeOffs.factor: Routing layer (Smart Client vs. Proxy Router)
tradeOffs.pro: Proxy routers (Vitess `vtgate`, Citus coordinator) centralize topology metadata and shield application code from shard splits.
tradeOffs.con: Adds an extra network hop (0.5–2ms) and requires scaling the proxy tier as stateless infrastructure.

tradeOffs.factor: Resharding granularity (Fixed Modulo vs. Virtual Shards)
tradeOffs.pro: Virtual shards / range splits (64 MB chunks in CockroachDB, keyspace intervals in Vitess) move only the affected slice during scale-out.
tradeOffs.con: Requires a distributed metadata service (etcd, ZooKeeper, or Raft) to keep routing maps consistent across clients.

failureModes.name: Tail-shard write hotspot
failureModes.description: Range-partitioned tables keyed by `created_at` or sequential IDs route every new insert to the highest range, saturating one node's CPU and disk while N-1 shards sit idle.
failureModes.mitigation: Prefix the shard key with a high-cardinality attribute (`tenant_id`, `org_id`) or a 2-byte hash prefix, or switch to hash partitioning for write-heavy append logs.

failureModes.name: Scatter-gather tail latency amplification
failureModes.description: Queries missing the shard key fan out to all 32 or 64 shards; if any single shard experiences a GC pause or compaction spike, overall p99 matches the slowest shard.
failureModes.mitigation: Require the shard key in all OLTP query predicates via linter/ORM guards, and maintain an asynchronous projection (e.g., OpenSearch or a secondary lookup table) for cross-shard search.

failureModes.name: Celebrity tenant skew
failureModes.description: Even with `hash(tenant_id)`, one enterprise customer generates 35% of total writes, exhausting IOPS on its assigned physical host.
failureModes.mitigation: Use virtual shards so the heavy tenant's keyspace range can be isolated onto dedicated hardware, or sub-shard the hot tenant with a salted key (`tenant_id#0..7`).

failureModes.name: Split-brain routing metadata
failureModes.description: During a shard split or primary failover, stale routing caches send writes to the old shard owner, causing silent data divergence or failed constraints.
failureModes.mitigation: Use epoch/generation numbers in the routing protocol so the old shard rejects writes with `MOVED` / `RECOVERING` once ownership transfers in etcd or Raft.

commonMistakes: Choosing `hash(user_id)` early when 40% of internal admin and billing queries filter by `merchant_id`, forcing full-cluster scatter-gather on critical paths.
Modulo-hashing directly by physical node count (`id % 8`), which forces a massive full-table reshuffle when expanding from 8 to 12 nodes.
Assuming global auto-increment sequences will remain cheap; centralized sequence generators become a single point of contention unless replaced with UUIDv7, Snowflake IDs, or per-shard hi/lo ranges.
Leaving foreign keys and cross-shard joins in place via application-level N+1 loops instead of colocation (`tenant_id` in every child table) or denormalized read models.
Delaying resharding automation until disk hits 90% full, leaving insufficient headroom for double-buffering snapshots during live chunk migration.

sections.content:
## The idea

Database sharding divides a logical table into horizontally disjoint subsets (shards), each hosted on an independent database primary with its own CPU, buffer pool, WAL, and storage volume. Unlike read replicas—which copy 100% of the data and only offload `SELECT` queries—sharding splits both reads and writes so cluster capacity scales linearly with node count.

Two dominant partitioning functions govern how rows map to shards. **Range partitioning** divides the keyspace into contiguous, non-overlapping intervals (`[0000–3FFF]`, `[4000–7FFF]`) tracked in a sorted range map. **Hash partitioning** applies a uniform hash (such as `xxhash64` or `Murmur3`) to the shard key and maps the digest onto a consistent hash ring or a fixed pool of virtual buckets (e.g., 1,024 vbuckets) assigned to physical primaries.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an orders service handling 40,000 writes/sec across 16 physical PostgreSQL primaries managed via a routing proxy and an etcd metadata store.

1. **Key selection & colocation**: `orders`, `order_items`, and `payments` all carry `merchant_id` as their shard key so an entire checkout's rows live on the same physical shard and commit in a single local ACID transaction.
2. **Routing lookup**: An incoming `INSERT INTO orders (merchant_id, order_id, ...)` hits the stateless router (`vtgate` / Citus coordinator). The router computes `keyspace_id = xxhash64(merchant_id)` and checks its in-memory routing map (cached from etcd with a generation epoch).
3. **Single-shard execution**: The router forwards the query over a persistent PgBouncer pool directly to Shard 11's primary. Latency overhead is ~0.8ms.
4. **Online range split**: When Shard 11 grows past 500 GB, the control plane splits its keyspace `[A000–AFFF]` into `[A000–A7FF]` and `[A800–AFFF]`, streams a consistent snapshot plus WAL/binlog delta to Shard 17, pauses writes on `[A800–AFFF]` for <500ms, updates the etcd epoch, and resumes traffic on Shard 17.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Range vs. Hash vs. Directory partitioning
sections.content:
## Range vs. Hash vs. Directory partitioning

Range partitioning stores a sorted boundary map (e.g., CockroachDB splits ranges at 64 MB by default), which makes prefix and range scans fast because adjacent keys sit together in the same RocksDB/B-tree SSTables. However, sequential keys write to a single tail range unless prefixed by a tenant or hash bucket.

Hash partitioning sacrifices range locality for uniform write distribution. Consistent hashing or virtual buckets (e.g., 256–4,096 vbuckets) ensures that adding a physical node only moves `1/N` of the buckets rather than reshuffling the entire table.

Directory-based (lookup) sharding stores an explicit `entity_id -> shard_id` table in Redis or a small replicated DB. It handles arbitrary per-tenant placement and easy VIP isolation, but every query pays a lookup hop and the directory itself becomes a critical availability dependency.

## Partitioning strategies compared

| Strategy | Write Distribution | Range Scans (`BETWEEN`) | Resharding Cost | Primary Risk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Contiguous Range** | Skewed on monotonic keys | Fast (1–2 shards) | Split/merge 64 MB–1 GB ranges | Tail-shard hotspot |
| **Consistent Hash / Vbuckets** | Uniform across nodes | Scatter-gather (all shards) | Move `1/N` virtual buckets | Cross-shard scan latency |
| **Composite `(tenant, ts)`** | Uniform across tenants | Fast within a tenant | Split hot tenant ranges | Celebrity tenant skew |
| **Directory Lookup** | Fully customizable | Depends on placement | Update directory + migrate | Directory bottleneck/SPOF |

## Failure modes

The most frequent production outage in sharded clusters is **stale routing after a split or failover**. If a client caches an old shard map and writes to the demoted primary before its lease expires, split-brain writes occur. Enforcing fencing tokens (epoch numbers checked on every write at the storage node) eliminates this.

Second is **cross-shard transaction deadlock and 2PC coordinator failure**. If a distributed 2PC coordinator crashes after phase 1 `PREPARE`, participating shards hold row locks indefinitely until a coordinator recovers or an operator manually resolves prepared transactions. Prefer colocation by shard key or asynchronous Sagas over 2PC on high-throughput OLTP paths.

## Operationalizing resharding & global indexes

Live resharding must be zero-downtime: snapshot a consistent LSN/GTID position on the source shard, stream ongoing WAL/binlog changes to the target shard until lag drops under 100ms, briefly fence writes (`READ ONLY` for <1s), flip the metadata epoch, and drop the migrated keyspace from the source.

For queries that cannot include the shard key (e.g., looking up a user by `email` when the table is sharded by `user_id`), maintain an asynchronous global secondary index via Debezium CDC into a separate lookup table sharded by `email`—accepting ~50–200ms eventual consistency in exchange for single-shard read latency.

## Practical checklist

- Verify >90% of OLTP reads and writes include the chosen shard key so scatter-gather stays rare.
- Over-provision logical virtual shards (e.g., 256 or 1,024) from day one even on 4 physical hosts.
- Replace database `SERIAL`/`AUTO_INCREMENT` with UUIDv7 or Snowflake IDs to avoid centralized ID bottlenecks.
- Enforce epoch/fencing-token validation on storage nodes to reject stale-route writes during failovers.
- Rehearse a live shard split in staging under synthetic write load and measure cutover pause duration.
