concepts.name: Heaps & Priority Queues

relationships.description: Dijkstra relies on a min-priority queue.
Top-K is a common coding pattern solved with heaps.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

concepts.tagline: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a contiguous array that maintains the heap-order invariant in O(log n) per update and O(1) for min/max inspection.

spark.summary: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a contiguous array that maintains the heap-order invariant in O(log n) per update and O(1) for min/max inspection.
spark.keyTakeaway: Packing a complete tree into a flat array gives O(log n) priority operations with L1-cache-friendly memory access, making binary and 4-ary heaps faster in practice than theoretically tighter pointer-based heaps.

concept.whyItMatters: Whenever a system needs the smallest or largest element from a changing stream—Dijkstra's shortest path, OS task schedulers, timer wheels, event-driven simulators, or top-k analytics—sorting the whole set on every insert ($O(n \log n)$) is prohibitively slow. A heap gives you $O(1)$ peek and $O(\log n)$ push/pop with zero pointer overhead.
whenToUse: Dynamic top-k / streaming quantiles: keeping the 100 largest elements across 100 million events using a size-k min-heap in $O(n \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ memory.
Graph shortest paths & MSTs (Dijkstra, Prim, A*): repeatedly popping the minimum-distance frontier vertex.
Multi-way external merge sort & LSM-tree compaction: merging k sorted SSTables or log files in $O(n \log k)$ time.
whenNotToUse: You need fast arbitrary search, range queries (`x <= k <= y`), or predecessor/successor lookups—use a balanced BST (B-tree, Red-Black tree) or skip list instead.
The dataset is static and queried once—`quickselect` finds the k-th element in $O(n)$ expected time without maintaining a heap.
Priorities are small bounded integers (e.g., 0–1023 ms timers)—a bucketed hierarchical timing wheel or radix heap gives $O(1)$ amortized operations.
keyPoints: Implicit array layout stores node `i`'s parent at `(i - 1) >> 1` and children at `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`, eliminating 16–24 bytes of left/right/parent pointers per node.
Floyd's bottom-up `heapify` builds a valid heap from an unsorted array in $O(n)$ time (not $O(n \log n)$), because half the nodes are leaves needing 0 swaps and most others sit near the bottom.

Standard heaps (`heapq` in Python, `PriorityQueue` in Java) do not support $O(\log n)$ arbitrary deletion or `decreaseKey`; you either maintain an external `pos[id]` index map (indexed heap) or push duplicate entries and skip stale pops (lazy deletion).

A $d$-ary heap (commonly $d = 4$) flattens tree height from $\log_2 n$ to $\log_4 n$ and aligns child scans within a single 64-byte CPU cache line, outperforming binary heaps on `decreaseKey`-heavy graph workloads.
Heaps are not stable by default: equal-priority items pop in arbitrary order unless you augment the key with a monotonic sequence counter `(priority, seq_id)`.

examples.title: Streaming Top-K heavy hitters in log aggregation
examples.scenario: An observability pipeline ingests 500,000 request-latency records per second and needs the 50 slowest endpoints over a 1-minute window (30M events) within a strict 10 MB memory budget.
examples.outcome: Using a fixed-capacity min-heap of size 50, each incoming event is compared against `heap[0]` in $O(1)$. Over 99.9% of events are smaller and discarded immediately; only larger ones trigger `heapreplace` in $O(\log 50) \approx 6$ comparisons, keeping memory under 4 KB.

examples.title: Lazy deletion vs. indexed heap in Dijkstra on road networks
examples.scenario: A routing engine computes shortest paths on a 20M-edge road graph where vertices are relaxed multiple times.
examples.outcome: With an indexed 4-ary heap (`pos[nodeId]`), `decreaseKey` updates the vertex in-place in $O(\log_4 V)$ without inflating heap size. When memory is plentiful, lazy deletion (pushing `(new_dist, node)` and ignoring pops where `dist > best_dist[node]`) avoids maintaining `pos[]` and is simpler to vectorize.

tradeOffs.pro: Indexed heaps keep heap size strictly $\le V$ and support true $O(\log n)$ `decreaseKey` and arbitrary removal.
tradeOffs.con: Requires a parallel `pos[id]` hash map or array updated on every swap, increasing constant-factor overhead and code complexity.

tradeOffs.pro: Cuts tree height in half (faster `siftUp` on `decreaseKey`) and fits 4 children into one 64-byte L1 cache line.
tradeOffs.con: `siftDown` during `pop` must compare $d$ children per level instead of 2, making `pop` slightly slower if comparisons are expensive (e.g., string keys).

tradeOffs.pro: Contiguous array layout gives predictable cache prefetching and 3–5x faster wall-clock time on real hardware.
tradeOffs.con: Fibonacci heaps offer $O(1)$ amortized `decreaseKey` theoretically, but pointer chasing causes L2/L3 cache misses and high memory overhead.

failureModes.name: Mutating priority keys in-place
failureModes.description: Code modifies an object's `priority` field after pushing it into `PriorityQueue` or `heapq`, silently corrupting the heap invariant so `pop()` returns non-minimum elements.
failureModes.mitigation: Treat heap keys as immutable; use an indexed heap `updateKey(id, newPriority)` method or push a new tuple and mark the old entry stale.

failureModes.name: Integer overflow in comparator subtraction
failureModes.description: A Java/C++ comparator written as `(a, b) -> a.score - b.score` overflows signed 32-bit `int` when comparing `INT_MIN` and positive numbers, flipping sort order.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use `Integer.compare(a.score, b.score)` or explicit `<` / `>` comparisons.

failureModes.name: Memory blowup with lazy deletion
failureModes.description: In dense graphs with frequent priority updates, lazy deletion leaves millions of stale entries inside the heap, degrading `pop()` to $O(\log E)$ and exhausting RAM.
failureModes.mitigation: Switch to an indexed heap when $|E| \gg |V|$, or compact/rebuild the heap in $O(n)$ whenever `stale_count > active_count`.

failureModes.name: Starvation from unstable priority ties
failureModes.description: Jobs with identical priority (e.g., `priority = 0`) are popped in heap-swap order rather than FIFO, starving older tasks.
failureModes.mitigation: Include a monotonic insertion counter `(priority, seq_id, payload)` so ties break deterministically in FIFO order.

commonMistakes: Building a heap by calling `heappush` $n$ times ($O(n \log n)$) instead of `heapify` ($O(n)$) when all elements are known upfront.
Calling `remove(obj)` on Java's `PriorityQueue` inside a hot loop without realizing it performs an $O(n)$ linear scan.
Using a max-heap when solving top-k largest elements instead of a size-k min-heap (which lets you discard small items in $O(1)$).
Confusing `heap[1..k]` in array order with sorted order—only `heap[0]` is guaranteed to be the extremum; reading the rest sorted requires $k$ pops.
Forgetting thread safety: `heapq` and `PriorityQueue` are not thread-safe; concurrent producers/consumers need a lock or `PriorityBlockingQueue`.

sections.content:
## The idea

A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree—every level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right—satisfying the **heap-order property**: in a min-heap, every parent's key is less than or equal to its children's keys (`A[parent(i)] <= A[i]`).

Because the tree is complete, it needs no node objects or pointers. Storing it level-by-level in a flat 0-indexed array maps tree navigation to cheap bit shifts: `parent(i) = (i - 1) >> 1`, `left(i) = (i << 1) + 1`, and `right(i) = (i << 1) + 2`. Every modification restores the invariant with one of two loops: **`siftUp`** (bubble a newly inserted or decreased key toward the root) or **`siftDown`** (sink a replaced root toward the leaves by swapping with its smaller child).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **Floyd's $O(n)$ `heapify`** followed by a `pop` on `[40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 5]`:

1. **Bottom-up `heapify`**: Start at the last non-leaf index `n // 2 - 1 = 2` (`30`) and `siftDown` backward to index `0`:
   - `i = 2` (`30`): child `5` (`5`) is smaller -> swap -> `[40, 10, 5, 50, 20, 30]`.
   - `i = 1` (`10`): children `50`, `20` are both `>= 10` -> no swap.
   - `i = 0` (`40`): smaller child is `i = 2` (`5`) -> swap `40` and `5` -> `[5, 10, 40, 50, 20, 30]`; continue sinking `40` at `i = 2` against child `i = 5` (`30`) -> swap -> **`[5, 10, 30, 50, 20, 40]`**.
2. **`popMin()`**:
   - Save `min = A[0]` (`5`). Move last element `A[5]` (`40`) to `A[0]` and shrink length to 5: `[40, 10, 30, 50, 20]`.
   - `siftDown(0)`: `40` compares children `10` and `30`, swaps with `10` -> `[10, 40, 30, 50, 20]`; at `i = 1`, `40` compares children `50` and `20`, swaps with `20` -> **`[10, 20, 30, 50, 40]`**.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Why Floyd's heapify is O(n) and d-ary heaps win on cache
sections.content:
## Why Floyd's heapify is O(n) and d-ary heaps win on cache

Building a heap by inserting $n$ items one by one takes $\sum_{i=1}^n \log i = \Theta(n \log n)$ in the worst case because each new item starts at the bottom and may `siftUp` to the root. **Floyd's `heapify`** flips the direction: it runs `siftDown` from `n/2 - 1` down to `0`. At height $h$, there are at most $\lceil n / 2^{h+1} \rceil$ nodes, and each sinks at most $h$ levels. Summing over all heights gives $n \sum_{h=1}^{\infty} h / 2^{h+1} = n$ comparisons—strictly $O(n)$.

In modern CPUs, pointer-heavy structures like Fibonacci heaps suffer L2/L3 cache misses (~10–60 ns per miss). A **4-ary heap** (`parent = (i - 1) >> 2`, `first_child = (i << 2) + 1`) packs all 4 children of a node into adjacent memory (16–32 bytes), fitting inside a single **64-byte L1 cache line**. It halves tree depth compared to a binary heap, cutting `decreaseKey` swaps by 50%.

## Priority queue implementation trade-offs

| Variant | `push` | `popMin` | `decreaseKey` | Memory / Cache |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Binary Heap** | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\log n)$ | $O(n)$ without index; $O(\log n)$ indexed | 1 contiguous array; best for general use |
| **4-ary Heap** | $O(\log_4 n)$ | $O(4 \log_4 n)$ | $O(\log_4 n)$ indexed | 4 children fit in 1 cache line; faster in Dijkstra |
| **Lazy-Delete Binary** | $O(\log E)$ | $O(\log E)$ amortized | $O(\log E)$ (push duplicate) | Simpler code; bloats to $O(E)$ entries |
| **Fibonacci Heap** | $O(1)$ | $O(\log n)$ amortized | $O(1)$ amortized | Heavy pointers; poor L1/L2 cache locality |
| **Balanced BST (TreeSet)** | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\log n)$ (remove + insert) | Supports range queries; ~3x higher RAM per node |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded heap growth in streaming top-k**: Using a max-heap of size $n$ and calling `pop()` $k$ times wastes $O(n)$ memory; always invert the comparator to a fixed-size-$k$ min-heap so memory stays $O(k)$.
- **Non-transitive or NaN comparators**: Pushing IEEE-754 `NaN` floats into a heap breaks total ordering (`NaN < x` and `x < NaN` are both `false`), permanently trapping elements in wrong subtrees.
- **Stale index corruption in indexed heaps**: Forgetting to update `pos[id]` on *both* elements during a swap (or deleting an item from `pos` before swapping it to the end) causes out-of-bounds panics.
- **Comparator allocation pressure**: In Python (`heapq`), custom key functions aren't supported directly; wrapping every item in a new tuple or wrapper object on every push creates GC churn in tight loops.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Practical variants: two-heap median & indexed timers
sections.content:
## Practical variants: two-heap median & indexed timers

Two-heap tracking maintains a **running median** in $O(\log n)$ per insert and $O(1)$ query: a max-heap stores the lower half of numbers and a min-heap stores the upper half, rebalancing whenever their sizes differ by more than 1.

For **system timers and schedulers** (e.g., Go's runtime network poller, which uses a **4-ary min-heap** for `time.Timer`), an indexed heap lets `timer.Reset()` or `timer.Stop()` adjust deadlines in $O(\log_4 n)$ without leaving expired timers clogging the queue.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use `heapify` ($O(n)$) instead of repeated `push` ($O(n \log n)$) when initializing from a batch.
- [ ] For top-$k$ largest items, use a **min-heap** capped at size $k$ (and a max-heap for top-$k$ smallest).
- [ ] Add a monotonic sequence number `(priority, seq, item)` whenever equal-priority items require FIFO stability.
- [ ] Reject or sanitize `NaN` keys before insertion to preserve total ordering.
- [ ] Choose an indexed 4-ary heap over lazy deletion when `decreaseKey` frequency exceeds `pop` frequency (e.g., dense graphs or timer resets).

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Heap Priority Queue Algorithms

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a contiguous array that maintains the heap-order invariant in O(log n) per update and O(1) for min/max inspection.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Contiguous Heap Array applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SiftUp / SiftDown Engine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SiftUp / SiftDown Engine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Treat heap keys as immutable; use an indexed heap `updateKey(id, newPriority)` method or push a new tuple and mark the old entry stale.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Packing a complete tree into a flat array gives O(log n) priority operations with L1-cache-friendly memory access, making binary and 4-ary heaps faster in practice than theoretically tighter pointer-based heaps.
Avoid trap: Building a heap by calling `heappush` $n$ times ($O(n \log n)$) instead of `heapify` ($O(n)$) when all elements are known upfront.
Avoid trap: Calling `remove(obj)` on Java's `PriorityQueue` inside a hot loop without realizing it performs an $O(n)$ linear scan.
When to reach for it: Dynamic top-k / streaming quantiles: keeping the 100 largest elements across 100 million events using a size-k min-heap in $O(n \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ memory.
When to reach for it: Graph shortest paths & MSTs (Dijkstra, Prim, A*): repeatedly popping the minimum-distance frontier vertex.

putItTogether.outcome: Using a fixed-capacity min-heap of size 50, each incoming event is compared against `heap[0]` in $O(1)$. Over 99.9% of events are smaller and discarded immediately; only larger ones trigger `heapreplace` in $O(\log 50) \approx 6$ comparisons, keeping memory under 4 KB.

concepts.name: Helm Chart Releases

relationships.description: Connects Helm Chart Releases to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned charts and tracks each deployment as an immutable, numbered release revision stored in-cluster for repeatable upgrades and rollbacks.

spark.summary: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned charts and tracks each deployment as an immutable, numbered release revision stored in-cluster for repeatable upgrades and rollbacks.
spark.keyTakeaway: Helm's value lies in atomic, revision-tracked releases (`--atomic --wait`) and parameterized reuse—treat rendered manifests as immutable build outputs and never mix manual `kubectl edit` into Helm-managed resources.

concept.whyItMatters: Deploying a microservice to Kubernetes touches 6–15 YAML objects (`Deployment`, `Service`, `Ingress`, `HPA`, `ServiceAccount`, `ConfigMap`, `PodDisruptionBudget`). Copy-pasting YAML across dev, staging, and prod drifts immediately. Helm renders Go templates against layered `values.yaml` overrides, applies them in dependency order, waits for readiness probes, and stores compressed release snapshots (`sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<N>`) so a broken deploy can roll back in one command.
whenToUse: Packaging third-party infrastructure (ingress-nginx, Prometheus, cert-manager, Kafka operators) distributed as OCI or HTTP Helm repositories.
Standardizing internal microservice deployments across dozens of teams via a shared library or golden base chart.
Needing one-command atomic upgrades (`helm upgrade --install --atomic`) with pre/post-upgrade hooks (e.g., DB schema migrations) and instant revision rollback.
whenNotToUse: Simple, single-team apps with 2–3 static manifests where plain Kustomize overlays avoid Go-template string-escaping headaches.
GitOps pipelines where Argo CD or Flux must see every rendered Kubernetes resource in Git before applying—use `helm template` in CI rather than running `helm upgrade` imperatively.
Managing stateful multi-step day-2 operations (failover, backup/restore, shard rebalancing) better handled by a custom Kubernetes Operator.
keyPoints: `Chart.yaml` separates the chart's own SemVer `version` (template changes) from `appVersion` (the container image tag deployed).
Values merge left-to-right with increasing precedence: chart `values.yaml` < parent chart values < `-f env.yaml` (later files win) < `--set` / `--set-string` flags.
Helm v3 stores each release revision as a gzipped, base64-encoded JSON blob inside a Kubernetes `Secret` (`sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<rev>`) in the release namespace.
Lifecycle hooks (`pre-install`, `post-upgrade`, `pre-rollback`) run Kubernetes `Job`s or `Pod`s outside normal release ownership unless given `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy`.
Helm v3.8+ supports OCI registries (`oci://ghcr.io/org/chart`) natively, unifying container image and chart signing/distribution via Cosign and SBOMs.

examples.title: Atomic canary-safe upgrade with DB migration hook
examples.scenario: A payments API rolls out `v2.4.0` requiring an additive PostgreSQL migration before new pods start serving traffic.
examples.outcome: A `Job` annotated with `helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade` and `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded` runs the migration first. `helm upgrade payments oci://registry/payments --version 2.4.0 --atomic --wait --timeout 5m` pauses; if the new `Deployment` pods fail readiness within 5 minutes, Helm automatically rolls back to revision `v11`.

examples.title: Avoiding 1 MiB etcd Secret limit on large umbrella charts
examples.scenario: A platform team bundles 18 microservices and large ConfigMaps into a single umbrella chart, causing `helm upgrade` to fail with `Secret "sh.helm.release.v1.core.v42" is invalid: data: Too long: must have at most 1048576 bytes`.
examples.outcome: They split the umbrella into per-service releases, set `--history-max 10` to prune old revisions, and move multi-megabyte static assets out of `ConfigMap` templates.

tradeOffs.pro: Helm supports loops, conditionals, helper partials (`_helpers.tpl`), and typed schema validation (`values.schema.json`).
tradeOffs.con: Whitespace-sensitive YAML inside Go templates (`{{- ... | nindent 8 }}`) is hard to read and debug compared to Kustomize's strategic-merge patches.

tradeOffs.pro: `helm upgrade --atomic` handles hooks, readiness waits, and automatic rollback directly from CI.
tradeOffs.con: CI pipelines need cluster kubeconfig access, and drift from manual `kubectl` edits goes unnoticed unless a GitOps controller reconciles continuously.

tradeOffs.pro: One command stands up an entire environment with shared global values.
tradeOffs.con: Couples failure domains: one broken subchart blocks the whole release and risks hitting Kubernetes' 1 MiB etcd Secret size limit.

failureModes.name: Stuck `pending-upgrade` release lock
failureModes.description: A CI runner is killed mid-deploy, leaving the latest Secret in `status: pending-upgrade`. Every subsequent `helm upgrade` fails with `another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress`.
failureModes.mitigation: Run `helm rollback <release> <last-deployed-rev>` (or `helm history` to verify the last `deployed` revision) rather than deleting the Secret manually.

failureModes.name: Implicit type coercion with `--set`
failureModes.description: Passing `--set image.tag=123456` or `--set app.id=1e5` makes Helm parse the value as a float64 (`1.23456e+05`), breaking container image pulls or pod env vars.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use `--set-string`, quote values in `-f values.yaml`, and enforce types with `values.schema.json`.

failureModes.name: Orphaned hook Jobs blocking re-deploys
failureModes.description: A `pre-upgrade` Job without `hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation` already exists on the second upgrade, failing with `jobs.batch "migrate" already exists`.
failureModes.mitigation: Include `"helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded` on all hook resources and give Jobs immutable or revision-suffixed names (`{{ .Release.Revision }}`).

failureModes.name: Manual `kubectl edit` drift overwritten silently
failureModes.description: An on-call engineer patches `replicas: 10` via `kubectl scale`, and the next `helm upgrade` resets `replicas` back to `3` from `values.yaml`.
failureModes.mitigation: Run `helm diff upgrade` in CI before applying, omit `replicas` from the Deployment template when an HPA manages scaling, and restrict production `kubectl` write RBAC.

commonMistakes: Leaving `--history-max` at `10` or unlimited without checking Secret count, or conversely setting it to `0` (infinite) and bloating etcd.
Hardcoding `replicas` inside `Deployment` when a `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` is enabled, causing Helm upgrades to reset autoscaled replica counts.
Using `helm upgrade --force` routinely—`--force` deletes and recreates resources (causing downtime on `Service` or `PVC` immutability errors) instead of patching.
Modifying `values.yaml` without running `helm lint` and `helm template` in CI, letting broken indentation reach the cluster.
Storing plaintext database passwords in `values.yaml` inside Git instead of referencing External Secrets / Sealed Secrets.

sections.content:
## The idea

Helm is a **package manager and release state machine** for Kubernetes. A **chart** is a directory (or `.tgz` / OCI artifact) containing `Chart.yaml` metadata, `values.yaml` defaults, optional `values.schema.json`, and Go `text/template` files under `templates/`.

When you run `helm upgrade --install`, Helm does not just pipe YAML to `kubectl apply`. It merges values, renders templates deterministically, diffs the desired manifests against the **previous release revision** stored in-cluster, computes a 3-way strategic merge patch, executes ordered lifecycle hooks, waits for workload readiness, and writes a new immutable revision record (`v1`, `v2`, `v3`...).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace `helm upgrade --install orders oci://ghcr.io/acme/orders --version 1.8.2 -f prod.yaml --set-string image.tag=a3f9c12 --atomic --wait --timeout 5m`:

1. **Pull & Validate**: Helm pulls the OCI chart artifact, verifies its `values.schema.json` against the merged values (`values.yaml` + `prod.yaml` + `--set-string`), and renders `templates/*.yaml` locally.
2. **Lock Revision (`pending-upgrade`)**: Helm reads `sh.helm.release.v1.orders.v7` from the target namespace, computes the diff, and writes `v8` with `status: pending-upgrade`.
3. **Pre-Upgrade Hooks**: Any resource tagged `helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade` (sorted by `helm.sh/hook-weight`, e.g., `-5` before `0`) is created and watched until completion.
4. **Apply & Wait**: Helm applies updated `ConfigMap`, `Service`, and `Deployment` manifests. With `--wait`, it polls the Kubernetes API until all new `Deployment` pods pass `readinessProbe`.
5. **Commit or Atomic Rollback**: If all pods become Ready within `5m`, Helm updates `v8` to `status: deployed` and marks `v7` as `superseded`. If a pod `CrashLoopBackOff`s past `5m`, `--atomic` automatically triggers a rollback to `v7` and exits non-zero in CI.

data.title: Helm atomic upgrade and revision state machine

edges.label: Pull chart + verify
edges.title: Fetch immutable chart
edges.description: Pulls versioned chart archive from OCI registry and validates `values.schema.json`.

edges.label: Read v7 + write v8 (pending)
edges.title: Create pending revision
edges.description: Diffs rendered manifests against `v7` and persists `v8` as `pending-upgrade`.

edges.label: Run pre-upgrade hooks
edges.title: Execute ordered hooks
edges.description: Runs `pre-upgrade` Jobs (e.g., DB migrations) sorted by `hook-weight`.

edges.label: Apply manifests + --wait
edges.title: Patch workloads & poll readiness
edges.description: Applies `Deployment`/`Service` patches and waits up to `--timeout` for Ready pods.

edges.label: Commit deployed / rollback
edges.title: Finalize revision state
edges.description: Marks `v8` `deployed` (and `v7` `superseded`), or `--atomic` reverts to `v7` on failure.

data.caption: Helm tracks every release revision in-cluster as a compressed Secret, enabling deterministic 3-way diffs and automatic rollback on failed readiness checks.

sections.content:
## Values precedence, hooks & checksum annotations

A classic Kubernetes pitfall occurs when you update a `ConfigMap`, run `helm upgrade`, and existing pods keep running with stale configuration because the `Deployment` pod spec didn't change. Helm solves this cleanly via a **template checksum annotation**:

```yaml
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
```

Whenever `configmap.yaml` renders differently, the `checksum/config` SHA-256 changes, triggering a rolling restart of the `Deployment`. Similarly, `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` protects stateful resources (like `PersistentVolumeClaim`s or `Namespace`s) from deletion during `helm uninstall`.

## Kubernetes packaging & deployment comparison

| Aspect | Helm (`helm upgrade`) | Kustomize (`kubectl apply -k`) | GitOps + Helm (Argo CD) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Parameterization** | Go templates + `values.yaml` + JSON Schema | Overlay patches (`patchesStrategicMerge`) | Helm `values` rendered by controller |
| **Revision tracking** | In-cluster Secrets (`v1`, `v2`, ...) | None natively (relies on Git history) | Git commit SHA + Argo sync history |
| **Lifecycle hooks** | Native (`pre-upgrade`, `post-install`) | None (external CI scripts) | Maps Helm hooks to Argo Sync Waves |
| **Drift detection** | Only on `helm diff` / next upgrade | Only on `kubectl diff` | Continuous reconciliation loop |
| **Atomic rollback** | Built-in `--atomic --wait` | Manual `git revert` + re-apply | Automated self-heal / manual rollback |

## Failure modes

- **1 MiB Secret overflow**: Storing large files or 50+ historical revisions in `sh.helm.release.v1.*` hits etcd's 1 MiB object limit. Cap `--history-max 10` and keep large payloads in object storage.
- **Helm + Argo CD hook impedance mismatch**: If you use Argo CD to deploy Helm charts, Argo runs `helm template` and translates `helm.sh/hook` into `argocd.argoproj.io/hook`, but `pre-rollback` hooks are not executed by Argo CD.
- **Race conditions on CRDs**: Helm's `crds/` directory installs CRDs once on `helm install` and **never upgrades or deletes them** on `helm upgrade` to avoid wiping custom resources. Manage CRD upgrades in a dedicated chart or pre-sync step.
- **Non-deterministic `lookup` or `randAlphaNum` functions**: Using `randAlphaNum` inside a `Secret` template regenerates a new password on *every* `helm upgrade`, breaking running apps. Use `lookup` to preserve existing values or manage secrets externally.

## Chart testing, OCI distribution & security

Treat charts like application code. Run `helm lint --strict`, `helm template` piped into `kubeconform` (verifying against the target Kubernetes API version, e.g., `1.30.0`), and `helm unittest` for template logic before publishing.

Publish charts as **OCI artifacts** (`helm package` -> `helm push app-1.8.2.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts`), sign them with `cosign sign`, and pin exact chart versions in production pipelines rather than floating ranges (`^1.8.0`).

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Add `values.schema.json` to catch missing required keys or wrong types at render time.
- [ ] Always deploy with `--atomic --wait --timeout <duration> --history-max 10` in imperative CI.
- [ ] Add `checksum/config` and `checksum/secret` annotations to pod templates so config edits trigger rolling restarts.
- [ ] Omit `replicas` from `Deployment` templates whenever an `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` is active.
- [ ] Set `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded` on all hook `Job`s.
- [ ] Validate rendered YAML with `helm lint` and `kubeconform` in CI, and use `helm diff` before production upgrades.

interviewProblems.title: Helm Chart Releases
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Helm Chart Releases. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned charts and tracks each deployment as an immutable, numbered release revision stored in-cluster for repeatable upgrades and rollbacks.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Kubernetes API Server applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Release Secrets (etcd).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Release Secrets (etcd) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Run `helm rollback <release> <last-deployed-rev>` (or `helm history` to verify the last `deployed` revision) rather than deleting the Secret manually.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Helm's value lies in atomic, revision-tracked releases (`--atomic --wait`) and parameterized reuse—treat rendered manifests as immutable build outputs and never mix manual `kubectl edit` into Helm-managed resources.
Avoid trap: Leaving `--history-max` at `10` or unlimited without checking Secret count, or conversely setting it to `0` (infinite) and bloating etcd.
Avoid trap: Hardcoding `replicas` inside `Deployment` when a `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` is enabled, causing Helm upgrades to reset autoscaled replica counts.
When to reach for it: Packaging third-party infrastructure (ingress-nginx, Prometheus, cert-manager, Kafka operators) distributed as OCI or HTTP Helm repositories.
When to reach for it: Standardizing internal microservice deployments across dozens of teams via a shared library or golden base chart.

putItTogether.title: Putting Helm Chart Releases Together
putItTogether.summary: Helm's value lies in atomic, revision-tracked releases (`--atomic --wait`) and parameterized reuse—treat rendered manifests as immutable build outputs and never mix manual `kubectl edit` into Helm-managed resources.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Helm Chart Releases before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: A `Job` annotated with `helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade` and `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded` runs the migration first. `helm upgrade payments oci://registry/payments --version 2.4.0 --atomic --wait --timeout 5m` pauses; if the new `Deployment` pods fail readiness within 5 minutes, Helm automatically rolls back to revision `v11`.

concepts.name: Hexagonal Architecture

relationships.description: Connects Hexagonal Architecture to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.

spark.summary: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.
spark.keyTakeaway: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.

concept.whyItMatters: In traditional layered architectures (`Controller -> Service -> Repository -> DB`), business rules inevitably leak framework annotations (`@Entity`, `@Transactional`, HTTP status codes) and SQL row shapes. When you need to support a Kafka consumer alongside REST, swap Stripe for Adyen, or migrate from DynamoDB to Postgres, every service method breaks. Hexagonal Architecture places the domain model at the center with zero external imports, forcing all I/O to translate at the edge.
whenToUse: Core business domains with complex invariants (billing, order state machines, risk scoring, ledger accounting) that outlive web frameworks and databases.
Systems with multiple entry points (REST API, gRPC, CLI, Kafka consumer) driving the exact same use cases.
Teams that want fast, deterministic unit tests for 90% of business rules without spinning up Docker/Testcontainers on every save.
whenNotToUse: Thin CRUD microservices or admin back-offices with almost no domain logic beyond validating JSON and writing rows.
Data-intensive ETL or reporting pipelines where SQL window functions and bulk set operations *are* the business logic; forcing them through domain objects kills performance.
Early-stage prototypes or hackathons where speed of iteration matters more than 5-year maintainability.
keyPoints: Driving (Primary) Ports are interfaces exposed *by* the application core (e.g., `PlaceOrderUseCase`), invoked by Driving Adapters (REST controller, gRPC handler, Kafka listener).
Driven (Secondary) Ports are interfaces defined *by* the core for what it needs (e.g., `OrderRepository`, `PaymentGateway`), implemented by Driven Adapters (Postgres, Stripe, in-memory fakes).

The Dependency Rule is strict and one-way: source-code imports only point inward (`adapters -> application -> domain`). The domain package has zero imports from Spring, FastAPI, Hibernate, or AWS SDKs.
Adapters own their own DTOs and ORM models (`OrderEntity`, `StripeChargeResponse`) and map them to/from pure domain entities (`Order`, `Money`) at the boundary.
Architectural fitness functions (ArchUnit in Java, `import-linter` in Python, `depguard` in Go) enforce the boundary automatically in CI so convenience imports don't erode it over time.

examples.title: Multi-channel order placement (REST + Kafka)
examples.scenario: An e-commerce checkout service accepts synchronous orders via `POST /v1/orders` and asynchronous subscription renewals from a `billing.renewals` Kafka topic.
examples.outcome: Both the Spring `OrderRestController` and `RenewalKafkaConsumer` (driving adapters) call the same `PlaceOrderPort.execute(PlaceOrderCommand)` use case. Validation, inventory reservation, and idempotency rules live once in the core, and swapping Postgres for an in-memory `FakeOrderRepository` lets the test suite run 400 domain tests in 120 ms.

examples.title: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) for a legacy ERP
examples.scenario: A modern fulfillment service must query a 15-year-old SOAP ERP that uses cryptic 3-letter status codes (`X9`, `P2`) and nullable XML strings.
examples.outcome: The `ErpInventoryAdapter` implements the clean `StockLookupPort` interface and translates `X9` -> `StockStatus.BACKORDERED` inside the adapter. No legacy ERP terminology ever enters the fulfillment domain model.

tradeOffs.pro: Domain logic is 100% decoupled from frameworks, enabling sub-second in-memory tests and painless major framework upgrades.
tradeOffs.con: Requires extra interfaces, mappers, and package structure—creating boilerplate for simple pass-through operations.

tradeOffs.pro: ORM lazy-loading bugs, JSON serialization quirks, and DB column renames stay trapped inside adapters.
tradeOffs.con: Converting `OrderEntity <-> Order <-> OrderResponseDto` adds repetitive mapping code and minor allocation overhead on high-throughput paths.

tradeOffs.pro: Core use cases stay explicit about consistency boundaries (e.g., via a `UnitOfWork` port).
tradeOffs.con: Without care, hiding persistence behind a `Repository` port can accidentally split one logical unit of work into multiple autocommit queries.

failureModes.name: Leaky ORM abstractions
failureModes.description: Putting `@Entity`, `@Column`, or SQLAlchemy `Base` directly on domain classes so `OrderRepository` returns framework-tracked proxies, causing `LazyInitializationException` in the domain.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep domain models as plain POJOs/dataclasses/structs and map from separate ORM entities inside the persistence adapter.

failureModes.name: Anemic pass-through boilerplate
failureModes.description: Every single `GET /users/{id}` query is wrapped in a `GetUserPort`, `GetUserUseCase`, `UserReadRepository`, and 4 identical DTOs with zero logic.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply CQRS pragmatically: use full Hexagonal ports for commands/writes with invariants, and allow thin read-only query handlers to project directly from the DB.

failureModes.name: Boundary erosion via shared utility imports
failureModes.description: A developer imports `org.springframework.http.HttpStatus` or `sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError` inside a domain service for convenience.
failureModes.mitigation: Add an automated CI check (ArchUnit / `import-linter` / Go `depguard`) that fails the build if `domain` imports any adapter or framework package.

failureModes.name: Mock-heavy tests drifting from real SQL behavior
failureModes.description: All tests run against an in-memory `HashMap` fake repository, passing in CI while production fails on a Postgres unique constraint or `NULL` handling.
failureModes.mitigation: Run a shared **contract test suite** against both the in-memory fake (every save) and the real Postgres/Kafka adapter via Testcontainers (in CI).

commonMistakes: Putting business logic inside driving adapters (controllers) or driven adapters (SQL queries / stored procedures) instead of the domain.
Naming ports after the technology (`PostgresOrderPort`, `KafkaEventPort`) instead of the domain intent (`OrderRepository`, `OrderEventPublisher`).
Returning HTTP status codes or framework exceptions from use cases instead of domain-specific result types or exceptions.
Splitting a single transaction across two repository calls without a `UnitOfWork` / transaction boundary port.
Enforcing 1-to-1 interface-per-class ceremony everywhere instead of reserving ports for genuine I/O boundaries.

sections.content:
## The idea

Proposed by Alistair Cockburn in 2005, **Hexagonal Architecture** (formally **Ports and Adapters**) reframes an application from a vertical stack (`UI -> Logic -> DB`) into an **inside/outside** symmetry. The **inside** (the hexagon) contains only pure domain entities, value objects, and application use cases. The **outside** contains every external actor: web browsers, gRPC callers, cron jobs, relational databases, Redis caches, and third-party webhooks.

Nothing outside touches the inside directly. Instead, the core defines **Ports** (technology-agnostic interfaces): **Driving Ports** on the left (what the app *offers*) and **Driven Ports** on the right (what the app *needs*). **Adapters** live strictly outside the hexagon, translating external protocols (HTTP JSON, SQL rows, Protobuf) into domain calls and back.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `TransferFunds` use case in a banking service:

1. **Driving Adapter (`RestTransferController`)**: Receives `POST /v1/transfers` with `{ "from": "acc_1", "to": "acc_2", "cents": 5000 }`, validates HTTP headers/JWT, maps JSON into a `TransferCommand`, and calls the driving port `TransferFundsPort.execute(cmd)`.
2. **Application Core (`TransferFundsService`)**: Runs inside a `UnitOfWork` port. It loads `Account` aggregates via the driven port `AccountRepository.findById(...)`, calls `fromAccount.debit(Money.usd(5000))` and `toAccount.credit(...)` (enforcing overdraft invariants in pure domain code), saves both accounts, and emits `FundsTransferredEvent` through `DomainEventPublisher`.
3. **Driven Adapters**:
   - `PostgresAccountAdapter` implements `AccountRepository`, mapping `Account` domain objects to `accounts_tbl` rows via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
   - `OutboxEventAdapter` implements `DomainEventPublisher`, writing the event to an `outbox` table in the same SQL transaction.
4. **Unit Test Swap**: In `TransferFundsTest`, `PostgresAccountAdapter` is replaced with `InMemoryAccountRepository`. Zero Spring context, zero Docker, and zero network calls—testing overdraft rules and double-entry balance invariants in < 1 ms.

data.title: Ports & Adapters dependency inversion flow

edges.label: Calls Driving Port
edges.title: Translate external input
edges.description: REST or Kafka adapter converts JSON/bytes into a `Command` and invokes the driving port.

edges.label: Enforce invariants
edges.title: Execute pure domain logic
edges.description: Domain entities validate business rules with zero framework or DB imports.

edges.label: Invokes Repository Port
edges.title: Dependency-inverted persistence
edges.description: Core calls `AccountRepository` interface; Postgres adapter implements it and maps rows.

edges.label: Invokes Gateway / Event Port
edges.title: Emit events or call external APIs
edges.description: Core calls `PaymentGateway` or `EventPublisher` port; adapter handles HTTP/ACL.

edges.label: Returns Domain Result
edges.title: Map outcome to protocol
edges.description: Driving adapter maps domain result or error to HTTP 201/422 or Kafka ack.

data.caption: All source-code dependencies point inward toward the hexagon; driven adapters implement interfaces owned by the core via Dependency Inversion.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Driving vs. driven ports and transaction boundaries
sections.content:
## Driving vs. driven ports and transaction boundaries

A frequent point of confusion is **who owns the interface**. In Hexagonal Architecture, the **core owns both**:

- **Driving Ports** (e.g., `PlaceOrderUseCase`) are *implemented by* the application service and *called by* controllers or CLI runners.
- **Driven Ports** (e.g., `OrderRepository`) are *called by* the application service and *implemented by* infrastructure adapters.

Because the core cannot import `@Transactional` without violating the dependency rule, model atomicity explicitly using a **`TransactionPort`** (or `UnitOfWork` closure: `tx.run(() -> { ... })`) implemented by the persistence adapter, or keep `@Transactional` in a thin application-wiring layer outside the pure domain entities.

## Architecture pattern comparison

| Dimension | Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) | Traditional 3-Tier Layered | Clean / Onion Architecture |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dependency direction** | Outside -> Inside (via DIP) | Top -> Down (`Controller -> Service -> DB`) | Outer rings -> Inner rings (concentric) |
| **Primary boundary** | Inside (Core) vs. Outside (I/O) | Horizontal technical layers | Enterprise rules -> App rules -> Adapters |
| **Domain isolation** | Zero framework/DB imports | ORM `@Entity` often shared across all tiers | Zero framework/DB imports |
| **Test speed** | < 1 ms per use case with fakes | Slow (often requires DB/Spring test context) | < 1 ms per use case with fakes |
| **Best fit** | Long-lived domain services, multi-channel I/O | Simple CRUD APIs, rapid prototypes | Large enterprise domains with strict layering |

## Failure modes

- **God-port proliferation**: Defining a single `DatabasePort` with 40 methods forces every test fake to stub 40 methods. Keep driven ports small and cohesive (Interface Segregation Principle, e.g., `OrderReader`, `OrderWriter`).
- **Adapter logic creep**: Putting discount calculations inside a REST controller or eligibility filters inside a SQL `WHERE` clause splits business truth across tiers.
- **Fake-vs-Prod divergence**: In-memory fakes that don't enforce unique keys, transaction isolation, or pagination sorting create false confidence. Always pair fakes with a shared **Repository Contract Test** run against real Postgres in CI.
- **Over-mapping simple reads**: Running complex read dashboards through aggregate hydration (`N` entities + mappers) causes severe latency; bypass domain aggregates for read-only CQRS projections.

## Enforcing boundaries with fitness functions

Architecture diagrams rot unless automated tests enforce them. Add a build-time dependency check in CI:

- **Java / Kotlin**: Use **ArchUnit** (`noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..adapter..", "org.springframework..", "jakarta.persistence..")`).
- **Python**: Use **`import-linter`** contracts (`type = forbidden`) forbidding `domain` from importing `fastapi`, `sqlalchemy`, or `boto3`.
- **Go**: Place `domain` in an internal package and enforce import rules with **`depguard`** in `golangci-lint`.

Pair this with a **contract test suite**: an abstract test class verifying `save()`, `findById()`, optimistic locking, and not-found behavior, executed against both `InMemoryOrderRepo` and `TestcontainersPostgresOrderRepo`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify `domain` and `application` packages have zero imports from web frameworks, ORMs, or cloud SDKs.
- [ ] Name ports after domain capabilities (`PaymentGateway`, `OrderRepository`), not vendor implementations (`StripeClient`, `PostgresRepo`).
- [ ] Keep ORM entities and JSON DTOs inside `adapter` packages and map them explicitly at the boundary.
- [ ] Enforce package dependency rules automatically in CI using ArchUnit, `import-linter`, or `depguard`.
- [ ] Run a shared contract test suite against both in-memory fakes (fast unit loop) and real Testcontainers adapters (CI).
- [ ] Use thin read-only query projections (CQRS) for complex reporting endpoints instead of forcing them through domain aggregates.

interviewProblems.title: Hexagonal Architecture
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Hexagonal Architecture. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Driven DB Adapter applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Driven External Adapter.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Driven External Adapter experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Keep domain models as plain POJOs/dataclasses/structs and map from separate ORM entities inside the persistence adapter.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.
Avoid trap: Putting business logic inside driving adapters (controllers) or driven adapters (SQL queries / stored procedures) instead of the domain.
Avoid trap: Naming ports after the technology (`PostgresOrderPort`, `KafkaEventPort`) instead of the domain intent (`OrderRepository`, `OrderEventPublisher`).
When to reach for it: Core business domains with complex invariants (billing, order state machines, risk scoring, ledger accounting) that outlive web frameworks and databases.
When to reach for it: Systems with multiple entry points (REST API, gRPC, CLI, Kafka consumer) driving the exact same use cases.

putItTogether.title: Putting Hexagonal Architecture Together
putItTogether.summary: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Hexagonal Architecture before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Both the Spring `OrderRestController` and `RenewalKafkaConsumer` (driving adapters) call the same `PlaceOrderPort.execute(PlaceOrderCommand)` use case. Validation, inventory reservation, and idempotency rules live once in the core, and swapping Postgres for an in-memory `FakeOrderRepository` lets the test suite run 400 domain tests in 120 ms.

concepts.name: Hinted Handoff & Repair

relationships.description: Connects Hinted Handoff & Repair to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Hinted handoff buffers writes on healthy coordinator nodes when a target replica is temporarily unreachable, while read repair and anti-entropy Merkle-tree repair reconcile silent divergence over time.

spark.summary: Hinted handoff buffers writes on healthy coordinator nodes when a target replica is temporarily unreachable, while read repair and anti-entropy Merkle-tree repair reconcile silent divergence over time.
spark.keyTakeaway: Hinted handoff preserves write availability during brief outages (minutes to a few hours), not durability guarantees; you still need read repair and scheduled anti-entropy repair to prevent zombie data and silent entropy.

concept.whyItMatters: In leaderless or dynamo-style stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak, DynamoDB-style quorums), nodes restart, suffer GC pauses, or experience transient network partitions daily. Without hinted handoff, a single downed replica drops write availability for consistency levels like ANY or forces coordinators to fail writes; without read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy, replicas permanently drift out of sync and resurrected nodes can serve stale values or reintroduce deleted rows (tombstone zombies).
whenToUse: High-availability AP/tunable-consistency clusters (e.g., Cassandra with RF=3, CL=LOCAL_ONE or LOCAL_QUORUM) where brief node restarts (5–30 minutes) must not stall writes.
Geo-distributed or multi-AZ deployments experiencing transient cross-AZ packet loss where coordinators can buffer hints locally until peers recover.
Workloads with skewed read/write ratios where background anti-entropy (nodetool repair) and probabilistic read repair close consistency gaps without blocking the write path.
whenNotToUse: Strictly linearizable systems (e.g., etcd/Raft or Spanner Paxos) where unacknowledged writes to a minority cannot be buffered as hints on non-owning nodes without violating consensus.
Extended replica outages exceeding max_hint_window_in_ms (typically 3 hours in Cassandra); storing hints longer risks coordinator disk exhaustion and replay storms.
Write-heavy workloads running near coordinator disk IOPS or heap limits, where hint serialization and replay compete directly with live mutations.
keyPoints: Hints are stored on the coordinator (or a designated proxy) as (target_host_id, mutation, timestamp) and are NOT counted toward quorum acknowledgments like LOCAL_QUORUM—only ConsistencyLevel.ANY counts a hint as a successful write.
Bounded hint windows (e.g., Cassandra's max_hint_window_in_ms = 10800000 ms / 3 hours) prevent unbounded disk growth when a node is permanently dead rather than transiently flapping.
Read repair runs synchronously (blocking on digest mismatches when CL > ONE) or asynchronously in the background, reconciling only the specific keys that are actively read.

Anti-entropy repair uses Merkle trees—hierarchical cryptographic hashes over token ranges—to pinpoint divergent sub-ranges between replicas in O(log N) tree traversal without streaming entire SSTables.

Tombstone retention (gc_grace_seconds, default 10 days in Cassandra) must exceed the anti-entropy repair interval; otherwise a down node can miss a delete tombstone and resurrect deleted data upon recovery.

examples.title: Rolling Kernel Patch on a 12-Node Cassandra Cluster
examples.scenario: An SRE team performs a rolling OS patch across 12 Cassandra nodes (RF=3, writes at LOCAL_QUORUM). Each node is drained and rebooted for 8 minutes. During each 8-minute window, coordinators buffer mutations destined for the rebooting node in /var/lib/cassandra/hints at ~4,500 hints/sec (~2.16M hints total per node reboot).
examples.outcome: Writes continue with zero client errors at p99 = 6.2 ms. Once the patched node rejoins via Gossip, coordinators throttle hint replay at hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (1024 KB/s per node), draining the 8-minute backlog in ~11 minutes without triggering full-range Merkle-tree repairs.

examples.title: Silent Bit-Rot and Cold-Key Divergence Resolved by Incremental Repair
examples.scenario: A ScyllaDB cluster stores 40 TB of IoT telemetry where 70% of partitions are write-once and rarely read after 24 hours. A network switch flap drops 0.4% of async replica writes over 6 hours—too brief to trip alerts, and cold keys never trigger read repair.
examples.outcome: Weekly incremental anti-entropy repair exchanges 32-level Merkle trees per vnode token range, isolating the 160 GB of divergent sub-ranges and streaming only the mismatched SSTable blocks rather than transferring all 40 TB.

tradeOffs.factor: Write Availability vs. Coordinator Disk & Replay Pressure
tradeOffs.pro: Coordinators absorb mutations during transient peer outages, keeping write success rates near 100% even when a replica is down.
tradeOffs.con: Hints consume local coordinator disk, JVM/memory buffers, and network bandwidth during replay, risking cascading latency spikes when multiple nodes recover simultaneously.

tradeOffs.factor: Read Repair vs. Read Tail Latency
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronously repairs hot keys on the fly when CL >= QUORUM, keeping frequently accessed records convergent without waiting for scheduled repairs.
tradeOffs.con: Requires digest requests to all replicas (or R+1) and extra round-trips on mismatch, inflating p99 read latency by 1.5x–3x during replica divergence.

tradeOffs.factor: Full Merkle-Tree Repair vs. Cluster CPU/I/O Overhead
tradeOffs.pro: Guarantees eventual consistency even for cold, never-read keys and ensures tombstones propagate before gc_grace_seconds expires.
tradeOffs.con: Building Merkle trees requires full SSTable scans and compaction/streaming I/O; poorly throttled repairs can double disk utilization and starve foreground queries.

failureModes.name: Hint Replay Storm
failureModes.description: A node returns after a 2.5-hour outage while 20 coordinators each hold gigabytes of queued hints. Unthrottled parallel replay saturates the recovering node's NIC, memtables, and compaction threads, causing it to fail health checks and flap.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap max_hint_window_in_ms (e.g., 1–3 hours), enforce hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (e.g., 1024 KB/s divided across active peers), and pause hint delivery if the target's pending compaction queue exceeds threshold.

failureModes.name: Zombie Data Resurrection
failureModes.description: A replica stays offline longer than gc_grace_seconds (e.g., 10 days). Healthy replicas purge expired delete tombstones via compaction. When the offline node returns—or a stale hint arrives—the pre-delete value reappears because the tombstone is gone.
failureModes.mitigation: Run anti-entropy repair strictly within gc_grace_seconds (e.g., every 3–5 days for a 10-day grace period), and never re-add a node that has been down longer than gc_grace_seconds without wiping and bootstrapping it fresh.

failureModes.name: Hint Disk Exhaustion on Coordinators
failureModes.description: During a prolonged AZ isolation, coordinators accumulate hints for an entire unreachable rack until /var/lib/cassandra/hints fills the root or data volume, crashing healthy coordinators.
failureModes.mitigation: Mount hints on a dedicated volume or enforce max_hints_file_size_in_mb and total hint disk caps; disable hinted handoff for cross-DC links when WAN links are saturated.

failureModes.name: Merkle-Tree Over-Streaming (Coarse Granularity)
failureModes.description: With a fixed-depth Merkle tree (e.g., depth 15 = 32,768 leaves) over a multi-terabyte token range, a single divergent key forces streaming an entire leaf bucket of tens of megabytes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use virtual nodes (vnodes) or sub-range repair (e.g., Cassandra Reaper) to keep per-repair token ranges small, and enable incremental repair so already-repaired SSTables are excluded from future tree builds.

commonMistakes: Assuming hinted handoff satisfies LOCAL_QUORUM—hints do NOT count as quorum acks; only ConsistencyLevel.ANY accepts a hint as a write success.
Disabling scheduled nodetool repair because hinted handoff and read repair are enabled, leaving cold keys permanently inconsistent and tombstones unpropagated.
Setting gc_grace_seconds shorter than the actual repair cycle, guaranteeing deleted records will resurrect as zombies after a node outage.
Running full-cluster repairs simultaneously on all nodes instead of staggering sub-range repairs with tools like Cassandra Reaper, triggering cluster-wide compaction storms.
Replacing a dead node with a new node using the same IP without running `nodetool assassinate` or proper bootstrap, causing coordinators to replay stale hints onto an empty ring slot.

sections.content:
## The idea

Distributed databases without a single leader (Dynamo, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak) decouple write availability from strict replica liveness. When a client writes a key with replication factor `RF=3`, the coordinator routes the mutation to all three owning replicas in parallel. If Replica C is temporarily unreachable—due to a 90-second GC pause, a rolling restart, or a top-of-rack switch flap—the coordinator cannot immediately deliver the mutation to C.

**Hinted handoff** solves the short-term gap: the coordinator writes a *hint* to its own local disk containing the target node's UUID, the mutation payload, and the original write timestamp. Once Gossip signals that Replica C is back online, the coordinator streams the queued hints to C in the background. Crucially, hinted handoff is a best-effort optimization for transient outages, not a durability guarantee: if the coordinator itself dies before replaying the hint, or if Replica C stays down past `max_hint_window_in_ms` (default 3 hours), the hint is dropped.

**Read repair** and **anti-entropy repair** close the remaining consistency gaps. Read repair compares data or SHA-256/MD5 digests across replicas during live reads and patches stale replicas with the newest timestamped value. Anti-entropy repair runs offline on a schedule, building **Merkle trees** over token ranges so replicas exchange compact tree hashes and stream only the mismatched key ranges—ensuring even cold, never-read data converges and delete tombstones propagate before `gc_grace_seconds` expires.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a 6-node Cassandra cluster (`RF=3`, `CL=LOCAL_QUORUM`, `max_hint_window_in_ms=10800000`) handling an e-commerce inventory update `UPDATE stock SET qty = 42 WHERE sku = 'SKU-901'` at timestamp `t = 1731430000000000` (microseconds).

1. **Write & Hint Capture**: The client sends the write to Coordinator `N1`. Consistent hashing maps `'SKU-901'` to replicas `N2`, `N4`, and `N5`. `N2` and `N4` acknowledge within 2.1 ms, satisfying `LOCAL_QUORUM` (2 of 3). `N5` is rebooting, so its TCP socket refuses connections. Because `N5` has been down for less than 3 hours, `N1` appends the mutation to `/var/lib/cassandra/hints/N5-uuid-1731430000.hints` and returns `200 OK` to the client.
2. **Hint Replay on Recovery**: Four minutes later, `N5` finishes rebooting and announces `STATUS=NORMAL` via Gossip. `N1` detects the state transition, opens its hint file for `N5`, and streams the buffered mutations at `1024 KB/s`. `N5` applies the write using Last-Write-Wins (LWW) timestamp `1731430000000000`, and `N1` deletes the hint segment once acknowledged.
3. **Read Repair on Mismatch**: Suppose a second write `qty = 41` at `t + 5s` suffered a dropped packet to `N4` while `N1`'s hint buffer was briefly disabled. Later, a client reads `'SKU-901'` at `LOCAL_QUORUM`: `N1` requests the full row from `N2` and a 32-byte digest from `N4`. The digests mismatch (`N2` has `qty=41`, `N4` has `qty=42`). `N1` fetches the full row from `N4`, resolves LWW (`t + 5s` wins), returns `qty=41` to the client, and issues a blocking read-repair mutation to `N4`.
4. **Anti-Entropy Merkle Repair**: Every 4 days (well inside the 10-day `gc_grace_seconds`), Cassandra Reaper triggers an incremental repair on token range `[0x4000, 0x4FFF]`. `N2`, `N4`, and `N5` each compute a depth-15 Merkle tree over unrepaired SSTables in that range (~1 MB each), exchange the root and branch hashes, find 3 divergent leaf buckets out of 32,768, and stream only those ~18 MB of missing rows.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / How hinted handoff, read repair, and Merkle repair complement each other
sections.content:
## How hinted handoff, read repair, and Merkle repair complement each other

No single repair mechanism is sufficient on its own in an AP/tunable-consistency store:

- **Hinted handoff** is *write-triggered* and *push-based*. It has near-zero impact on read latency and handles 95%+ of routine rolling restarts and brief network blips. However, it fails if the coordinator crashes before replay or if the outage outlives `max_hint_window_in_ms`.
- **Read repair** is *read-triggered* and *lazy*. Using digest requests (comparing hashes rather than full payloads across replicas), it catches divergence on hot keys without scheduling overhead. Yet cold keys—such as archived orders or historical logs—are never read and therefore never repaired by read repair.
- **Anti-entropy repair** is *schedule-triggered* and *exhaustive*. By hashing token sub-ranges into Merkle trees, replicas detect every divergent key—hot or cold—including missing delete tombstones. Its cost is background disk I/O and network streaming, which is why modern deployments use **incremental repair** (marking already-repaired SSTables) and **sub-range orchestration** (splitting a 256-vnode ring into thousands of small tasks) to bound cluster impact.

## Repair mechanism comparison

| Mechanism | Trigger | Scope | Latency Impact | Primary Failure Gap |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hinted Handoff** | Write fails to reach a replica | Missed writes within `max_hint_window` (e.g., 3h) | Adds coordinator disk append (~0.2 ms); zero read impact | Lost if coordinator dies or outage > hint window |
| **Blocking Read Repair** | Read digest mismatch (`CL > ONE`) | Actively read keys only | Inflates p99 read latency (extra RTT + mutation) | Never repairs cold, unread keys |
| **Background Read Repair** | Probabilistic or async mismatch | Actively read keys only | None on foreground read response | Eventual only; can lag under high load |
| **Full / Incremental Merkle Repair** | Scheduled cron / Reaper (every 3–7d) | Entire token range (hot + cold + tombstones) | High background CPU, disk scan, and streaming I/O | Can cause compaction storms if unthrottled |

## Failure modes

- **Tombstone resurrection (Zombie data)**: If a node is offline for 12 days while `gc_grace_seconds` is 10 days (864,000 s), healthy nodes compact away delete tombstones on Day 11. When the offline node returns on Day 12, its pre-delete SSTables still hold the deleted row—and anti-entropy repair treats that row as *missing* on the healthy nodes, propagating the deleted data back across the entire cluster.
- **Hint replay storm & GC/compaction collapse**: When a node recovers after 2.9 hours of downtime in a 10,000 writes/sec cluster, 20 coordinators may simultaneously flush ~5 GB of hints. Without `hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb`, the recovering node's memtables flush thousands of tiny SSTables, triggering an L0 compaction backlog and OOMs.
- **Coordinator disk saturation**: Storing hints on the same NVMe volume as live SSTables means a multi-hour rack outage can fill the disk to 100%, halting all writes on healthy coordinators.
- **Merkle-tree validation memory spikes**: Computing deep Merkle trees across wide partitions or uncompacted SSTables allocates significant off-heap/heap buffers and random IOPS, degrading foreground p99 latency.

## Tuning parameters & operational math

Three formulas govern safe operation in Cassandra/ScyllaDB-class systems:

1. **Hint Disk Budget**: `Peak_Hint_Bytes = Write_Rate_Bytes_Per_Sec * (RF - 1) * Outage_Hours * 3600 / Healthy_Coordinators`. At 20 MB/s cluster ingest (`RF=3`) and 1 downed node out of 12 for 3 hours, coordinators accumulate `~39 GB` per coordinator (~470 GB total) if all writes miss that replica—requiring explicit `max_hints_directory_size` caps.
2. **Replay Drain Time**: `Drain_Seconds = Total_Hint_KB / (Throttle_KB_Per_Sec * Active_Coordinators_Targeting_Node)`. Remember Cassandra's `hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb` is divided by the number of *all* nodes in the cluster or per-coordinator depending on version—verify throughput via `nodetool netstats`.
3. **Tombstone Safety Invariant**: Always enforce `Repair_Cycle + Max_Repair_Duration + Outage_Detection_Buffer < gc_grace_seconds`. With `gc_grace_seconds = 864000` (10 days), target a complete incremental repair every 3–4 days.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Set `max_hint_window_in_ms` to 3 hours (10800000 ms) or less; never rely on hints for multi-day outages.
- [ ] Place `/var/lib/cassandra/hints` on a dedicated volume or configure a hard disk-space cap so hints cannot starve SSTables.
- [ ] Schedule automated sub-range incremental repairs (e.g., Cassandra Reaper) to complete every 3–5 days, strictly below `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days).
- [ ] Throttle hint replay (`hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb`) and repair streaming (`stream_throughput_outbound_megabits_per_sec`) based on 30% of available NIC/disk headroom.
- [ ] Monitor `HintedHandoff` pending counts, `ReadRepair` rates, and `Compaction` pending tasks; alert if any repair cycle misses its `gc_grace_seconds` deadline.
- [ ] Wipe and re-bootstrap any node that has been offline longer than `gc_grace_seconds` instead of rejoining it directly.
