interviewProblems.title: Hinted Handoff & Repair
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Hinted Handoff & Repair. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Hinted handoff buffers writes on healthy coordinator nodes when a target replica is temporarily unreachable, while read repair and anti-entropy Merkle-tree repair reconcile silent divergence over time.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Replicas N2 & N4 applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Replica N5.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Replica N5 experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap max_hint_window_in_ms (e.g., 1–3 hours), enforce hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (e.g., 1024 KB/s divided across active peers), and pause hint delivery if the target's pending compaction queue exceeds threshold.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Hinted handoff preserves write availability during brief outages (minutes to a few hours), not durability guarantees; you still need read repair and scheduled anti-entropy repair to prevent zombie data and silent entropy.
Avoid trap: Assuming hinted handoff satisfies LOCAL_QUORUM—hints do NOT count as quorum acks; only ConsistencyLevel.ANY accepts a hint as a write success.
Avoid trap: Disabling scheduled nodetool repair because hinted handoff and read repair are enabled, leaving cold keys permanently inconsistent and tombstones unpropagated.
When to reach for it: High-availability AP/tunable-consistency clusters (e.g., Cassandra with RF=3, CL=LOCAL_ONE or LOCAL_QUORUM) where brief node restarts (5–30 minutes) must not stall writes.
When to reach for it: Geo-distributed or multi-AZ deployments experiencing transient cross-AZ packet loss where coordinators can buffer hints locally until peers recover.

putItTogether.title: Putting Hinted Handoff Repair Together
putItTogether.summary: Hinted handoff preserves write availability during brief outages (minutes to a few hours), not durability guarantees; you still need read repair and scheduled anti-entropy repair to prevent zombie data and silent entropy.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Hinted Handoff Repair before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Writes continue with zero client errors at p99 = 6.2 ms. Once the patched node rejoins via Gossip, coordinators throttle hint replay at hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (1024 KB/s per node), draining the 8-minute backlog in ~11 minutes without triggering full-range Merkle-tree repairs.

concepts.name: HTTP Semantics & Caching

relationships.description: Connects HTTP Semantics & Caching to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: HTTP caching (RFC 9111) uses explicit freshness lifetimes, validation headers (ETag/Last-Modified), and Vary keys so browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies serve safe, fast responses without stale leaks.

spark.summary: HTTP caching (RFC 9111) uses explicit freshness lifetimes, validation headers (ETag/Last-Modified), and Vary keys so browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies serve safe, fast responses without stale leaks.
spark.keyTakeaway: Separate immutable static assets (Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable) from dynamic APIs (Cache-Control: no-cache + ETag revalidation), and use Vary carefully so you never fragment cache hit ratios or leak user-specific responses.

concept.whyItMatters: Every uncached request that hits an origin server pays full TLS/origin compute, database I/O, and cross-region RTT (50–250 ms). Properly configured HTTP caching offloads 70–95% of traffic to edge CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront) and browser caches, cutting p95 latency under 15 ms. Conversely, a single misconfigured Cache-Control or missing Vary header can cache authenticated PII on a shared CDN and serve User A's account page to User B.
whenToUse: Content-hashed static assets (JS, CSS, fonts, images) where filenames change on every build, enabling 1-year immutable caching.
Public or semi-static read APIs (catalogs, feature flags, product pages) where 10–60 second edge TTLs plus stale-while-revalidate absorb traffic spikes.
Large payloads (JSON schemas, media manifests) where ETag / If-None-Match conditional requests turn 500 KB downloads into 300-byte 304 Not Modified responses.
whenNotToUse: Personalized, authenticated, or financial endpoints unless explicitly marked Cache-Control: private, no-store (or private, max-age=0, must-revalidate).
Real-time transactional state (live inventory counts, payment status) where even a 2-second stale read breaks business invariants.
Non-idempotent or state-mutating methods (POST, PUT, DELETE), which RFC 9111 forbids standard caches from serving without explicit invalidation.
keyPoints: Cache-Control directives govern storage and freshness: `no-store` forbids all caching; `no-cache` allows storage but mandates origin revalidation before every reuse; `private` restricts storage to the browser, blocking shared CDNs.

Freshness lifetime is computed from `s-maxage` (shared caches only) -> `max-age` -> `Expires`, compared against the response `Age` header; `stale-while-revalidate` lets caches serve slightly expired content while refreshing asynchronously.
Conditional validation uses strong/weak `ETag` (`If-None-Match`) or `Last-Modified` (`If-Modified-Since`) to return `304 Not Modified` without resending the response body.

The `Vary` header defines secondary cache keys (e.g., `Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language`); `Vary: User-Agent` or `Vary: Cookie` destroys CDN cache hit ratios by creating thousands of distinct keys.

Unsafe methods (`POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`) must invalidate matching cached URI entries on compliant caches, while `GET` and `HEAD` are safe and cacheable by default when freshness headers are present.

examples.title: Immutable Asset Hashing + Stale-While-Revalidate on a Retail Storefront
examples.scenario: A storefront serves `app.8f3c2a.js` (420 KB) and `/api/v1/catalog/featured` (65 KB JSON, updated every 5 minutes) behind Fastly.
examples.outcome: Static bundles carry `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, yielding a 99.4% browser/CDN hit rate and zero 304 round-trips. The catalog endpoint returns `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` with a strong `ETag`, keeping edge p99 latency at 12 ms while masking origin 502 blips.

examples.title: Preventing Cross-User Cache Poisoning on an Authenticated BFF
examples.scenario: An engineering team places Cloudflare in front of `/api/me/profile`, which authenticates via a session cookie and omits `Cache-Control`. A misconfigured CDN page rule caches all 200 OK responses for 5 minutes.
examples.outcome: By enforcing `Cache-Control: private, no-store` on all authenticated routes and `Vary: Authorization` where token-scoped responses are edge-cached, the team eliminates PII leakage while keeping public `/pricing` pages cached at 96% hit ratio.

tradeOffs.factor: Long TTLs vs. Instant Content Updates
tradeOffs.pro: Maximizes edge offload (95%+) and shields origins from thundering herds.
tradeOffs.con: Requires content-hashed filenames or active purge APIs (e.g., Cloudflare/Fastly surrogate-key purges) to retract bad deploys.

tradeOffs.pro: `no-cache` with `ETag` saves bandwidth via `304 Not Modified` while guaranteeing freshness on every request.
tradeOffs.con: Still incurs a full network round-trip to the origin (or shielding POP) to validate the ETag on every load.

tradeOffs.factor: Granular Vary Headers vs. Cache Hit Ratio
tradeOffs.pro: Prevents serving compressed gzip bytes to non-gzip clients or wrong-language pages.
tradeOffs.con: Every unique value combination of `Vary` headers multiplies cache keys; `Vary: *` or `Vary: User-Agent` collapses hit rates toward 0%.

failureModes.name: Authenticated PII Cache Leak
failureModes.description: An endpoint returns user-specific data with `Cache-Control: public` or no `Cache-Control` header behind a permissive CDN rule, causing the shared cache to serve one user's data to subsequent visitors.
failureModes.mitigation: Default all authenticated API middleware to `Cache-Control: private, no-store` and add automated CI/gateway assertions that block `public` or `s-maxage` when `Set-Cookie` or `Authorization` is present.

failureModes.name: Cache Key Explosion via Unbounded Vary
failureModes.description: Returning `Vary: User-Agent` or `Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept` splits a single popular URL into tens of thousands of cache variants across Chrome/Safari/Firefox minor versions.
failureModes.mitigation: Normalize `Accept-Encoding` at the CDN edge to `{gzip, br, identity}` and strip `Vary: User-Agent` in favor of responsive CSS or normalized device-class headers.

failureModes.name: Thundering Herd on Synchronized TTL Expiry
failureModes.description: A hot endpoint with `s-maxage=60` expires simultaneously across 50 edge POPs, sending 50x–500x concurrent origin requests that overwhelm database connections.
failureModes.mitigation: Combine `s-maxage=60` with `stale-while-revalidate=120` and `stale-if-error=600`, plus request coalescing (collapsed forwarding) at the reverse proxy/CDN.

failureModes.name: Misunderstanding no-cache vs. no-store
failureModes.description: Developers set `Cache-Control: no-cache` expecting sensitive medical or financial payloads never to be written to disk, unaware that browsers still store the response locally and merely revalidate it.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `Cache-Control: no-store` for sensitive data that must never touch disk or shared memory, and reserve `no-cache` for payloads that should be cached but revalidated.

commonMistakes: Confusing `no-cache` (store, but revalidate before reuse) with `no-store` (do not store anywhere).
Omitting `immutable` on fingerprinted static assets, causing browsers on manual reload (F5) to fire unnecessary `If-None-Match` revalidation bursts.
Setting both `Expires` and `Cache-Control` with conflicting values, forgetting that `Cache-Control: max-age` / `s-maxage` always overrides `Expires` per RFC 9111.
Returning weak ETags (`W/"abc"`) for byte-range requests (`Range: bytes=0-1023`), which RFC 9110 forbids for `206 Partial Content` coalescing.
Using `Vary: Cookie` on public marketing pages because an analytics cookie is present, reducing CDN cache hit rate to near zero.

sections.content:
## The idea

HTTP is not merely a transport framing protocol—**RFC 9110** (Semantics) and **RFC 9111** (Caching) encode a distributed caching contract directly into request and response headers. Every intermediary—browser cache, corporate proxy, Varnish/Nginx reverse proxy, and global CDN—reads the same headers to answer two questions: *Can I store this response?* and *Can I reuse it without asking the origin?*

**Storage rules** come from `Cache-Control`: `no-store` forbids persistence; `private` allows only single-user browser caches; `public` permits shared caches. **Freshness rules** compare a response's calculated lifetime (`s-maxage` for shared caches, else `max-age`, else `Expires - Date`) against its `Age`. While `Age < lifetime`, the response is *fresh* and served directly from cache in 1–15 ms.

Once `Age >= lifetime` (or if `no-cache` was specified), the entry becomes *stale*. Rather than discarding it, the cache sends a **conditional request** (`If-None-Match: "v42"` or `If-Modified-Since`) to the origin. If the resource has not changed, the origin replies `304 Not Modified` with an empty body and refreshed headers, resetting freshness without transferring megabytes of payload.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a product catalog request `GET /v1/products/42` with `Accept-Encoding: br` traversing a Browser -> Cloudflare Edge POP -> Origin API (Node/Go + Postgres):

1. **Cold Cache Miss (`t = 0s`)**: The browser has no entry. Cloudflare hashes the primary key `(GET, https://api.example.com/v1/products/42)` and misses. It forwards the request to Origin. Origin queries Postgres (18 ms) and responds `200 OK` with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=15, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=120`, `ETag: "9d4f2a"`, and `Vary: Accept-Encoding`.
2. **Shared & Private Storage**: Cloudflare stores the Brotli-compressed body keyed by `(URL, Accept-Encoding=br)` with a 60-second shared TTL. The browser stores it for 15 seconds (`max-age=15`).
3. **Fresh Edge Hit (`t = 25s`)**: A second user in the same city requests `/v1/products/42`. Cloudflare sees `Age: 25 < s-maxage: 60` and returns `200 OK` in 9 ms—Origin sees zero traffic.
4. **Stale-While-Revalidate (`t = 75s`)**: Another user arrives at `t = 75s`. The 60s `s-maxage` has expired, but `75s < 60s + 120s` (`stale-while-revalidate`). Cloudflare immediately serves the stale cached response in 9 ms while asynchronously sending `GET /v1/products/42` with `If-None-Match: "9d4f2a"` to Origin.
5. **304 Revalidation**: Origin checks the row version, sees it is still `"9d4f2a"`, and returns `304 Not Modified` (no body, 220 bytes of headers). Cloudflare resets `Age: 0` for another 60 seconds.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Cache keys, Vary, and surrogate keys
sections.content:
## Cache keys, Vary, and surrogate keys

By default, an HTTP cache keys entries by `(HTTP Method, Scheme, Host, Path + Query)`. Two subtle mechanisms control key cardinality and invalidation:

- **`Vary` (Secondary Cache Keys)**: When an origin returns `Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language`, the cache stores separate variants per header value tuple. Avoid `Vary: User-Agent` or `Vary: Cookie`—a single popular endpoint can fracture into 50,000+ cold keys. If you must vary on auth or device type, normalize at the edge into a coarse header (e.g., `X-Device-Class: mobile|desktop`).
- **`Surrogate-Key` / `Cache-Tag`**: URL-based purging fails when a single product update affects `/products/42`, `/category/shoes`, and `/search?q=running`. CDNs like Fastly and Cloudflare support `Surrogate-Key: product-42 cat-shoes` (stripped before reaching the browser), enabling O(1) tag-based invalidation across thousands of cached URLs simultaneously while keeping `s-maxage` high (e.g., 24 hours).

## Cache-Control directive reference

| Directive | Browser Storage | Shared CDN Storage | Revalidation Behavior | Typical Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | Yes (1 year) | Yes (1 year) | None, even on reload | Content-hashed JS/CSS/fonts (`app.8f3c2a.js`) |
| `public, s-maxage=60, max-age=10` | Yes (10s) | Yes (60s) | Revalidates after respective TTL | Public APIs where edge can be warmer than browser |
| `no-cache` | Yes | Yes (if `public`) | Must revalidate (`304`) before every use | HTML shells (`index.html`) pointing to hashed assets |
| `private, no-store` | No | No | Never stored; full fetch every time | Banking, PII, `/api/me`, auth tokens |
| `stale-while-revalidate=120` | Yes | Yes | Serves stale during window, refreshes async | Catalogs, feeds, CMS pages tolerating brief staleness |

## Failure modes

- **Web cache poisoning via unkeyed headers**: If an origin reads `X-Forwarded-Host` or `X-Original-URL` to build script URLs in HTML without listing that header in `Vary`, an attacker can send a crafted header on a cache miss and poison the CDN entry for all subsequent users.
- **Cache stampede on TTL expiration**: Without `stale-while-revalidate` or request coalescing (collapsed forwarding), a hot key expiring at `s-maxage=60` unleashes hundreds of simultaneous origin queries.
- **Set-Cookie stripping or accidental caching**: Sending `Set-Cookie` on a `200 OK` with `Cache-Control: public` can either cache a session cookie for all users or cause CDNs to silently bypass caching.
- **Query string cache busting abuse**: Attackers appending `?cb=random123` to bypass CDN caches and hit the origin directly unless query parameters are allowlisted in the CDN cache key.

## Designing cacheable APIs & HTML shells

A reliable web architecture pairs **two distinct caching tiers**:

1. **HTML Entrypoints (`index.html`)**: Serve with `Cache-Control: no-cache` (or `s-maxage=10, stale-while-revalidate=60`) and a strong `ETag`. Clients always get the latest deployment manifest via a fast `304` check.
2. **Fingerprinted Assets & Read APIs**: Serve JS/CSS/images with content hashes and `max-age=31536000, immutable`. For read APIs, strip cookies on public endpoints, prefer `Surrogate-Key` invalidation over tiny TTLs, and set `stale-if-error=86400` so the CDN continues serving the last good response if the origin returns `500`/`502`/`504`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Default all authenticated or user-scoped endpoints to `Cache-Control: private, no-store`.
- [ ] Use `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` for all content-hashed static bundles.
- [ ] Add `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error` on public read APIs to eliminate stampedes and mask origin blips.
- [ ] Audit `Vary` headers; never emit `Vary: User-Agent` or `Vary: *` on CDN-fronted routes.
- [ ] Enable request coalescing (collapsed forwarding) at the reverse proxy/CDN for cache misses.
- [ ] Ensure `Surrogate-Key` / `Cache-Tag` headers are stripped at the edge before forwarding responses to browsers.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: HTTP caching (RFC 9111) uses explicit freshness lifetimes, validation headers (ETag/Last-Modified), and Vary keys so browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies serve safe, fast responses without stale leaks.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Edge CDN / Varnish applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Origin API.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Origin API experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Default all authenticated API middleware to `Cache-Control: private, no-store` and add automated CI/gateway assertions that block `public` or `s-maxage` when `Set-Cookie` or `Authorization` is present.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Separate immutable static assets (Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable) from dynamic APIs (Cache-Control: no-cache + ETag revalidation), and use Vary carefully so you never fragment cache hit ratios or leak user-specific responses.
Avoid trap: Confusing `no-cache` (store, but revalidate before reuse) with `no-store` (do not store anywhere).
Avoid trap: Omitting `immutable` on fingerprinted static assets, causing browsers on manual reload (F5) to fire unnecessary `If-None-Match` revalidation bursts.
When to reach for it: Content-hashed static assets (JS, CSS, fonts, images) where filenames change on every build, enabling 1-year immutable caching.
When to reach for it: Public or semi-static read APIs (catalogs, feature flags, product pages) where 10–60 second edge TTLs plus stale-while-revalidate absorb traffic spikes.

putItTogether.summary: Separate immutable static assets (Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable) from dynamic APIs (Cache-Control: no-cache + ETag revalidation), and use Vary carefully so you never fragment cache hit ratios or leak user-specific responses.

The catalog endpoint returns `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` with a strong `ETag`, keeping edge p99 latency at 12 ms while masking origin 502 blips.

concepts.name: HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing

relationships.description: Connects HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.

spark.summary: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.
spark.keyTakeaway: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern web pages and microservice meshes issue 40–150 concurrent requests per origin. HTTP/1.1 forces browsers to open 6 parallel TCP connections (each paying a 1-RTT TCP + 1–2-RTT TLS handshake and cold slow-start) and still stalls behind slow responses. HTTP/2 collapses all traffic onto one warmed TCP+TLS connection, compresses repetitive headers by 75–90% via HPACK, and lets gRPC stream bidirectional RPCs at high throughput.
whenToUse: Browser-to-CDN or API-gateway traffic over reliable broadband/fiber where a page loads dozens of concurrent assets or API calls from the same origin.
Internal microservice-to-microservice communication (especially gRPC over HTTP/2) where long-lived multiplexed connections eliminate connection-pool churn and TLS handshake overhead.
Bandwidth-constrained mobile or API workloads with large, repetitive headers (Authorization JWTs, cookies, trace IDs) that benefit from HPACK stateful compression.
whenNotToUse: Lossy cellular or last-mile networks (>2% packet loss) where a single dropped TCP packet stalls all 100 multiplexed HTTP/2 streams simultaneously; prefer HTTP/3 (QUIC).
Legacy L4 load balancers without L7 awareness—because HTTP/2 reuses one long-lived TCP connection, L4 round-robin pins all RPCs from a client pod to a single backend pod.

Large single-file bulk downloads over high-BDP (bandwidth-delay product) links if the server's HTTP/2 stream flow-control window is undersized (e.g., 64 KB default), throttling throughput below a single HTTP/1.1 socket.
keyPoints: Every HTTP/2 message is split into binary frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`, `SETTINGS`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, `RST_STREAM`, `GOAWAY`) tagged with a 31-bit `Stream ID` (odd = client-initiated, even = server-initiated).

Multiplexing allows interleaved frames from dozens of concurrent streams (typically `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 100` to `256`) on one TCP connection, removing HTTP/1.1 application-layer HoL blocking.
HPACK (RFC 7541) compresses headers using a static table (61 common entries), a per-connection dynamic table (default 4,096 bytes), and Huffman encoding—cutting typical header overhead by ~80%.
Two-level credit-based flow control (`WINDOW_UPDATE` per stream and per connection, initial window 65,535 bytes) prevents a single fast sender from flooding a slow receiver's buffers.
Because all streams ride one TCP byte stream, a single lost TCP segment blocks delivery of *all* HTTP/2 streams at the kernel receive buffer until retransmitted (TCP head-of-line blocking).

examples.title: gRPC Microservice Mesh with Envoy L7 Load Balancing
examples.scenario: A checkout service makes 12,000 RPS to an inventory service (20 pods) over gRPC/HTTP2. Initially, an AWS NLB (L4) routes connections: each checkout pod opens 1 long-lived HTTP/2 connection, pinning all 1,200 RPS from that pod to 1 lucky inventory pod while others sit idle.
examples.outcome: Inserting Envoy sidecars configured for L7 HTTP/2 load balancing distributes individual HTTP/2 streams across all 20 inventory pods via least-request, cutting p99 latency from 84 ms to 11 ms while keeping TCP/TLS handshakes near zero.

examples.title: Eliminating Domain Sharding on a Media Web App
examples.scenario: Under HTTP/1.1, a web app sharded assets across `static1..static4.example.com` to get 24 parallel sockets, paying 4x TLS handshakes and DNS lookups.
examples.outcome: Consolidating onto a single HTTP/2 origin (`cdn.example.com`) with connection coalescing reduced time-to-interactive by 380 ms on 4G and cut TLS CPU usage on edge proxies by 62%.

tradeOffs.factor: Single Connection Efficiency vs. TCP Head-of-Line Blocking
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates repeated TCP/TLS handshakes, lets TCP congestion window grow large (cwnd) quickly, and maximizes header compression across streams.
tradeOffs.con: At 2–5% packet loss, one dropped packet stalls every concurrent stream on that connection, making HTTP/2 slower than 6 parallel HTTP/1.1 connections in high-loss regimes.

tradeOffs.factor: HPACK Stateful Dynamic Table vs. Per-Connection Memory & Ordering
tradeOffs.pro: Compresses repeated 1 KB+ cookies and JWTs down to 2-byte table indices.
tradeOffs.con: Requires strict in-order frame processing per connection and consumes per-connection RAM (4–64 KB) at proxies handling 100k+ concurrent clients.

tradeOffs.factor: Long-Lived Connections vs. L4 Load Balancing
tradeOffs.pro: Avoids ephemeral port exhaustion and connection setup latency.
tradeOffs.con: Breaks naive L4 connection-level load balancing; new backend pods receive zero traffic until existing connections cycle via `GOAWAY` or `max_connection_age`.

failureModes.name: TCP Head-of-Line Blocking Under Packet Loss
failureModes.description: A single dropped TCP packet on a mobile link causes the OS kernel to hold all subsequent in-flight HTTP/2 frames in the socket buffer until Fast Retransmit / RTO completes, stalling CSS, JS, and API calls together.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable HTTP/3 (QUIC) on edge CDNs so independent streams no longer share a single kernel TCP byte stream, keeping HTTP/2 as fallback.

failureModes.name: L4 Load Balancer Hot-Spotting (Connection Pinning)
failureModes.description: When gRPC/HTTP2 clients connect through an L4 LB, a single persistent TCP connection carries thousands of multiplexed RPCs to one backend replica, causing CPU saturation while peer replicas sit at 5% CPU.
failureModes.mitigation: Use L7-aware proxies (Envoy, Nginx, ALB) that multiplex/demultiplex streams per request, or configure server-side `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` (e.g., 5 minutes + jitter) to send `GOAWAY` and force periodic reconnects.

failureModes.name: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DoS (CVE-2023-44487)
failureModes.description: An attacker opens thousands of streams with `HEADERS` and immediately cancels them with `RST_STREAM` in the same packet burst, forcing the server to allocate/teardown request contexts while bypassing `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`.
failureModes.mitigation: Patch HTTP/2 stacks (Envoy, Go `x/net/http2`, Nginx) to rate-limit consecutive `RST_STREAM` frames per connection and terminate abusive connections with `GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM)`.

failureModes.name: Undersized Flow-Control Window Throttling
failureModes.description: Keeping the default 65,535-byte stream window on a 100 ms RTT link caps single-stream throughput at `65,535 / 0.1s ≈ 655 KB/s` (~5.2 Mbps) regardless of 1 Gbps link capacity.
failureModes.mitigation: Tune `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (e.g., 1–4 MB) and BDP auto-tuning on proxies/gRPC servers for high-bandwidth transfers.

commonMistakes: Keeping HTTP/1.1 domain sharding (`cdn1..cdn4`) after upgrading to HTTP/2, which prevents multiplexing and wastes TLS handshakes.
Leaving gRPC clients behind an L4 load balancer without `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` or client-side round-robin, starving newly scaled pods.
Assuming HTTP/2 Server Push is still useful—Chrome and major browsers removed Server Push in 2022; use `103 Early Hints` (`Link: rel=preload`) instead.
Setting `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` too high (e.g., 10,000) on memory-constrained servers, allowing a single client to exhaust heap.
Forgetting to tune HTTP/2 flow-control windows (`initial_stream_window_size`) on high-latency WAN links, capping throughput to a few Mbps.

sections.content:
## The idea

HTTP/1.1 is a text-based, sequential protocol: on a single TCP socket, Response B cannot start until Response A finishes completely. Even with HTTP pipelining, a slow `/api/report` response blocks all smaller responses behind it (**application-layer head-of-line blocking**). Browsers worked around this by opening 6 TCP connections per origin and sharding domains—multiplying TLS handshakes and fighting TCP slow-start.

**HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)** replaces plain-text messages with a **binary framing layer** over a single TCP+TLS connection. Every request and response is assigned a unique 31-bit **Stream ID** and broken into small frames (up to `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, default 16 KB). Frames from dozens of concurrent streams are interleaved on the wire and reassembled at the receiver.

To eliminate per-request overhead, **HPACK (RFC 7541)** replaces repeated ASCII header strings with integer indices into a static table and a connection-scoped dynamic table. Meanwhile, credit-based **flow control** (`WINDOW_UPDATE` frames) ensures a fast stream cannot starve other streams or overflow proxy buffers—without closing the underlying TCP socket.

## Concrete walkthrough

Follow a browser loading `https://app.example.com` that needs `/app.js` (180 KB) and `/api/user` (2 KB, slow DB query taking 120 ms) over a single HTTP/2 connection (RTT = 30 ms):

1. **Connection Preface & Settings**: After 1-RTT TCP and 1-RTT TLS 1.3 (ALPN `h2`), client and server exchange `SETTINGS` frames agreeing on `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 100`, `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE = 1048576` (1 MB), and `HEADER_TABLE_SIZE = 4096`.
2. **Concurrent Stream Initiation**: At `t = 0 ms`, the browser opens **Stream 1** (`HEADERS` for `/app.js`, `END_STREAM`) and **Stream 3** (`HEADERS` for `/api/user`, `END_STREAM`) back-to-back in a single TCP segment. HPACK encodes `:method: GET` and `:scheme: https` as 1-byte static-table indices and stores `authorization: Bearer ...` in the dynamic table.
3. **Interleaved Delivery (No App HoL Blocking)**: At `t = 15 ms`, the server immediately begins sending `DATA` frames for Stream 1 (`/app.js`) in 16 KB chunks while `/api/user` is still querying Postgres. By `t = 45 ms`, `/app.js` finishes (`END_STREAM` on Stream 1) even though Stream 3 hasn't sent a single byte yet.
4. **Flow Control & Completion**: At `t = 135 ms`, Postgres returns the user record. The server sends `HEADERS` (referencing the dynamic table) + `DATA` (`END_STREAM`) on Stream 3. If `/app.js` had been 5 MB, the browser would send `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames every ~512 KB to replenish the server's send credits.

sections.content:
## HPACK compression and stream lifecycle

Each HTTP/2 stream transitions through a strict state machine (`idle` -> `open` -> `half-closed (local/remote)` -> `closed`). A client cannot reuse a Stream ID; when Stream IDs approach `2^31 - 1`, the connection gracefully shuts down via `GOAWAY` (carrying the `last_stream_id` processed so the client knows which in-flight streams are safe to retry on a new connection).

**HPACK (RFC 7541)** avoids the CRIME/BREACH compression side-channel attacks that broke SPDY's GZIP header compression. Instead of sliding-window DEFLATE, HPACK uses:
1. **Static Table**: 61 pre-populated common pairs (e.g., index 2 = `:method: GET`, index 8 = `:status: 200`).
2. **Dynamic Table**: A FIFO ring buffer (default 4 KB) per connection direction storing custom headers like `x-request-id` or `authorization`.
3. **Huffman Coding**: Compresses string literals by ~30% when not yet in the dynamic table.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 comparison
sections.content:
## HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 comparison

| Dimension | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) | HTTP/3 (RFC 9114 / QUIC) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transport** | TCP + TLS (6+ sockets/origin) | Single TCP + TLS 1.3 socket | Single UDP + QUIC (built-in TLS 1.3) |
| **Wire Format** | Plain-text ASCII lines | Binary frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`) | Binary frames over QUIC streams |
| **App-Layer HoL Blocking** | Yes (1 active response/socket) | No (interleaved streams) | No (independent QUIC streams) |
| **Transport HoL Blocking** | Per-socket only | **Yes** (1 lost TCP packet stalls all streams) | **No** (loss on Stream A doesn't stall Stream B) |
| **Header Compression** | None (uncompressed ASCII) | HPACK (static + dynamic table) | QPACK (out-of-order safe dynamic table) |
| **Connection Migration** | Breaks on IP change (Wi-Fi -> 5G) | Breaks on IP change | Seamless via QUIC Connection ID |

## Failure modes

- **TCP head-of-line blocking**: On a 3% packet-loss mobile link, TCP stalls the entire HTTP/2 connection waiting for retransmission, making page load slower than HTTP/1.1's 6 independent sockets.
- **L4 load-balancer pinning**: Long-lived HTTP/2 connections bypass L4 round-robin, overloading early-started backend pods during autoscaling events.
- **RST_STREAM Rapid Reset floods**: Malicious clients open and immediately `RST_STREAM` thousands of streams per second, exhausting server CPU/memory unless strict reset rate limits are enforced.
- **Dynamic table memory bloat**: Proxies accepting large `SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE` values across hundreds of thousands of idle connections can exhaust RAM.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Operational tuning for Envoy, Nginx, and gRPC
sections.content:
## Operational tuning for Envoy, Nginx, and gRPC

When running HTTP/2 in production:
- **Edge/CDN**: Enable HTTP/2 alongside HTTP/3 (`Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400`) so lossy clients upgrade to QUIC automatically.
- **gRPC / Microservices**: Always terminate HTTP/2 at an L7 proxy (Envoy/Linkerd/Istio) or use client-side xDS/DNS lookaside load balancing. Set `max_connection_age: 300s` + `max_connection_age_grace: 30s` so `GOAWAY` drains connections cleanly during rolling deploys.
- **Flow Control**: Raise `initial_stream_window_size` from 64 KB to 1–4 MB and `initial_connection_window_size` to 4–16 MB for high-BDP cross-region links.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Remove legacy HTTP/1.1 domain sharding so browsers coalesce streams onto one HTTP/2 connection.
- [ ] Use L7 load balancing (or `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` + `GOAWAY`) for gRPC/HTTP2 microservice pools.
- [ ] Tune `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (1–4 MB) if serving large payloads over >50 ms RTT links.
- [ ] Cap `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` (e.g., 100–256) and enable `RST_STREAM` rate limiting against Rapid Reset DoS.
- [ ] Replace deprecated HTTP/2 Server Push with `103 Early Hints` for critical CSS/fonts.
- [ ] Pair HTTP/2 with HTTP/3 (QUIC) at the edge to eliminate TCP head-of-line blocking on lossy networks.

interviewProblems.title: HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Single TCP + TLS 1.3 applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Envoy / Origin Server.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Envoy / Origin Server experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enable HTTP/3 (QUIC) on edge CDNs so independent streams no longer share a single kernel TCP byte stream, keeping HTTP/2 as fallback.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
Avoid trap: Keeping HTTP/1.1 domain sharding (`cdn1..cdn4`) after upgrading to HTTP/2, which prevents multiplexing and wastes TLS handshakes.
Avoid trap: Leaving gRPC clients behind an L4 load balancer without `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` or client-side round-robin, starving newly scaled pods.
When to reach for it: Browser-to-CDN or API-gateway traffic over reliable broadband/fiber where a page loads dozens of concurrent assets or API calls from the same origin.

When to reach for it: Internal microservice-to-microservice communication (especially gRPC over HTTP/2) where long-lived multiplexed connections eliminate connection-pool churn and TLS handshake overhead.

putItTogether.title: Putting Http2 Connection Multiplexing Together
putItTogether.summary: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Http2 Connection Multiplexing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.

putItTogether.outcome: Inserting Envoy sidecars configured for L7 HTTP/2 load balancing distributes individual HTTP/2 streams across all 20 inventory pods via least-request, cutting p99 latency from 84 ms to 11 ms while keeping TCP/TLS handshakes near zero.

concepts.name: Hybrid Vector & Keyword Search

relationships.description: Connects Hybrid Vector & Keyword Search to llm prompt engineering in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Hybrid vector search combines sparse lexical scoring (BM25) with dense semantic embeddings (HNSW/IVF) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and optional cross-encoder reranking to achieve high recall on both exact identifiers and conceptual queries.

spark.summary: Hybrid vector search combines sparse lexical scoring (BM25) with dense semantic embeddings (HNSW/IVF) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and optional cross-encoder reranking to achieve high recall on both exact identifiers and conceptual queries.
spark.keyTakeaway: Dense vectors alone miss exact SKUs, error codes, and proper nouns, while BM25 misses synonyms; run both in parallel, fuse with RRF (k=60), and cross-encoder rerank only the top 20–50 candidates.

concept.whyItMatters: Pure semantic (dense vector) search excels at paraphrased intent ('how to fix memory leak in JVM') but routinely fails on exact tokens like `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET`, `SKU-4920B`, or `RFC 9113`, where a single character difference shouldn't be blurred into nearby embeddings. Conversely, BM25 nails exact keywords and rare acronyms but returns zero results when a user searches 'car' for a doc titled 'automobile'. Hybrid search captures both signals in <30–50 ms and dramatically cuts RAG hallucinations.
whenToUse: Enterprise RAG, documentation search, and support knowledge bases where users mix natural-language questions with exact product codes, API names, or error strings.
E-commerce catalog search combining conceptual intent ('warm waterproof jacket for winter hiking') with exact brand/model/SKU filters.
Code and log search where exact symbol names (`NullPointerException`, `max_hint_window_in_ms`) coexist with semantic descriptions.
whenNotToUse: Pure exact-match lookups (primary key, UUID, order ID) where a B-tree or inverted index alone is faster, deterministic, and 10x cheaper.
Tiny datasets (<5,000 short records) where brute-force cosine similarity or SQLite FTS5 fits in memory and avoids HNSW index complexity.
Ultra-low-latency (<5 ms) autocomplete where running a transformer embedding model on the query path blows the latency budget.
keyPoints: Sparse retrieval (BM25 / SPLADE) scores exact term frequency and inverse document frequency (IDF), excelling at rare tokens, SKUs, and acronyms.

Dense retrieval embeds queries and chunks into fixed vectors (e.g., 768–1536 dims via `text-embedding-3-small` or `bge-m3`) indexed in HNSW graphs for ~10 ms approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) lookup.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (`RRF_score(d) = sum(1 / (k + rank_i(d)))`, typically `k = 60`) merges uncalibrated BM25 scores and cosine similarities using rank positions alone—no brittle score normalization required.

Metadata pre-filtering (e.g., `tenant_id = 'acme' AND year >= 2025`) must be integrated into the HNSW traversal (single-stage filtered ANN in Qdrant/Milvus/Elasticsearch) to avoid empty top-k results from post-filtering.
Two-stage retrieval sends the top 50–100 RRF candidates to a cross-encoder reranker (`bge-reranker-v2-m3` or Cohere Rerank) to jointly attend over `(query, doc)` tokens, boosting NDCG@10 by 8–18%.

examples.title: Developer Docs & Error-Code RAG Assistant
examples.scenario: A cloud platform indexes 180,000 API doc chunks in Qdrant (1024-dim dense HNSW + BM25 sparse vectors). A developer queries: `why does webhook return ERR_HMAC_MISMATCH_401`.
examples.outcome: Dense search alone ranks generic OAuth/401 guides above the exact HMAC page because the rare error token wasn't well-represented in the embedding model's pretraining. BM25 ranks the exact `ERR_HMAC_MISMATCH_401` section #1; RRF (`k=60`) + cross-encoder reranking places it at rank #1 with 0.94 relevance, eliminating support tickets.

examples.title: E-Commerce Catalog Search with Tenant & Stock Pre-Filtering
examples.scenario: A marketplace with 4M SKUs in Milvus / OpenSearch runs hybrid search for `ergonomic mesh chair under 300` with `in_stock = true AND price <= 300`.
examples.outcome: Single-stage filtered HNSW + BM25 evaluates the stock/price bitset during graph traversal, returning 40 valid in-stock matches in 24 ms (vs. post-filtering returning only 3 results out of top-40).

tradeOffs.pro: Combining BM25 + HNSW + cross-encoder reranking consistently outperforms either retriever alone across BEIR benchmarks.
tradeOffs.con: Requires maintaining both an inverted index and a vector HNSW graph (higher RAM: ~4–6 GB per 1M 1024-dim float32 vectors without quantization) plus GPU/CPU budget for reranking.

tradeOffs.factor: RRF (Rank-Based) vs. Linear Score Fusion (alpha * dense + (1-alpha) * sparse)
tradeOffs.pro: RRF needs zero score calibration and is resilient to BM25's unbounded `[0, inf)` scale vs. cosine's `[-1, 1]`.
tradeOffs.con: Discards score magnitude gaps (e.g., a 0.99 exact match vs. a 0.51 weak match look identical if both are rank #1).

tradeOffs.pro: Full cross-attention between query and document tokens resolves subtle negation and multi-hop phrasing.
tradeOffs.con: Adds 40–150 ms per query on GPU (or 200+ ms on CPU) for top-50 candidates, unsuitable for <10 ms typeahead.

failureModes.name: Post-Filtering Recall Collapse
failureModes.description: Running unconstrained top-20 ANN first and then filtering by `tenant_id = 'acme'` (which owns 1% of rows) leaves 0–1 results after filtering.
failureModes.mitigation: Use engines with single-stage filtered HNSW (bitset evaluation inside graph traversal) or partition indexes by high-selectivity tenant keys.

failureModes.name: Naïve Score Addition Without Normalization
failureModes.description: Summing raw BM25 scores (e.g., 14.7) directly with cosine similarity (0.82) causes BM25 to dominate 18:1, silently disabling semantic search.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (`k=60`) or min-max/z-score normalization per query before weighted combination.

failureModes.name: Chunk Boundary Context Loss
failureModes.description: Splitting documents at fixed 500-character boundaries cuts headings from paragraphs or splits tables, causing both BM25 and embeddings to miss the relationship.
failureModes.mitigation: Use structure-aware chunking (Markdown/HTML headers, 10–15% overlap) and prepend document title/section breadcrumbs to each chunk before embedding.

failureModes.name: Aggressive Quantization Recall Drop
failureModes.description: Compressing 1536-dim float32 vectors straight to 1-bit binary quantization without oversampling + rescoring drops recall@10 by 10–20% on nuanced queries.
failureModes.mitigation: Use int8 scalar quantization (minimal recall loss, 4x RAM savings) or oversample top-100 binary candidates and rescore against full-precision vectors on disk.

commonMistakes: Adding raw BM25 and cosine similarity scores without RRF or normalization.
Applying metadata filters *after* top-k ANN retrieval instead of inside the HNSW traversal.
Sending 500+ candidates to a cross-encoder reranker, blowing the p99 latency budget.
Using the same embedding model on queries and documents without required instruction prefixes (e.g., `query: ` vs. `passage: ` for E5/BGE models).
Storing unindexed raw float32 vectors at scale without int8/PQ quantization or disk-backed mmap, causing OOMs.

sections.content:
## The idea

Modern search faces a fundamental split: **lexical retrieval (BM25)** matches exact character tokens weighted by rarity (IDF), while **dense vector retrieval (HNSW)** maps text into continuous geometric space so semantically similar phrases cluster together.

Neither is sufficient alone. Dense encoders compress a 300-token chunk into a single vector, inevitably blurring exact identifiers like `CVE-2023-44487`, `x-amz-request-id`, or `SKU-9910`. Meanwhile, BM25 is blind to synonyms (`latency spike` vs. `p99 tail regression`) and paraphrased intent.

**Hybrid vector search** executes both retrievers in parallel over the same corpus (with shared metadata filters), merges the two ranked lists via **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**, and optionally passes the top 20–50 candidates through a **cross-encoder reranker** that reads query and document together for final precision.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a query `"kafka consumer lag spike after rebalance"` against a 500,000-chunk engineering runbook index in Qdrant/OpenSearch:

1. **Query Preparation**: The gateway generates a 1024-dim dense vector `v_q` (12 ms) and tokenizes the query for BM25 (`kafka`, `consumer`, `lag`, `spike`, `rebalance`). Both branches carry the pre-filter `org_id = 'payments'`.
2. **Parallel Retrieval**:
   - **Dense HNSW branch** traverses the multi-layer proximity graph with the `org_id` bitset filter and returns top-50 chunks (`14 ms`), surfacing conceptually relevant articles on *cooperative sticky assignor* and *partition revocation*.
   - **BM25 branch** queries the inverted index (`8 ms`) and returns top-50 chunks matching the exact rare terms `rebalance` and `lag`.
3. **RRF Fusion (`k = 60`)**: A chunk ranked #2 in Dense (`1/62 = 0.0161`) and #1 in BM25 (`1/61 = 0.0164`) scores `0.0325`, beating a chunk ranked #1 only in Dense (`0.0164`).
4. **Cross-Encoder Reranking**: The top-30 fused chunks are scored in a single GPU batch by `bge-reranker-v2-m3` (`38 ms`), promoting the exact runbook covering `max.poll.interval.ms` rebalance storms to rank #1. Total search latency: **~72 ms**.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Score fusion math: RRF vs. linear combination
sections.content:
## Score fusion math: RRF vs. linear combination

**Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** is the industry default because it requires zero tuning across heterogeneous score distributions:

`RRF(d) = 1 / (k + rank_dense(d)) + 1 / (k + rank_sparse(d))`

With `k = 60`, rank #1 contributes `0.01639`, rank #10 contributes `0.01429`, and rank #50 contributes `0.00909`. Documents appearing in *both* lists naturally jump ahead of single-signal matches. When domain tuning is required (e.g., favoring exact SKU matches 70/30), use **min-max normalized linear combination** (`0.7 * norm_bm25 + 0.3 * norm_dense`) or **Distribution-Based Score Fusion (DBSF)**, which normalizes each list using `mean ± 3 * stddev`.

## Retrieval stage trade-offs

| Stage | Signal Type | Typical Latency (500K chunks) | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **BM25 / Inverted** | Exact tokens + IDF | 5–12 ms | SKUs, error codes, rare proper nouns | Blind to synonyms & paraphrasing |
| **Dense HNSW (int8)** | Bi-encoder cosine | 8–20 ms | Synonyms, cross-lingual, intent | Blurs exact IDs & negations |
| **RRF Fusion (k=60)** | Rank positions | <1 ms | Calibration-free, boosts dual hits | Ignores raw confidence gaps |
| **Cross-Encoder** | Full token cross-attention | 35–120 ms (top-30) | Highest NDCG@10 precision | Too slow for >100 candidates |

## Failure modes

- **Post-filtering empty results**: Filtering *after* top-k ANN fails whenever selectivity is <5%. Always use single-stage filtered HNSW.
- **Uncalibrated score addition**: Adding raw BM25 (`0..25+`) to cosine (`0..1`) silently breaks semantic recall.
- **Missing model prefixes**: Asymmetric models (`e5-large`, `bge`) degrade sharply if `query:` / `passage:` prefixes are omitted.
- **Stale index / delete drift**: Updating a document without deleting its old chunks leaves phantom results in both BM25 and HNSW.

## Memory & quantization sizing

At 1 million 1024-dim vectors:
- **Float32 HNSW (`M=16`)**: `1M * 1024 * 4 bytes = 4.1 GB` raw vectors + `~0.5 GB` graph edges (`~4.6 GB` RAM).
- **Int8 Scalar Quantization**: Cuts vector RAM 4x to `~1.0 GB` (+ `0.5 GB` graph) with <1% recall@10 drop.
- **Binary Quantization + Oversample**: Cuts RAM 32x (`~128 MB`), provided you fetch top-100 and rescore against disk-backed float32/int8 vectors.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Run BM25 and dense HNSW in parallel with single-stage metadata pre-filtering.
- [ ] Start with RRF (`k=60`) before attempting weighted linear fusion.
- [ ] Cap cross-encoder reranking to top 20–50 fused candidates to hold p99 under 100 ms.
- [ ] Use structure-aware chunking (300–600 tokens) with title/heading breadcrumbs prepended.
- [ ] Apply int8 scalar quantization once vector RAM exceeds 50% of node memory.
- [ ] Evaluate recall@20 and NDCG@10 on a golden query set covering both exact IDs and paraphrased questions.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Hybrid vector search combines sparse lexical scoring (BM25) with dense semantic embeddings (HNSW/IVF) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and optional cross-encoder reranking to achieve high recall on both exact identifiers and conceptual queries.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: BM25 Inverted Index applies the primary invariant and coordinates with RRF + Cross-Encoder.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, RRF + Cross-Encoder experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use engines with single-stage filtered HNSW (bitset evaluation inside graph traversal) or partition indexes by high-selectivity tenant keys.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Dense vectors alone miss exact SKUs, error codes, and proper nouns, while BM25 misses synonyms; run both in parallel, fuse with RRF (k=60), and cross-encoder rerank only the top 20–50 candidates.
Avoid trap: Adding raw BM25 and cosine similarity scores without RRF or normalization.
Avoid trap: Applying metadata filters *after* top-k ANN retrieval instead of inside the HNSW traversal.
When to reach for it: Enterprise RAG, documentation search, and support knowledge bases where users mix natural-language questions with exact product codes, API names, or error strings.
When to reach for it: E-commerce catalog search combining conceptual intent ('warm waterproof jacket for winter hiking') with exact brand/model/SKU filters.

putItTogether.title: Putting Hybrid Vector Search Together
putItTogether.summary: Dense vectors alone miss exact SKUs, error codes, and proper nouns, while BM25 misses synonyms; run both in parallel, fuse with RRF (k=60), and cross-encoder rerank only the top 20–50 candidates.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Hybrid Vector Search before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Dense search alone ranks generic OAuth/401 guides above the exact HMAC page because the rare error token wasn't well-represented in the embedding model's pretraining. BM25 ranks the exact `ERR_HMAC_MISMATCH_401` section #1; RRF (`k=60`) + cross-encoder reranking places it at rank #1 with 0.94 relevance, eliminating support tickets.

concepts.name: Idempotency & Message Deduplication

relationships.description: Consumers must tolerate redelivery.
Outbox publishing pairs with idempotent consumers.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

concepts.tagline: Idempotency keys and deduplication logs ensure that network retries, at-least-once message deliveries, and double-clicks execute state mutations at most once while returning the original cached outcome.

spark.summary: Idempotency keys and deduplication logs ensure that network retries, at-least-once message deliveries, and double-clicks execute state mutations at most once while returning the original cached outcome.
spark.keyTakeaway: Because distributed networks only guarantee at-least-once delivery, every mutating API and consumer must pair a client-generated idempotency key with an atomic database/transaction check—not a separate read-then-write.

concept.whyItMatters: In distributed systems, timeouts are ambiguous: when a client or Kafka consumer times out waiting for an ACK, it cannot tell whether the server crashed before processing or after committing. Retrying without idempotency double-charges credit cards, mints duplicate orders, or corrupts inventory balances. Combining client-supplied `Idempotency-Key` headers (or event IDs) with atomic persistence turns at-least-once transport into effectively-once business effects.
whenToUse: Payment, billing, and ledger APIs (e.g., Stripe-style `POST /v1/charges` with `Idempotency-Key` UUIDv4) where duplicate execution causes financial loss.
Event-driven consumers reading from at-least-once brokers (Kafka, SQS Standard, SNS, RabbitMQ) that redeliver messages on consumer rebalance or visibility timeout expiry.
Mobile or flaky-network clients that automatically retry timed-out POST/PATCH requests.
whenNotToUse: Naturally idempotent operations (`PUT /users/42` full replacement, `DELETE /sessions/9`, or `SET status = 'PAID'`) where re-running yields the identical state without side-effect logs.
Read-only `GET`/`HEAD` endpoints that perform no mutations.
High-throughput fire-and-forget telemetry/metrics where storing a deduplication key per event costs more than the 0.01% duplicate rate.
keyPoints: Idempotency is an end-to-end property: the client generates a unique key (UUIDv4) *before* the first attempt and reuses that exact key across all retries of the same logical operation.

Always validate a payload hash (e.g., SHA-256 of request body) alongside the key; reusing the same `Idempotency-Key` with a different amount or target must return `422 Unprocessable Entity` / `409 Conflict`.

Atomic state transitions are mandatory: insert the key (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` or DynamoDB `attribute_not_exists(pk)`) inside the same DB transaction as the business write, or use a Redis `SET NX EX` lock with an explicit `IN_PROGRESS` state.

Concurrent duplicate requests arriving while the first is still `IN_PROGRESS` should return `409 Conflict` (or `425 Too Early` with `Retry-After`) rather than running in parallel or returning an empty response.

Kafka's `enable.idempotence=true` deduplicates *broker-level* producer retries via `(PID, SequenceNumber)`, and transactional outbox + consumer-side `processed_events` tables deduplicate *application-level* side effects.

examples.title: Stripe-Pattern Payment Charge API in PostgreSQL
examples.scenario: A mobile checkout app sends `POST /v1/payments` (`amount=4999`, `Idempotency-Key: 9b1deb4d-...`). The gateway times out at 3s due to a slow 3DS bank call and retries 2 seconds later while the first request is still running, then retries a third time after it commits.
examples.outcome: Attempt 1 inserts `(key, payload_hash, status='IN_PROGRESS')` in Postgres. Attempt 2 hits the unique key while `IN_PROGRESS` and receives `409 Conflict` (`Retry-After: 2`). Attempt 1 commits the ledger row and updates the idempotency record to `status='COMPLETED', response_code=201, response_body=...`. Attempt 3 reads the completed record and replays the exact `201 Created` JSON without charging the card again.

examples.title: Kafka Consumer Deduplication via Atomic Processed-Events Table
examples.scenario: An order-fulfillment consumer reads `OrderPaid` events from Kafka (`at-least-once`). After updating inventory in Postgres for `event_id=evt_8821`, the consumer crashes before committing its Kafka offset, causing a rebalance and redelivery of `evt_8821`.
examples.outcome: Inside a single Postgres transaction, the consumer executes `INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES ('evt_8821') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. On redelivery, `rowcount == 0`, so the consumer skips the inventory decrement and commits the Kafka offset cleanly.

tradeOffs.factor: Same-DB Transaction vs. Redis Dedup Cache
tradeOffs.pro: Inserting the dedup key in the same ACID transaction as the business mutation guarantees zero split-brain between state and dedup record.
tradeOffs.con: Adds write IOPS and storage growth to the primary OLTP database, requiring TTL partitioning/pruning (e.g., 24h–7d retention).

tradeOffs.factor: Strict In-Progress Locking vs. Optimistic Parallelism
tradeOffs.pro: Returning `409` on concurrent duplicate keys prevents race conditions and duplicate external API calls (e.g., to Stripe/Adyen).
tradeOffs.con: If the worker holding `IN_PROGRESS` crashes without a lease timeout, the key stays locked until TTL expiry unless a lease/heartbeat or recovery state machine is implemented.

tradeOffs.factor: Dedup Retention Window vs. Storage Cost
tradeOffs.pro: Longer retention (e.g., 7–30 days) protects against delayed batch retries and dead-letter queue (DLQ) replays.
tradeOffs.con: Keeping millions of UUID keys and cached JSON responses bloats indexes unless stored in time-partitioned tables or DynamoDB TTL items.

failureModes.name: Check-Then-Act Race Condition
failureModes.description: Two identical retries simultaneously execute `SELECT * FROM idempotency WHERE key = ?`, both see `NULL`, and both execute the payment charge before either writes the key.
failureModes.mitigation: Use an atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` / `UNIQUE` constraint or Redis `SET key value NX EX 3600`—never a separate `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Split-Brain (Redis + Postgres)
failureModes.description: The service writes the business row to Postgres and then crashes before writing the dedup key to Redis (or writes Redis first and Postgres rolls back), causing either a missed dedup or a permanently blocked key.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep the idempotency/processed_events table in the same ACID database as the business mutation, or use the Transactional Outbox pattern.

failureModes.name: Orphaned IN_PROGRESS Lock After Worker Crash
failureModes.description: A worker sets `status='IN_PROGRESS'` and is OOM-killed mid-request; every subsequent client retry gets `409 Conflict` forever.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach a short lease timestamp (`locked_until = now() + 30s`) to `IN_PROGRESS` records—if expired and no external side effect was started, allow safe takeover or query the downstream provider by the same idempotency key.

failureModes.name: Key Reuse with Mutated Payload
failureModes.description: A buggy client hardcodes an `Idempotency-Key` across two different orders ($10 then $500) and silently receives the cached $10 response.
failureModes.mitigation: Store `request_hash = SHA256(method + path + canonical_body)` with the key and reject mismatches with `422 Unprocessable Entity`.

commonMistakes: Generating the idempotency key on the server instead of the client—server-generated keys cannot detect client network retries.
Implementing deduplication with a non-atomic `GET` followed by `SET` or `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.
Forgetting to pass the idempotency key downstream to external payment gateways or webhooks, causing duplicate external calls on internal retries.
Omitting payload-hash verification, allowing accidental key reuse to return a stale response for a different request.
Using `SETNX` in Redis without an expiration (`EX`), leaking memory indefinitely until eviction.

sections.content:
## The idea

In an unreliable network, **at-least-once delivery** is the practical baseline: HTTP clients retry on `504`/timeout, and message brokers (Kafka, SQS) redeliver unacknowledged events after consumer crashes. Without protection, retrying a non-idempotent operation like `POST /transfers` or `decrement_stock` executes the side effect multiple times.

**Idempotency** means applying an operation multiple times produces the same system state and observable result as applying it once. For naturally non-idempotent operations (creating a charge, appending a ledger entry), we achieve this via an **idempotency key** (client-generated UUIDv4) or **message ID** paired with an atomic deduplication store.

The core pattern has three phases: (1) **Acquire** the key atomically (`IN_PROGRESS` + payload hash), (2) **Execute** the business mutation and persist the serialized response inside the same ACID boundary (or atomic state machine), and (3) **Replay** the stored response on any subsequent retry with the same key.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace `POST /v1/transfers` (`amount=25000`, `to='acct_88'`, `Idempotency-Key: 7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7`):

1. **Request 1 (Initial)**: The API computes `req_hash = SHA256(canonical_json)`. Inside a Postgres transaction, it runs `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys(key, req_hash, status, locked_until) VALUES ($1, $2, 'IN_PROGRESS', now() + interval '30 seconds') ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING`. It inserts 1 row and commits the lock.
2. **Request 2 (Concurrent Retry at +1.2s)**: The mobile client timed out at 1s and retries with the same key. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` inserts 0 rows. The server selects the existing row, verifies `req_hash` matches, sees `status = 'IN_PROGRESS'` with `locked_until > now()`, and immediately returns `409 Conflict` with `Retry-After: 2`.
3. **Completion of Request 1 (+2.4s)**: After debiting the sender and crediting `acct_88` inside a single DB transaction, the server updates `idempotency_keys` in that same commit: `status = 'COMPLETED', response_code = 201, response_body = '{"transfer_id":"tr_501"}'`. 
4. **Request 3 (Post-Commit Retry at +3.5s)**: The client retries once more. The server finds `status = 'COMPLETED'` and returns the exact cached `201 Created` JSON (`{"transfer_id":"tr_501"}`) in 2 ms without touching the ledger.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Messaging deduplication: Kafka, SQS, and the Outbox pattern
sections.content:
## Messaging deduplication: Kafka, SQS, and the Outbox pattern

API idempotency is only half the story; asynchronous pipelines need two additional layers:

- **Producer-to-Broker**: Kafka's `enable.idempotence=true` assigns every producer a `ProducerID` (`PID`) and monotonic `SequenceNumber` per partition, so broker-level retries on network blips are deduplicated before appending to the log. AWS SQS FIFO offers a 5-minute `MessageDeduplicationId` window.
- **Broker-to-Consumer**: Neither Kafka's idempotent producer nor SQS prevents a consumer from processing a message twice after a crash before offset commit/delete. Consumers must maintain a `processed_events(event_id PRIMARY KEY, processed_at)` table in the same database as their state updates and check/insert it inside the same transaction.
- **Transactional Outbox**: When an API must update Postgres *and* publish a Kafka event, write the event to an `outbox` table in the same Postgres transaction and let Debezium (CDC) or a poller publish it—giving the event a deterministic `event_id` for downstream consumers.

## Deduplication implementation comparison

| Approach | Atomicity Guarantee | Concurrency Handling | Best Suited For | Main Limitation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Same-DB `idempotency_keys` Table** | Full ACID with business write | `ON CONFLICT` + `IN_PROGRESS` lease (`409`) | Payments, orders, ledger APIs | Adds OLTP storage; needs TTL pruning |
| **Redis `SET NX EX` + Cache** | Separate from SQL DB (risk of split-brain) | Atomic lock via Lua / `SET NX` | High-QPS soft dedup, rate/click guards | Lost on Redis failover unless RDB/AOF + DB backup |
| **Consumer `processed_events` Table** | Full ACID with consumer state update | `PRIMARY KEY` violation skips duplicate | Kafka / SQS / RabbitMQ consumers | Only protects single-DB consumers |
| **SQS FIFO `MessageDeduplicationId`** | Broker-enforced 5-min window | Drops duplicate enqueue attempts | Short-window task queues | 5-minute hard cap; doesn't cover consumer crashes |

## Failure modes

- **External side-effect split-brain**: Calling a third-party API (e.g., Stripe) *inside* a Postgres transaction that later rolls back leaves an external charge with no local DB record. Instead, pass the same `Idempotency-Key` to Stripe, commit a `PENDING_EXTERNAL` state first, call Stripe outside the DB lock, then finalize.
- **Expired dedup window on DLQ replay**: If `idempotency_keys` is pruned after 24 hours, replaying a 3-day-old dead-letter queue batch re-executes old mutations.
- **Unbounded table growth**: Storing full 50 KB response bodies for 10M requests/day adds 500 GB/day; use daily range partitions (`DROP TABLE` instead of `DELETE`) and cap cached body sizes.
- **Leased lock starvation**: Setting `locked_until` to 10 minutes on a 2-second endpoint traps clients in `409` loops after a single pod crash.

## Key design & retention rules

1. **Scope keys per tenant/user**: Key the unique constraint on `(tenant_id, idempotency_key)` so Tenant A cannot collide with or probe Tenant B's keys.
2. **Keep `IN_PROGRESS` leases tight**: Set `locked_until` to `2x–3x` the endpoint's p99 timeout (e.g., 15–30 seconds).
3. **Partition by time**: Use Postgres declarative daily partitions or DynamoDB `ttl` attributes (24–72 hours for APIs, 7–30 days for async `processed_events`) to drop expired keys with zero vacuum overhead.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Require client-generated UUIDv4 `Idempotency-Key` headers on all non-idempotent `POST`/`PATCH` endpoints.
- [ ] Scope uniqueness to `(tenant_id, key)` and verify `SHA-256(request_body)` matches (`422` on mismatch).
- [ ] Acquire `IN_PROGRESS` atomically (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` or `SET NX EX`) with a bounded lease timeout.
- [ ] Commit the business mutation and cached response in the same ACID transaction.
- [ ] Propagate the idempotency key to downstream webhooks and payment providers.
- [ ] Pair at-least-once consumers with a `processed_events` table and time-partitioned TTL cleanup.

interviewProblems.title: Idempotency & Message Deduplication
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Idempotency & Message Deduplication. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Idempotency keys and deduplication logs ensure that network retries, at-least-once message deliveries, and double-clicks execute state mutations at most once while returning the original cached outcome.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Payment / Order API applies the primary invariant and coordinates with ACID Ledger + Dedup DB.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, ACID Ledger + Dedup DB experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use an atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` / `UNIQUE` constraint or Redis `SET key value NX EX 3600`—never a separate `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Because distributed networks only guarantee at-least-once delivery, every mutating API and consumer must pair a client-generated idempotency key with an atomic database/transaction check—not a separate read-then-write.
Avoid trap: Generating the idempotency key on the server instead of the client—server-generated keys cannot detect client network retries.
Avoid trap: Implementing deduplication with a non-atomic `GET` followed by `SET` or `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.
When to reach for it: Payment, billing, and ledger APIs (e.g., Stripe-style `POST /v1/charges` with `Idempotency-Key` UUIDv4) where duplicate execution causes financial loss.
When to reach for it: Event-driven consumers reading from at-least-once brokers (Kafka, SQS Standard, SNS, RabbitMQ) that redeliver messages on consumer rebalance or visibility timeout expiry.

putItTogether.title: Putting Idempotency And Deduplication Together
putItTogether.summary: Because distributed networks only guarantee at-least-once delivery, every mutating API and consumer must pair a client-generated idempotency key with an atomic database/transaction check—not a separate read-then-write.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Idempotency And Deduplication before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Attempt 1 inserts `(key, payload_hash, status='IN_PROGRESS')` in Postgres. Attempt 2 hits the unique key while `IN_PROGRESS` and receives `409 Conflict` (`Retry-After: 2`). Attempt 1 commits the ledger row and updates the idempotency record to `status='COMPLETED', response_code=201, response_body=...`. Attempt 3 reads the completed record and replays the exact `201 Created` JSON without charging the card again.

concepts.name: Immutable Infrastructure

relationships.description: Connects Immutable Infrastructure to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Servers, containers, and OS images are never patched or reconfigured in place; every change triggers a fresh build, test, and atomic replacement of running instances.

spark.summary: Servers, containers, and OS images are never patched or reconfigured in place; every change triggers a fresh build, test, and atomic replacement of running instances.
spark.keyTakeaway: Replace, don't repair: baking artifacts once into versioned images eliminates configuration drift, snowflakes, and partial-upgrade outages.

concept.whyItMatters: Mutable fleets accumulate undocumented hotfixes, stale libraries, and divergent kernel states over months of SSH sessions and Ansible runs. Immutable infrastructure moves mutation to build time so production nodes are disposable, byte-identical replicas of a tested artifact.
whenToUse: Auto-scaling cloud fleets (AWS ASG, GCP MIG, Kubernetes) where nodes are frequently created and destroyed under load.
Regulated or security-sensitive environments requiring reproducible SBOMs, cryptographic image signing (Cosign/AMI), and 24-hour CVE rebuild SLAs.
Multi-region deployments where identical runtime behavior across US-East, EU-Central, and AP-South is mandatory.
whenNotToUse: Stateful single-node databases (PostgreSQL primary, bare-metal Ceph OSDs) where destroying the host risks petabyte-scale data movement.
Bare-metal or legacy on-prem hardware without PXE/iPXE automated provisioning or API-driven hypervisors.
Early-stage local prototyping where 10-minute Packer AMI bake cycles slow down tight edit-compile-debug loops.
keyPoints: Build-time mutation only: tools like Packer, Docker BuildKit, or Nix bake OS packages, binaries, and systemd units into a sealed artifact.
Read-only runtime filesystems: distributions like Bottlerocket and Talos Linux mount `/` as read-only SquashFS protected by dm-verity, blocking runtime tampering.
Instance metadata and env injection: immutable images stay environment-agnostic by reading secrets and config at boot via IMDSv2, Vault, or Kubernetes ConfigMaps.
Atomic traffic cutover: Blue/Green or Canary rollouts drain ALB/Envoy connections from old instances only after new instances pass `/healthz`.
Digest pinning over mutable tags: deploying `sha256:9f86d08...` instead of `:latest` guarantees that a scale-out event at 03:00 boots the exact same bits.

examples.title: AWS Golden AMI Pipeline with Packer & Terraform
examples.scenario: A fintech API running 80 EC2 `c6i.xlarge` instances needs an OpenSSL security patch across three AWS regions without downtime.
examples.outcome: CI runs `packer build` to produce a hardened Ubuntu 24.04 AMI (`ami-0a91f...`), verifies it with InSpec, updates the Terraform Launch Template, and triggers an ASG Instance Refresh (`MinHealthyPercentage=90`) that replaces all 80 nodes in 18 minutes with zero SSH access.

examples.title: Kubernetes Cluster Upgrade on Talos Linux
examples.scenario: Platform engineering must upgrade 45 bare-metal Kubernetes worker nodes from kernel 6.1 to 6.6 while keeping latency-sensitive gRPC workloads online.
examples.outcome: Because Talos has no SSH daemon or package manager, `talosctl upgrade` streams a signed SquashFS image to the inactive A/B boot partition, cordons and drains each node via PDBs, and reboots into the verified kernel in under 90 seconds per node.

tradeOffs.pro: Rollbacks take seconds by shifting load balancer targets back to the previous ASG or ReplicaSet.
tradeOffs.con: Small config or one-line script fixes require a full image build (3–15 minutes) instead of a 5-second `scp`.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates 'works on node-04' mysteries because every instance is derived from the exact same immutable hash.
tradeOffs.con: No SSH or package tools (`tcpdump`, `strace`) in production forces teams to invest in eBPF sidecars, ephemeral debug containers, and centralized logs.

tradeOffs.pro: Predictable artifact retention with clear lineage between Git commit SHA and running AMI/container digest.
tradeOffs.con: Daily base-image rebuilds across dozens of microservices generate terabytes of EBS snapshots and ECR layers requiring lifecycle pruning.

failureModes.name: Boot-Time Cloud-Init Drift
failureModes.description: Teams leave `apt-get update && apt-get install` inside `user_data` scripts; an upstream PyPI or Ubuntu mirror outage breaks auto-scaling at peak traffic.
failureModes.mitigation: Bake 100% of OS and application dependencies into the Packer/Docker image and restrict `user_data` to fast local wiring (env vars, hostname).

failureModes.name: Mutable Tag Hijacking (`:latest`)
failureModes.description: A scale-out event pulls `:prod` after a bad push, creating a split-brain fleet running two different binary versions under the same tag.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce immutable image tags and SHA-256 digests in Kubernetes admission controllers (Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper) and Terraform.

failureModes.name: Slow Image Pulls During Traffic Spikes
failureModes.description: Bloated 4 GB container images cause `ImagePullBackOff` or 5-minute cold starts when HPA scales from 10 to 100 pods.
failureModes.mitigation: Use multi-stage distroless builds (<100 MB), pre-warm EBS snapshots (AWS Fast Snapshot Restore), or enable eStargz lazy-pulling.

failureModes.name: Stateful Data Loss on Instance Termination
failureModes.description: An engineer stores local upload caches or SQLite files on instance ephemeral NVMe; an ASG replacement silently wipes customer data.
failureModes.mitigation: Externalize all state to RDS, S3, or detached EBS/PVCs with `Retain` reclaim policies and mount root filesystems read-only.

commonMistakes: Leaving SSH port 22 open 'just in case', which inevitably tempts engineers to apply undocumented hotfixes during incidents.
Hardcoding environment-specific secrets or database URLs inside the baked image instead of injecting them at runtime.
Forgetting to configure graceful connection draining (`deregistration_delay` / `preStop` sleep), causing 502 errors during instance replacement.
Skipping automated smoke tests against the newly baked AMI before promoting its ID to production Terraform state.
Never garbage-collecting old AMIs and container layers, leading to silent AWS snapshot quota exhaustion.

sections.content:
## The idea

Traditional server management treats machines like pets: you provision an OS once, then run Chef, Puppet, or Ansible repeatedly over months to mutate packages, sysctl flags, and binaries in place. Every failed run, manual hotfix, or skipped reboot leaves behind subtle state differences—configuration drift.

Immutable infrastructure treats compute instances like cattle by splitting the lifecycle into two strict phases. In the **build phase**, a pipeline starts from a clean base, installs dependencies, compiles or copies the application, runs security scans, and seals the result into a read-only artifact (an AWS AMI, GCP Image, or OCI container digest). In the **runtime phase**, instances boot from that artifact, fetch only environment-specific configuration (via IMDS, Vault, or Kubernetes Secrets), and never accept in-place mutations. When a CVE drops or code changes, you build a new artifact, spin up fresh instances, verify health, shift traffic, and terminate the old fleet.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider releasing `checkout-api` v2.14.0 on AWS EC2:

1. **Bake & Sign**: GitHub Actions triggers `packer build` from `ubuntu-24.04-minimal`. Packer installs the compiled Go binary, configures `systemd`, applies CIS Level 1 `sysctl` hardening, removes `openssh-server`, and outputs `ami-08f3c1e2a94b7d112`.
2. **Provision**: Terraform updates `aws_launch_template.checkout` with the new AMI ID and runs `aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh` with `InstanceWarmup=120` and `MinHealthyPercentage=90`.
3. **Verify & Drain**: New instances boot, read `DB_HOST` and TLS certs from AWS Secrets Manager, and pass `GET /healthz` on port 8080. Once the ALB marks a new target healthy, it shifts traffic and sends `SIGTERM` to an old instance, waiting 30 seconds (`deregistration_delay`) for in-flight HTTP/2 requests to finish before terminating it.
4. **Rollback**: If p99 latency spikes from 40 ms to 300 ms, Terraform or the ASG reverts the Launch Template to `ami-04d2a991c...`—no reverse-Ansible playbooks required.
