concepts.tagline: OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access without sharing user passwords, using distinct grant flows tailored to confidential backends, public SPAs/mobile apps, headless devices, and service-to-service workloads. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flows in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.

spark.summary: OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access without sharing user passwords, using distinct grant flows tailored to confidential backends, public SPAs/mobile apps, headless devices, and service-to-service workloads. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flows in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) for any user-facing login and Client Credentials for machine-to-machine calls; never use Implicit or ROPC.

concept.whyItMatters: Exposing user passwords to third-party apps or storing long-lived credentials in browser JavaScript creates catastrophic blast radii. OAuth 2.0 separates authentication (often via OpenID Connect) from scoped, revocable, short-lived access tokens so compromised clients cannot take over an entire account.
whenToUse: Granting third-party or first-party web/mobile apps scoped, revocable access to user resources via `Authorization Code + PKCE`.
Authenticating backend microservices or batch jobs to internal APIs via `Client Credentials` without a human user in the loop.
Authorizing input-constrained devices (smart TVs, CLI tools) via the `Device Authorization Grant` (RFC 8628).
whenNotToUse: Using `Implicit` flow (`response_type=token`) for SPAs; it leaks access tokens in browser URL fragments, history, and Referer headers.
Using `Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC)` to collect raw user passwords in your own login form, bypassing MFA, SSO, and federated IdPs.
Treating an opaque OAuth 2.0 access token as user identity proof; use an OpenID Connect (OIDC) `id_token` or `/userinfo` endpoint for authentication.
keyPoints: PKCE (RFC 7636) binds the authorization request to the token exchange using a per-session `code_verifier` and SHA-256 `code_challenge`, preventing authorization code interception on public and confidential clients alike.
Always validate the `state` parameter (cryptographically random, bound to the user's browser session) on the `/callback` endpoint to block Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) login attacks.
Use short-lived access tokens (5–15 minutes) paired with Refresh Token Rotation (`refresh_token` invalidated on single use) and reuse detection to limit stolen token windows.
For SPAs, the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern keeps `client_secret` and refresh tokens in an HttpOnly, SameSite cookie on a confidential server rather than browser `localStorage`.
Confidential server-to-server workloads use `grant_type=client_credentials` with mTLS or `private_key_jwt` (RFC 7523) instead of static shared secrets.

examples.title: Migrating a React SPA from Implicit Flow to Auth Code + PKCE via BFF
examples.scenario: A SaaS dashboard used `response_type=token` (Implicit flow) and stored 24-hour JWTs in `localStorage`, exposing tokens to any third-party analytics XSS vulnerability.
examples.outcome: Moving token exchange into an API Gateway BFF using Authorization Code + PKCE (`S256`) and issuing `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies eliminated token exposure in browser JS and cut token lifetime to 10 minutes with silent server-side refresh.

examples.title: Headless CLI Authentication with RFC 8628 Device Flow
examples.scenario: A developer CLI tool needed to access a cloud deployment API on SSH-only Linux servers where opening a local browser redirect to `localhost:8080` failed.
examples.outcome: Implementing Device Authorization Grant (`POST /oauth/device/code`) let the CLI display an 8-character `user_code` and verification URL; the developer approved it on their laptop browser while the CLI polled `/oauth/token` every 5 seconds.

tradeOffs.pro: Direct SPA PKCE requires zero session-management backend and works with static CDN hosting.
tradeOffs.con: Tokens reside in browser memory or storage (vulnerable to XSS), whereas a BFF keeps tokens server-side behind `HttpOnly` cookies.

tradeOffs.factor: JWT Access Tokens vs. Opaque Reference Tokens
tradeOffs.pro: Self-contained JWTs allow resource servers to verify signatures (`JWKS`) locally in <1ms without calling the authorization server.
tradeOffs.con: JWTs cannot be immediately revoked before expiration without maintaining a distributed revocation list or short 5-minute TTLs.

tradeOffs.factor: Refresh Token Rotation vs. Static Refresh Tokens
tradeOffs.pro: Rotating refresh tokens on every `/token` call detects replay if either the legitimate client or an attacker reuses an old token, revoking the entire token family.
tradeOffs.con: Concurrent browser tabs racing to refresh the same token can trigger false-positive reuse revocations without a brief 5–10s grace window or single-flight lock.

failureModes.name: Authorization Code Interception
failureModes.description: On mobile or desktop apps with custom URI schemes (`myapp://callback`), a malicious app registers the same scheme and steals the `code` from the redirect.
failureModes.mitigation: Mandate PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) on the authorization server; the attacker cannot exchange the stolen `code` without the original `code_verifier`.

failureModes.name: Open Redirect & Token Leakage
failureModes.description: Wildcard `redirect_uri` matching (e.g., `https://app.example.com/*`) lets an attacker redirect the authorization code to an attacker-controlled open redirect path.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce exact byte-for-byte `redirect_uri` matching in the authorization server configuration; never allow wildcard paths or query-string prefixes.

failureModes.name: CSRF on Callback Endpoint
failureModes.description: An attacker initiates an OAuth flow with their own account and tricks a victim into visiting the attacker's `/callback?code=...` URL, binding the victim's session to the attacker's account.
failureModes.mitigation: Generate a 128-bit random `state` value stored in an `HttpOnly` cookie before redirecting, and reject any callback where `state` is missing or mismatched.

failureModes.name: Confused Deputy / Token Replay Across Audiences
failureModes.description: A resource server accepts a valid JWT issued for a different API because it only checks signature and `exp`, ignoring the `aud` (audience) and `scope` claims.
failureModes.mitigation: Validate `iss`, `aud` (must match the exact resource server identifier), `exp`, and required `scope` on every API request.

commonMistakes: Using `client_secret` inside a mobile app or SPA bundle—public clients cannot keep secrets, so any secret shipped in client code is compromised immediately.
Confusing OAuth 2.0 (authorization) with OpenID Connect (authentication) and skipping `id_token` `nonce` and `aud` validation.
Setting refresh token lifetimes to infinite without idle timeouts or rotation, leaving stolen sessions active for years.
Passing `access_token` in URL query parameters (`?access_token=...`), which leaks credentials into proxy logs, browser history, and Referer headers.
Skipping `PKCE` on confidential web servers—OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE for all Authorization Code flows to close code-injection vectors.

sections.content:
## The idea

OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is a **delegation framework**, not an authentication protocol. It defines four roles: the **Resource Owner** (user), the **Client** (app requesting access), the **Authorization Server** (IdP issuing tokens), and the **Resource Server** (API hosting protected data).

Instead of handing the Client a user's password, the Authorization Server authenticates the user on its own trusted domain, obtains consent for specific `scope` strings (e.g., `orders:read`), and issues a short-lived `access_token` to the Client. The Client presents that token as a Bearer credential (`Authorization: Bearer <token>`) to the Resource Server.

## Concrete walkthrough

Here is the exact **Authorization Code + PKCE** flow for a web or mobile client:

1. **Generate PKCE & State**: The Client generates a 64-byte random `code_verifier`, computes `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))`, and creates a random `state` token bound to the user's session.
2. **Authorization Redirect**: The Client redirects the user's browser to `GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=web-app&redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/cb&scope=openid+profile+orders:read&state=xyz&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256`.
3. **User Auth & Consent**: The Authorization Server authenticates the user (password + WebAuthn/MFA) and redirects back to `redirect_uri?code=auth_9f8a&state=xyz`.
4. **State Verification & Token Exchange**: The Client verifies `state == xyz`, then makes a back-channel `POST /oauth/token` sending `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code=auth_9f8a`, `redirect_uri`, `client_id`, and the raw `code_verifier`.
5. **PKCE Validation & Token Issue**: The Authorization Server hashes `code_verifier`, confirms it matches the stored `code_challenge`, invalidates `auth_9f8a` (single-use), and returns `{access_token (10m), refresh_token (7d), id_token}`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Choosing the right grant type and OIDC layering
sections.content:
## Choosing the right grant type and OIDC layering

OAuth 2.1 consolidates the specification around four surviving patterns:

- **Authorization Code + PKCE**: Mandatory for all interactive user flows (confidential web backends, SPAs, native mobile).
- **Client Credentials (`grant_type=client_credentials`)**: For service-to-service calls with no user context. Prefer `private_key_jwt` (signed JWT assertion) or mTLS over static `client_secret` strings.
- **Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628)**: For CLI tools, smart TVs, and IoT devices lacking a browser.
- **Refresh Token Grant**: Silent renewal of short-lived access tokens; pair with **DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession, RFC 9449)** when sender-constraining tokens is required.

**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** sits cleanly on top of OAuth 2.0 by adding the `openid` scope, returning a signed JWT `id_token` containing `sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nonce` so the Client knows *who* logged in.

## OAuth 2.0 grant flow comparison

| Grant Flow | Client Type | User Involved? | Primary Mechanism | Status in OAuth 2.1 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Auth Code + PKCE** | Confidential & Public | Yes | Temp `code` + SHA-256 `code_verifier` | **Recommended default** |
| **Client Credentials** | Confidential (Backend) | No | `client_id` + `private_key_jwt` / mTLS | **Recommended for M2M** |
| **Device Authorization** | Input-constrained | Yes (2nd device) | `device_code` polling + `user_code` | **Supported (RFC 8628)** |
| **Implicit (`token`)** | Public (Legacy SPA) | Yes | Access token in URL `#fragment` | **Removed / Deprecated** |
| **ROPC (`password`)** | First-party legacy | Yes | Raw username & password to `/token` | **Removed / Deprecated** |

## Failure modes

**1. Missing `aud` Validation in Multi-Tenant APIs**: If Service A and Service B share the same IdP, a token minted for `aud: service-a` with `scope: read` can be replayed against Service B unless Service B explicitly rejects tokens whose `aud` claim does not include `service-b`.

**2. Refresh Token Race Conditions**: In SPAs making 5 parallel API calls when a 10-minute access token expires, all 5 requests may try to use the same single-use `refresh_token`. Request #1 succeeds and rotates the token; Requests #2–#5 trigger reuse detection and revoke the user's entire session.

**3. `alg: none` or Key Confusion Attacks**: Weak JWT libraries that trust the unverified token header's `alg` field can be tricked into accepting unsigned tokens or verifying RS256 public keys as HS256 HMAC secrets.

## Production hardening & token lifecycle

Hardening an OAuth 2.0 deployment requires defense-in-depth across client and server:

- **Pin Algorithms & Keys**: Resource servers should hardcode allowed signing algorithms (e.g., `RS256` or `ES256`), cache IdP JWKS keys with `kid` lookup, and reject `alg=none`.
- **Single-Flight Refresh**: Wrap client-side token refresh in a mutex/promise queue so concurrent 401 responses share one `/oauth/token` call.
- **Sender-Constrained Tokens**: For high-security financial APIs (FAPI 2.0), bind tokens to the client's TLS certificate (mTLS `cnf.x5t#S256`) or ephemeral keypair (DPoP) so stolen Bearer tokens cannot be replayed from another host.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Require `code_challenge_method=S256` (PKCE) on all Authorization Code grants; disable Implicit and ROPC.
- [ ] Register exact `redirect_uri` values with no wildcards or open redirects.
- [ ] Generate and verify a cryptographic `state` parameter (and `nonce` for OIDC `id_token`) per login.
- [ ] Keep access token TTLs to 5–15 minutes and enable refresh token rotation with reuse detection.
- [ ] Validate `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `alg`, and `scope` on every Resource Server endpoint.
- [ ] Use a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) with `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookies for browser SPAs.

interviewProblems.title: OAuth2 Authorization Flows
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on OAuth2 Authorization Flows. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access without sharing user passwords, using distinct grant flows tailored to confidential backends, public SPAs/mobile apps, headless devices, and service-to-service workloads. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flows in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Authorization Server applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Resource Server (API).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Resource Server (API) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Mandate PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) on the authorization server; the attacker cannot exchange the stolen `code` without the original `code_verifier`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) for any user-facing login and Client Credentials for machine-to-machine calls; never use Implicit or ROPC.
Avoid trap: Using `client_secret` inside a mobile app or SPA bundle—public clients cannot keep secrets, so any secret shipped in client code is compromised immediately.
Avoid trap: Confusing OAuth 2.0 (authorization) with OpenID Connect (authentication) and skipping `id_token` `nonce` and `aud` validation.
When to reach for it: Granting third-party or first-party web/mobile apps scoped, revocable access to user resources via `Authorization Code + PKCE`.
When to reach for it: Authenticating backend microservices or batch jobs to internal APIs via `Client Credentials` without a human user in the loop.

putItTogether.title: Putting Oauth2 Authorization Flows Together
putItTogether.summary: Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) for any user-facing login and Client Credentials for machine-to-machine calls; never use Implicit or ROPC.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Oauth2 Authorization Flows before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Moving token exchange into an API Gateway BFF using Authorization Code + PKCE (`S256`) and issuing `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies eliminated token exposure in browser JS and cut token lifetime to 10 minutes with silent server-side refresh.

concepts.name: Observability-Driven Testing

relationships.description: Connects Observability-Driven Testing to contract testing in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Observability-driven testing (ODT) instruments tests and production traffic with structured traces, logs, and metrics so assertions verify internal distributed execution paths rather than just final HTTP status codes. It bridges pre-merge integration suites and controlled production experiments like canary analysis and chaos engineering.

spark.summary: Observability-driven testing (ODT) instruments tests and production traffic with structured traces, logs, and metrics so assertions verify internal distributed execution paths rather than just final HTTP status codes. It bridges pre-merge integration suites and controlled production experiments like canary analysis and chaos engineering.
spark.keyTakeaway: Emit OpenTelemetry trace context (`traceparent`) from every integration and E2E test so failures link directly to the exact microservice span, SQL query, or async consumer that broke—and reuse those same SLO telemetry queries to gate production canaries.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional assertions (`assert response.status_code == 200`) miss silent partial failures—like a dropped Kafka event, a cache stampede, or an N+1 query regression that doubles p99 latency. ODT turns rich telemetry into verifiable test assertions and extends verification into production safely.
whenToUse: Testing asynchronous, event-driven, or microservice architectures (Kafka/SQS pipelines, saga orchestrators) where final state is eventual and black-box HTTP checks are flaky.
Gating progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) using automated canary analysis against real latency, error, and saturation SLIs.
Validating resilience under fault injection (Chaos Mesh, Gremlin, Toxiproxy) by asserting that circuit breakers, retries, and fallbacks fire as instrumented.
whenNotToUse: Pure unit tests of deterministic in-memory business logic or math functions—telemetry instrumentation adds unnecessary setup overhead over fast unit assertions.
Teams lacking basic structured logging or distributed tracing in staging/prod; ODT requires consistent OpenTelemetry context propagation first.
Replacing contract testing (Pact) or static type checking; ODT verifies runtime behavior, not compile-time schema compatibility.
keyPoints: Propagate W3C `traceparent` headers from test runners (Playwright, pytest, JUnit) into backend services and message brokers so each test run produces one unified distributed trace.
Assert on trace spans and structured events (e.g., `assert span('payment.charge').attributes['retry_count'] == 0` or `db.query_count <= 5`) using tools like Tracetest or Malabi.
Separate **synthetic test traffic** (`baggage: test_run_id=...`) from real user SLIs so load/chaos tests do not pollute production error budgets.
Use feature flags + dynamic telemetry sampling (100% head/tail sampling for `test_run_id` headers) to capture full forensic traces on flaky or failing tests.
Extend ODT to production via **Testing in Production**: shadow traffic, dark launches, and automated canary rollbacks driven by Prometheus/Datadog/Honeycomb queries.

examples.title: Catching Silent N+1 Queries in CI with Trace-Based Assertions
examples.scenario: An e-commerce checkout API passed all functional integration tests (`201 Created`), yet every deploy risked introducing ORM lazy-loading regressions that spiked RDS CPU in production.
examples.outcome: Adding Tracetest assertions on the CI OpenTelemetry trace (`span[db.system=postgresql].count <= 6` and `duration < 45ms` for a 5-item cart) caught two N+1 regressions before merge without writing brittle SQL mock assertions.

examples.title: Automated Canary Gating with Argo Rollouts & Prometheus
examples.scenario: A search ranking service deployed 6 times daily; manual dashboard watching during 10% canaries missed a 2x tail-latency regression on cold cache keys.
examples.outcome: Wiring an Argo Rollouts `AnalysisTemplate` to query `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` and `5xx` error rates every 60s for 10 minutes automatically aborted bad rollouts within 3 minutes and linked the failing `trace_id` to Slack.

tradeOffs.factor: Trace-Based Assertions vs. Mocked Unit Tests
tradeOffs.pro: Tests real serialization, network headers, SQL plans, and async broker handoffs with zero mock drift.
tradeOffs.con: Slower execution (seconds vs. milliseconds) and requires an ephemeral OTel collector/backend (Jaeger, Tempo, or Honeycomb) in CI.

tradeOffs.factor: 100% Test Trace Capture vs. Storage Cost
tradeOffs.pro: Tail-based or header-triggered sampling (`test_run_id` present) guarantees zero missing spans when debugging a rare race condition.
tradeOffs.con: High-volume load tests with 100% tracing enabled can overwhelm OTel Collector memory or blow through vendor ingest quotas.

tradeOffs.factor: Testing in Production (Canaries) vs. Staging-Only Gates
tradeOffs.pro: Exposes real data distributions, DNS/TLS quirks, and third-party API latency that staging mocks never reproduce.
tradeOffs.con: Requires strict blast-radius controls (1%–5% traffic splits, synthetic test accounts, idempotent mutations) to protect real users.

failureModes.name: Broken Context Propagation Across Async Queues
failureModes.description: A Kafka or SQS producer omits `traceparent` in message headers, splitting one test trace into disconnected orphan traces and causing trace assertions to time out.
failureModes.mitigation: Use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation for Kafka/SQS/RabbitMQ headers and add a CI smoke check verifying parent-child `trace_id` continuity across async boundaries.

failureModes.name: Async Span Flush Race in Short-Lived Tests
failureModes.description: The test runner queries Jaeger/Tempo 100ms after the HTTP response returns, before the service's `BatchSpanProcessor` (default 5s delay) flushes spans.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure shorter flush intervals (`OTEL_BSP_SCHEDULE_DELAY=500`) in test environments and poll the trace backend with exponential backoff up to 5–10 seconds.

failureModes.name: Test Traffic Polluting Production SLOs
failureModes.description: Synthetic E2E or chaos tests running against production trigger false-positive PagerDuty alerts and burn real customer error budgets.
failureModes.mitigation: Tag all synthetic traffic with `synthetic=true` in OTel baggage/attributes and filter `synthetic!="true"` out of all SLO burn-rate and alerting queries.

failureModes.name: Brittle Span Name Coupling
failureModes.description: Tests assert on exact internal function names or auto-generated span strings that break whenever a developer refactors a private helper.
failureModes.mitigation: Assert on stable OpenTelemetry semantic conventions (`http.status_code`, `db.operation`, `messaging.destination.name`) and explicit domain span names.

commonMistakes: Relying on `sleep(5)` in async tests instead of polling the trace/telemetry backend for the expected completion span.
Allowing the OpenTelemetry `BatchSpanProcessor` to drop spans silently under CI load without checking `otelcol_exporter_send_failed_spans`.
Running chaos experiments without defining steady-state telemetry hypotheses (e.g., error rate < 0.5%, fallback hit rate > 99%) beforehand.
Instrumenting only HTTP ingress and ignoring downstream database, Redis, and third-party webhook spans.
Leaving 100% debug trace sampling enabled in load tests, crashing the OTel Collector with OOMKills.

sections.content:
## The idea

Traditional testing treats a distributed system like a black box: send an input, wait, and assert on the output. When a 6-service workflow fails—or succeeds slowly because of 40 redundant database queries—black-box tests either miss the regression entirely or fail with an unhelpful timeout.

**Observability-driven testing (ODT)** flips the model to white-box runtime verification. It uses the same **OpenTelemetry (OTel)** traces, structured logs, and metrics that power production debugging as **first-class test assertions** in CI and **automated quality gates** during progressive production rollouts.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an async order-fulfillment flow (`POST /orders` -> Order Service -> Kafka `orders.created` -> Inventory Service -> Postgres) tested in CI with Tracetest and OpenTelemetry:

1. **Inject Trace Context**: The test runner generates `traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01` (sampling flag `01` forces 100% capture) and sends `POST /orders`.
2. **Propagate Across Boundaries**: Order Service records an HTTP server span, writes to Postgres, and injects `traceparent` into the Kafka message headers before returning `202 Accepted`.
3. **Async Worker Execution**: Inventory Service consumes the Kafka event, extracts `traceparent` as its parent span, reserves stock in Postgres, and emits its own spans to the OTel Collector.
4. **Query & Assert on Telemetry**: After `202 Accepted`, the test runner polls Tempo/Jaeger by `trace_id` (`4bf92f35...`). It asserts: (a) `POST /orders` status == `202`, (b) Kafka consumer span `inventory.reserve` completed with `status.code == OK`, (c) total `db.system=postgresql` spans <= 4, and (d) end-to-end trace duration < 250ms.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Span assertions, chaos verification, and canary analysis
sections.content:
## Span assertions, chaos verification, and canary analysis

ODT spans three operational stages:

1. **CI Trace Assertions**: Validate internal invariants—no unindexed full-table scans (`db.rows_examined`), zero unexpected retries, and exact event fan-out counts.
2. **Chaos & Fault-Injection Verification**: Tools like Chaos Mesh or Toxiproxy inject 300ms network latency or kill a Redis pod while tests assert that the `resilience4j.circuitbreaker` span transitions to `OPEN` and serves cached fallback data within 50ms.
3. **Progressive Production Verification**: Argo Rollouts or Flagger shifts 5% of live traffic to the canary and runs PromQL/Honeycomb queries comparing canary vs. baseline `http_server_duration_p99` and `5xx` rate, auto-promoting or rolling back without human intervention.

## Traditional testing vs. observability-driven testing

| Dimension | Traditional Black-Box Testing | Observability-Driven Testing (ODT) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Signal** | HTTP response body & status code | Full OTel trace tree, span attributes, & SLIs |
| **Async / Event Workflows** | Fragile `sleep()` or DB polling loops | Deterministic polling on downstream consumer spans |
| **Performance Regressions** | Caught late in separate load tests | Caught per-PR via `db.query_count` & span duration |
| **Failure Triage** | Grep container logs to guess cause | Direct deep-link to failing `trace_id` & exact span |
| **Production Coverage** | Stops at pre-prod staging | Extends to automated canary & chaos verification |

## Failure modes

**1. High-Cardinality Label Explosion from Test Runs**: Putting a unique `test_run_id` into a Prometheus metric label (`http_requests_total{test_run_id="..."}`) creates millions of time series and OOMs Prometheus. Always put `test_run_id` in **trace attributes and structured logs**, never in Prometheus metric labels.

**2. Telemetry Pipeline Lag Causing Flaky CI**: If the CI OTel Collector buffers batches for 5–10 seconds, trace assertions fail intermittently. Use an in-memory or fast-flush collector config (`send_batch_size: 100`, `timeout: 200ms`) in CI.

**3. False Confidence from Unrepresentative Synthetic Data**: Canaries with low traffic (<10 req/min) lack statistical power for p99 comparisons; pair canary gating with synthetic probe traffic or minimum sample thresholds.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Integrating ODT into CI/CD and production
sections.content:
## Integrating ODT into CI/CD and production

To adopt ODT incrementally without rewriting existing suites:

- **Week 1 (Context Propagation)**: Add OTel SDKs and pass `traceparent` from Playwright/API tests; print the Jaeger/Tempo trace URL on any test failure.
- **Week 2 (Invariant Assertions)**: Add 3–5 high-value trace assertions on critical checkout/auth flows (max DB queries, zero `ERROR` spans, required async consumer completion).
- **Week 3 (Canary Gating)**: Reuse those exact PromQL/OTel queries in Argo Rollouts `AnalysisTemplate` so pre-prod and prod share one source of truth.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Propagate W3C `traceparent` and `baggage` across HTTP, gRPC, and message brokers (Kafka/SQS).
- [ ] Force sampling (`sampled=1`) on CI and synthetic test requests; exclude `synthetic=true` from prod SLOs.
- [ ] Never attach unbounded `test_run_id` values to Prometheus metric labels (use trace/log attributes only).
- [ ] Tune CI `BatchSpanProcessor` flush delay to `<= 500ms` to avoid assertion race conditions.
- [ ] Assert on semantic attributes (`db.system`, `http.status_code`, `rpc.grpc.status_code`) rather than private function names.
- [ ] Gate production canaries with automated SLI queries (p99 latency, 5xx rate, saturation) for 5–15 minutes.

interviewProblems.title: Observability-Driven Testing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Observability-Driven Testing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Observability-driven testing (ODT) instruments tests and production traffic with structured traces, logs, and metrics so assertions verify internal distributed execution paths rather than just final HTTP status codes. It bridges pre-merge integration suites and controlled production experiments like canary analysis and chaos engineering.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: OTel Collector + Tempo applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Assertion / Canary Gate.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Assertion / Canary Gate experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation for Kafka/SQS/RabbitMQ headers and add a CI smoke check verifying parent-child `trace_id` continuity across async boundaries.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Emit OpenTelemetry trace context (`traceparent`) from every integration and E2E test so failures link directly to the exact microservice span, SQL query, or async consumer that broke—and reuse those same SLO telemetry queries to gate production canaries.
Avoid trap: Relying on `sleep(5)` in async tests instead of polling the trace/telemetry backend for the expected completion span.
Avoid trap: Allowing the OpenTelemetry `BatchSpanProcessor` to drop spans silently under CI load without checking `otelcol_exporter_send_failed_spans`.
When to reach for it: Testing asynchronous, event-driven, or microservice architectures (Kafka/SQS pipelines, saga orchestrators) where final state is eventual and black-box HTTP checks are flaky.
When to reach for it: Gating progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) using automated canary analysis against real latency, error, and saturation SLIs.

putItTogether.title: Putting Observability Driven Testing Together
putItTogether.summary: Emit OpenTelemetry trace context (`traceparent`) from every integration and E2E test so failures link directly to the exact microservice span, SQL query, or async consumer that broke—and reuse those same SLO telemetry queries to gate production canaries.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Observability Driven Testing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Adding Tracetest assertions on the CI OpenTelemetry trace (`span[db.system=postgresql].count <= 6` and `duration < 45ms` for a 5-item cart) caught two N+1 regressions before merge without writing brittle SQL mock assertions.

concepts.name: Observability Golden Signals

relationships.description: Connects Observability Golden Signals to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: The Four Golden Signals—Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation—form the minimal, high-signal metric foundation for monitoring any user-facing distributed system. Measuring them with histograms (not averages) and separating successful vs. failed request latencies exposes tail regressions and capacity cliffs before outages hit.

spark.summary: The Four Golden Signals—Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation—form the minimal, high-signal metric foundation for monitoring any user-facing distributed system. Measuring them with histograms (not averages) and separating successful vs. failed request latencies exposes tail regressions and capacity cliffs before outages hit.
spark.keyTakeaway: Instrument every service boundary with Prometheus/OTel histograms for Latency (p50/p95/p99, splitting 2xx from 5xx), Traffic (RPS), Errors (explicit + policy), and Saturation (the tightest resource bottleneck)—and alert on SLO error-budget burn rates rather than raw CPU spikes.

concept.whyItMatters: Dashboards crammed with 80 infrastructure graphs hide the few symptoms users actually feel. The Four Golden Signals (from Google's SRE handbook) give on-call engineers an immediate triage framework: if you can only measure four things on a service, measure these four.
whenToUse: Designing baseline SLIs, SLOs, and executive health dashboards for any HTTP, gRPC, or streaming microservice.
Triaging live incidents to isolate whether degradation stems from downstream latency, traffic surges, code errors, or resource exhaustion.
Building multi-window, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts that page humans only when user-facing error budgets are genuinely threatened.
whenNotToUse: Debugging a single user's failed request or pinpointing which line of code threw an exception—use distributed traces and structured logs for root cause.
Monitoring offline batch/ETL jobs where throughput, queue age, and completion freshness matter more than interactive request latency.
Replacing business KPIs (checkout conversion, payment authorization rate), which complement technical signals.
keyPoints: **Latency**: Track request duration using histograms (e.g., `http_server_request_duration_seconds`) and report p50, p95, and p99—never averages, which mask 10-second tail stalls. Always separate fast-failing `5xx` error latency from successful `2xx` latency.
**Traffic**: Measure demand in domain-appropriate units—requests per second (RPS) for APIs, messages/sec for Kafka consumers, or active concurrent sessions for WebSockets.
**Errors**: Capture explicit failures (`5xx`, uncaught exceptions), implicit failures (`200 OK` with an empty or stale payload), and policy failures (rate-limit `429` or SLA violations > 1,000ms).
**Saturation**: Measure how full your most constrained resource is *before* it hits 100%—thread pool utilization, DB connection pool wait queue, JVM heap after GC, or CPU CFS throttling.
Pair the Golden Signals with **USE** (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for hardware/infrastructure and **RED** (Rate, Errors, Duration) for request-driven microservices.

examples.title: Separating 5xx Error Latency Exposes Hidden Checkout Stall
examples.scenario: A checkout API's blended p99 latency dropped from 240ms to 90ms during an outage, confusing on-call engineers because a broken Redis connection was failing fast in 2ms with `500` errors.
examples.outcome: Splitting `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` by `status_class="2xx"` vs. `"5xx"` immediately revealed that `2xx` p99 had actually spiked to 1,800ms on fallback DB queries while `5xx` fast-fails skewed the blended curve.

examples.title: Catching Connection Pool Saturation Before 503 Outage
examples.scenario: Service CPU sat at a healthy 35%, yet every afternoon at peak traffic the API started timing out.
examples.outcome: Tracking HikariCP `hikaricp_connections_pending` (Saturation) showed the 20-connection DB pool hitting 100% utilization and queuing threads 15 minutes before `504` errors appeared, prompting pool sizing and slow-query tuning.

tradeOffs.factor: Native Histograms vs. Fixed Bucket Histograms
tradeOffs.pro: Fixed Prometheus buckets (`le="0.1", "0.25", "0.5", "1.0"`) are universally supported, while OTel exponential/native histograms preserve accurate p99 across shifting scales without manual bucket tuning.
tradeOffs.con: Over-specified fixed buckets (`20+` buckets x high-cardinality labels) multiply time-series cardinality by 20x.

tradeOffs.factor: Symptom-Based SLO Alerts vs. Cause-Based Resource Alerts
tradeOffs.pro: Alerting on Golden Signal SLO burn rate (Latency + Errors) cuts false-positive pages by 70%+ because high CPU without latency/error impact doesn't wake engineers.
tradeOffs.con: Rapidly growing saturation (e.g., disk filling at 92%) still needs a proactive warning ticket before it causes an abrupt 100% error cliff.

tradeOffs.pro: Server-side metrics are cheap and always available, while client/synthetic RUM metrics capture DNS, TLS, and CDN latency invisible to origin pods.
tradeOffs.con: Client-side telemetry is noisy across user networks and cannot observe internal microservice saturation.

failureModes.name: Averaging Latency Hides Tail Outages
failureModes.description: Reporting `avg(duration)` shows 45ms even when 2% of requests (all mobile checkouts) time out at 10,000ms.
failureModes.mitigation: Export HDR/Prometheus histograms and compute `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` and `0.99` over `rate(...[5m])`.

failureModes.name: Silent 200 OK Implicit Errors
failureModes.description: A degraded recommendation engine returns `HTTP 200` with an empty JSON array `[]`; `5xx` error rate stays at `0.0%` while conversion plummets.
failureModes.mitigation: Emit explicit domain error/fallback counters (`recommendation_fallback_total{reason="timeout"}`) and include them in the service's Error SLI.

failureModes.name: High-Cardinality Label Explosion
failureModes.description: Adding `user_id`, `request_id`, or unnormalized URL paths (`/users/12345`) to Golden Signal metrics crashes Prometheus/Mimir.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict metric labels to bounded dimensions (`service`, `route_template`, `method`, `status_class`); keep `user_id` and `trace_id` in traces/logs or exemplars.

failureModes.name: Averaging Across Multi-Pod Saturation
failureModes.description: Alerting on cluster-wide average CPU (40%) misses one hot shard or single-threaded Node.js/Python worker pinned at 100% CPU.
failureModes.mitigation: Aggregate saturation using `max()` or `p99()` across pods (`max(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total)`) rather than cluster `avg()`.

commonMistakes: Computing client-side quantiles (`Summary` metrics) on individual pods and then averaging them across pods in Grafana—quantiles cannot be averaged mathematically.
Grouping `4xx` client typos (`404`, `400`) into server error alerts, causing noisy pages whenever a bot scrapes invalid URLs.
Using CPU utilization as the sole Saturation metric while ignoring memory pressure, disk IOPS, Kafka consumer lag, and thread/connection pool queues.
Setting static thresholds (`latency > 200ms for 1m`) instead of multi-window SLO burn-rate alerts (`14.4x` burn over 5m/1h).
Missing Prometheus **exemplars** on latency histograms, forcing engineers to hunt manually for a `trace_id` during a p99 spike.

sections.content:
## The idea

Coined in Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* book, the **Four Golden Signals** define the essential telemetry needed to understand user experience and system headroom: **Latency**, **Traffic**, **Errors**, and **Saturation**.

Instead of building dashboards around arbitrary internal counters, Golden Signals organize monitoring around **external symptoms** (Latency, Traffic, Errors) and **leading capacity indicators** (Saturation). When Latency or Errors degrade, Traffic and Saturation immediately tell you *why*—whether a sudden 3x traffic spike pushed the database pool to 100% saturation, or a bad deploy introduced `500` errors at flat traffic.

## Concrete walkthrough

Here is how a payment API instrumented with **OpenTelemetry** and **Prometheus** exposes and correlates all four signals during a flash sale:

1. **Traffic**: `sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service="payments"}[1m]))` jumps from 1,200 RPS to 4,800 RPS.
2. **Saturation**: `max(hikaricp_connections_active / hikaricp_connections_max)` hits `1.0` (100%), and `hikaricp_connections_pending` climbs from 0 to 140 queued threads.
3. **Latency**: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{status_class="2xx"}[2m])))` degrades from 45ms to 1,400ms as threads wait for DB connections.
4. **Errors**: Requests exceeding the 2,000ms gateway timeout fail with `504`; `sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{status_class="5xx"}[1m])) / sum(rate(...[1m]))` crosses 2.5%, triggering a fast-burn SLO page with a linked Grafana **exemplar** `trace_id` pointing straight to `hikaricp.acquire`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Mapping Golden Signals to RED and USE
sections.content:
## Mapping Golden Signals to RED and USE

Two popular mnemonics operationalize the Four Golden Signals depending on the layer:

- **RED Method (Request-driven services)**: **R**ate (Traffic), **E**rrors, **D**uration (Latency). Ideal for microservices, API gateways, and serverless functions. It omits Saturation because container orchestrators often surface saturation separately.
- **USE Method (Infrastructure resources)**: **U**tilization (% busy), **S**aturation (queue depth/throttling), **E**rrors (hardware/dropped packets). Ideal for CPUs, NVMe disks, network interfaces, Kubernetes nodes, and DB connection pools.

Together, **RED + Saturation** gives you the complete Four Golden Signals.

## Golden Signals reference specification

| Signal | What to Measure | Preferred Metric Type | Key Pitfall to Avoid |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Latency** | `p50`, `p95`, `p99` request duration (`2xx` vs `5xx`) | Histogram / Native Histogram | Averaging latency or mixing fast `5xx` errors with `2xx` |
| **Traffic** | RPS, Kafka msgs/sec, active streams | Counter (`rate()`) | Counting health-check `/healthz` pings in user traffic |
| **Errors** | `5xx`, policy rejections, silent fallbacks | Counter (`rate()` ratio) | Paging on client `404`s or ignoring `200` empty responses |
| **Saturation** | Pool queue depth, CFS CPU throttle, lag | Gauge / Histogram | Watching cluster-wide avg CPU instead of `max()` per pod |

## Failure modes

**1. Low-Traffic Alert Flapping**: At 2 AM when traffic drops to 0.5 RPS, two transient network blips yield a 10% error rate for 2 minutes. Without minimum-sample gating or multi-window burn rates (`1h` + `5m`), on-call gets woken up for a non-incident.

**2. Healthcheck Pollution**: Load balancer `/healthz` probes (every 2s from 20 nodes) inflate Traffic and artificially lower p99 Latency if not excluded via `route!="/healthz"`.

**3. Metric Scrape Gaps**: If a service's `/metrics` endpoint blocks on a slow lock or exceeds Prometheus `scrape_timeout` (default 10s), all four signals go blank right when the service is most saturated.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / From Golden Signals to SLO burn-rate alerting
sections.content:
## From Golden Signals to SLO burn-rate alerting

Raw threshold alerts (`p99 > 500ms`) cause pager fatigue. Instead, convert Latency and Errors into **SLIs** (e.g., `99.9%` of requests `< 300ms` and non-`5xx` over 30 days = `43.2m` monthly error budget) and alert using Google SRE's multi-window burn-rate pattern:

- **Page (Urgent)**: `14.4x` burn rate over both `1h` AND `5m` windows (burns 2% of monthly budget in 1 hour).
- **Page (High)**: `6x` burn rate over both `6h` AND `30m` windows (burns 5% of monthly budget in 6 hours).
- **Ticket (Low)**: `1x`–`3x` burn rate over `3d` / `6h`—investigate during business hours.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Instrument every service with OTel/Prometheus histograms for Latency, splitting `2xx` and `5xx`.
- [ ] Exclude `/healthz` and `/metrics` from Traffic, Latency, and Error SLIs.
- [ ] Bound all metric labels (`service`, `route_template`, `status_class`); ban `user_id` or raw URLs.
- [ ] Monitor Saturation on the tightest bottleneck (DB pool pending, Kafka lag, CPU throttling) using `max()`.
- [ ] Enable Prometheus **exemplars** on latency/error histograms to link directly to distributed traces.
- [ ] Replace static threshold pages with multi-window SLO burn-rate alerts.

interviewProblems.title: Observability Golden Signals
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Observability Golden Signals. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The Four Golden Signals—Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation—form the minimal, high-signal metric foundation for monitoring any user-facing distributed system. Measuring them with histograms (not averages) and separating successful vs. failed request latencies exposes tail regressions and capacity cliffs before outages hit.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: SLO Burn-Rate Rules applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Grafana + On-Call.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Grafana + On-Call experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Export HDR/Prometheus histograms and compute `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` and `0.99` over `rate(...[5m])`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Instrument every service boundary with Prometheus/OTel histograms for Latency (p50/p95/p99, splitting 2xx from 5xx), Traffic (RPS), Errors (explicit + policy), and Saturation (the tightest resource bottleneck)—and alert on SLO error-budget burn rates rather than raw CPU spikes.
Avoid trap: Computing client-side quantiles (`Summary` metrics) on individual pods and then averaging them across pods in Grafana—quantiles cannot be averaged mathematically.
Avoid trap: Grouping `4xx` client typos (`404`, `400`) into server error alerts, causing noisy pages whenever a bot scrapes invalid URLs.
When to reach for it: Designing baseline SLIs, SLOs, and executive health dashboards for any HTTP, gRPC, or streaming microservice.
When to reach for it: Triaging live incidents to isolate whether degradation stems from downstream latency, traffic surges, code errors, or resource exhaustion.

putItTogether.title: Putting Observability Golden Signals Together
putItTogether.summary: Instrument every service boundary with Prometheus/OTel histograms for Latency (p50/p95/p99, splitting 2xx from 5xx), Traffic (RPS), Errors (explicit + policy), and Saturation (the tightest resource bottleneck)—and alert on SLO error-budget burn rates rather than raw CPU spikes.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Observability Golden Signals before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Splitting `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` by `status_class="2xx"` vs. `"5xx"` immediately revealed that `2xx` p99 had actually spiked to 1,800ms on fallback DB queries while `5xx` fast-fails skewed the blended curve.

concepts.name: On-Call Escalation Policies

relationships.description: Connects On-Call Escalation Policies to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: On-call escalation defines deterministic routing, acknowledgment SLAs, and tiered handoffs so production incidents reach the right responder fast without burning out engineers. Effective escalation pairs automated multi-channel paging (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with explicit severity tiers, Incident Commander (IC) roles, and blameless post-incident feedback loops.

spark.summary: On-call escalation defines deterministic routing, acknowledgment SLAs, and tiered handoffs so production incidents reach the right responder fast without burning out engineers. Effective escalation pairs automated multi-channel paging (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with explicit severity tiers, Incident Commander (IC) roles, and blameless post-incident feedback loops.
spark.keyTakeaway: Keep Tier-1 pages strictly actionable with a 5-minute acknowledgment timeout before escalating to a secondary, separate the Incident Commander from hands-on debuggers on SEV-1/SEV-2, and enforce a 48-hour SLA to fix or delete any noisy alert.

concept.whyItMatters: Even the most resilient architecture fails unexpectedly. Without clear escalation paths, critical outages stall in unmonitored Slack channels for 40 minutes while the wrong team guesses who owns a failing database or payment gateway—multiplying customer impact and engineer burnout.
whenToUse: Operating 24/7 production services with explicit availability SLOs (99.9%+) where delayed human intervention violates customer SLAs.
Scaling beyond a single 6-person team into multi-team microservice ownership where incidents cross network, database, and application boundaries.
Formalizing SEV-1/SEV-2 incident command, executive stakeholder updates, and customer status-page communications.
whenNotToUse: Non-urgent warnings (disk at 75%, staging test failures, dependency deprecation notices)—route these to Jira/Linear tickets or async Slack digests, never pages.
Replacing automated self-healing (Kubernetes liveness probes, autoscaling, circuit breakers) with human toil.
Paging teams for services they did not build and have no code/config authority to fix or roll back.
keyPoints: **Clear Ownership & Service Catalog**: Every alert must map to a single owning team in Backstage/PagerDuty with a runbook URL; unowned alerts are a production bug.
**Timed Multi-Layer Escalation**: Level 1 (Primary) gets 5 minutes to ACK via push/SMS/voice; on timeout, page Level 2 (Secondary), then Level 3 (Engineering Manager / Domain Lead) at 15 minutes.

**Severity-Driven Mobilization**: Define objective SEV-1 (total outage/data loss), SEV-2 (partial degradation/SLO burn), and SEV-3 (minor/workaround) criteria so responders know immediately whether to open a war room.

**Role Separation (ICS)**: On SEV-1/SEV-2, appoint an **Incident Commander (IC)** to coordinate timelines, communications, and parallel tracks while Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) focus purely on mitigation.
**Alert Hygiene & Toil Caps**: Track pages per shift; if an on-call engineer receives >2–3 non-actionable pages per week, treat alert tuning as P0 engineering work.

examples.title: Cutting Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA) from 22m to 3m via Tiered Escalation
examples.scenario: A fintech platform routed all alerts into a shared `#prod-alerts` Slack channel; a midnight Redis failover sat unseen for 22 minutes because engineers muted Slack overnight.
examples.outcome: Migrating critical SLO burn alerts to PagerDuty with a 5-minute push-to-phone-call escalation and automatic fallback to the Secondary + Platform Lead cut MTTA to 2.8 minutes and eliminated missed pages.

examples.title: Stopping Cross-Team Ping-Pong with IC Role & Service Graph
examples.scenario: During a SEV-1 checkout outage, Frontend blamed API Gateway, Gateway blamed Auth, and no one checked the shared RDS connection pool for 35 minutes.
examples.outcome: Introducing a mandatory SEV-1 Incident Commander (IC) rotation plus PagerDuty's service-dependency graph let the IC pull in the DB and Auth SMEs into one Zoom bridge within 4 minutes and resolve the pool exhaustion in 12 minutes.

tradeOffs.factor: Fast Escalation Timeout (3–5m) vs. Longer Window (15m)
tradeOffs.pro: A 5-minute ACK timeout ensures sleeping or commuting engineers don't delay SEV-1 recovery.
tradeOffs.con: Too short a timeout (<2m) double-pages the secondary responder while the primary is simply unlocking their phone or laptop.

tradeOffs.factor: Dedicated SRE On-Call vs. 'You Build It, You Run It'
tradeOffs.pro: Product engineers fixing their own pages feel immediate pain from flaky deploys and fix root causes 3x faster.
tradeOffs.con: Small product teams (<4 engineers) suffer severe burnout on 24/7 rotations without follow-the-sun pairing or shared platform tiers.

tradeOffs.factor: Automated War-Room Creation vs. Manual Triage
tradeOffs.pro: Tools like Incident.io or FireHydrant auto-create a Slack channel, Zoom link, Jira ticket, and status page draft in <10 seconds.
tradeOffs.con: Auto-declaring full war rooms on noisy SEV-3 alerts creates alarm fatigue; reserve auto-bridging for SEV-1/SEV-2.

failureModes.name: Alert Fatigue & Pager Desensitization
failureModes.description: High-volume, non-actionable pages (e.g., transient CPU spikes that self-recover in 90s) train engineers to blindly ACK pages and go back to sleep.
failureModes.mitigation: Delete or downgrade any alert that doesn't require immediate human action; require every page to link to a tested runbook.

failureModes.name: Single-Point-of-Failure Hero Dependency
failureModes.description: Every hard database or Kubernetes incident escalates informally to one senior staff engineer who isn't even on rotation, leading to burnout and knowledge silos.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce shadow shifts for new engineers, document tribal knowledge in runbooks during postmortems, and rotate IC duties.

failureModes.name: Notification Pipeline Blindness
failureModes.description: An AWS region outage knocks out your self-hosted Alertmanager or Slack webhook, so nobody gets paged during the biggest outage of the year.
failureModes.mitigation: Host alerting/paging on an independent SaaS or separate region (PagerDuty, Opsgenie) and run a continuous 'dead man's switch' heartbeat check (e.g., Healthchecks.io).

failureModes.name: Missing Handoff Context Across Shifts
failureModes.description: An ongoing SEV-2 incident is handed off at 9 AM without summarizing mitigated symptoms, active feature flags, or pending rollbacks, causing the incoming shift to repeat work.
failureModes.mitigation: Mandate a structured 5-minute shift handoff template (Active Incidents, Silenced Alerts, Deployed Mitigations, Next Check-in).

commonMistakes: Creating alerts without a `runbook_url`—forcing a half-asleep engineer at 3 AM to read source code to figure out what a metric means.
Routing pages solely to Slack or email instead of phone/SMS/high-priority push notifications that bypass Do Not Disturb.
Allowing a single engineer to act as both Incident Commander and sole hands-on debugger during a multi-team SEV-1.
Skipping blameless postmortems or failing to track action items to completion, guaranteeing the same outage repeats next quarter.
Keeping a 2-person or 3-person 24/7 rotation—anything under 6–8 engineers guarantees chronic sleep deprivation and attrition.

sections.content:
## The idea

**On-call escalation** is the human-routing state machine that sits behind your monitoring stack. When an automated system cannot self-heal an SLO violation, escalation ensures the alert reaches an empowered engineer within minutes, provides immediate diagnostic context, and—if that engineer is unavailable or overwhelmed—automatically widens the circle to backups, adjacent service owners, and an Incident Commander (IC).

Good escalation optimizes two metrics simultaneously: **Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA)** for customers, and **sleep/cognitive load preservation** for engineers.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a 02:14 AM SEV-1 payment gateway degradation from alert firing to resolution:

1. **Trigger & Deduplicate (02:14)**: Prometheus/Alertmanager fires `PaymentsHighErrorBurn` (`14.4x` SLO burn) and groups 12 related pod alerts into one PagerDuty incident with `runbook_url` and Grafana dashboard links.
2. **Level 1 Page (02:14–02:19)**: PagerDuty pushes a critical alert (bypassing iOS/Android DND) to Primary On-Call A. No ACK arrives within 5 minutes.
3. **Level 2 Escalation (02:19)**: PagerDuty automatically escalates to Secondary On-Call B via SMS + voice call. B ACKs at 02:20 (`MTTA = 6m`), opens the linked runbook, and sees upstream Stripe webhook timeouts + elevated DB locks.
4. **SEV-1 Mobilization (02:23)**: B runs `/incident declare sev1` in Slack (Incident.io), auto-paging the **Incident Commander (IC)** rotation and opening `#inc-412-payments` + a Zoom bridge.
5. **Parallel Mitigation (02:25–02:38)**: The IC assigns B to roll back the 01:50 deploy while paging the Database On-Call to inspect lock contention, updating the external status page every 15 minutes until SLO burn drops to 0.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Designing escalation policies and ICS roles
sections.content:
## Designing escalation policies and ICS roles

A resilient escalation policy separates **initial triage** from **major incident command**:

- **4-Tier Escalation Ladder**: L1 Primary (0–5m) -> L2 Secondary (5–10m) -> L3 Team Lead/EM (10–20m) -> L4 VP/On-Call Director (20m+).
- **Incident Command System (ICS) Roles**: For SEV-1/SEV-2, assign: (1) **Incident Commander** (owns decisions and coordination, never touches terminals), (2) **Operations / Tech Lead** (directs SMEs and rollbacks), and (3) **Communications Lead** (updates Statuspage and customer support).
- **Follow-the-Sun Rotations**: Split 24-hour coverage across 2–3 geographic hubs (e.g., US-West, EU, APAC) with 8–12 hour day shifts so engineers rarely wake up at 3 AM.

## Incident severity & escalation matrix

| Severity | Customer Impact Criteria | Page Urgency | Required Roles | Status Update Cadence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SEV-1** | Full outage, data loss, or security breach | Immediate 24/7 (5m ACK) | IC + Ops + Comms + SMEs | Every 15–30 min |
| **SEV-2** | Major feature degraded or >5% error SLO burn | Immediate 24/7 (5m ACK) | IC + Service Owner | Every 60 min |
| **SEV-3** | Minor impact with automated/manual workaround | Business hours / Slack | Single On-Call Engineer | Daily / at resolution |
| **SEV-4** | Cosmetic bug or staging failure | Ticket only (no page) | Product backlog | Normal sprint triage |

## Failure modes

**1. Escalation Loop / Dead-End Schedules**: An engineer leaves the company and their PagerDuty user is deactivated, leaving a gap in the rotation where pages drop or loop endlessly. Audit rotations automatically via CI/Terraform (`pagerduty_schedule`) synced to HR/Okta groups.

**2. Over-Escalation to Executives Too Early**: Paging VPs at minute 5 on every transient alert trains leadership to ignore pages and intimidates junior responders.

**3. Postmortem Without Alert Cleanup**: Teams write thorough 5-page postmortems on the root cause while leaving the 40 noisy alerts that masked the real signal untouched.

## Measuring & sustaining healthy on-call rotations

Track operational health metrics for your on-call program just like service SLOs:

- **Target Toil Budget**: <= 2 off-hours pages per 7-day shift per engineer. Any alert firing >2x/week without a code/config fix is auto-reviewed.
- **GameDays**: Run quarterly Chaos/GameDay drills during business hours (e.g., terminating a primary AZ or injecting DNS failure) to verify escalation paths, runbook accuracy, and IC handoffs before a real 2 AM outage.
- **Compensatory Time Off**: Provide automatic recovery time after disruptive overnight SEV-1 responses to prevent cumulative burnout.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Maintain at least 6–8 engineers per 24/7 rotation (or use follow-the-sun regional handoffs).
- [ ] Configure 5-minute L1 -> L2 -> L3 escalation timeouts with push, SMS, and voice fallback.
- [ ] Require `runbook_url`, severity, and owning team metadata on 100% of paging alerts.
- [ ] Separate Incident Commander (coordination) from SMEs (mitigation) on all SEV-1/SEV-2 events.
- [ ] Run an external dead-man's-switch heartbeat monitor to detect broken alerting pipelines.
- [ ] Review page volume weekly and delete or fix any non-actionable alert within 48 hours.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on On-Call Escalation Policies. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: On-call escalation defines deterministic routing, acknowledgment SLAs, and tiered handoffs so production incidents reach the right responder fast without burning out engineers. Effective escalation pairs automated multi-channel paging (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with explicit severity tiers, Incident Commander (IC) roles, and blameless post-incident feedback loops.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Level 2: Secondary / SME applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SEV-1 Incident Commander.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SEV-1 Incident Commander experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Delete or downgrade any alert that doesn't require immediate human action; require every page to link to a tested runbook.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Keep Tier-1 pages strictly actionable with a 5-minute acknowledgment timeout before escalating to a secondary, separate the Incident Commander from hands-on debuggers on SEV-1/SEV-2, and enforce a 48-hour SLA to fix or delete any noisy alert.
Avoid trap: Creating alerts without a `runbook_url`—forcing a half-asleep engineer at 3 AM to read source code to figure out what a metric means.
Avoid trap: Routing pages solely to Slack or email instead of phone/SMS/high-priority push notifications that bypass Do Not Disturb.
When to reach for it: Operating 24/7 production services with explicit availability SLOs (99.9%+) where delayed human intervention violates customer SLAs.
When to reach for it: Scaling beyond a single 6-person team into multi-team microservice ownership where incidents cross network, database, and application boundaries.

putItTogether.title: Putting On Call Escalation Together
putItTogether.summary: Keep Tier-1 pages strictly actionable with a 5-minute acknowledgment timeout before escalating to a secondary, separate the Incident Commander from hands-on debuggers on SEV-1/SEV-2, and enforce a 48-hour SLA to fix or delete any noisy alert.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for On Call Escalation before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Migrating critical SLO burn alerts to PagerDuty with a 5-minute push-to-phone-call escalation and automatic fallback to the Secondary + Platform Lead cut MTTA to 2.8 minutes and eliminated missed pages.

concepts.name: Onion Architecture

relationships.description: Connects Onion Architecture to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.

spark.summary: An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.
spark.keyTakeaway: Isolate your core business logic from Spring, SQLAlchemy, or Kafka by defining repository and gateway interfaces inside the domain/application ring and implementing them in the outermost infrastructure ring.

concept.whyItMatters: In traditional N-tier architectures, business services directly import ORM entities and database clients, coupling domain rules to schema quirks and framework lifecycles. When you upgrade Hibernate, swap PostgreSQL for DynamoDB, or test complex pricing rules, you end up booting a 6-second application context or mocking SQL cursors. Onion Architecture inverts those dependencies so pure domain logic compiles and runs in under 15 milliseconds with zero I/O.
whenToUse: Core business domains with rich invariants, state machines, or regulatory rules (e.g., billing ledgers, underwriting, order fulfillment) that outlive web frameworks.
Long-lived services where swapping persistence engines, message brokers, or external vendor APIs (e.g., Stripe to Adyen) must not require rewriting business logic.
Teams that want fast, deterministic unit tests for 80%+ of their codebase without spinning up Docker/Testcontainers for every rule variation.
whenNotToUse: Simple CRUD microservices, admin backends, or BFFs where 90% of the code is validating JSON and writing rows to a single table.
Short-lived prototypes, hackathons, or early-stage MVPs where mapping between domain objects, DTOs, and ORM models slows down iteration.
Read-heavy reporting or analytics pipelines (e.g., dbt, Spark jobs) whose primary job is executing set-based SQL transformations rather than enforcing entity invariants.
keyPoints: The Dependency Rule is absolute: source code dependencies may only point inward toward the Domain Model; inner rings never import classes from outer rings.
The Domain Model ring holds pure entities, value objects, and domain events with zero framework annotations (no `@Entity`, `@Column`, or `@Autowired`).
The Domain Services and Application Services rings orchestrate use cases and define output ports (interfaces like `PaymentGateway` or `OrderRepository`).
The Infrastructure and UI rings sit on the outside, implementing those ports with concrete adapters (JPA, jOOQ, gRPC, Kafka consumers, FastAPI routers).
Boundary enforcement should be automated in CI using tools like ArchUnit (Java) or import-linter (Python) so accidental outer-ring imports fail the build.

examples.title: Payment Ledger Migration from MySQL/JPA to CockroachDB
examples.scenario: A fintech ledger service originally coupled Hibernate `@Entity` classes directly to settlement rules. Moving to multi-region CockroachDB required changing transaction retry semantics and primary key generation.
examples.outcome: After refactoring to Onion Architecture, settlement invariants lived in pure Java `LedgerEntry` aggregates while `JpaLedgerRepository` implemented a `LedgerRepository` port. Swapping in a jOOQ-based CockroachDB adapter took 4 days with zero changes to the 340 domain unit tests.

examples.title: ArchUnit Guardrails in a Spring Boot Order Service
examples.scenario: As an e-commerce team grew from 6 to 30 engineers, developers began injecting `RestTemplate` and `KafkaTemplate` directly into domain calculators, causing 9-second test boots and circular dependencies.
examples.outcome: Adding an ArchUnit `onionArchitecture()` check in Gradle CI rejected 14 PRs that leaked `org.springframework` or `jakarta.persistence` into `..domain..`, cutting the core test suite runtime from 42 seconds to 1.8 seconds.

tradeOffs.pro: Domain logic stays completely portable and free of ORM lazy-loading surprises or framework magic.
tradeOffs.con: Requires explicit mappers between domain aggregates, persistence entities, and API DTOs—adding 15–25% more files per feature.

tradeOffs.pro: In-memory fakes implementing repository ports run thousands of business-rule tests in milliseconds.
tradeOffs.con: Mocks and fakes can drift from real SQL constraints (unique indexes, lock behavior), so contract tests against real DBs are still mandatory.

tradeOffs.pro: Write-side aggregates enforce strict transactional consistency without leaking SQL into domain rules.
tradeOffs.con: Complex paginated reads or joins feel awkward through pure repository ports and often need a dedicated CQRS read-model bypass.

failureModes.name: Anemic Domain Model
failureModes.description: Engineers strip behavior out of domain entities into giant Application Services, leaving entities as dumb getter/setter bags while duplicating validation across use cases.
failureModes.mitigation: Push invariant checks and state transitions (`order.confirm()`, `wallet.debit(amount)`) directly onto domain aggregates and keep Application Services thin.

failureModes.name: Leaky ORM Abstractions
failureModes.description: Putting `@Entity` or `@JsonProperty` annotations on domain classes or returning Hibernate `PersistentBag` proxies from repositories ties domain behavior to an active DB session.
failureModes.mitigation: Maintain separate persistence models in the infrastructure package and map explicitly at the repository boundary.

failureModes.name: Mapping Fatigue & N+1 Regressions
failureModes.description: Blindly loading full aggregate graphs through generic `findById()` ports for simple read endpoints causes severe N+1 query storms.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Onion Architecture for command/write paths and allow slim, read-only query projections (CQRS) that map SQL rows straight to response DTOs.

failureModes.name: Architectural Drift in Growing Teams
failureModes.description: Without automated checks, urgent hotfixes introduce direct imports from `infrastructure` into `domain`, silently collapsing the onion back into a big ball of mud.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce ring boundaries in CI with ArchUnit (`Architectures.onionArchitecture()`) or Python `import-linter` contracts.

commonMistakes: Confusing runtime call flow with compile-time dependency direction—outer controllers call inner services, but inner services depend only on interfaces.
Creating a 1:1 `IRepository` interface for every database table instead of designing ports around aggregate roots.
Putting transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`) inside domain entities instead of wrapping use cases in the Application Service or an outer decorator.
Over-abstracting standard library utilities (e.g., wrapping `java.time.Clock` is useful for tests, wrapping `StringUtils` is pure noise).
Using MapStruct or reflection mappers blindly across boundaries, hiding missing fields until runtime.

sections.content:
## The idea

Coined by Jeffrey Palermo in 2008, **Onion Architecture** solves a recurring rot in layered N-tier systems: the database sits at the bottom of the dependency graph, so every layer above it—business logic, services, and UI—transitively couples to SQL schemas and ORM frameworks.

Onion Architecture flips the graph using the **Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)**. Instead of the domain depending on a `PostgresOrderRepository`, the inner rings define an `OrderRepository` interface (port), and the outer infrastructure ring provides `PostgresOrderRepository` (adapter). Everything compiles from the outside in, while the core remains pure language primitives and domain types.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an e-commerce `PlaceOrder` use case handling inventory reservation and payment capture:

1. **UI / Web Ring (`OrderController`)**: Deserializes the HTTP `POST /orders` payload into a `PlaceOrderCommand` and invokes `PlaceOrderUseCase.execute(cmd)`.
2. **Application Service Ring (`PlaceOrderUseCase`)**: Starts a transaction boundary, loads the `Cart` via the `CartRepository` interface, and calls `Order.createFrom(cart)`.
3. **Domain Model Ring (`Order`, `Money`)**: Pure Java/Python objects verify that `cart.items()` is non-empty, compute totals using `Money` value objects, and transition status to `PENDING_PAYMENT`.
4. **Infrastructure Ring (`JpaOrderRepository`, `StripePaymentAdapter`)**: Implements the interfaces defined inside the application/domain rings, translating `Order` into a `orders` table row and calling Stripe's `/v1/payment_intents` API.

data.title: Inward Dependency Direction vs. Runtime Execution Flow

edges.label: 1. Dispatch Command
edges.title: Controller invokes Use Case
edges.description: Maps JSON request to a framework-free PlaceOrderCommand and calls the application service.

edges.label: 2. Enforce Invariants
edges.title: Execute pure domain logic
edges.description: Domain aggregate validates line items, discounts, and state transitions with zero I/O.

edges.label: 3. Call Port Interface
edges.title: Polymorphic dispatch to adapter
edges.description: Application service calls OrderRepository.save(), which routes at runtime to the Postgres adapter.

edges.label: 4. Implements Port (DIP)
edges.title: Compile-time inward dependency
edges.description: Infrastructure imports the Application/Domain port interface; the domain never imports SQL or Stripe.

edges.label: 5. Return Result DTO
edges.title: Return outcome to caller
edges.description: Returns OrderId and status without leaking JPA entities or internal exceptions to the HTTP layer.

data.caption: Runtime control flows from UI through Application Services to Infrastructure adapters, while compile-time source dependencies point strictly inward toward the Domain Model.

sections.content:
## Anatomy of the four rings

Each ring has a strict boundary on what it may import:

- **Domain Model (Center)**: Entities, Value Objects, Aggregates, and Domain Events. Allowed imports: language standard library only.
- **Domain Services**: Stateless business logic spanning multiple aggregates (e.g., currency conversion policies or FX spread calculations).
- **Application Services**: Use-case orchestrators (`PlaceOrderUseCase`), transaction coordination, and output port interfaces (`OrderRepository`, `EventPublisher`).
- **Infrastructure & UI (Outer)**: Web controllers, CLI handlers, JPA/SQLAlchemy repositories, Kafka producers, and DI wiring (`Spring @Configuration` or FastAPI `Depends`).

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Onion vs. Layered vs. Hexagonal vs. Clean
sections.content:
## Onion vs. Layered vs. Hexagonal vs. Clean

| Dimension | Classic N-Tier | Onion Architecture | Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) | Clean Architecture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dependency Direction** | Top-down (UI -> Biz -> DB) | Strictly inward toward Domain | Symmetric inward toward Core | Strictly inward toward Entities |
| **Core Organizing Unit** | Database tables & services | Domain Model & Services | Application Core + Ports | Entities & Use Case Interactors |
| **Framework Coupling** | High (ORM leaks into services) | Zero in inner 3 rings | Zero inside hexagon | Zero inside Entities/Use Cases |
| **Primary Strength** | Fast initial CRUD scaffolding | Rich domain modeling (DDD) | Clean I/O & protocol swapping | Explicit use-case boundaries |
| **CI Enforcement Tooling** | Rarely enforced | ArchUnit `onionArchitecture()` | ArchUnit / import-linter | ArchUnit / module boundaries |

## Failure modes

1. **Bypassing Reads Through Heavy Aggregates**: Fetching a 12-table aggregate just to render a 3-column summary table kills DB performance. Keep Onion ports for write commands and allow a direct read-only query service for dashboards.
2. **Framework Annotations Creeping Inward**: Adding `@Transactional`, `@Validated`, or `@Entity` into the domain package defeats portability and reintroduces 5-second test boots.
3. **Leaky Exceptions**: Letting `PSQLException` or `DataIntegrityViolationException` bubble uncaught through a repository port forces the Application Service to import database driver packages to handle unique-key conflicts; translate them into domain exceptions like `DuplicateOrderException` inside the adapter.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Enforcing boundaries with ArchUnit and Python Protocols
sections.content:
## Enforcing boundaries with ArchUnit and Python Protocols

Conventions decay unless CI rejects violations. In Java/Kotlin, **ArchUnit** provides a first-class rule:

```java
Architectures.onionArchitecture()
  .domainModels("com.acme.orders.domain.model..")
  .domainServices("com.acme.orders.domain.service..")
  .applicationServices("com.acme.orders.application..")
  .adapter("persistence", "com.acme.orders.infra.postgres..")
  .adapter("rest", "com.acme.orders.infra.web..");
```

In Python, define ports as `typing.Protocol` classes inside `domain/ports.py` and enforce unidirectional package imports in CI using `import-linter` (`type = layers`), ensuring `domain` never imports `sqlalchemy`, `fastapi`, or `boto3`.

## Practical checklist

- **Zero framework imports in `domain/`**: Verify with `grep` or ArchUnit that no ORM, HTTP, or DI annotations exist inside the domain package.
- **Separate persistence models**: Map between `Order` (domain) and `OrderJpaEntity` (infrastructure) at the repository boundary.
- **Translate infrastructure errors**: Convert SQL unique-constraint or HTTP 429 errors into domain-meaningful exceptions inside adapters.
- **Use CQRS for heavy reads**: Let read-only reporting endpoints bypass aggregate hydration via slim query projections.
- **Automate in CI**: Fail pull requests automatically on any outward dependency violation.
