concepts.tagline: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.

spark.summary: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.
spark.keyTakeaway: CPU-bound Python threads can now scale across cores without multiprocessing pickle overhead, provided C-extensions declare Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED and shared mutable state is synchronized.

concept.whyItMatters: For three decades, Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) forced CPU-bound workloads into multiprocessing—duplicating multi-gigabyte model weights or lookup tables across processes and serializing data over pipes. Free-threaded CPython (3.13t experimental, 3.14+ maturing) unlocks true multi-core shared-memory parallelism for pure Python, hybrid AI/data pipelines, and in-process request serving.
whenToUse: CPU-bound pure-Python workloads (parsing, validation, AST transforms, simulations) that previously required multiprocessing.
Multi-threaded services sharing large read-only or concurrent in-memory structures (4+ GB embeddings, feature tables, caches) without IPC serialization.
Mixed I/O + CPU pipelines where asyncio or thread pools process payloads in-process without spawning worker subprocesses.
whenNotToUse: Single-threaded scripts or latency-sensitive single-core loops where the ~5-10% atomic/biased-refcount overhead of 3.13t slows execution.
Workloads relying on legacy C-extensions that have not declared Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED, which silently re-enable the GIL at import time.
Purely I/O-bound workloads (HTTP/DB fan-out) where asyncio already handles 10,000+ concurrent sockets with lower memory per task than OS threads.
keyPoints: PEP 703 replaces the GIL with Biased Reference Counting (BRC), mimalloc per-thread heaps, and stop-the-world cyclic GC.
Single-threaded execution in Python 3.13t carries roughly 5-10% overhead compared to standard GIL builds due to thread-safe refcounting and specialized bytecode.
Built-in containers (list, dict, set) remain memory-safe via per-object critical sections, but compound read-modify-write operations still require explicit locks.
Importing any C-extension without Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED (or without PYTHON_GIL=0) automatically re-enables the GIL at runtime with a warning.
Immortal objects (PEP 683) for None, True, False, small ints, and interned strings avoid cross-thread reference count contention.

examples.title: Shared 4 GB Lookup Table Across 16 Worker Threads
examples.scenario: A feature-enrichment service previously ran 16 multiprocessing workers, each holding a copy of a 4 GB dictionary (64 GB total RSS) and paying ~120 MB/s pickle IPC tax.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Python 3.13t ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) shares one 4.2 GB in-memory dictionary across all 16 threads, cutting RAM by ~93% and achieving a 10.5x CPU speedup.

examples.title: Silent GIL Re-Activation by Legacy C-Extension
examples.scenario: A team deploys a multi-threaded image-metadata pipeline on python3.13t, but imports an unpatched C-based XML parser without checking sys._is_gil_enabled().
examples.outcome: CPython logs a RuntimeWarning and re-enables the GIL at import time, collapsing 8-core throughput back to 1 core until the extension is updated or isolated.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates N-process memory duplication and pickle serialization overhead for shared in-memory data.
tradeOffs.con: Incurs ~5-10% single-thread CPU overhead in 3.13t due to biased refcounting and critical-section checks.

tradeOffs.pro: Per-object critical sections prevent interpreter segfaults on concurrent list/dict access.
tradeOffs.con: Application-level race conditions (e.g., d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1) now surface as real data races if unguarded.

tradeOffs.pro: Core libraries like NumPy, Cython, PyTorch, and Cryptography are actively adopting Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED.
tradeOffs.con: Long-tail C-extensions using global C state or borrowed references can crash or force GIL fallback.

failureModes.name: Silent GIL Fallback on Import
failureModes.description: Importing a C-extension without Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED re-enables the global lock mid-process, eliminating multi-core scaling.
failureModes.mitigation: Assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False in startup health checks and run CI with PYTHON_GIL=0 to catch incompatible extensions.

failureModes.name: Lost-Update Data Races
failureModes.description: Code like counter += 1 or cache[k] += 1 relied accidentally on the GIL's bytecode-switch atomicity and now loses updates under parallel threads.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap compound read-modify-write invariants in threading.Lock or use queue.Queue for producer-consumer handoffs.

failureModes.name: Stop-the-World GC Tail Latency
failureModes.description: Cyclic garbage collection pauses all Python threads simultaneously to trace object graphs safely.
failureModes.mitigation: Avoid reference cycles in hot worker loops, pool long-lived objects, and monitor GC pause durations.

failureModes.name: False Sharing on Shared Counters
failureModes.description: Multiple threads mutating adjacent objects or shared global counters bounce CPU L1/L2 cache lines across cores.
failureModes.mitigation: Aggregate metrics in thread-local variables (threading.local()) and merge periodically.

commonMistakes: Assuming free-threaded Python makes application code thread-safe automatically without locks around compound state mutations.
Deploying python3.13t without verifying sys._is_gil_enabled() == False after all third-party imports.
Replacing asyncio with 5,000 OS threads for network I/O, wasting ~8 MB stack virtual memory and scheduler overhead per thread.
Benchmarking only 1-thread speed and concluding nogil is slower without testing multi-core throughput.
Using global mutable caches without threading.Lock or copy-on-write snapshots.

sections.content:
## The idea

CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) existed because reference counting (`Py_INCREF` / `Py_DECREF`) is not atomic: two threads incrementing a reference count simultaneously without synchronization can corrupt memory and cause use-after-free crashes. Making every refcount an atomic CPU `LOCK XADD` instruction, however, would destroy single-threaded performance.

PEP 703 (shipping as the optional `python3.13t` build in Python 3.13 and advancing in 3.14+) solves this without tanking single-threaded speed by combining **Biased Reference Counting (BRC)**, **mimalloc** thread-safe heaps, **immortal objects** (PEP 683), and **per-object critical sections**. Each object tracks an owning thread ID: the owning thread updates its local refcount with cheap non-atomic instructions, while other threads use a separate atomic shared refcount field.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose an 8-core service runs `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)` on `python3.13t` to parse and score 100,000 JSON documents against a shared 2 GB in-memory rule graph:

1. **Startup check**: After importing dependencies, the app verifies `assert not sys._is_gil_enabled()`. All C-extensions (`orjson`, `numpy`, etc.) declare `Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED`.
2. **Thread-local allocation**: Each worker thread allocates temporary parsed dicts from its own **mimalloc** heap with zero global allocator lock contention.
3. **Immortal & biased reads**: Reads against shared `None`, `True`, small ints, and the read-only rule graph hit immortal objects (zero refcount writes) or BRC shared counters.
4. **Scaling**: Instead of 8 processes x 2 GB (`16 GB` RSS) plus `pickle` serialization overhead, the single process uses `~2.4 GB` RSS and saturates all 8 cores (~6.5x–7.2x speedup).

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Choosing between asyncio, threads (nogil), and multiprocessing
sections.content:
## Choosing between asyncio, threads (nogil), and multiprocessing

Free-threaded Python does not replace `asyncio` or `multiprocessing`—it fills the massive middle ground that used to be broken:

- **Use `asyncio`** for high-concurrency network I/O (1,000–50,000 open HTTP/WebSocket/DB connections) where memory per task (~KB) beats OS thread stacks (~MB).
- **Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` on `3.13t+`** for CPU-bound Python work, parallel inference preprocessing, and shared large read-only state.
- **Use `multiprocessing`** when you need hard fault isolation (segfaulting C libraries, OOM containment) or must run legacy C-extensions that still require the GIL.

## Python concurrency runtime comparison

| Model | CPU Scaling | Memory Sharing | Per-Worker RAM | Typical Overhead |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Standard Threads (GIL)** | 1 core (Python bytecode) | Zero-copy shared heap | ~8 MB stack | GIL contention (`sys.setswitchinterval`) |
| **Free-Threaded (`3.13t`)** | N cores (true parallel) | Zero-copy shared heap | ~8 MB stack | ~5–10% single-thread BRC overhead |
| **Multiprocessing** | N cores (OS processes) | Copy-on-write / `SharedMemory` | Full interpreter + dataset copy | `pickle` IPC (~50–200 MB/s bottleneck) |
| **Asyncio (Event Loop)** | 1 core | Zero-copy shared heap | ~2–5 KB coroutine | Blocked by any sync CPU call >1 ms |

## Failure modes

Teams migrating to `python3.13t` encounter four distinct production surprises:

- **Silent GIL re-activation**: Loading one unported `.so` wheel flips the interpreter back to GIL-enabled mode. Always verify `sys._is_gil_enabled() is False` in CI and startup probes.
- **Compound race conditions**: Statements like `if k not in cache: cache[k] = compute(k)` are no longer serialized by the GIL; two threads will both compute and overwrite.
- **C-extension segfaults**: Legacy C extensions using `PyList_GET_ITEM` borrowed references without critical sections can crash under concurrent mutation.
- **Oversubscription**: Running 32 Python threads that each call BLAS/OpenMP (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=16`) spawns 512 native threads and thrashes CPU caches.

## Safe migration strategy

Adopt free-threaded Python incrementally:

1. **Audit wheels**: Check C-extension support (NumPy, SciPy, Cython 3.1+, PyO3/Rust, Cryptography) and run test suites with `PYTHON_GIL=0`.
2. **Guard shared state**: Audit module-level globals, memoization dicts, and metrics counters; protect them with `threading.Lock` or thread-local buffers.
3. **Pin native thread pools**: Set `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` and `MKL_NUM_THREADS=1` when fanning out across Python worker threads.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Install the `t`-suffixed runtime (`python3.13t` or `python3.14t`) and verify `sys._is_gil_enabled()` returns `False`.
- [ ] Run integration tests with `PYTHON_GIL=0` so any incompatible C-extension fails loudly instead of silently re-enabling the GIL.
- [ ] Replace `multiprocessing` worker pools that share large read-only models/dicts with `ThreadPoolExecutor`.
- [ ] Audit all shared mutable dicts, counters, and lazy-init singletons for explicit `threading.Lock` protection.
- [ ] Cap `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` to avoid thread oversubscription when calling NumPy/BLAS inside Python threads.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Critical Section Lock applies the primary invariant and coordinates with STW Cyclic GC.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, STW Cyclic GC experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False in startup health checks and run CI with PYTHON_GIL=0 to catch incompatible extensions.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: CPU-bound Python threads can now scale across cores without multiprocessing pickle overhead, provided C-extensions declare Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED and shared mutable state is synchronized.
Avoid trap: Assuming free-threaded Python makes application code thread-safe automatically without locks around compound state mutations.
Avoid trap: Deploying python3.13t without verifying sys._is_gil_enabled() == False after all third-party imports.
When to reach for it: CPU-bound pure-Python workloads (parsing, validation, AST transforms, simulations) that previously required multiprocessing.
When to reach for it: Multi-threaded services sharing large read-only or concurrent in-memory structures (4+ GB embeddings, feature tables, caches) without IPC serialization.

concepts.tagline: LLM quantization compresses 16-bit model weights and KV caches into 8-bit or 4-bit representations (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) to slash VRAM usage by 2-4x and accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.

spark.summary: LLM quantization compresses 16-bit model weights and KV caches into 8-bit or 4-bit representations (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) to slash VRAM usage by 2-4x and accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.
spark.keyTakeaway: Because autoregressive LLM decode is memory-bandwidth bound at low batch sizes, moving from FP16 to INT4/FP8 cuts HBM reads per token by 2-4x while keeping accuracy loss under ~1% when activation outliers are protected.

concept.whyItMatters: A 70B-parameter LLM in FP16 consumes ~140 GB just for weights—requiring two 80 GB H100s before serving a single token—and autoregressive decoding reads all 140 GB from HBM for every single generated token. Quantization fits that 70B model onto a single 48 GB or 80 GB GPU and multiplies decode throughput by shrinking memory traffic.
whenToUse: Serving 7B-70B+ models on fewer GPUs (e.g., fitting Llama-3.1-70B INT4 onto a single 80 GB A100/H100 instead of 2x GPUs).
Accelerating memory-bandwidth-bound decode latency (tok/s per user) in interactive chat and coding copilots.
Compressing long-context KV caches with FP8 (E4M3) to double or quadruple concurrent batch size at 32k-128k context.
whenNotToUse: Tiny models (<3B parameters) running at high batch sizes on H100s where inference is already compute-bound and INT4 dequantization overhead can hurt.
Sub-4-bit (INT2 / 1.58-bit) post-training quantization on complex reasoning or multi-step code generation without quantization-aware training (QAT).
Hardware lacking native INT8/FP8 Tensor Cores or fused dequantize-GEMM kernels (e.g., older GPUs running unoptimized INT4).
keyPoints: LLM inference has two distinct phases: compute-bound prefill (processing the prompt in parallel) and memory-bandwidth-bound decode (1 token at a time).
On an H100 (3.35 TB/s HBM3), reading 140 GB (FP16) caps batch-1 decode near ~24 tok/s, whereas 35 GB (INT4) raises the bandwidth ceiling near ~95 tok/s.
Activation outliers (~1% of channels with >6.0 magnitude) break naive Round-To-Nearest (RTN) INT4; AWQ, GPTQ, and SmoothQuant preserve those salient channels.
FP8 (E4M3) on Hopper/Ada Tensor Cores delivers near-lossless (<0.2% MMLU drop) W8A8 compute speedup for both prefill and decode.
KV-cache quantization (FP8/INT8) is often just as important as weight quantization at 32k+ context lengths where KV cache dominates VRAM.

examples.title: Single-GPU 70B Serving with AWQ + FP8 KV Cache
examples.scenario: A production team needs to serve Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct with 8k context on 80 GB A100 GPUs using vLLM.
examples.outcome: Using AWQ 4-bit weights (~38 GB VRAM) and FP8 KV cache leaves ~35 GB for paged KV blocks, fitting on 1 GPU instead of 2 and cutting per-token cost by ~50% with <0.8% benchmark drop.

examples.title: Naive RTN INT4 Collapse on Structured JSON Output
examples.scenario: A team applies naive Round-To-Nearest INT4 quantization without calibration to an 8B extraction model.
examples.outcome: Unscaled activation outliers distort attention projections, spiking JSON schema parse failures from 0.4% to 11%; switching to calibrated AWQ (128 calibration samples) restores 0.5% failure rate.

tradeOffs.pro: INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ/Q4_K_M) reduces weight memory by ~3.5-4x compared to FP16.
tradeOffs.con: Requires fused dequantize-GEMM kernels (Marlin/ExLlamaV2) and risks minor reasoning degradation on edge prompts.

tradeOffs.pro: W4A16 maximizes single-user decode speed by minimizing HBM reads.
tradeOffs.con: W8A8 (FP8) uses native Tensor Cores to accelerate compute-bound prefill and high-batch throughput, which W4A16 cannot.

tradeOffs.pro: AWQ/GPTQ calibration on 128-512 domain samples preserves accuracy much better than zero-shot RTN.
tradeOffs.con: Adds a 10-45 minute offline quantization step and requires domain-representative calibration text.

failureModes.name: Outlier Channel Clipping
failureModes.description: Naive min-max quantization scales an entire weight tensor to fit one extreme outlier, crushing normal weights into 1-2 bits.
failureModes.mitigation: Use group-wise quantization (group_size=128) paired with AWQ activation scaling or SmoothQuant.

failureModes.name: Dequantization Kernel Bottleneck at High Batch
failureModes.description: W4A16 models dequantize weights to FP16 in registers; at batch=64+, compute saturates and W4A16 becomes slower than FP8 W8A8.
failureModes.mitigation: Benchmark at target concurrency (e.g., batch=32 vs batch=1) and switch to FP8 W8A8 on H100/L40S for high-batch serving.

failureModes.name: Calibration Dataset Mismatch
failureModes.description: Calibrating GPTQ exclusively on English prose degrades accuracy on SQL, Python, or multilingual prompts.
failureModes.mitigation: Include a representative mix of code, JSON, and target-language samples in the 256-sample calibration set.

failureModes.name: KV-Cache OOM Under Long Context
failureModes.description: Compressing weights from 140 GB to 35 GB still OOMs if 100 concurrent 32k-token requests allocate 60+ GB of FP16 KV cache.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable PagedAttention with FP8 KV-cache quantization (--kv-cache-dtype fp8 in vLLM).

commonMistakes: Evaluating quantized models only on WikiText perplexity instead of task-specific evals like HumanEval, GSM8K, or strict JSON schema adherence.
Using W4A16 on H100s for high-concurrency batch workloads where FP8 W8A8 delivers higher total tokens/sec.
Forgetting to quantize the KV cache when serving 32k-128k context windows.
Deploying uncalibrated RTN INT4 instead of AWQ, GPTQ, or GGUF K-quants (Q4_K_M).
Ignoring kernel support—running GPTQ without Marlin or ExLlamaV2 kernels leaves 2-3x decode speed on the table.

## The idea

Autoregressive LLM generation is split into two physically opposite regimes. **Prefill** processes all prompt tokens in parallel as large matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM), making it **compute-bound** (limited by Tensor Core TFLOPS). **Decode** generates one token per step per sequence, multiplying a thin activation vector against every weight matrix in the network—making it **memory-bandwidth bound**.

Quantization maps 16-bit floating-point numbers (`BF16`/`FP16`) onto smaller discrete grids (`FP8`, `INT8`, `INT4`) using affine scaling (`x_q = round(x / scale) + zero_point`). By shrinking weights 2x–4x, decode steps move 2x–4x fewer bytes across GPU HBM3 buses, directly multiplying tokens/sec while freeing VRAM for larger batches and longer KV caches.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose we deploy **Llama-3.1-70B** (`80 layers`, GQA `8` KV heads) on an **80 GB H100** (`3.35 TB/s` HBM3):

1. **FP16 baseline**: Weights alone require `70B * 2 bytes = 140 GB`, so it cannot fit on 1x H100. Across 2x H100s with tensor parallelism, batch-1 decode reads 140 GB/token.
2. **AWQ INT4 quantization (`group_size=128`)**: Using 256 calibration prompts, AWQ identifies the top ~1% salient weight channels (driven by large activation magnitudes) and scales them up before rounding to 4 bits. Packed weights drop to `~38 GB`.
3. **Fused Marlin kernel execution**: During decode in `vLLM`, the Marlin kernel loads packed INT4 weights from HBM (`38 GB` per pass), dequantizes them to FP16 inside GPU shared memory/registers on the fly, and multiplies against FP16 activations—cutting HBM traffic by ~3.7x.
4. **FP8 KV cache**: Enabling `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` halves KV-cache memory per token, leaving `~36 GB` for PagedAttention blocks.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Why naive rounding fails: activation outliers
sections.content:
## Why naive rounding fails: activation outliers

Transformer activations in models >6B parameters exhibit systematic **outlier features**: roughly 0.1%–1% of hidden dimensions consistently reach magnitudes 10x–100x larger than the median. Naive min-max quantization stretches the quantization grid to cover the outlier, squeezing 99% of normal values into a handful of buckets and destroying accuracy.

Modern schemes solve this in three ways:
- **LLM.int8()**: Keeps the ~0.1% outlier columns in FP16 and quantizes the remaining 99.9% to INT8.
- **SmoothQuant (W8A8)**: Migrates quantization difficulty from activations (`X`) into weights (`W`) via a diagonal scale `s`: `Y = (X diag(s)^-1)(diag(s) W)`.
- **AWQ (W4A16)**: Protects the top ~1% salient weight channels identified by activation magnitude without storing mixed-precision exceptions.

## Quantization schemes compared

| Format / Method | Bitwidth (W/A) | Memory vs FP16 | Hardware Target | Accuracy & Speed Profile |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **FP8 (E4M3)** | W8 / A8 | ~50% | H100, L40S, RTX 4090 | <0.2% drop; accelerates both prefill & decode |
| **AWQ (Marlin)** | W4 / A16 | ~28% | A100, H100, L4, 3090/4090 | <0.8% drop; fastest low-batch decode |
| **GPTQ (Marlin)** | W4 / A16 | ~28% | A100, H100, consumer GPUs | Hessian-aware rounding; strong at `group_size=128` |
| **GGUF (`Q4_K_M`)** | Mixed 4/6-bit | ~30% | Apple Silicon, CPU, llama.cpp | Mixed precision for attention/FFN sensitivity |
| **NF4 (QLoRA)** | W4 / BF16 | ~25% | Fine-tuning on 24-48 GB GPUs | Information-theoretically optimal for normal weights |

## Failure modes

Production deployments of quantized LLMs commonly fail in four ways:

- **High-batch W4A16 slowdown**: At batch sizes >32, W4A16's register dequantization adds ALU overhead that makes it *slower* than FP8 W8A8 on Hopper GPUs.
- **Silent tool-calling / JSON breakage**: Perplexity barely moves (+0.15), yet strict JSON bracket balancing or tool-argument extraction degrades noticeably on 3-bit or uncalibrated 4-bit models.
- **Missing fused kernels**: Loading a GPTQ checkpoint without `marlin` or `exllamav2` falls back to slow PyTorch dequantize-then-matmul, running slower than FP16.
- **Unquantized KV cache**: A 70B INT4 model serving 128k context still hits OOM if KV cache remains in FP16.

## How to benchmark before shipping

Never ship a quantized checkpoint on perplexity alone. Run a 3-layer gate:

1. **Task-specific evals**: Measure exact-match accuracy on your production prompts (tool calls, SQL, RAG citations) against the BF16 baseline.
2. **Throughput vs. concurrency curve**: Sweep concurrency (`1, 8, 32, 64, 128` requests) measuring Time-To-First-Token (`TTFT` p95) and Inter-Token Latency (`ITL` p95).
3. **VRAM headroom check**: Verify peak KV-cache utilization under max context length with PagedAttention enabled.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Choose **FP8 (W8A8)** on H100/L40S when serving medium-to-high batch concurrency; choose **AWQ + Marlin (W4A16)** for single-GPU 70B or low-latency decode.
- [ ] Enable **FP8 KV-cache** (`--kv-cache-dtype fp8`) for workloads with >8k average context length.
- [ ] Calibrate AWQ/GPTQ on 128–512 domain-matched samples (including code/JSON if used in production).
- [ ] Confirm fused kernels (`Marlin`, `FlashInfer`, `CUTLASS FP8`) are active in engine startup logs.
- [ ] Run end-to-end JSON schema, tool-calling, and RAG faithfulness regressions against the FP16/BF16 baseline.

concepts.name: Quorum Read/Write Tuning

relationships.description: Connects Quorum Read/Write Tuning to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Quorum tuning balances strong consistency, tail latency, and fault tolerance in replicated databases by choosing replication factor N, write quorum W, and read quorum R—where W + R > N guarantees read-your-writes overlap.

spark.summary: Quorum tuning balances strong consistency, tail latency, and fault tolerance in replicated databases by choosing replication factor N, write quorum W, and read quorum R—where W + R > N guarantees read-your-writes overlap.
spark.keyTakeaway: Tune W + R > N (typically N=3, W=2, R=2) for strong overlap, or drop to W=1 / R=1 only when you explicitly accept stale reads and asynchronous read-repair.

concept.whyItMatters: Every distributed datastore without a single strict leader (Dynamo, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak) forces an explicit per-query trade-off between consistency, availability, and p99 latency. Misconfigured quorums either cause silent lost updates and stale reads when W + R <= N, or trigger avoidable outages during rolling restarts when W or R is set too high.
whenToUse: Tuning Dynamo-style leaderless databases (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB-like architectures) per workload using N, W, and R.
Balancing p99 read/write latency against durability in multi-AZ or multi-region clusters (LOCAL_QUORUM vs EACH_QUORUM).
Designing degraded-mode fallback policies when a datacenter loses one or more replica nodes.
whenNotToUse: Consensus-backed strongly linearizable databases (etcd, CockroachDB, Spanner) where Raft/Paxos mandates majority (floor(N/2)+1) and cannot be weakened per-query.
Single-node databases or strict primary-standby setups without multi-replica quorum routing.
Transactional multi-key ACID workflows where leaderless LWW (Last-Write-Wins) quorums still allow write skew without lightweight transactions.
keyPoints: Strict overlap requires W + R > N so at least one replica in the read quorum holds the latest acknowledged write.
Preventing concurrent write conflicts requires W > N / 2; otherwise two disjoint write quorums can succeed simultaneously.
For N=3, QUORUM (W=2, R=2) tolerates 1 node failure for both reads and writes while capping tail latency at the 2nd-fastest replica.
W + R > N does not guarantee linearizability in Dynamo/Cassandra without monotonic clocks or Paxos/LWT, because partial writes can still leak to subsequent reads.
Background repair (read repair, hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy) is mandatory to heal lagging replicas even under strict quorums.

examples.title: Cassandra Session Store: N=3, LOCAL_QUORUM (W=2, R=2)
examples.scenario: A user-profile service stores sessions in a 3-AZ Cassandra cluster (N=3) and needs to survive a single-AZ maintenance restart without stale reads.
examples.outcome: With W=2 and R=2 (2+2 > 3), 1 down node causes zero errors, p99 latency tracks the 2nd-fastest AZ (~4 ms), and read-your-writes holds.

examples.title: Flash-Sale Degradation Trap: Dropping to W=1, R=1
examples.scenario: To shave 3 ms off checkout latency, a team switches an inventory counter from QUORUM to ONE (W=1, R=1) with N=3.
examples.outcome: Because 1 + 1 <= 3, readers hit stale replicas before async replication arrives, overselling limited stock and losing updates under LWW clock skew.

tradeOffs.pro: Higher W and R (e.g., W=2, R=2 for N=3) enforce overlapping quorums and immediate read-repair on digest mismatch.
tradeOffs.con: Wait time is bounded by the W-th or R-th slowest replica instead of the fastest replica (W=1/R=1).

tradeOffs.pro: Increasing N from 3 to 5 with W=3, R=3 survives 2 simultaneous node failures (1 planned + 1 crash).
tradeOffs.con: Increases storage footprint by 67% and cross-node write amplification.

tradeOffs.pro: EACH_QUORUM guarantees every datacenter sees writes before acknowledgment.
tradeOffs.con: Adds full cross-region RTT (~70-150 ms) to every write and fails writes if any remote DC loses quorum.

failureModes.name: Sloppy Quorum Stale Read
failureModes.description: When hinted handoff accepts writes on non-home nodes during a partition, a strict R quorum on home nodes misses the hinted write.
failureModes.mitigation: Disable sloppy quorums for strongly consistent workloads and rely on strict home-replica quorums.

failureModes.name: NTP Clock Skew Under Last-Write-Wins (LWW)
failureModes.description: A node with a clock skewed +500 ms ahead wins every LWW tie-break, silently dropping newer writes from other coordinators.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce tight NTP/chrony sync, use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC), or use Paxos/LWT for contended keys.

failureModes.name: Partial Write Leakage (Non-Linearizable Read)
failureModes.description: A write fails after updating 1 of 2 required replicas (returning an error to the client), yet a subsequent R=2 read sees and repairs that partial write.
failureModes.mitigation: Document that W+R>N gives eventual/read-your-writes only for acknowledged writes; use LWT/Raft if atomic rollback is required.

failureModes.name: Hinted Handoff Storm on Recovery
failureModes.description: A node down for >3 hours exceeds max_hint_window_in_ms, or floods the cluster with gigabytes of replayed hints upon rejoin.
failureModes.mitigation: Run scheduled incremental Merkle-tree repairs (nodetool repair) within gc_grace_seconds and throttle hint replay.

commonMistakes: Assuming W + R > N alone provides strict serializability/linearizability in leaderless LWW stores.
Using N=3, W=3, R=1 for write-heavy durability without realizing a single dead node halts 100% of writes.
Using ALL in multi-AZ clusters, turning any single-node GC pause into a cluster-wide p99 spike or outage.
Skipping periodic anti-entropy repairs, leading to 'zombie deletes' when tombstones expire past gc_grace_seconds.
Choosing EACH_QUORUM for writes when LOCAL_QUORUM + async cross-DC replication meets business RPO.

sections.content:
## The idea

In a leaderless replicated store (popularized by Amazon's Dynamo paper and implemented in Apache Cassandra and ScyllaDB), every key is replicated across `N` nodes. Rather than locking all `N` replicas, a coordinator fans out reads and writes in parallel and returns as soon as `W` (write quorum) or `R` (read quorum) replicas acknowledge.

By the pigeonhole principle, if **`W + R > N`**, any read quorum of size `R` must intersect any write quorum of size `W` in at least one node. That overlapping node carries the highest timestamped value, allowing the coordinator to return fresh data and trigger **read repair** on stale replicas.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a write followed by a read on a **Cassandra `N=3, W=2, R=2` (`QUORUM`)** cluster:

1. **Write (`W=2`)**: Client sends `UPDATE balance = 500 (ts=102)` to the coordinator. The coordinator forwards the mutation to replicas `R1`, `R2`, and `R3`.
2. **Quorum satisfied**: `R1` (`2 ms`) and `R2` (`4 ms`) persist to commitlog + memtable and ack. `R3` is experiencing a `40 ms` GC pause. The coordinator returns `200 OK` to the client at `4 ms`.
3. **Read (`R=2`)**: Another client reads `balance` with `R=2`. The coordinator requests the full row from `R1` and a cryptographic digest from `R3` (optimizing bandwidth).
4. **Digest mismatch & read repair**: `R1` has `ts=102 (500)` while `R3` has `ts=101 (400)`. The digests mismatch. The coordinator fetches full data from both, returns `500` (`ts=102`) to the client, and issues an async read-repair write (`ts=102`) to heal `R3`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Why W + R > N is not full linearizability
sections.content:
## Why W + R > N is not full linearizability

A common misconception is that `W + R > N` makes a Dynamo/Cassandra cluster linearizable. Two subtleties break linearizability:

1. **Failed-write leakage**: If a write updates `R1` and then times out before reaching `R2`, the client receives a `WriteTimeoutException`. However, `R1` still holds the new value; a later `R=2` read hitting `R1` and `R3` will return—and repair—the "failed" write.
2. **Concurrent write races**: Without Paxos/Raft (`SERIAL` / `LOCAL_SERIAL`), two concurrent writers rely on physical wall-clock LWW timestamps, which can invert ordering under NTP drift.

## Common quorum profiles (N=3 and N=5)

| Profile | N / W / R | Tolerated Failures (W / R) | Tail Latency | Best Workload Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Balanced Quorum** | `3 / 2 / 2` | 1 / 1 | 2nd-fastest of 3 | General OLTP, user profiles, sessions |
| **Read-Optimized** | `3 / 3 / 1` | 0 / 2 | Fastest of 3 (reads) | Read-heavy catalogs where write downtime is rare |
| **Write-Optimized** | `3 / 1 / 3` | 2 / 0 | Fastest of 3 (writes) | High-ingest telemetry that tolerates slow/brittle reads |
| **Eventual Fast** | `3 / 1 / 1` | 2 / 2 | Fastest of 3 | Append-only logs, metrics, non-critical caches |
| **High-Resilience** | `5 / 3 / 3` | 2 / 2 | 3rd-fastest of 5 | Survives 1 planned maintenance + 1 sudden crash |

## Failure modes

Quorum systems degrade in four predictable ways:

- **Rolling-restart outage on `W=N`**: Setting `W=3` for `N=3` means any single-node upgrade or reboot blocks all writes.
- **Cross-region latency explosion**: Using `EACH_QUORUM` forces writes to wait for remote-DC RTTs (~80–150 ms) and fails writes if any DC loses a majority.
- **Clock-skew overwrite**: A coordinator with a fast clock stamps writes 1 second in the future, making every subsequent write from normal nodes silently lose LWW.
- **Zombie deletes**: If a down node misses a tombstone and rejoins after `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days) without repair, old data resurrects.

## Multi-datacenter quorum tuning

In multi-region deployments (`RF=3` per DC), prefer **`LOCAL_QUORUM` for both reads and writes** paired with sticky regional routing. Clients get ~3–5 ms local latency and strong intra-DC consistency, while cross-DC replication proceeds asynchronously. Reserve `EACH_QUORUM` or `SERIAL` (Paxos LWT) strictly for global uniqueness checks or financial balances.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify `W + R > N` and `W > N/2` for any table requiring read-your-writes consistency.
- [ ] Use `LOCAL_QUORUM` instead of `QUORUM` or `ALL` in multi-DC clusters to avoid cross-region tail latency.
- [ ] Schedule incremental Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs (`nodetool repair`) well within `gc_grace_seconds`.
- [ ] Monitor NTP/chrony clock drift across all coordinators and use Paxos/LWT (`SERIAL`) for contended updates.
- [ ] Upgrade to `N=5, W=3, R=3` for tier-0 tables that must survive a rolling restart plus an unexpected node failure.

interviewProblems.title: Quorum Read/Write Tuning
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Quorum Read/Write Tuning. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Quorum tuning balances strong consistency, tail latency, and fault tolerance in replicated databases by choosing replication factor N, write quorum W, and read quorum R—where W + R > N guarantees read-your-writes overlap.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Replica 2 (AZ-b) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Replica 3 (AZ-c).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Replica 3 (AZ-c) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Disable sloppy quorums for strongly consistent workloads and rely on strict home-replica quorums.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Tune W + R > N (typically N=3, W=2, R=2) for strong overlap, or drop to W=1 / R=1 only when you explicitly accept stale reads and asynchronous read-repair.
Avoid trap: Assuming W + R > N alone provides strict serializability/linearizability in leaderless LWW stores.
Avoid trap: Using N=3, W=3, R=1 for write-heavy durability without realizing a single dead node halts 100% of writes.
When to reach for it: Tuning Dynamo-style leaderless databases (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB-like architectures) per workload using N, W, and R.
When to reach for it: Balancing p99 read/write latency against durability in multi-AZ or multi-region clusters (LOCAL_QUORUM vs EACH_QUORUM).

putItTogether.title: Putting Quorum Tuning Together
putItTogether.summary: Tune W + R > N (typically N=3, W=2, R=2) for strong overlap, or drop to W=1 / R=1 only when you explicitly accept stale reads and asynchronous read-repair.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Quorum Tuning before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: With W=2 and R=2 (2+2 > 3), 1 down node causes zero errors, p99 latency tracks the 2nd-fastest AZ (~4 ms), and read-your-writes holds.

concepts.name: RAG Retrieval Pipelines

relationships.description: Connects RAG Retrieval Pipelines to llm prompt engineering in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Production RAG retrieval combines semantic chunking, hybrid dense (HNSW) + sparse (BM25/SPLADE) search, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), metadata pre-filtering, and cross-encoder reranking to deliver high-precision context to LLMs.

spark.summary: Production RAG retrieval combines semantic chunking, hybrid dense (HNSW) + sparse (BM25/SPLADE) search, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), metadata pre-filtering, and cross-encoder reranking to deliver high-precision context to LLMs.
spark.keyTakeaway: Dense vector search alone misses exact SKUs and error codes; hybrid retrieval (BM25 + HNSW) fused via RRF and narrowed by a cross-encoder reranker boosts precision while cutting LLM prompt tokens.

concept.whyItMatters: An LLM can only reason over the context it receives. Naive "embed 500-char chunks + cosine top-5" pipelines fail on exact identifiers, leak cross-tenant data when ACLs are applied too late, and flood the LLM with noisy chunks that trigger hallucinations and high token bills.
whenToUse: Grounding LLM answers in private, rapidly changing enterprise docs, support runbooks, or product catalogs.
Queries mixing semantic intent ('how to fix timeout') with exact tokens ('ERR_CONNECTION_RESET', 'SKU-9040').
Multi-tenant applications requiring strict document-level RBAC/ACL enforcement before chunks ever reach the LLM.
whenNotToUse: Small, static corpora (<50k tokens) that fit cleanly inside a prompt cache with zero retrieval latency or chunking loss.
Structured analytical queries ('sum Q3 revenue by region') where Text-to-SQL or APIs beat unstructured chunk retrieval.
Real-time streaming telemetry where indexing lag makes vector stores perpetually stale.
keyPoints: Hybrid search pairs dense embeddings (e.g., BGE-M3 / text-embedding-3-large) with lexical BM25/SPLADE so neither synonyms nor exact codes are missed.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF: sum(1 / (k + rank)), k=60) merges dense and sparse rankings cleanly without score-normalization tuning.
Cross-encoder rerankers (e.g., Cohere Rerank v3, bge-reranker-v2-m3) jointly score query+chunk pairs, pruning top-50 candidates to top-5 high-precision chunks.
Metadata pre-filtering (tenant_id, ACLs, date) must execute inside the vector/lexical index—post-filtering can return zero valid results.
Parent-child (small-to-big) chunking retrieves crisp 256-token child chunks for matching, then injects their 1,024-token parent section for LLM coherence.

examples.title: Hybrid Support Copilot for Exact Hardware SKUs
examples.scenario: A dense-only Qdrant pipeline fails when engineers search for 'AX-9040-V2 firmware rollback', returning generic router docs instead of the exact SKU manual.
examples.outcome: Adding BM25 + dense HNSW fused with RRF (k=60) and a bge-reranker-v2-m3 top-50->5 stage lifts Recall@5 by 18% and cuts LLM input tokens by 70%.

examples.title: Multi-Tenant ACL Pre-Filtering Fix
examples.scenario: A SaaS RAG service fetches top-10 vector matches globally and filters out unauthorized tenant_id rows afterward.
examples.outcome: For smaller tenants, all 10 global hits belong to larger tenants, leaving 0 context chunks; moving tenant_id and ACLs into HNSW pre-filtering fixes empty responses and eliminates leakage risk.

tradeOffs.pro: Boosts NDCG@5 by ~8-15% and slashes irrelevant context sent to the LLM.
tradeOffs.con: Adds ~40-90 ms of GPU inference latency per query on top-50 candidates.

tradeOffs.pro: Small chunks (200-300 tokens) yield sharper embedding similarity without topic dilution.
tradeOffs.con: Small chunks lose surrounding headers/conditions unless paired with parent-document expansion.

tradeOffs.pro: Hybrid dense + BM25 captures both conceptual paraphrases and exact identifiers.
tradeOffs.con: Requires maintaining synchronized dense HNSW and inverted lexical indices.

failureModes.name: Post-Retrieval ACL Starvation
failureModes.description: Filtering permissions after top-K vector search drops authorized results when other tenants dominate the top K.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply tenant_id and group ACL filters as pre-filters inside Qdrant, Milvus, OpenSearch, or pgvector.

failureModes.name: Chunk Boundary Context Shredding
failureModes.description: Fixed 500-character splits cut tables, code blocks, or 'NOT recommended' caveats away from their subject.
failureModes.mitigation: Use structure-aware Markdown/HTML splitters and parent-child retrieval (match child, return parent).

failureModes.name: Stale Index & Orphaned Chunks
failureModes.description: Updating a source document appends new chunks without deleting old chunk IDs, causing contradictory answers.
failureModes.mitigation: Key chunks deterministically by (doc_id, chunk_index) and run atomic delete-by-doc_id upserts.

failureModes.name: Lost-in-the-Middle Context Overload
failureModes.description: Stuffing 20+ unranked chunks into the prompt degrades LLM attention on middle passages and raises hallucination.
failureModes.mitigation: Rerank top-50 down to top-5/8 and place highest-scoring chunks at the start and end of the context window.

commonMistakes: Relying on pure cosine similarity for domains rich in part numbers, error codes, legal citations, or acronyms.
Splitting PDFs and Markdown tables mid-row with naive fixed character windows.
Applying RBAC/tenant filters in application code after vector search instead of inside the index.
Shipping without offline retrieval metrics (Recall@K, MRR, NDCG@10) and only eyeballing 5 sample prompts.
Passing top-25 raw chunks directly to the LLM instead of reranking down to top-5.

sections.content:
## The idea

A production RAG pipeline is a multi-stage information retrieval funnel, not a single vector lookup. Dense bi-encoder embeddings excel at semantic similarity ('memory leak' <-> 'OOM killer'), but compress away exact lexical tokens ('CVE-2024-3094', '0x80070005'). Conversely, BM25 excels at exact terms but misses synonyms.

Modern pipelines solve this with **two-stage hybrid retrieval**: a fast **Stage 1 recall layer** runs dense HNSW vector search and sparse BM25/SPLADE in parallel (pre-filtered by tenant ACLs), merges them with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**, and passes the top ~50 candidates to a **Stage 2 cross-encoder reranker** that jointly attends over `(query, chunk)` pairs to emit the top 5–8 highest-signal chunks.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a user query `"Why did checkout fail with ERR_IDEMPOTENCY_409?"`:

1. **Query prep & ACLs**: Extract `tenant_id=acme` and `role=eng` pre-filters; optionally expand abbreviations.
2. **Parallel Stage-1 recall**:
   - **Dense (HNSW, `1024-dim` BGE-M3)** returns top-50 semantically related checkout retry docs.
   - **Sparse (BM25 / OpenSearch)** returns top-50 docs containing the exact token `ERR_IDEMPOTENCY_409`.
3. **RRF fusion (`k=60`)**: Each doc gets `score = 1/(60 + rank_dense) + 1/(60 + rank_sparse)`, promoting docs strong in either or both lists.
4. **Stage-2 cross-encoder rerank**: `bge-reranker-v2-m3` scores the top-50 fused chunks in ~55 ms, selecting the top-5.
5. **Parent-child expansion**: Each matched 256-token child chunk expands to its 1,024-token parent section before entering the LLM prompt.

sections.content:
## Chunking & ingestion architecture

Retrieval quality is capped by ingestion quality:

- **Structure-first splitting**: Parse PDFs/HTML into Markdown headings, tables, and code blocks first; never split a table or code fence in half.
- **Parent-child (small-to-big)**: Index `256-token` child chunks for crisp vector matching, but store a `parent_id` pointing to the `1,024-token` section so the LLM sees complete context.
- **Contextual headers**: Prepend `doc_title > section_h2 > updated_at` to each chunk before embedding so pronoun-heavy paragraphs ('It must be rotated every 90 days') stay grounded.

## Retrieval stage latency & quality breakdown

| Stage | Typical Latency | Candidate Pool | Primary Strength | Failure Without It |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dense HNSW** | ~10–25 ms | Top 50 | Paraphrases, synonyms, conceptual intent | Misses exact error codes, SKUs, and IDs |
| **BM25 / SPLADE** | ~8–20 ms | Top 50 | Exact identifiers, acronyms, rare terms | Misses semantic phrasing mismatches |
| **RRF (`k=60`)** | <1 ms | Top 50 merged | Scale-invariant rank merging | Requires brittle min-max score tuning |
| **Cross-Encoder** | ~40–90 ms | 50 -> Top 5 | Full query-chunk token attention | Noisy top-20 floods LLM and raises cost |

## Failure modes

RAG pipelines silently degrade in four ways:

- **Post-filtering empty sets**: Applying permissions after top-K retrieval starves minority tenants.
- **Stale chunk orphans**: Re-ingesting edited docs without deleting prior chunk IDs causes old policies to outrank new ones.
- **Embedding model drift**: Mixing query embeddings from model v2 against document embeddings from model v1 silently destroys cosine similarity.
- **Table flattening**: Naive PDF text extractors scramble multi-column financial or spec tables into unreadable word soup.

## Evaluating retrieval separately from generation

Always decouple **retrieval evals** from **LLM generation evals**:

1. **Retrieval metrics**: Build a 100–300 query golden set with labeled relevant `doc_ids` and track `Recall@20` (Stage 1) and `NDCG@5` / `MRR` (Stage 2).
2. **Generation metrics**: Measure groundedness/faithfulness (does the answer contradict or extrapolate beyond retrieved chunks?) and citation accuracy using frameworks like `RAGAS` or LLM-as-a-judge.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce `tenant_id` and ACL predicates as **pre-filters** inside the vector and lexical indices.
- [ ] Combine dense HNSW + BM25/SPLADE with **RRF (`k=60`)** instead of dense-only search.
- [ ] Add a **cross-encoder reranker** (`top-50 -> top-5`) to maximize precision and cut LLM input tokens.
- [ ] Use **structure-aware chunking** with contextual headers (`doc_title > section`) and atomic `delete-by-doc_id` upserts.
- [ ] Track `Recall@20` and `NDCG@5` on a golden query set before changing chunk sizes, embedders, or prompts.

concepts.name: Randomized Algorithms

relationships.description: Connects Randomized Algorithms to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Randomized algorithms trade deterministic worst-case guarantees for dramatic gains in simplicity, memory efficiency, and average-case speed by injecting controlled pseudo-randomness into branching, sampling, or hashing.

spark.summary: Randomized algorithms trade deterministic worst-case guarantees for dramatic gains in simplicity, memory efficiency, and average-case speed by injecting controlled pseudo-randomness into branching, sampling, or hashing.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use Las Vegas algorithms when you need 100% exact answers with probabilistic runtime (e.g., randomized QuickSort), and Monte Carlo algorithms when tiny, bounded error probabilities unlock massive memory or latency savings (e.g., HyperLogLog, Miller-Rabin).

concept.whyItMatters: Adversarial or skewed inputs routinely degrade deterministic algorithms to quadratic time or force prohibitive memory footprints. A single random pivot defeats sorted-input QuickSort attacks, Power-of-Two-Choices load balancing slashes max server queue depth from O(ln n / ln ln n) to O(ln ln n / ln 2), and HyperLogLog counts 1 billion distinct users in 1.5 KB instead of 32 GB.
whenToUse: Defeating worst-case input patterns in sorting, hashing, and routing without complex deterministic balancing (e.g., randomized QuickSort, universal hashing).
Approximating cardinalities, quantiles, or frequencies over high-throughput streams where exact state exceeds RAM (e.g., HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch, reservoir sampling).
Breaking symmetry and thundering-herd synchronization in distributed protocols (e.g., exponential backoff with full jitter, Raft randomized election timeouts of 150-300 ms).
whenNotToUse: Financial ledgers, billing, or compliance counters where even a 0.81% relative error or rare false positive is legally unacceptable.
Safety-critical real-time control loops (avionics, braking) requiring strict deterministic worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds.
Small datasets (under 100,000 items) where exact hash sets or deterministic sorts fit comfortably in L3 cache or a few megabytes of RAM.
keyPoints: Las Vegas algorithms (e.g., randomized QuickSort, randomized Skip Lists) always return the exact right answer; only their runtime is a random variable.
Monte Carlo algorithms (e.g., Miller-Rabin primality, Bloom filters, HyperLogLog) run in fixed time/space and bound error probability exponentially via independent trials or hash bits.
Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) sampling probes two random backends and picks the less loaded one, cutting max load from O(ln n / ln ln n) to O(ln ln n / ln 2) with O(1) coordination.
Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R) maintains a uniform k-item sample over an unbounded stream of unknown length N in O(k) memory.
PRNG choice matters: use SplitMix64 or Xoshiro256++ for simulation/sketches, SipHash-2-4 for hash-flooding resistance, and CSPRNGs (getrandom / SecureRandom) for security or election tie-breaking.

examples.title: Distinct Daily Active Users at Edge Scale with HyperLogLog
examples.scenario: An analytics ingestion tier processes 400,000 events/sec across 50M daily unique user IDs. Storing exact 64-bit IDs per metric bucket in Redis Sets would consume ~3.2 GB per day per dimension.
examples.outcome: Switching to Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT (16,384 6-bit registers = 12 KB per key) reduces memory by >99.9% while keeping standard error at 1.04 / sqrt(16384) = 0.81%.

examples.title: Envoy Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) Load Balancing
examples.scenario: A 200-pod microservice fleet behind an L7 proxy experiences tail-latency spikes under pure round-robin when 10% of pods hit GC pauses or noisy-neighbor CPU throttling.
examples.outcome: Enabling Envoy's LEAST_REQUEST policy with choice_count=2 samples two random healthy endpoints and picks the one with fewer active requests, cutting p99 latency by 45% without global state.

tradeOffs.pro: Doubling HyperLogLog registers or Count-Min Sketch width cuts error smoothly while staying orders of magnitude smaller than exact sets.
tradeOffs.con: Zero-error exactness is impossible in sublinear space; cardinality deltas smaller than ~1% cannot be reliably distinguished.

tradeOffs.pro: Randomization eliminates complex deterministic rebalancing trees or global coordination locks.
tradeOffs.con: Non-deterministic execution complicates unit tests, bug reproduction, and incident postmortems unless PRNG seeds are logged.

tradeOffs.pro: Fast non-cryptographic PRNGs (Xoshiro256++, MurmurHash3) run in ~1-3 ns per call.
tradeOffs.con: Predictable seeds or weak hashes expose hash tables and load balancers to algorithmic complexity DoS attacks.

failureModes.name: Seed Synchronization / Correlated Jitter
failureModes.description: Containers booted from the same image at the same second initialize PRNGs with identical timestamps or static seeds, causing synchronized retry storms.
failureModes.mitigation: Seed PRNGs from OS entropy (/dev/urandom, getrandom()) combined with instance PID/UUID, and verify jitter spread in chaos tests.

failureModes.name: Hash-Flooding Collision Attack
failureModes.description: An attacker crafts keys that collide in a non-keyed hash function (e.g., plain MurmurHash), degrading a randomized hash map or sketch to worst-case behavior.
failureModes.mitigation: Use keyed cryptographic or DoS-resistant hashes like SipHash-2-4 with a per-process secret seed rotated on restart.

failureModes.name: Biased Sampling via Modulo Reduction
failureModes.description: Mapping a 32-bit PRNG output to [0, N) using `rand() % N` introduces modulo bias when 2^32 is not divisible by N, skewing reservoir or shuffle distributions.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Lemire's fast range reduction or rejection sampling (`ThreadLocalRandom.nextInt(n)` / `crypto/rand.Int`) to guarantee strict uniformity.

failureModes.name: Under-Dimensioned Monte Carlo Trials
failureModes.description: Running too few independent rounds (e.g., k=3 in Miller-Rabin or narrow Count-Min width w) allows false positives to slip into production.
failureModes.mitigation: Size parameters from target error bounds (e.g., k=40 for Miller-Rabin gives <= 4^-40 error; w = ceil(e / epsilon) for Count-Min Sketch).

commonMistakes: Using `Math.random()` or `java.util.Random` (48-bit LCG with global atomic CAS contention) in hot multi-threaded paths instead of `ThreadLocalRandom` or Xoshiro256++.
Forgetting to persist or log the PRNG seed in randomized tests and simulations, making flaky failures impossible to reproduce.
Using a non-cryptographic PRNG for security tokens, session IDs, or leader-election tie-breakers where predictability is exploitable.
Assuming HyperLogLog or Bloom filters support item deletion without switching to Counting Bloom Filters or exact backing stores.
Applying naive `rand()` inside Fisher-Yates shuffles with a 32-bit seed for decks > 13 elements (13! > 2^32), making most permutations unreachable.

sections.content:
## The idea

Deterministic algorithms must handle every conceivable input, so adversaries or pathological production data can force worst-case behavior. Randomized algorithms shift the source of uncertainty from the *input* to *internal coin flips*. By choosing pivots, hash seeds, or sample candidates randomly, no fixed input can reliably trigger worst-case paths.

Two foundational families govern the design space:
- **Las Vegas algorithms** never lie: they always produce the exact correct output, while their execution time is a random variable concentrated tightly around the expectation (e.g., randomized QuickSort runs in $O(n \log n)$ with probability $1 - O(n^{-c})$).
- **Monte Carlo algorithms** run within a strict time or memory budget and accept a mathematically bounded probability of error (e.g., Miller-Rabin primality testing, HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch). Repeating $k$ independent trials drives one-sided error down exponentially ($p^k$).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider routing 100,000 RPS across $n = 100$ backend pods using **Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C)** instead of pure random or global least-connections:

1. **Request arrival**: A client request hits the edge proxy (e.g., Envoy).
2. **Two-sample probe**: The proxy draws two distinct indices $i, j \in [0, 99]$ uniformly using a thread-local PRNG (`Xoshiro256++`).
3. **Local queue comparison**: It reads its in-memory active-request counters `inflight[i]` and `inflight[j]` (zero cross-proxy RPCs).
4. **Dispatch & increment**: If `inflight[i] <= inflight[j]`, it increments `inflight[i]` and forwards the request to pod $i$; otherwise pod $j$.
5. **Completion**: On response or timeout, the proxy decrements the chosen pod's counter.

Under pure random placement of $n$ balls into $n$ bins, the fullest bin reaches $\approx \frac{\ln n}{\ln \ln n}$ ($\approx 3$–$4\times$ average). Checking just **two** random choices drops the maximum load exponentially to $\frac{\ln \ln n}{\ln 2} + O(1)$—typically within 1–2 requests of the global optimum—while avoiding the lock contention and stale-state herding of global least-loaded routing.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Las Vegas vs. Monte Carlo & PRNG selection
sections.content:
## Las Vegas vs. Monte Carlo & PRNG selection

Choosing the right class of randomness and generator prevents subtle production bugs:

- **Amplifying Monte Carlo confidence**: A single Miller-Rabin witness catches a composite number with probability $\ge 3/4$. Running $k = 40$ independent bases lowers the false-prime probability to $\le 4^{-40} \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-25}$—lower than hardware cosmic-ray bit flips.
- **Streaming sketches**: **HyperLogLog** hashes each item into a 64-bit integer, uses the first $b$ bits (e.g., $b=14 \implies m=16,384$ buckets) to pick a register, and records the longest run of leading zeros in the remaining bits. **Count-Min Sketch** uses $d$ pairwise-independent hash functions across $w$ counters, taking the `min` across rows to eliminate overcounting bias from collisions.
- **PRNG hygiene**: Never share a single `java.util.Random` across threads (atomic CAS contention stalls cores). Use `ThreadLocalRandom` or `Xoshiro256++` for speed, and `SecureRandom` / `crypto/rand` whenever an attacker could observe outputs and predict future choices.

## Canonical randomized algorithms compared

| Algorithm | Class | Time / Space | Error / Guarantee | Primary Production Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Randomized QuickSort | Las Vegas | $O(n \log n)$ expected, $O(\log n)$ stack | 100% exact output | In-memory sorting immune to pre-sorted inputs |
| Miller-Rabin ($k=40$) | Monte Carlo | $O(k \log^3 n)$ time | $\le 4^{-40}$ false-prime rate | RSA/ECC key generation in OpenSSL / BoringSSL |
| HyperLogLog ($b=14$) | Monte Carlo | $O(1)$ update, 12 KB RAM | $\pm 0.81\%$ standard error | Redis `PFCOUNT`, BigQuery `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` |
| Count-Min Sketch | Monte Carlo | $O(d)$ update, $O(w \cdot d)$ RAM | Overestimates by $\le \varepsilon N$ w.p. $1-\delta$ | Heavy-hitter / DDoS IP tracking in network telemetry |
| Power-of-Two-Choices | Randomized routing | $O(1)$ per request | Max load $O(\ln \ln n / \ln 2)$ | Envoy `LEAST_REQUEST`, NGINX, linkerd2-proxy |

## Failure modes

- **Correlated PRNG seeds**: Containers starting in lockstep with `time(NULL)` seeds generate identical backoff jitter, turning randomized retries into a synchronized thundering herd.
- **Modulo bias**: Computing `rand() % N` when $2^{32} \bmod N \neq 0$ over-weights lower indices; in weighted routing or reservoir sampling, this skews traffic distribution.
- **Hash-collision DoS**: Using unseeded MurmurHash or FNV-1a in public-facing sketches or hash tables lets attackers craft colliding keys that blind heavy-hitter detectors.
- **Non-reproducible test flakiness**: Unseeded randomized property tests fail once every 500 CI runs and cannot be debugged unless the failing seed is printed in test output.

## Production patterns & observability

- **Deterministic replay via logged seeds**: Pass an explicit `uint64_t seed` into simulation, shuffling, and sampling engines; emit the seed in structured logs on any assertion failure.
- **Bounded jitter formulas**: Use AWS-style **Full Jitter** (`random_between(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`) or **Decorrelated Jitter** (`min(cap, random_between(base, sleep * 3))`) rather than fixed-window retries.
- **Sketch mergeability**: HyperLogLog registers and Count-Min arrays with identical seeds and dimensions merge losslessly via element-wise `max` (HLL) or `+` (CMS), enabling lock-free per-core aggregation before periodic reduction.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Classify the requirement: exactness required (Las Vegas) vs. bounded approximation acceptable (Monte Carlo).
- [ ] Verify thread-local PRNGs (`ThreadLocalRandom`, `Xoshiro256++`) are used on hot paths—no global mutexes or atomic seed CAS.
- [ ] Seed from OS CSPRNG (`/dev/urandom` / `getrandom`) at startup; use `SipHash-2-4` if keys are attacker-controlled.
- [ ] Eliminate modulo bias using rejection sampling or Lemire's fast range mapping.
- [ ] Document and monitor error budgets (e.g., HLL register precision $b$, CMS $\varepsilon/\delta$) and log seeds in randomized test suites.

interviewProblems.title: Randomized Algorithms
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Randomized Algorithms. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Randomized algorithms trade deterministic worst-case guarantees for dramatic gains in simplicity, memory efficiency, and average-case speed by injecting controlled pseudo-randomness into branching, sampling, or hashing.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Backend Pod A applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Backend Pod B.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Backend Pod B experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Seed PRNGs from OS entropy (/dev/urandom, getrandom()) combined with instance PID/UUID, and verify jitter spread in chaos tests.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use Las Vegas algorithms when you need 100% exact answers with probabilistic runtime (e.g., randomized QuickSort), and Monte Carlo algorithms when tiny, bounded error probabilities unlock massive memory or latency savings (e.g., HyperLogLog, Miller-Rabin).
Avoid trap: Using `Math.random()` or `java.util.Random` (48-bit LCG with global atomic CAS contention) in hot multi-threaded paths instead of `ThreadLocalRandom` or Xoshiro256++.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to persist or log the PRNG seed in randomized tests and simulations, making flaky failures impossible to reproduce.
When to reach for it: Defeating worst-case input patterns in sorting, hashing, and routing without complex deterministic balancing (e.g., randomized QuickSort, universal hashing).
When to reach for it: Approximating cardinalities, quantiles, or frequencies over high-throughput streams where exact state exceeds RAM (e.g., HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch, reservoir sampling).

putItTogether.title: Putting Randomized Algorithms Intro Together
putItTogether.summary: Use Las Vegas algorithms when you need 100% exact answers with probabilistic runtime (e.g., randomized QuickSort), and Monte Carlo algorithms when tiny, bounded error probabilities unlock massive memory or latency savings (e.g., HyperLogLog, Miller-Rabin).
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Randomized Algorithms Intro before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Switching to Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT (16,384 6-bit registers = 12 KB per key) reduces memory by >99.9% while keeping standard error at 1.04 / sqrt(16384) = 0.81%.

concepts.name: Rate Limiting Algorithms, Token Buckets & Redis Lua

relationships.description: Rate limiting stores counter states inside high-speed in-memory caches.

provenance.title: System Design HLD Example: Distributed Rate Limiter
Sliding Window Technique
Nested loops cause slow O(N squared) complexity on subarray problems. | Sliding Window

concepts.tagline: Rate limiting enforces caps on request or resource consumption per caller, tenant, or endpoint over time to protect downstream capacity, ensure fair multi-tenant sharing, and blunt abuse.

spark.summary: Rate limiting enforces caps on request or resource consumption per caller, tenant, or endpoint over time to protect downstream capacity, ensure fair multi-tenant sharing, and blunt abuse.
spark.keyTakeaway: Pair an in-memory local limiter (token bucket) for sub-millisecond burst protection with a Redis Lua sliding-window or token-bucket store for global tenant quotas, and always return HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`.

concept.whyItMatters: Without rate limiting, a single buggy client retry loop, scraper, or noisy tenant can saturate database connection pools and cause cascading 503 outages for every customer. Well-tuned limiters shed excess load at the edge in <1 ms while preserving headroom for healthy traffic.
whenToUse: Protecting public APIs, login/OTP endpoints, and expensive compute routes (LLM inference, PDF export) from abuse, scraping, and brute-force attacks.
Enforcing tiered SaaS commercial quotas (e.g., Free: 60 req/min, Pro: 1,000 req/min) and preventing noisy-neighbor starvation in multi-tenant platforms.
Shielding downstream databases or third-party webhooks with fixed concurrency or RPS ceilings.
whenNotToUse: Internal health-check, readiness, and Prometheus metrics scrape paths—throttling these triggers false-positive pod restarts.
When the bottleneck is purely slow downstream processing rather than request rate; use adaptive concurrency limits (e.g., Vegas/Gradient2) or backpressure instead.
Strictly idempotent, cache-absorbed static CDN assets where edge PoPs already absorb 99%+ of traffic cheaply.
keyPoints: Token Bucket allows controlled bursts up to bucket capacity `B` while capping sustained average rate at `R` tokens/sec—ideal for interactive APIs.
Leaky Bucket (queue-based) smooths bursty ingress into a constant egress rate, protecting brittle downstream sinks at the cost of queueing latency.
Fixed Window Counters suffer from 2x boundary-burst spikes at minute/hour rollovers; Sliding Window Counters eliminate boundary spikes with O(1) memory.
Distributed rate limiting requires atomic read-modify-write (Redis Lua scripts or Envoy `ratelimit` gRPC) to prevent race conditions across gateway replicas.
Standardize responses with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests`, `Retry-After`, and IETF `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset` headers.

examples.title: Stripe-Style Dual-Layer Token Bucket & Concurrency Limiter
examples.scenario: A payment API serves 100 req/s per merchant in live mode, but bursts of webhook-triggered queries occasionally spike to 250 req/s for 2 seconds.
examples.outcome: A Redis-backed Token Bucket (refill=100/s, capacity=200) absorbs short legitimate bursts, while a separate concurrency semaphore caps slow `/v1/reports` queries at 10 in-flight per merchant.

examples.title: Envoy Global Rate Limit + Local Failover
examples.scenario: An API gateway cluster of 40 Envoy pods enforces a 5,000 req/hr quota per API key via a central Redis-backed `ratelimit` gRPC service.
examples.outcome: When a Redis shard experiences a 400 ms failover, Envoy's `failure_mode_deny: false` (fail-open) + local per-pod 200 req/s circuit-breaker cap prevents a total outage while still blocking runaway floods.

tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous Redis Lua checks enforce exact cross-region or cross-pod quotas.
tradeOffs.con: Adds 0.5-2 ms network RTT per request and makes Redis availability a critical-path dependency.

tradeOffs.pro: Fail-open preserves user traffic if the rate-limit store goes down.
tradeOffs.con: Leaves origin servers exposed to overload during a limiter outage unless backed by a local fallback limiter.

tradeOffs.factor: Sliding Window Log vs. Sliding Window Counter
tradeOffs.pro: Sliding Window Log (Redis `ZSET` of timestamps) is 100% exact to the millisecond.
tradeOffs.con: Stores O(N) timestamps per key, blowing up RAM for high-rate tenants; Sliding Window Counter approximates it in O(1) space.

failureModes.name: Hot-Key Contention in Redis
failureModes.description: A single global or mega-tenant key (e.g., `rl:global` or a major customer) routes 100k RPS to one Redis shard, saturating its single-threaded event loop.
failureModes.mitigation: Batch token leases locally at the gateway (e.g., fetch 50 tokens at a time) or shard the key across N slots (`key:{0..15}`) with N-way split quotas.

failureModes.name: Fixed-Window Boundary Stampede
failureModes.description: A client sends 1,000 requests at 12:00:59 and another 1,000 at 12:01:01, hitting 2x the intended 1,000 req/min limit in 2 seconds.
failureModes.mitigation: Replace fixed windows with Sliding Window Counter (weighted interpolation of current and previous bucket) or Token Bucket.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm Amplification
failureModes.description: Blocked clients immediately retry 429 responses in a tight loop, multiplying ingress load on the rate limiter itself.
failureModes.mitigation: Return explicit `Retry-After` headers, reject early at the L7 edge/WAF before auth/DB work, and require exponential backoff + jitter in SDKs.

failureModes.name: Proxy IP Spoofing / Shared NAT Collisions
failureModes.description: Keying strictly on `X-Forwarded-For` allows header spoofing, while keying on raw IP throttles an entire corporate NAT or mobile carrier.
failureModes.mitigation: Parse only trusted proxy hops for client IP, and key authenticated endpoints on `tenant_id` or `api_key_hash` rather than IP alone.

commonMistakes: Using separate `GET` then `INCR` commands in Redis without a Lua script, creating race conditions under concurrent requests.
Leaving Redis keys without `EXPIRE` / `PEXPIRE` TTLs, causing unbounded memory growth from one-off caller IPs.
Rate limiting after expensive JWT signature verification, body parsing, or DB lookups instead of at the outermost edge.
Applying identical limits to `GET /health`, `POST /login`, and `POST /export` instead of endpoint-tiered cost weights.
Returning `500` or `503` instead of `429 Too Many Requests`, confusing client SDKs into aggressive immediate retries.

sections.content:
## The idea

Rate limiting decouples **incoming demand** from **system capacity** by enforcing a strict admission budget over time. Every request is classified by a rate-limit key—such as `ip`, `api_key`, `tenant_id:route`, or `user_id`—and checked against a stateful quota before expensive business logic executes.

Production limiters balance three competing goals: **burst tolerance** (letting legitimate users load a dashboard with 15 parallel API calls), **steady-state smoothing** (keeping average RPS within DB/CPU budgets), and **low-overhead enforcement** (deciding allow/deny in $< 1\text{ ms}$ without becoming the bottleneck).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an API gateway enforcing a **100 req/s sustained, 200-request burst** Token Bucket per API key using an atomic Redis Lua script (`EVALSHA`):

1. **Request arrives** at Envoy/NGINX with `Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...`. The gateway extracts `key = rl:sk_live_98a` and current timestamp `now_ms`.
2. **Atomic Lua execution**: Redis runs the script single-threaded:
   - Fetches `tokens` and `last_refill_ms` from the hash `rl:sk_live_98a` (initializing to `tokens = 200` if missing).
   - Computes `elapsed = max(0, now_ms - last_refill_ms)` and `refilled = min(200, tokens + elapsed * 0.1)` (100 tokens/1000 ms).
   - If `refilled >= 1`, sets `tokens = refilled - 1`, updates `last_refill_ms = now_ms`, sets `PEXPIRE` to 10s, and returns `{1, floor(tokens), 0}`.
   - Otherwise returns `{0, 0, ceil((1 - refilled) / 0.1)}` (milliseconds until 1 token is available).
3. **Gateway response**: On `1`, the request forwards upstream with `RateLimit-Remaining`. On `0`, the gateway immediately returns `HTTP 429` with `Retry-After: 1`.

sections.content:
## Local, centralized, and hybrid architectures

- **Local in-memory limiting**: Zero network overhead (~50 ns), but each of $K$ gateway pods tracks only $1/K$ of the quota. Uneven load balancing causes premature 429s or under-enforcement.
- **Centralized Redis/Valkey**: Exact global counts across all pods, but every request pays a network hop and Redis becomes a hot-spot risk.
- **Hybrid token leasing (best of both)**: Gateways keep a local token bucket and periodically lease batches (e.g., 50 tokens or 100 ms of quota) from Redis asynchronously. This cuts Redis QPS by 50x while keeping global drift bounded to one lease window.

## Rate limiting algorithms compared

| Algorithm | Memory per Key | Burst Handling | Boundary Spike | Best Fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Token Bucket | O(1) (2 numbers) | Up to capacity `B` | None | General public APIs (Stripe, GitHub) |
| Leaky Bucket (Queue) | O(queue size) | Smooths to fixed rate | None | Protecting legacy/brittle downstream sinks |
| Fixed Window Counter | O(1) (1 integer) | Up to limit per window | **2x spike** at edges | Coarse abuse blocks where 2x spike is tolerable |
| Sliding Window Log | O(N) timestamps | Exact over rolling window | None | Low-rate strict limits (e.g., 5 OTPs / 15 min) |
| Sliding Window Counter | O(1) (2 integers) | Weighted interpolation | Negligible (<1%) | High-scale distributed APIs needing low RAM |

## Failure modes

- **Hot-key Redis saturation**: Millions of requests hitting one shared key (e.g., unauthenticated `/public` endpoint) bottleneck a single Redis core.
- **Distributed clock skew**: Using client/gateway wall-clock timestamps inside Redis Lua scripts causes negative elapsed times if one gateway's NTP drifts; always use `redis.call('TIME')` inside Lua.
- **Retry storms**: Returning `429` without `Retry-After` or jitter guidance causes aggressive clients to hammer the gateway even harder.
- **Fail-closed cascading outage**: Blocking all traffic when Redis times out turns a cache blip into a full platform outage.

## Production patterns & observability

- **Weighted cost budgets**: Charge `cost = 1` for `GET /items/{id}` and `cost = 25` for `POST /search/export` against the same tenant token bucket so heavy endpoints cannot starve cheap ones.
- **Shadow / dry-run mode**: Deploy new limits with `enforce: false` for 7 days, emitting `ratelimit_would_deny_total` metrics to spot legitimate enterprise bursts before enforcing.
- **Standardized headers**: Emit `RateLimit-Policy`, `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset` on both `200` and `429` responses so well-behaved SDKs self-throttle proactively.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Choose Token Bucket or Sliding Window Counter for O(1) memory without 2x fixed-window boundary spikes.
- [ ] Execute distributed checks atomically (Redis Lua with `TIME` and `PEXPIRE` TTLs) to prevent race conditions and memory leaks.
- [ ] Configure a fail-open policy paired with a local per-pod safety-net limiter.
- [ ] Exempt `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and internal control-plane heartbeats from tenant rate limits.
- [ ] Return HTTP `429` with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-*` headers, and validate limits in shadow mode first.
