concepts.name: Split-Brain Prevention

relationships.description: Connects Split-Brain Prevention to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Split-brain happens when a network partition splits a distributed cluster into isolated groups that both elect a primary and accept conflicting writes; preventing it requires strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1), time-bounded leases, and monotonic fencing tokens.

spark.summary: Split-brain happens when a network partition splits a distributed cluster into isolated groups that both elect a primary and accept conflicting writes; preventing it requires strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1), time-bounded leases, and monotonic fencing tokens.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never rely on heartbeats alone to declare a peer dead—pair majority quorum (odd node count >= 3) with monotonic fencing tokens checked by the storage layer so a paused old primary can never corrupt data.

concept.whyItMatters: A single 15-second split-brain event in a primary-replica database or distributed lock service allows two leaders to commit conflicting transactions (e.g., double-spending balances or diverging PostgreSQL LSNs), requiring painful manual data reconciliation or full cluster rebuilds.
whenToUse: Operating stateful primary-replica databases (PostgreSQL via Patroni, MySQL Group Replication) with automated failover.
Building distributed lock managers, leader-elected controllers, or consensus stores (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Raft).
Managing shared block/object storage (Ceph, DRBD, Pacemaker) where two writers would corrupt filesystem metadata.
whenNotToUse: Stateless, idempotent microservices behind a load balancer where any instance can serve requests independently.
AP/eventual-consistency stores (e.g., Cassandra, DynamoDB multi-master with CRDTs or LWW) intentionally designed to accept concurrent writes and merge them later.
Single-node deployments where no automated failover exists (manual promotion avoids accidental dual-primary).
keyPoints: Majority Quorum (`floor(N / 2) + 1`) guarantees any two quorums overlap in at least one node—3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 nodes tolerate 2.
A 2-node cluster cannot form a safe majority quorum (half of 2 is 1); always deploy 3 nodes or add a lightweight Witness/Arbitrator in a 3rd failure domain.
Leases alone are vulnerable to asymmetric clock drift or long JVM/hypervisor pauses (a 20s GC pause outlives a 10s lease, leaving the old leader thinking it still holds the lock).
Fencing tokens (monotonically increasing epoch/term numbers issued by the consensus store) must be validated by the storage/target server to reject stale writes.
STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head) uses out-of-band power/hypervisor APIs (IPMI, AWS EC2 StopInstances) to guarantee an unreachable node is truly dead before failover.

examples.title: Fencing Tokens Stopping a GC-Paused Leader
examples.scenario: Service Node A acquires a distributed lease (`epoch=33`) in etcd to write to an object store, then freezes for 25 seconds during a JVM Stop-The-World GC pause. etcd expires the lease at 10s and grants `epoch=34` to Node B.
examples.outcome: When Node A wakes up and sends its buffered write tagged with `epoch=33`, the storage server sees `last_seen_epoch=34` and rejects Node A's stale request with `412 Precondition Failed`.

examples.title: PostgreSQL + Patroni 3-Node Quorum Failover
examples.scenario: A primary PostgreSQL node in AZ-1 loses network connectivity to AZ-2 and AZ-3 while remaining reachable by a few local app servers.
examples.outcome: Because AZ-1 holds only 1 of 3 etcd votes, Patroni in AZ-1 fails to renew its leader key, immediately demotes local Postgres to read-only (`pg_rewind` on rejoin), while AZ-2/AZ-3 form a 2/3 quorum and promote the replica cleanly.

tradeOffs.pro: Strict majority quorum guarantees zero split-brain writes during any network partition.
tradeOffs.con: If >= `ceil(N / 2)` nodes are unreachable (e.g., 2 of 3 nodes down), the entire cluster stops accepting writes until quorum returns.

tradeOffs.pro: 5 nodes survive 2 simultaneous failures (e.g., 1 planned maintenance + 1 sudden crash) without losing quorum.
tradeOffs.con: Increases write commit latency (must replicate to 3 nodes instead of 2) and adds 67% more infrastructure cost.

tradeOffs.factor: Fencing Tokens vs. STONITH Hardware Fencing
tradeOffs.pro: Fencing tokens work purely in software over standard protocols (HTTP `If-Match`, Raft term checks) with zero hardware dependencies.
tradeOffs.con: Requires the downstream resource to understand and enforce monotonic tokens; legacy filesystems/SANs often require STONITH power-off instead.

failureModes.name: Even-Node Cluster Without Witness
failureModes.description: A 2-node active-passive pair splits down the middle; if each side promotes itself on heartbeat loss, both accept writes.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use an odd number of voting members (3 or 5) or place a lightweight quorum witness in a 3rd AZ/region.

failureModes.name: Asymmetric Partition / Zombie Leader
failureModes.description: Old leader loses contact with peers but stays reachable by clients, continuing to serve stale reads or attempt writes before its lease expires.
failureModes.mitigation: Use ReadIndex / leader leases in Raft for linearizable reads, demote immediately on failed lease renewal, and enforce fencing tokens on all writes.

failureModes.name: Hypervisor Pause / Clock Jump
failureModes.description: A VM live-migration or NTP step causes a node's wall clock to lag or jump, breaking lease-expiry assumptions.
failureModes.mitigation: Use monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) for lease intervals, keep conservative safety margins, and rely on storage-side fencing tokens rather than timing alone.

failureModes.name: Dual-STONITH Shootout
failureModes.description: Two partitioned nodes simultaneously send IPMI/cloud-API power-off commands to each other, taking down the entire cluster.
failureModes.mitigation: Gate STONITH behind quorum checks, or configure asymmetric fencing delays (e.g., Node 1 waits 0s, Node 2 waits 5s).

commonMistakes: Deploying a 2-node cluster with automated failover and no 3rd-AZ witness.
Using `wall-clock` (`CLOCK_REALTIME`) instead of monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) to measure lease expiration.
Assuming a distributed lock (like Redis Redlock without fencing) prevents stale writes after a client process pauses.
Placing 2 of 3 consensus nodes in the same availability zone or rack—losing that single AZ loses quorum.
Rejoining a fenced old primary without `pg_rewind` or log truncation, causing silent replication corruption.

sections.content:
## The idea

**Split-brain** occurs when a network partition divides a cluster into two or more isolated sub-networks and more than one side believes it is the active authority. In a stateful system, two concurrent primaries inevitably generate **divergent histories** that cannot be merged automatically.

Preventing split-brain rests on three interlocking guarantees:

1. **Mathematical Quorum (`floor(N / 2) + 1`):** Only a partition containing a strict majority of voting nodes may elect a leader or commit writes. By the pigeonhole principle, two majorities always share at least one overlapping node.
2. **Time-Bounded Leases & Demotion:** A leader holds a renewable lease (e.g., `10s` TTL in etcd/Consul) and must demote itself to read-only the instant renewal fails—before any peer can safely take over.
3. **Storage-Side Fencing:** Because process pauses (GC, swap, VM migration) can freeze a leader past its lease expiry, the storage or target system must enforce a **monotonic fencing token** (or hardware STONITH) so late packets from a zombie leader are rejected.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a **3-AZ Patroni + etcd PostgreSQL failover** combined with **storage-level fencing** during a partition:

1. **Steady state:** `Node-A` (AZ-1) holds etcd leader lease `term=42` (`ttl=10s`, `loop_wait=2s`). `Node-B` (AZ-2) and `Node-C` (AZ-3) stream WAL replication.
2. **Network partition (`t = 0s`):** AZ-1 is cut off from AZ-2 and AZ-3. `Node-A` can still talk to a few AZ-1 app pods, so it thinks it is healthy.
3. **Self-demotion (`t = 2s–6s`):** `Node-A` attempts to renew its `term=42` lease in etcd, but cannot reach `Node-B` or `Node-C` (1/3 votes < quorum of 2). Before its `10s` TTL expires, Patroni on `Node-A` **forcibly demotes local PostgreSQL to read-only**.
4. **Quorum election (`t = 10s`):** `Node-B` and `Node-C` form a 2/3 majority in etcd, expire `term=42`, and elect `Node-B` as primary with **`term=43`**.
5. **Zombie protection:** Even if `Node-A` had frozen in a 20-second kernel/GC stall before demoting and later flushed a write tagged `epoch=42` to a shared volume or conditional store, the store sees `current_epoch=43 > 42` and **rejects the write**. When AZ-1 heals, `Node-A` runs `pg_rewind` to discard any uncommitted local WAL and rejoins as a replica.

sections.content:
## Quorum math and failure-domain placement

Consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos, ZAB) require `Q = floor(N / 2) + 1` votes:

- **N = 3:** Quorum = 2, fault tolerance = **1 node**. Place 1 node in each of 3 AZs (`1 + 1 + 1`). Never place `2 + 1` across 2 AZs—if the 2-node AZ goes down, quorum is lost.
- **N = 5:** Quorum = 3, fault tolerance = **2 nodes**. Ideal for production etcd/ZooKeeper where one node can be down for OS patching while still surviving a sudden crash.
- **Even N (2 or 4):** Adds zero fault tolerance over `N - 1` (`4` nodes still have quorum `3`, tolerating only `1` failure) while increasing replication overhead. If you only have 2 database servers, run a tiny **quorum witness** in a 3rd AZ/region.

## Split-brain prevention mechanisms compared

| Mechanism | How It Stops Split-Brain | Guarantees Against GC/Clock Pause? | Typical Systems |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Majority Quorum (Raft/Paxos)** | Only `> N/2` partition can elect a leader | Yes (for consensus state) | etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper, CockroachDB |
| **Monotonic Fencing Tokens** | Target storage rejects writes with `token < max_seen` | **Yes** (enforced at write time) | HDFS NameNode, Chubby, S3/DynamoDB conditional writes |
| **STONITH / Power Fencing** | Cuts power/network to unreachable node via IPMI/Cloud API | **Yes** (node is physically halted) | Pacemaker/Corosync, Linux DRBD, Ceph |
| **TTL Leases Alone** | Leader steps down if lease isn't renewed in `T` seconds | **No** (vulnerable to pauses `> T`) | Naive Redis locks, un-fenced leader election |

## Failure modes

- **Silent Stale Reads from Zombie Leader:** Even if writes are fenced, an isolated old primary can still serve stale reads to clients unless reads also go through quorum (`ReadIndex`) or use bounded leader leases with monotonic clocks.
- **Split-Brain in Async Replicas:** Promoting an asynchronous PostgreSQL/MySQL replica before draining the old primary loses committed transactions on the old primary that hadn't replicated yet (**RPO > 0**), causing diverged timelines.
- **Witness Co-Location:** Running the 3rd-vote witness on the same physical host or VPC subnet as Node 1 turns a 3-node cluster into a single-point-of-failure 2-node cluster in disguise.
- **Fencing Token Wrap or Non-Persistence:** If the storage node resets `max_seen_epoch` to `0` on reboot, a stale zombie packet can slip through after a restart.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Lightweight fencing with cloud conditional writes
sections.content:
## Lightweight fencing with cloud conditional writes

You don't always need a dedicated etcd cluster to get strong fencing. Modern cloud object and NoSQL stores provide atomic **compare-and-swap (CAS)** primitives:

- **Amazon S3 / GCS:** Use `If-Match: <ETag>` or `If-None-Match: *` on lease/manifest objects so only the holder of the latest ETag can commit a checkpoint.
- **DynamoDB:** Use `ConditionExpression: "epoch = :expected"` to increment a monotonic `epoch` attribute and attach that `epoch` to every downstream mutation.
- **Kubernetes Leases:** `coordination.k8s.io/v1` `Lease` objects use optimistic concurrency (`resourceVersion`) inside Kubernetes' etcd-backed API server.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Deploy an **odd number** of consensus/voting nodes (3 or 5) distributed across **>= 3 independent failure domains** (AZs).
- [ ] Never run a 2-node active-passive cluster with auto-failover without a 3rd-AZ witness.
- [ ] Pair leader leases with **monotonic fencing tokens** validated by the downstream storage/database.
- [ ] Configure STONITH (IPMI or Cloud Stop-Instance) for shared-disk/block clusters where software fencing isn't possible.
- [ ] Use monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) for all lease-expiry timers.
- [ ] Chaos-test network partitions (e.g., `iptables DROP` between AZs) and `SIGSTOP` pauses on the leader to verify zero dual-primary writes.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Split-brain happens when a network partition splits a distributed cluster into isolated groups that both elect a primary and accept conflicting writes; preventing it requires strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1), time-bounded leases, and monotonic fencing tokens.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: New Leader (Node B) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Fenced Storage / Target.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Fenced Storage / Target experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always use an odd number of voting members (3 or 5) or place a lightweight quorum witness in a 3rd AZ/region.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never rely on heartbeats alone to declare a peer dead—pair majority quorum (odd node count >= 3) with monotonic fencing tokens checked by the storage layer so a paused old primary can never corrupt data.
Avoid trap: Deploying a 2-node cluster with automated failover and no 3rd-AZ witness.
Avoid trap: Using `wall-clock` (`CLOCK_REALTIME`) instead of monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) to measure lease expiration.
When to reach for it: Operating stateful primary-replica databases (PostgreSQL via Patroni, MySQL Group Replication) with automated failover.
When to reach for it: Building distributed lock managers, leader-elected controllers, or consensus stores (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Raft).

putItTogether.title: Putting Split Brain Prevention Together
putItTogether.summary: Never rely on heartbeats alone to declare a peer dead—pair majority quorum (odd node count >= 3) with monotonic fencing tokens checked by the storage layer so a paused old primary can never corrupt data.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Split Brain Prevention before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.

putItTogether.outcome: When Node A wakes up and sends its buffered write tagged with `epoch=33`, the storage server sees `last_seen_epoch=34` and rejects Node A's stale request with `412 Precondition Failed`.

concepts.name: SQL Injection Prevention

relationships.description: Connects SQL Injection Prevention to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: SQL injection (CWE-89) happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers alter query structure; preventing it requires strict code-data separation via parameterized queries (prepared statements), allowlists for dynamic identifiers, and least-privilege database roles.

spark.summary: SQL injection (CWE-89) happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers alter query structure; preventing it requires strict code-data separation via parameterized queries (prepared statements), allowlists for dynamic identifiers, and least-privilege database roles.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never sanitize or regex-escape SQL values—bind every user input through wire-level parameterized queries (`Parse`/`Bind`) and restrict dynamic table/column/sort names to static compile-time allowlists.

concept.whyItMatters: SQL injection remains one of the highest-impact vulnerabilities (OWASP Top 10 A03:2021 / CWE-89) because a single unparameterized `WHERE` or `ORDER BY` clause exposes the entire database—allowing full table exfiltration (`UNION SELECT`), authentication bypass, or OS/file access (`xp_cmdshell`, `COPY TO PROGRAM`) in seconds via automated tools like `sqlmap`.
whenToUse: Every database query across web APIs, background workers, GraphQL resolvers, and internal admin tools that touches user or external input.
Dynamic search, filter, and sorting endpoints where column names or `ASC`/`DESC` directions are chosen by the client (pair prepared statements with strict allowlists).
Stored procedures and dynamic SQL inside PostgreSQL/SQL Server using `EXECUTE ... USING` or `sp_executesql`.
whenNotToUse: Do not rely on regex input blacklists (stripping `'`, `--`, or `UNION`) as a primary defense—encoding tricks and SQL dialect quirks bypass them.
Do not rely on Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) alone; WAFs are a defense-in-depth layer, never a substitute for parameterized queries.
Do not assume an ORM (`Hibernate`, `SQLAlchemy`, `Prisma`) makes you immune—raw query escape hatches (`.raw()`, `text()`, `createNativeQuery()`) reintroduce SQLi if formatted with strings.
keyPoints: Parameterized queries (JDBC `PreparedStatement`, psycopg3 `%s`, Go `db.Query($1)`) send the SQL template (`Parse`) and parameter values (`Bind`) separately at the wire protocol level—data can never become SQL syntax.
Parameters only bind **literal values** (`WHERE email = $1`), NOT identifiers (table names, column names) or keywords (`ASC`/`DESC`); dynamic identifiers require a strict `Map`/`Set` allowlist.
Always apply **least-privilege DB roles**: web app users should never connect as `superuser`, `db_owner`, or `postgres`.
Stored procedures are NOT automatically safe if they concatenate strings internally (`EXEC('SELECT ... ' + @input)`); they must use `USING` or `sp_executesql`.
Defense in depth—PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS), read-only replicas for reporting, and SAST rules (Semgrep/CodeQL)—limits blast radius if a bug slips through.

examples.title: Safe Dynamic Search & Sorting Endpoint
examples.scenario: An e-commerce catalog API accepts `category`, `max_price`, `sort_by`, and `sort_dir` query parameters from users.
examples.outcome: `category` and `max_price` are bound via `PreparedStatement` placeholders (`?`), while `sort_by` is looked up in an immutable `Map.of("price", "p.unit_price", "rating", "p.avg_rating")` and `sort_dir` is validated against `{"ASC", "DESC"}`—completely blocking `ORDER BY (CASE WHEN ...)` blind SQLi.

examples.title: PostgreSQL Stored Procedure & RLS Blast-Radius Reduction
examples.scenario: A multi-tenant B2B SaaS app runs parameterized queries as an `app_writer` role with PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (`CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)`).
examples.outcome: Even if a developer forgets a `WHERE tenant_id = $1` filter in a new endpoint, the database engine itself blocks cross-tenant data leakage.

tradeOffs.factor: Server-Side Prepared Statements vs. Client-Side Emulation
tradeOffs.pro: True wire-protocol preparation (`Parse`/`Bind`/`Execute`) enforces strict parser separation and caches query execution plans.
tradeOffs.con: In transaction-pooling proxies (PgBouncer in `transaction` mode), named prepared statements can collide across pooled connections unless configured with protocol-level unnamed statements or PgBouncer >= 1.21 prepared statement support.

tradeOffs.factor: ORM Query Builders vs. Raw Parameterized SQL
tradeOffs.pro: ORMs/query builders (Prisma, jOOQ, SQLAlchemy Core) parameterize values by default and catch schema mismatches early.
tradeOffs.con: Complex analytical CTEs or window functions often force developers into raw SQL methods where accidental f-strings/concatenation can sneak in.

tradeOffs.pro: Mapping user-facing sort keys (`"created"`) to hardcoded SQL identifiers (`"created_at"`) is 100% immune to injection and hides internal column names.
tradeOffs.con: Requires updating the allowlist map whenever a new sortable column is added.

failureModes.name: Second-Order SQL Injection
failureModes.description: User input (e.g., `admin'--` in a username) is safely stored via a prepared statement, then later concatenated unescaped into a background batch or password-reset SQL string.
failureModes.mitigation: Parameterize every query everywhere—never treat database-loaded strings as trusted SQL syntax.

failureModes.name: Unvalidated `ORDER BY` / `IN (...)` Clauses
failureModes.description: Developers parameterize `WHERE` values but interpolate `sort_by` directly or build `IN (${ids.join(',')})` strings.
failureModes.mitigation: Use static allowlists for `ORDER BY` / column names, and native array binding (`WHERE id = ANY($1::int[])` in Postgres) or dynamically generated `?,?,?` placeholders for `IN` lists.

failureModes.name: ORM Raw-SQL Escape Hatch
failureModes.description: Using `User.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")` or `entityManager.createNativeQuery("... " + name)` bypasses ORM parameterization.
failureModes.mitigation: Pass bind parameters as the second argument (`raw(sql, [name])`) and enforce Semgrep/CodeQL SAST rules banning string interpolation inside SQL calls.

failureModes.name: Over-Privileged Database Credentials
failureModes.description: Application connects as `postgres` or `sa`, turning a read-only injection into `COPY ... TO PROGRAM` remote code execution or `DROP TABLE`.
failureModes.mitigation: Grant only `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` on specific tables to the app role; revoke `CREATE` on `public` schema and disable `xp_cmdshell`.

commonMistakes: Escaping quotes with `addslashes()` or `.replace("'", "''")` instead of using prepared statements (vulnerable to multibyte encoding and non-quoted numeric contexts).
Using `LIKE '%' + ? + '%'` incorrectly by interpolating `?` inside quotes (`LIKE '%?%'`) instead of passing `"%" + term + "%"` as the bound parameter.
Assuming `IN (?)` binds an array in MySQL/JDBC—most drivers bind it as a single string unless expanded to `(?, ?, ?)` or using Postgres `= ANY($1)`.
Returning raw SQL exception stack traces (`PSQLException: ERROR: syntax error at or near...`) in HTTP 500 responses, handing attackers schema details.
Forgetting that stored procedures using string concatenation (`EXEC(@sql)`) are just as vulnerable as application-side concatenation.

sections.content:
## The idea

SQL injection happens because a SQL query is a **program** sent as text to a database parser. When an application builds that string by concatenating untrusted user input (`"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"`), the database parser cannot tell where the developer's SQL code ends and the user's data begins. An input like `' OR '1'='1` alters the **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)** of the query.

**Parameterized queries (Prepared Statements)** eliminate this class of vulnerability by enforcing **structural separation at the wire protocol level** (e.g., PostgreSQL's Extended Query Protocol `Parse` -> `Bind` -> `Execute`, or MySQL's `COM_STMT_PREPARE` / `COM_STMT_EXECUTE`):

1. **`Parse`:** The client sends the SQL template with placeholders (`SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = $1`) *before* any user data. The database compiles and locks the AST.
2. **`Bind`:** The client sends the raw user input (`"alice@example.com' OR '1'='1"`) as a typed binary/text parameter.
3. **`Execute`:** The engine compares the literal string against the `email` column—it is **never** re-parsed as SQL syntax.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how a **Java Spring / JDBC** or **Python psycopg3** search endpoint handles a malicious payload `q = "widget'; DROP TABLE orders; --"` and `sort = "price; DROP TABLE orders"`:

1. **Identifier allowlist check (before SQL):** The API looks up `sort` in an immutable map: `ALLOWED_SORTS = {"price": "unit_price", "newest": "created_at"}`. Since `"price; DROP TABLE orders"` is not a key, the API immediately rejects the request with `HTTP 400 Bad Request`—zero database round-trips.
2. **Wire-protocol `Parse` (valid `sort = "price"`):** The driver sends `SELECT id, name, unit_price FROM products WHERE name ILIKE $1 ORDER BY unit_price DESC LIMIT $2` to PostgreSQL. The planner compiles the AST once.
3. **Wire-protocol `Bind`:** The driver binds `$1 = "%widget'; DROP TABLE orders; --%"` (with `%` and `_` `LIKE` wildcards escaped) and `$2 = 25`.
4. **Safe execution:** PostgreSQL searches literally for product names containing that exact string, returns 0 rows, and never executes `DROP TABLE`. Even if `EXECUTE` were abused, the `app_readonly` role lacks `DROP` privileges.

sections.content:
## Handling tricky SQL constructs safely

Developers often fall back to string concatenation for three specific SQL patterns—each has a clean, safe alternative:

- **Dynamic `ORDER BY` / Column Names:** Parameters cannot bind identifiers. Map user input through a `dict`/`Map` (`{"date": "created_at", "total": "grand_total"}`) and reject unknown keys.
- **Variable-Length `IN (...)` Lists:** In PostgreSQL, bind a single array parameter: `WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[])`. In MySQL/SQLite, build the placeholder string dynamically using only `"?"` tokens (`", ".join(["?"] * len(ids))`) and pass `ids` as bound parameters.
- **`LIKE` Wildcard Escaping:** Prepared statements prevent SQLi in `LIKE`, but an attacker sending `%%%%` can trigger expensive full-table wildcard scans. Escape `\`, `%`, and `_` in the application before binding `f"%{escaped}%"`.

## SQL injection defense layers compared

| Control Layer | Protects Against | Fails / Bypassed When | Role in Defense-in-Depth |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Parameterized Queries (`Parse`/`Bind`)** | Value injection in `WHERE`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` | Developer concatenates identifiers (`ORDER BY`) or raw SQL strings | **Primary control** (mandatory) |
| **Static Identifier Allowlists** | Injection in `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, table/column names | Incomplete list or falling back to raw user string on miss | **Primary control** for dynamic SQL structure |
| **Least-Privilege DB Roles + RLS** | Privilege escalation (`DROP`, `COPY TO PROGRAM`, cross-tenant reads) | Does not stop read/write abuse of tables the role *is* allowed to access | **Blast-radius containment** |
| **SAST (Semgrep / CodeQL)** | Catches `f"SELECT ..."` or `+` concatenation in CI before deploy | Obfuscated multi-hop string builders across files | **Automated regression gate** |
| **WAF (ModSecurity CRS)** | Automated `sqlmap` noise and common payloads | Custom encoding, comments (`/**/`), or blind time-based payloads | **Perimeter noise reduction** (secondary) |

## Failure modes

- **PgBouncer Transaction Pooling Collisions:** Older PgBouncer setups in `transaction` pooling mode failed when drivers used named server-side prepared statements (`PREPARE stmt_1`). Ensure PgBouncer >= 1.21 with `max_prepared_statements > 0` or use unnamed protocol-level `Parse`/`Bind`—never disable parameterization by falling back to unsafe string escaping.
- **Blind / Time-Based Exfiltration:** Even when an endpoint returns only `200 OK` or `404` with no DB errors, attackers extract data bit-by-bit using `pg_sleep(5)` or `IF(SUBSTR(...), SLEEP(5), 0)`.
- **Stored Procedure String Concatenation:** Wrapping a concatenated query inside `CREATE FUNCTION` (`EXECUTE 'SELECT ... ' || user_input`) provides zero protection; use `EXECUTE 'SELECT ... WHERE id = $1' USING user_input`.
- **Verbose Error Leakage:** Returning raw SQL error strings in API responses lets attackers map table and column names in minutes.

## Automated verification in CI/CD

Preventing regressions requires automated checks alongside code review:

1. **SAST in Pull Requests:** Configure **Semgrep** or **CodeQL** rules (`java.lang.security.audit.sqli`, `python.lang.security.audit.formatted-sql-query`) to fail builds whenever string formatting touches a DB cursor or ORM raw-query method.
2. **Integration Tests with Injection Payloads:** Include test cases passing `' OR '1'='1`, `"; DROP TABLE users; --`, and `1; SELECT pg_sleep(5)` into search/sort endpoints to verify they return `0` results or `HTTP 400` in `< 50ms`.
3. **DB Role Audits:** Run a periodic CI/migration check asserting that the application DB role has `rolsuper = false`, `rolbypassrls = false`, and no `CREATE` grant on `public`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Bind 100% of query values using wire-level parameterized queries (`PreparedStatement`, `%s`, `$1`, `@p1`)—including inside ORM `.raw()` calls and stored procedures.
- [ ] Validate all dynamic table names, column names, and `ASC`/`DESC` directions against a hardcoded allowlist `Map`/`Set`.
- [ ] Use `= ANY($1)` (Postgres) or generated `?, ?, ?` placeholders for variable-length `IN` clauses.
- [ ] Connect the application with a least-privilege DB role (no superuser, no `DDL`, no OS command privileges) and enable Row-Level Security for multi-tenant tables.
- [ ] Suppress raw SQL error messages from HTTP responses; log full details internally only.
- [ ] Enforce Semgrep/CodeQL SQLi rules in CI to block accidental string interpolation.

interviewProblems.title: SQL Injection Prevention
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on SQL Injection Prevention. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: SQL injection (CWE-89) happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers alter query structure; preventing it requires strict code-data separation via parameterized queries (prepared statements), allowlists for dynamic identifiers, and least-privilege database roles.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: DB Driver (Wire Protocol) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with PostgreSQL / MySQL Engine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, PostgreSQL / MySQL Engine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Parameterize every query everywhere—never treat database-loaded strings as trusted SQL syntax.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never sanitize or regex-escape SQL values—bind every user input through wire-level parameterized queries (`Parse`/`Bind`) and restrict dynamic table/column/sort names to static compile-time allowlists.
Avoid trap: Escaping quotes with `addslashes()` or `.replace("'", "''")` instead of using prepared statements (vulnerable to multibyte encoding and non-quoted numeric contexts).
Avoid trap: Using `LIKE '%' + ? + '%'` incorrectly by interpolating `?` inside quotes (`LIKE '%?%'`) instead of passing `"%" + term + "%"` as the bound parameter.
When to reach for it: Every database query across web APIs, background workers, GraphQL resolvers, and internal admin tools that touches user or external input.
When to reach for it: Dynamic search, filter, and sorting endpoints where column names or `ASC`/`DESC` directions are chosen by the client (pair prepared statements with strict allowlists).

putItTogether.title: Putting Sql Injection Prevention Together
putItTogether.summary: Never sanitize or regex-escape SQL values—bind every user input through wire-level parameterized queries (`Parse`/`Bind`) and restrict dynamic table/column/sort names to static compile-time allowlists.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Sql Injection Prevention before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: `category` and `max_price` are bound via `PreparedStatement` placeholders (`?`), while `sort_by` is looked up in an immutable `Map.of("price", "p.unit_price", "rating", "p.avg_rating")` and `sort_dir` is validated against `{"ASC", "DESC"}`—completely blocking `ORDER BY (CASE WHEN ...)` blind SQLi.

concepts.name: SQL Query Tuning: Index Seeks, Scans, Clustered & Covering Indexes

relationships.description: Database indexing establishes core B-Tree vs LSM-Tree mechanics; SQL query tuning applies B-Tree seeks, scans, and covering index structures to optimize production relational queries.

SQL covering indexes achieve sub-5ms latency inside the database engine without cache invalidation complexity, whereas in-memory caches achieve sub-millisecond QPS at the cost of external RAM and cache-aside state management.
Sharding distributes tables horizontally across instances, but single-node partition performance remains fundamentally governed by clustered and covering index design.

concepts.tagline: SQL query tuning and indexing reduce disk I/O and CPU scans from O(N) full-table reads to O(log N) B+tree lookups and covering index-only scans using execution plans and selectivity statistics.

spark.summary: SQL query tuning and indexing reduce disk I/O and CPU scans from O(N) full-table reads to O(log N) B+tree lookups and covering index-only scans using execution plans and selectivity statistics.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always measure with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before adding indexes: a single well-ordered composite index (equality columns first, range/sort columns last) routinely cuts p99 latency from seconds to single-digit milliseconds without bloating write amplification.

concept.whyItMatters: At 10M+ rows, a missing or poorly ordered index forces sequential heap scans that saturate NVMe IOPS, evict shared buffers, and stall connection pools under concurrent OLTP load.
whenToUse: High-selectivity WHERE predicates (< 5–10% of rows) on large tables in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, or SQL Server.
Hot JOIN keys, ORDER BY / GROUP BY clauses, and pagination queries where avoiding an external disk sort cuts latency by 10x–100x.
Read-heavy endpoints that can be satisfied entirely from an index via covering columns (INCLUDE) without touching heap pages.
whenNotToUse: Tiny lookup tables (< 1,000 rows or a few 8 KB pages) where a sequential scan is faster than traversing B+tree levels.
Low-cardinality boolean or status flags (e.g., is_active = true matching 95% of rows) unless paired with a partial index (WHERE is_active = false).
Write-saturated append-only ingestion tables where every extra secondary index adds B+tree page splits, WAL volume, and vacuum overhead.
keyPoints: B+tree composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: place high-selectivity equality (=) columns first, then range (>, <, BETWEEN) or sort (ORDER BY) columns.
Covering indexes (CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (col)) enable Index-Only Scans in PostgreSQL when the visibility map confirms all-visible pages, eliminating random heap fetches.
Query planners rely on ANALYZE histograms and pg_stats (n_distinct, most_common_vals); stale statistics cause nested-loop vs. hash-join misestimates.
Non-sargable predicates like WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' or WHERE created_at + INTERVAL '1 day' > NOW() defeat standard B+tree indexes unless backed by an expression index.
Unused or duplicate indexes silently degrade INSERT/UPDATE throughput; audit pg_stat_user_indexes (idx_scan = 0) before creating new ones.

examples.title: PostgreSQL 16 multi-tenant order pagination
examples.scenario: An e-commerce API runs SELECT id, total_cents, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND status = 'PAID' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 on an 80M-row table, using only single-column indexes on tenant_id and created_at.
examples.outcome: Replacing both with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_status_created ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_cents) switches the plan from Bitmap Heap Scan + Top-N Heap Sort (1,420 ms, 48,000 shared buffer reads) to an Index-Only Scan (1.8 ms, 5 buffer hits).

examples.title: Partial index for unprocessed outbox events
examples.scenario: A Spring Boot service polls a 25M-row outbox table with WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 every 200 ms, while 99.9% of rows are already published.
examples.outcome: Creating CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_pending ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL shrinks the index from 1.9 GB to 4 MB, keeping it pinned in shared_buffers and dropping poll latency from 310 ms to 0.4 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Each targeted B+tree or GIN index turns multi-second table scans into sub-millisecond point or range lookups.
tradeOffs.con: Every INSERT, UPDATE on indexed columns, and DELETE must update all affected indexes, generating extra dirty pages, WAL bytes, and HOT-update disqualifications.

tradeOffs.factor: Composite covering indexes vs. storage footprint
tradeOffs.pro: INCLUDE columns satisfy queries with Index-Only Scans, avoiding random 8 KB heap page reads.
tradeOffs.con: Wider index tuples reduce B+tree fanout, increase tree depth, and consume more RAM in shared_buffers or InnoDB buffer pool.

tradeOffs.pro: GIN accelerates JSONB/full-text containment (@>) and BRIN tracks min/max per 128-page range at 1% of B+tree size for time-series data.
tradeOffs.con: GIN has expensive pending-list flushes on heavy writes, and BRIN degrades to full scans if physical rows are not correlated with insertion order.

failureModes.name: Parameter sniffing / plan instability
failureModes.description: A cached generic plan built for a rare tenant_id (10 rows, Nested Loop) is reused for a whale tenant (2M rows), causing CPU spikes and timeouts.
failureModes.mitigation: Use pg_stat_statements to spot high variance, force custom plans when needed (plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan), or partition skew-heavy tenants.

failureModes.name: Stale planner statistics after bulk loads
failureModes.description: Loading 5M rows without running ANALYZE leaves pg_class.reltuples outdated, tricking the optimizer into choosing Nested Loop joins over Hash Joins.
failureModes.mitigation: Run ANALYZE immediately after batch ETL/COPY jobs and tune autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor (e.g., 0.02 instead of 0.1) on large tables.

failureModes.name: Blocking DDL locks during index creation
failureModes.description: Running plain CREATE INDEX acquires a SHARE lock that blocks all concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements for minutes on large tables.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL) or ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE (MySQL) with lock_timeout set to 2s.

failureModes.name: Deep OFFSET pagination degradation
failureModes.description: SELECT ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500000 forces the engine to scan and discard 500,000 index entries on every page turn.
failureModes.mitigation: Switch to keyset (cursor) pagination: WHERE id > :last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 for constant O(log N) latency at any depth.

commonMistakes: Indexing every column individually instead of designing composite indexes matched to actual WHERE + ORDER BY predicates.
Putting a range column (created_at > ...) before an equality column (tenant_id = ...) in a composite B+tree index.
Using SELECT * on OLTP endpoints, which prevents Index-Only Scans and pulls large TOAST/text columns into memory.
Applying functions to indexed columns in WHERE clauses (e.g., DATE(created_at) = '2026-11-12') instead of half-open range bounds (>= '2026-11-12' AND < '2026-11-13').
Testing query plans on an empty or 1,000-row staging database where the planner naturally picks Sequential Scans.

sections.content:
## The idea

SQL query tuning aligns physical storage access paths with how the cost-based optimizer (CBO) estimates selectivity, join order, and I/O cost. Instead of scanning millions of 8 KB heap pages sequentially, you shape predicates to be sargable (search-argument-able) and build balanced B+tree, partial, or specialized indexes so the engine touches only the exact leaf pages and heap blocks required.

## Concrete walkthrough

1. Capture slow queries in production via `pg_stat_statements` sorted by `total_exec_time` and `shared_blks_read`.
2. Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)` on a representative bind parameter to compare `actual rows` vs. `estimated rows`.
3. Spot high-cost nodes: `Seq Scan` with heavy `Rows Removed by Filter`, `Sort Method: external merge Disk`, or `Nested Loop` multiplying a 100x underestimated row count.
4. Rewrite non-sargable expressions into range predicates and eliminate `OFFSET` in favor of keyset cursors.
5. Create a composite covering index `(equality_cols, range_or_sort_col) INCLUDE (select_cols)` using `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
6. Re-run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and verify `Heap Fetches: 0` (after `VACUUM`) and single-digit `shared hit` counts.

edges.label: Bind params
edges.title: Parse & bind
edges.description: Application sends a prepared query with concrete filter and limit parameters.

edges.label: Selectivity check
edges.title: Choose index path
edges.description: Optimizer estimates < 1% row selectivity from histograms and picks Index-Only Scan.

edges.label: Root → Leaf
edges.title: Traverse B+tree

sections.content:
## Composite key ordering and sargability

A B+tree stores keys lexicographically. An index on `(a, b, c)` supports predicates on `(a)`, `(a, b)`, and `(a, b, c)`, plus `ORDER BY b` when `a` is constrained by `=`. Once a range operator (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `IN` with many values) appears on column `b`, subsequent column `c` cannot use the tree order for filtering or sorting. Always place equality predicates first, sort/range columns second, and non-filtered projection columns inside `INCLUDE` so they do not bloat internal branch pages.

## Index types by workload

| Index Type | Engine Support | Best Workload | Size Overhead | Write Penalty |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **B+Tree** | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server | Equality, ranges, `ORDER BY`, prefix `LIKE 'abc%'` | Medium (15–30% of table) | Moderate (page splits + WAL) |
| **Partial B+Tree** | PostgreSQL, SQLite | Sparse states (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) | Very Low (1–5% of table) | Low (only matching rows) |
| **GIN** | PostgreSQL | JSONB `@>`, arrays, full-text `tsvector` | High (30–80% of table) | High (pending list / fastupdate) |
| **BRIN** | PostgreSQL | Append-only time-series (`created_at`) | Tiny (< 1% of B+tree) | Negligible |
| **Hash** | PostgreSQL (10+), Memory | Strict `=` on long strings/UUIDs | Medium | Low–Moderate |

## Failure modes

The most deceptive production outage is **planner cliff flipping**: a query runs in 3 ms for months until table growth crosses a cost threshold and PostgreSQL suddenly switches from an Index Scan to a Parallel Seq Scan, saturating disk read bandwidth. Equally dangerous are **HOT update breaks**—adding an index on a frequently updated column like `updated_at` prevents Heap-Only Tuple updates, doubling vacuum bloat—and **index bloat** from heavy churn, which requires periodic `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` or `pg_repack`.

## Observability and verification

Track `pg_stat_statements` weekly for `calls * mean_exec_time` and `shared_blks_read / calls`. Verify buffer efficiency (`shared hit` vs `shared read`) rather than wall-clock time alone, because warm OS page cache can hide an unindexed scan that will fail under cold-cache load. Pair `pg_stat_user_indexes` with `idx_scan = 0` checks over a full monthly billing cycle before dropping redundant indexes.

## Practical checklist

- Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` against production-scale data before writing migrations.
- Order composite B+tree columns as `(equality_cols, range_or_sort_col) INCLUDE (projection_cols)`.
- Replace `OFFSET` pagination with keyset cursors (`WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id)`).
- Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` with `lock_timeout = '2s'` in migrations.
- Keep `pg_stat_statements` enabled and prune unused indexes (`idx_scan = 0`) quarterly.

questions.title: Diagnosing Key Lookup vs Index Only Scan in Execution Plans
questions.prompt: In an execution plan for a query filtering on a secondary index, you observe an Index Seek followed by an expensive 'Key Lookup' (or 'Bookmark Lookup') consuming 85% of total query operator cost. What is the root cause and the most efficient resolution?

options.text: The table statistics are outdated; running ANALYZE TABLE will automatically convert the query to an Index Only Scan without index changes.
options.explanation: Statistics describe data distribution but cannot provide missing column data that is physically absent from secondary index leaf pages.

options.text: The secondary index satisfies the WHERE condition but lacks columns referenced in the SELECT clause, forcing the engine to fetch row data from the clustered index for each matching row. Solution: Add the missing projected columns to the index as key or INCLUDE columns (Covering Index).
options.explanation: Correct! Key Lookups occur whenever a non-clustered index does not cover all columns requested in the query. Expanding the index into a covering index eliminates the lookups.

options.text: The primary key is corrupted; rebuilding the clustered index with DROP and RECREATE will eliminate secondary lookups.
options.explanation: Key lookups are normal behavior for non-covering queries, not a sign of index corruption.

options.text: The database engine has exceeded max_connections and downgraded the execution plan to sequential I/O.
options.explanation: Connection limits affect client concurrency, not optimizer index covering decisions.

rubric.excellent: Identifies that missing projected columns trigger secondary-to-clustered random I/O lookups and prescribes a covering index with INCLUDE columns.
rubric.acceptable: Recognizes that the index is missing columns required by the query.
rubric.gap: Confuses key lookups with table corruption or outdated query statistics.

questions.sampleSolution: A Key Lookup occurs when an index seek satisfies query predicates but fails to provide columns in the SELECT projection. Creating a covering index (CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table (where_cols) INCLUDE (select_cols)) allows an Index Only Scan, dropping I/O to zero heap accesses.
questions.explanation: By storing unindexed projection columns in the leaf level of the index via INCLUDE, the engine resolves the query entirely within the index B-Tree.

interviewProblems.title: Architect High-QPS Multi-Tenant Query Indexing Under High Concurrency
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are the Principal Database Architect for a multi-tenant SaaS ledger processing 10,000 queries per second on a table with 200,000,000 rows. A critical endpoint executes: SELECT transaction_id, created_at, status, amount FROM ledger WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status IN ('PENDING', 'FAILED') AND created_at >= ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50. Currently, the query takes 3,500ms and causes 100% database CPU. How do you design the clustered index, composite secondary indexes, and query structure to guarantee sub-5ms p99 latency?
constraints: Zero downtime allowed during index deployment

dimensions.name: Composite Index Key Ordering
dimensions.description: Applying equality-before-range rules to minimize B-Tree leaf scan volume.

dimensions.name: Covering Index & Key Lookup Elimination
dimensions.description: Eliminating random page reads for projected columns (amount, transaction_id).

dimensions.name: Production Operational Safety
dimensions.description: Zero-downtime online index builds without table write locks.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: 1. Index Design: Create a composite covering index: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_ledger_tenant_status_date ON ledger (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (amount, transaction_id). Leading tenant_id provides exact partition seek. status IN (...) performs bounded range seeks. created_at DESC aligns perfectly with ORDER BY created_at DESC, eliminating in-memory sorting. INCLUDE (amount, transaction_id) satisfies SELECT completely, yielding an Index Only Scan with zero Key Lookups. 2. Operational Safety: Deploy via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (or ALGORITHM=INPLACE in MySQL) to prevent exclusive table locks, avoiding transaction pool starvation. 3. Result: B-Tree depth traversal requires 4 page reads, scanning at most 50 leaf entries, executing in <2ms directly from buffer cache.
commonPitfalls: Placing created_at as the leading column, forcing a scan across all tenants
Omitting amount from the index, causing 50 random Key Lookups per query
Running standard CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY, causing full table write locks

Avoid trap: Putting a range column (created_at > ...) before an equality column (tenant_id = ...) in a composite B+tree index.

concepts.tagline: Stacks (LIFO) and Queues (FIFO) are linear abstract data types providing O(1) push/pop or enqueue/dequeue operations to control execution order, backtracking, and asynchronous buffering.

spark.summary: Stacks (LIFO) and Queues (FIFO) are linear abstract data types providing O(1) push/pop or enqueue/dequeue operations to control execution order, backtracking, and asynchronous buffering.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use a dynamic array/ArrayDeque for both stacks and queues in Java and Python (avoiding legacy synchronized Stack or O(N) list.pop(0)), and switch to bounded ring buffers or monotonic deques when memory predictability or sliding-window O(1) extrema are required.

concept.whyItMatters: Stacks power every call stack, expression parser, and DFS traversal, while queues form the backbone of BFS, rate-limiting buffers, and producer-consumer pipelines across OS kernels and distributed brokers.
whenToUse: LIFO backtracking, undo/redo histories, bracket/AST parsing, monotonic stack problems (next greater element), and iterative DFS.
FIFO task scheduling, BFS shortest-path in unweighted graphs, level-order tree traversal, and decoupling bursty producers from steady consumers.
Sliding-window maximum/minimum or bounded-latency ring buffers using a double-ended queue (Deque).
whenNotToUse: Random-access lookups by index or key—use a contiguous array or hash map instead of scanning a stack or queue.
Priority-ordered processing where highest-urgency items must jump ahead of older ones—use a binary heap / PriorityQueue.
Durable multi-consumer event replay across restarts—in-memory queues lose state on crash; use Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Redis Streams.
keyPoints: Both stack push/pop and queue enqueue/dequeue run in amortized O(1) time and O(N) space when backed by a circular array or doubly-linked list.
In Java, prefer ArrayDeque<T> over java.util.Stack (which extends Vector and synchronizes every call) and over LinkedList (which allocates a node per element and hurts CPU cache locality).
In Python, use collections.deque (a doubly-linked list of 64-element blocks) for O(1) append/popleft; list.pop(0) is O(N) due to element shifting.
Bounded queues (e.g., ArrayBlockingQueue or Disruptor ring buffers) enforce backpressure so slow consumers do not trigger OutOfMemoryError.
Monotonic stacks and deques maintain sorted invariants by popping dominated elements on insertion, turning O(N*K) nested loops into O(N) single-pass algorithms.

examples.title: LMAX-style bounded ring buffer in a telemetry collector
examples.scenario: A Java ingestion service receives 120,000 metrics/sec and previously used an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, causing 4 GB heap growth and 1.2s GC stop-the-world pauses during downstream DB slowdowns.
examples.outcome: Switching to a pre-allocated 65,536-slot ArrayBlockingQueue (or ring buffer) caps queue memory at ~16 MB, eliminates per-event node allocations, and sheds excess load with HTTP 429 when full.

examples.title: Monotonic deque for 1-minute sliding window p100 latency
examples.scenario: A Python monitoring agent computes the max request latency over a moving 60-second window across 10M log events/day.
examples.outcome: Using collections.deque to store (timestamp, latency) pairs in decreasing latency order evicts expired timestamps from the left and smaller values from the right in O(1) amortized time per event.

tradeOffs.pro: Contiguous array slots fit in L1/L2 CPU cache lines and avoid per-element heap allocation and GC pressure.
tradeOffs.con: Unbounded array-backed structures require occasional O(N) resizing spikes unless capacity is pre-sized or bounded.

tradeOffs.pro: Bounded queues guarantee O(1) memory ceiling and propagate backpressure upstream before the process OOMs.
tradeOffs.con: Requires an explicit overflow policy (block producer, drop oldest, drop newest, or reject with 429/503).

tradeOffs.factor: Iterative explicit stack vs. Call-stack recursion
tradeOffs.pro: Heap-allocated ArrayDeque/list stacks handle millions of nodes without risking StackOverflowError (typically 1 MB thread stack in JVM, 1,000 frames in CPython).
tradeOffs.con: Slightly more verbose state management when simulating post-order or multi-phase recursion frames.

failureModes.name: Unbounded queue OOM under consumer stall
failureModes.description: Producers keep enqueuing into an unbounded queue while a downstream database stalls, exhausting heap memory and crashing the service.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use bounded capacity (e.g., ArrayBlockingQueue(capacity) or deque(maxlen=N)) with explicit rejection or circuit breaking.

failureModes.name: O(N^2) hidden complexity from list.pop(0)
failureModes.description: Using a Python list as a FIFO queue shifts all remaining elements on every pop(0), turning a 100k-item BFS into 5 billion memory moves.
failureModes.mitigation: Use collections.deque.popleft() or queue.Queue for O(1) head removal.

failureModes.name: Thread-stack overflow on deep trees/graphs
failureModes.description: Recursive DFS on a skewed 100,000-node linked graph exceeds the JVM/CPython call stack limit and crashes.
failureModes.mitigation: Convert recursion to an explicit heap-allocated stack (ArrayDeque in Java, list in Python).

failureModes.name: Head-of-line blocking in a single FIFO queue
failureModes.description: One slow 30-second export job at the front of a single-worker FIFO queue stalls thousands of 5 ms interactive requests behind it.
failureModes.mitigation: Partition queues by workload class (fast vs. bulk) or use fair/weighted scheduling across separate worker pools.

commonMistakes: Using java.util.Stack in new Java code instead of Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>().
Using LinkedList as a queue in Java when ArrayDeque is faster and uses ~4x less memory per element.
Forgetting to check isEmpty() before peek()/pop(), causing NoSuchElementException or IndexError.
Using an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue in ThreadPoolExecutor, which prevents maxPoolSize threads from ever spawning.
Mutating shared mutable objects after pushing them onto a queue without defensive copying or immutability.

sections.content:
## The idea

Stacks (Last-In, First-Out) and Queues (First-In, First-Out) restrict where elements enter and leave a sequence so that insertion and removal stay O(1) without shifting or searching. A stack models nested state and reversal; a queue models fair ordering and temporal decoupling between producers and consumers.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a circular-array queue (like `ArrayDeque` with capacity 8, `head = 0`, `tail = 0`, `mask = capacity - 1`):
1. **Enqueue (`offer(A)`, `offer(B)`, `offer(C)`)**: Write at `buf[tail]` and advance `tail = (tail + 1) & mask` -> `tail` moves to `3`.
2. **Dequeue (`poll()`)**: Read `buf[head]` (`A`), null out the slot to avoid GC retention, and advance `head = (head + 1) & mask` -> `head` moves to `1`.
3. **Wrap-around**: When `tail` reaches index `7` and `head` is at `2`, the next `offer` wraps `tail = (7 + 1) & 7 = 0` without copying any elements.
4. **Resize**: Only when `tail == head` (buffer full) does the structure allocate a `2x` array and copy `[head..end]` followed by `[0..tail]`, yielding amortized O(1) per operation.

sections.content:
## Monotonic stacks and deques

A monotonic stack maintains elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order by popping violating elements before pushing the new one. Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, guaranteeing O(N) total time across the entire array—ideal for next-greater-element, daily temperatures, and largest-rectangle-in-histogram problems. Extending this to a deque (`ArrayDeque` / `collections.deque`) lets you also evict expired indices from the front for O(N) sliding-window extrema.

## Java and Python implementation matrix

| Use Case | Java Choice | Python Choice | Time Complexity | Key Caveat |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Single-thread Stack** | `ArrayDeque<T>` (`push`/`pop`) | `list` (`append`/`pop`) | O(1) amortized | Avoid `java.util.Stack` (synchronized `Vector`) |
| **Single-thread Queue** | `ArrayDeque<T>` (`offer`/`poll`) | `collections.deque` (`append`/`popleft`) | O(1) amortized | Never use `list.pop(0)` (O(N)) |
| **Thread-safe Bounded Queue** | `ArrayBlockingQueue<T>` | `queue.Queue(maxsize=N)` | O(1) | Set explicit capacity to enforce backpressure |
| **Lock-free Concurrent Queue** | `ConcurrentLinkedQueue<T>` | `SimpleQueue` (unbounded) | O(1) | `size()` is O(N) in `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` |
| **Sliding Window Extrema** | `ArrayDeque<Integer>` (indices) | `collections.deque` (indices) | O(1) amortized | Store indices, not values, to detect window expiry |

## Failure modes

In production, the most common queue failure is **unbounded memory growth** when `Executors.newFixedThreadPool` pairs an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue` with slow downstream I/O. In algorithms, **off-by-one window eviction** in monotonic deques and **reference leaks** (forgetting to null out popped array slots in custom ring buffers) cause subtle bugs and GC memory leaks.

## Cache locality and concurrency

Modern CPUs prefetch sequential cache lines (64 bytes). An `ArrayDeque` stores references contiguously, whereas `LinkedList` scatters 32-byte node objects across the heap, causing pointer-chasing cache misses. For multi-producer, multi-consumer workloads, prefer `ArrayBlockingQueue` for strict bounds or `ConcurrentLinkedDeque` / LMAX Disruptor when lock contention on a single monitor limits throughput.

## Practical checklist

- Default to `ArrayDeque` (Java) and `collections.deque` (Python) for both stacks and queues.
- Always bound production work queues and define a `RejectedExecutionHandler` or HTTP 429 policy.
- Use iterative stacks (`ArrayDeque`) instead of recursion when tree/graph depth can exceed 1,000 nodes.
- Store array indices (not raw values) in monotonic stacks/deques so distance and window expiry are trivial.
- Null out cleared slots in custom array-backed stacks/queues to prevent loitering object references.

concepts.name: Strangler Fig Migration

relationships.description: Connects Strangler Fig Migration to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: The Strangler Fig pattern incrementally replaces a legacy monolith by intercepting traffic at an edge proxy or gateway, routing specific capabilities to new microservices while keeping existing flows running safely.

spark.summary: The Strangler Fig pattern incrementally replaces a legacy monolith by intercepting traffic at an edge proxy or gateway, routing specific capabilities to new microservices while keeping existing flows running safely.
spark.keyTakeaway: Migrate one bounded vertical slice at a time behind a reverse proxy (Envoy/NGINX) with dual-write or Debezium CDC data sync, shadow traffic verification, and instant feature-flag rollback—never a Big Bang cutover.

concept.whyItMatters: Big Bang rewrites freeze feature delivery for 12–24 months and routinely fail under parity gaps; Strangler Fig delivers production value in weeks with per-route blast-radius isolation.
whenToUse: Decomposing a revenue-critical legacy monolith (e.g., Java EE, Rails, or .NET) that cannot afford downtime or a multi-quarter feature freeze.
Extracting high-change or high-scale bottlenecks (e.g., checkout, search, or auth) into independent services with separate release cadences.
Migrating core data stores (e.g., Oracle to PostgreSQL) incrementally using Change Data Capture (CDC) and shadow reads.
whenNotToUse: Small applications (< 50k LOC) where a clean modularization or direct rewrite takes only a few weeks.
Tightly coupled batch jobs or shared-memory desktop/embedded systems with no network boundary to intercept.
Organizations lacking automated contract tests, observability, or CI/CD to operate distributed services safely.
keyPoints: Every migration follows three phases per slice: Coexist (proxy routes to monolith), Mirror/Verify (shadow traffic + CDC sync), and Cutover/Decommission.
An API gateway or L7 proxy (Envoy, NGINX, Kong, AWS ALB) decouples clients from backend topology via path, header, or percentage routing.
Data decoupling is the hardest part: avoid shared-database anti-patterns by using Debezium CDC outbox/binlog replication until the new service owns its schema.
Shadow (dark-launch) traffic replays live GET/idempotent requests to the new service asynchronously and diffs responses against the monolith before user-facing cutover.
Decommissioning the old code path is mandatory; an unretired monolith leaves you maintaining two systems indefinitely.

examples.title: Checkout extraction from a 10-year Java monolith
examples.scenario: A retail platform runs catalog, cart, checkout, and invoicing in one Oracle-backed monolith whose 45-minute deploy cycle blocks Black Friday scaling.
examples.outcome: Teams place Envoy in front of the monolith, stream order tables via Debezium CDC to a new PostgreSQL-backed Checkout service, mirror 100% of read traffic for 2 weeks with < 0.01% diff, then shift /api/v2/checkout from 1% -> 25% -> 100% with zero downtime.

examples.title: Legacy authentication strangle via JWT bridge
examples.scenario: A SaaS monolith relies on sticky PHP session cookies stored in Memcached, blocking new Go/Python microservices.
examples.outcome: An edge auth-proxy validates legacy session cookies and mints short-lived RS256 JWTs for downstream new services while new logins hit the standalone Auth service directly.

tradeOffs.factor: Incremental risk reduction vs. interim complexity
tradeOffs.pro: Each migrated slice ships to production independently with instant DNS/gateway rollback.
tradeOffs.con: During transition, teams must maintain routing rules, dual-auth bridges, and CDC pipelines across both systems.

tradeOffs.pro: CDC reads database transaction logs (WAL/binlog) asynchronously with guaranteed ordering and zero app-level 2PC locks.
tradeOffs.con: CDC introduces replication lag (typically 50–500 ms), requiring read-your-own-writes routing or sticky cutover windows.

tradeOffs.factor: Shared database shortcut vs. isolated schema
tradeOffs.pro: Pointing the new service at the old DB ships faster on day 1.
tradeOffs.con: Creates tight schema coupling and lock contention, preventing independent scaling and trapping you in a distributed monolith.

failureModes.name: Dual-write split-brain divergence
failureModes.description: Application code writes to both legacy and new databases without distributed transactions; partial failures silently corrupt state.
failureModes.mitigation: Never dual-write directly from app code on critical paths—use single-writer ownership plus transactional outbox or Debezium CDC.

failureModes.name: Circular monolith-to-microservice callbacks
failureModes.description: The extracted service calls back into the monolith synchronously, creating latency amplification and cascading failure loops.
failureModes.mitigation: Replicate needed read-only reference data into the new service via events/CDC and enforce acyclic dependency rules.

failureModes.name: Half-strangled zombie monolith
failureModes.description: Teams migrate 60% of endpoints, lose executive sponsorship, and leave both systems running in production for years.
failureModes.mitigation: Tie each slice's Definition of Done to deleting the dead monolith route and archiving its tables.

failureModes.name: Non-idempotent shadow traffic mutations
failureModes.description: Mirroring POST /payments or POST /orders traffic to the new service triggers duplicate charges or emails.
failureModes.mitigation: Only mirror safe GET/read endpoints, or intercept external side-effect adapters (payment gateways, SMTP) with no-op stubs in shadow mode.

commonMistakes: Starting with the most tangled core domain instead of a low-risk, well-bounded edge capability.
Allowing the new microservice to query the monolith's internal tables directly via SQL joins.
Skipping automated parity diffing between legacy and new responses before shifting live user traffic.
Forgetting session/auth token translation at the edge proxy, forcing users to log in twice.
Ignoring latency budgets—adding 3 extra proxy/service hops without tuning connection pooling and timeouts.

sections.content:
## The idea

Named after tropical strangler fig vines that grow around a host tree until the host rots away, the Strangler Fig pattern places an interception layer (API gateway or L7 proxy) in front of a legacy system. New features and extracted capabilities are built beside the monolith and gradually take over routes and data ownership until the legacy core can be safely powered down.

## Concrete walkthrough

1. **Place the seam**: Route all ingress traffic through an L7 gateway (e.g., Envoy) with default fallback to the legacy monolith.
2. **Select a bounded slice**: Pick a cohesive domain (e.g., `/v1/inventory`) with clear inputs/outputs and minimal foreign-key entanglement.
3. **Sync data via CDC**: Stream legacy table changes via Debezium (WAL/binlog -> Kafka) into the new service's dedicated database.
4. **Shadow & diff**: Enable Envoy traffic mirroring (`request_mirror_policies`) to send live read requests asynchronously to the new service and compare JSON payloads.
5. **Canary cutover**: Shift live traffic 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% while monitoring p99 latency, 5xx rates, and business invariants.
6. **Flip source of truth & prune**: Stop CDC into the new DB, reverse-sync if legacy reports still need it temporarily, and delete the legacy route.

sections.content:
## Breaking the shared database

Splitting compute without splitting data creates a distributed monolith. During migration, establish a **single source of truth** per table at any moment. Use Change Data Capture (Debezium) or a **Transactional Outbox** to replicate writes from the current owner to the shadow store. At cutover, drain the replication lag (or pause writes briefly for 1–2 seconds), flip ownership to the new service, and optionally run reverse-CDC if legacy reporting jobs still read the old tables.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Data sync and cutover strategies compared
sections.content:
## Data sync and cutover strategies compared

| Strategy | Consistency | Latency Impact | Operational Effort | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CDC (Debezium + Kafka)** | Eventual (50–500 ms) | Zero on legacy writes | Medium (connect cluster) | High-volume tables with strict zero-downtime needs |
| **Transactional Outbox** | Eventual (atomic local commit) | Minimal (+1 local insert) | Low–Medium | Domain events when migrating writes first |
| **App-level Dual Write** | Weak (split-brain risk) | 2x write latency | Low initially, high cleanup | Avoid for financial or inventory state |
| **Read-Through Proxy / Anti-Corruption Layer** | Strong | +1 network hop | Low | Thin wrapper when legacy DB stays temporarily |

## Failure modes

The biggest risk during cutover is **stale-read race conditions**: a user writes to the new service and immediately reads from a legacy endpoint before reverse-sync completes. Solve this by migrating all read and write endpoints of a bounded aggregate together, or by routing read-after-write sessions via a short-lived cookie/header to the new owner.

## Parity testing and observability

Attach a consistent `X-Correlation-ID` at the API gateway so distributed traces (OpenTelemetry) span both the monolith and the new service. In shadow mode, log structural diffs (ignoring non-deterministic fields like timestamps or UUIDs) and require 99.99% semantic parity over at least one full business cycle before shifting write traffic.

## Practical checklist

- Put an L7 proxy/gateway in front of the monolith before extracting any code.
- Pick a first slice with clear boundaries and low coupling (e.g., read-heavy catalog or notifications).
- Use CDC or an outbox instead of synchronous app-level dual writes.
- Run shadow read mirroring with automated response diffing before cutover.
- Delete the dead legacy endpoints and schema tables as soon as the new slice stabilizes.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The Strangler Fig pattern incrementally replaces a legacy monolith by intercepting traffic at an edge proxy or gateway, routing specific capabilities to new microservices while keeping existing flows running safely.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Debezium CDC applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Extracted Service.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Extracted Service experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Never dual-write directly from app code on critical paths—use single-writer ownership plus transactional outbox or Debezium CDC.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Migrate one bounded vertical slice at a time behind a reverse proxy (Envoy/NGINX) with dual-write or Debezium CDC data sync, shadow traffic verification, and instant feature-flag rollback—never a Big Bang cutover.
Avoid trap: Starting with the most tangled core domain instead of a low-risk, well-bounded edge capability.
Avoid trap: Allowing the new microservice to query the monolith's internal tables directly via SQL joins.
When to reach for it: Decomposing a revenue-critical legacy monolith (e.g., Java EE, Rails, or .NET) that cannot afford downtime or a multi-quarter feature freeze.
When to reach for it: Extracting high-change or high-scale bottlenecks (e.g., checkout, search, or auth) into independent services with separate release cadences.

concepts.name: Stream Watermarks & Late Data

relationships.description: Connects Stream Watermarks & Late Data to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

concepts.tagline: Watermarks track event-time progress in unbounded streams, telling stateful operators when a time window is complete enough to emit results—while allowed lateness and side outputs handle straggling events.

spark.summary: Watermarks track event-time progress in unbounded streams, telling stateful operators when a time window is complete enough to emit results—while allowed lateness and side outputs handle straggling events.
spark.keyTakeaway: In Apache Flink or Spark Structured Streaming, set watermarks to max_observed_event_time - bounded_out_of_orderness, pair them with allowedLateness for corrections, and route beyond-lateness events to a side output rather than silently dropping them.

concept.whyItMatters: Mobile apps, IoT sensors, and multi-region Kafka topics deliver events out of order; without event-time watermarks, tumbling windows either emit wrong counts prematurely or hold state in memory forever until OOM.
whenToUse: Event-time aggregations (tumbling, sliding, or session windows) in Apache Flink, Apache Beam, or Spark Structured Streaming.
Out-of-order streams from mobile clients offline-buffering events, multi-AZ producers, or cross-region replication.
Billing, fraud detection, or SLA alerting where results depend on when an event occurred rather than when the server ingested it.
whenNotToUse: Simple stateless per-event transformations (filtering, JSON enrichment, regex masking) that require no windowing.
Strict processing-time monitoring where wall-clock ingestion rate is the actual metric (e.g., raw Kafka consumer lag).
Batch-only workloads over bounded, already-complete daily Parquet files.
keyPoints: Event time (when the action happened) differs from processing time (when the Flink/Spark worker sees the record); watermarks bridge the two.
A watermark W(t) is a monotonic assertion that no more events with timestamp <= t are expected; when W(t) passes window_end, the window fires.
Bounded-out-of-orderness watermarks (maxEventTime - delta) trade latency for completeness: larger delta catches more late events but delays window emission and increases state size.
An idle Kafka partition stops advancing its local watermark and stalls the global min-watermark across all parallel subtasks unless withIdleness() is configured.
Events arriving after W(t) passes window_end + allowedLateness are dropped from state—route them to a Dead Letter / side output for batch reconciliation.

examples.title: Flink 1.19 mobile telemetry 1-minute tumbling windows
examples.scenario: A ride-hailing app buffers GPS pings during tunnel drops; 99% arrive within 15 seconds, while 0.8% arrive up to 2 minutes late.
examples.outcome: Configuring WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(15)) with allowedLateness(Time.minutes(2)) and sideOutputLateData(lateTag) emits fast 15s-delayed dashboards, retracts/updates windows for stragglers, and logs < 0.2% ultra-late pings to S3.

examples.title: Stalled watermark from an idle regional Kafka partition
examples.scenario: A 16-partition Kafka topic has low overnight traffic on partition 12; Flink's operator watermark takes the minimum across all 16 partitions, freezing all window emissions for 4 hours.
examples.outcome: Adding .withIdleness(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) marks silent partitions as idle so active partitions continue advancing the global watermark smoothly.

tradeOffs.pro: A generous out-of-orderness bound (e.g., 60s) reduces late-data retractions and downstream upserts.
tradeOffs.con: Every window waits 60s longer to emit and retains open RocksDB/heap state for 60s more.

tradeOffs.factor: Allowed lateness vs. state storage cost
tradeOffs.pro: Keeping window state open for allowedLateness lets the stream engine emit accurate updated totals for late arrivals.
tradeOffs.con: RocksDB state size grows linearly with lateness duration, increasing checkpoint size and recovery time.

tradeOffs.pro: Emitting early speculative triggers plus late updates keeps dashboards fresh and eventually accurate.
tradeOffs.con: Downstream sinks must support idempotent upserts (e.g., PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT or ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree) rather than append-only logs.

failureModes.name: Idle partition watermark stall
failureModes.description: One empty or skewed Kafka partition emits no events, pinning the operator's min-watermark in the past and halting all window outputs while state grows unboundedly.
failureModes.mitigation: Always configure idle-source detection (withIdleness in Flink) and alert on watermark-to-wall-clock lag.

failureModes.name: Clock skew poisoning maxEventTime
failureModes.description: A single buggy client sends a timestamp 10 years in the future, jumping the watermark to 2036 and causing all real-time events to be treated as late and dropped.
failureModes.mitigation: Clamp or quarantine future timestamps (event_time > processing_time + max_skew) at the ingestion/deserialization boundary.

failureModes.name: Silent data loss on late records
failureModes.description: Default window operators silently discard records arriving after window_end + allowedLateness, causing revenue/billing undercounts.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach a side output (lateOutputTag) to route ultra-late records to a cold-path Parquet/S3 reconciliation job.

failureModes.name: Unbounded state on high-cardinality session windows
failureModes.description: Long allowedLateness combined with millions of per-user session keys exhausts RocksDB disk/memory and times out checkpoints.
failureModes.mitigation: Bound session gaps, set explicit State TTL, and size RocksDB block cache + incremental checkpoints.

commonMistakes: Assuming watermarks are global wall-clock timers rather than data-driven metadata flowing inside the stream.
Forgetting that an operator with multiple upstream inputs advances its watermark to min(input_watermarks), not max.
Leaving idle-partition timeouts unset on topics with uneven key distribution.
Using append-only sinks (like plain CSV or unkeyed Kafka) when allowedLateness emits multiple updates per window.
Trusting untrusted client device clocks without clamping future timestamps.

sections.content:
## The idea

In distributed streaming, network jitter and offline buffering scramble event arrival order. A **watermark** `W(t)` is a special timestamped marker injected into the data stream asserting that no further events with `event_time <= t` are expected. It decouples correctness (event time) from infrastructure speed (processing time), giving stateful operators a deterministic signal to fire windows and garbage-collect old state.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose we aggregate 1-minute tumbling windows (`[12:00, 12:01)`) with a 10-second out-of-orderness bound (`delta = 10s`) and `allowedLateness = 30s`:
1. Events with timestamps `12:00:15`, `12:00:48`, and `12:01:05` arrive. `maxEventTime` becomes `12:01:05`, so `W = 12:00:55` (window `[12:00, 12:01)` stays open).
2. Event `12:01:12` arrives -> `W = 12:01:02`. Because `W >= 12:01:00`, the `[12:00, 12:01)` window **fires** its initial aggregate.
3. Window state is **retained** until `W` reaches `12:01:30` (`window_end + allowedLateness`).
4. A late event `12:00:52` arrives while `W = 12:01:15`: it enters the retained window and triggers an **updated emission**.
5. Once `W >= 12:01:30`, the window state is **purged**; any subsequent `12:00:xx` event is routed to the **side output**.

edges.label: Event (t)
edges.title: Extract event time
